title: Joey Zwillinger: From $4.1BN to $142M Market Cap;Why Public Markets Have Written Allbirds Off |E1078
key_insights: Allbirds' market capitalization dropped from a $3.75B IPO valuation to ~$127M due to a combination of external market factors and internal strategic missteps.
Despite the stock performance, the brand health remains strong, but suffers from low aided brand awareness (under 15% in the US).
The company is undergoing a strategic transition, pulling back on marketing and store growth to clean up inventory and refocus on its core 'active life' product category.
Zwillinger believes the consumer is in a more fragile situation than widely understood, and is structuring the business conservatively for the next 6 months.

The path to profitability involves getting back to basics, sharpening focus on core products, and leveraging their strong brand foundation to regain momentum, aiming for cash flow and EBITDA profitability in 2025.
fundraising_mentions: IPO at $3.75 billion valuation.
Current market cap around $127 million.
IPO price was $15 per share.
Current share price is around $1.
quotable: We have a mountain of cash, we have control of our destiny, and the fact that Wall Street's written us off... the markets are unforgiving and our market cap is a reflection of the fact that we've essentially been written off by people.
The consumer is in a more delicate and fragile situation than people understand and... it's going to be more difficult and there's going to be less spending than people think in the coming 6 months.
one_liner: Allbirds co-founder Joey Zwillinger discusses the stark contrast between the company's strong brand love and its public market struggles, detailing the tough decisions being made to steer the company back toward profitability.

title: WTF is Going On in VC? Are LPs Investing in New Funds? | 20VC #965
key_insights: The 'Postmates effect' where a #3 or #4 player in a market could achieve a billion-dollar exit is over; VCs are now looking for true market leaders again.
VCs are seeking a 'trifecta' in the current market: top-tier growth, top-quartile capital efficiency, and a clear path to winning a category.
Founders should avoid making drastic cuts to marketing and sales; instead, they should set data-driven budgets and trust their teams to optimize spend to maintain pipeline for the eventual recovery.
The market downturn's impact is not evenly distributed; sectors like healthcare and parts of e-commerce are still performing well.

LPs are becoming more selective, preferring to re-up with existing managers who have a track record of DPI (Distributions to Paid-In Capital), especially from 2021 exits, and are wary of managers who deployed capital too quickly at the peak.
Founders of companies that raised at massive valuations with long runways face a difficult path to exit, as generating a 10x return on the capital raised is highly improbable.
fundraising_mentions: Received a growth stage offer at 15x ARR for a top decile SaaS company with over $50M in revenue that is profitable or close to it.
Many growth investors (90%) are largely out of the market or only looking for bargains.
His own SaaStr fund one was $60 million raised in 2016.
A second-time founder with a multi-billion dollar exit was advised to raise all the capital he could 'now' rather than waiting for a later A or B round.
quotable: If you didn't have multiple billion dollar cash exits in 2021 you're not a good investor.
For Founders you have to understand that will never lead to a return of 2021. never.
When I see like a Founder cry I have no sympathy... it's supposed to be hard.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin discusses the current state of the VC and SaaS markets, explaining that the bar for investment has significantly risen and the boom times of 2021 will not return, while advising founders on navigating the downturn with capital efficiency and strategic budgeting.

title: Why CAC:LTV is a BS metric
guest_role: Head of Paid Acquisition / Growth at Stitch Fix
topics: Payback period as an alternative metric
key_insights: The 'lifetime' component of LTV is often undefinable for early-stage companies.
CAC:LTV is often too coarse, ignoring variations in customer quality across different channels and keywords.
Payback period is a superior metric, offering more granularity and removing the ambiguous 'lifetime' element.
Payback period should be calculated on a 'paid over paid' basis, using paid tags for accurate CPA.
LTV formulas are tools, not strategies, and can be misused to justify budget increases rather than optimizing for real value.
A deeper understanding of user psychology and creative quality provides a greater edge in performance marketing than purely mechanical optimization.
quotable: early in a company's Journey it's rare to have a real idea of what a reasonable customer lifetime is
this is a tool and not a strategy
one_liner: This episode debunks CAC:LTV as a flawed metric, advocating for a more granular payback period approach and emphasizing strategy over mechanical formula optimization in performance marketing.

title: Chime IPO: Are IPOs Hotter Than Ever?
key_insights: Meta's $14.8B investment in Scale AI is viewed as a strategic talent acquisition and messaging play to assert dominance in AI, rather than a traditional financial investment, causing major disruption for Scale's business with competitors like OpenAI.

The IPO market is roaring back, evidenced by Chime's 50% pop. This is attributed to high-quality companies pricing conservatively to reopen the market, creating momentum and attracting pent-up investor demand.

There is a strong venture capital bias towards backing the founding CEO through the entire lifecycle of a company, as replacing a founder is a high-risk, 'open-heart surgery' that often fails, even if it seems necessary.

In the current private markets, valuations for high-growth companies like Ramp ($16B) and Gusto ($9.3B) are driven by hyper-growth, market momentum, and strategic positioning, sometimes feeling lofty compared to public comps or margin quality.

Old guard tech companies face significant hurdles competing with the new, fast-moving AI-native startups. A company's existing ecosystem and customer base (like Salesforce) are critical, as it's difficult to compete for new customers from ground zero against focused players like Glean.
fundraising_mentions: Scale AI: Meta invested $14.83 billion for a 49% stake, with investors receiving the capital as a special dividend.
Ramp: Raised $200 million at a $16 billion valuation.
Gusto: Announced a tender offer at a $9.3 billion valuation with $900 million in ARR.
Perplexity: Raising a round with tranches at $15 billion and $18 billion valuations.
Chime: Went public and the stock popped 50%.
OpenAI: Received a $200 million defense contract from the Pentagon.
quotable: I would say the only durable moat in in the entire human data business is access to an audience.
Microsoft put down an offer tomorrow for $4 billion to acquire Handshake. Would you say yes? What? Absolutely not.
one_liner: The 20VC team and Handshake founder Garrett dissect Meta's shocking acquisition of Scale AI, the resurgence of the IPO market led by Chime, and the high-stakes strategic decisions shaping the future of AI and fintech.

title: George Bonaci, VP of Growth @Ramp: How Ramp Became the Fastest Growing SaaS Company Ever |E1264
key_insights: Growth should be approached as a science, focusing on forming hypotheses and running a high velocity of experiments rather than applying old playbooks.
A successful growth strategy involves managing a portfolio of bets with varying risk levels and time horizons, from short-term optimizations to long-term, high-risk swings.
When a growth channel proves effective, it's crucial to scale it to the point of saturation as quickly as possible rather than increasing spend incrementally.

Early-stage companies should hire junior, high-potential generalists for growth roles, as they are more adaptable and think from first principles, unlike senior hires who may rely on outdated playbooks.
Finding 'Alpha' in growth comes from either exploring nascent channels no one else is using or trying channels that everyone is convinced will not work, like B2B direct mail.
A good leader needs to know how to do everyone on their team's job, but poorly, to be dangerous enough to ask the right questions without micromanaging.
The most common mistake founders make is hiring for experience because they don't know what 'good' looks like, instead of doing the work to define 'good' and testing candidates against it.
fundraising_mentions: Mentions hiring a 'smart generalist' at the Series A stage.
quotable: I think the way that you find Alpha is either by doing things that no one else knows about I think another aspect is probably doing things that everyone is convinced will not work.
I think a good leader needs to know how to do everyone on their team's job but poorly and I think the poorly part is important.
one_liner: Ramp's VP of Growth, George Bonaci, details his scientific, experiment-driven framework for building one of the fastest-growing SaaS companies, covering everything from managing a portfolio of growth bets and finding 'Alpha' in overlooked channels to hiring high-potential talent.

title: Scooter Braun: I forgot who I was
guest_role: one of the biggest entrepreneurs in entertainment today behind well-known artists from Justin Bieber to Ariana Grande
key_insights: The speaker, Scooter Braun, initially confused his public persona with his true self.
External achievements and praise served as a distraction from internal self-work.
A period of deep unhappiness forced him to engage in significant personal introspection.
An intense self-work process (the Hoffman process) proved transformative for his well-being.
Prioritizing self-care and personal well-being can yield profound positive changes.
quotable: I forgot who I was
one week of choosing yourself can do for your well-being
one_liner: Scooter Braun reflects on his journey from defining himself by success to rediscovering his authentic self through intense personal work, emphasizing the importance of well-being over external validation.

title: How Cathie Wood Stays Positive When $ARKK Is Down 80-90%
key_insights: Conviction in investment theses during downturns is derived directly from intensive, data-driven research that is constantly being double and triple-checked.
When high-conviction stocks decrease significantly in price, the expected five-year rate of return for those assets increases, signaling a buying opportunity, not a time to sell.

ARK's strategy during risk-off periods involves averaging down on their positions and concentrating the portfolio into their highest conviction names, reducing the number of holdings from 58 to around 32-33.
Concerns about company solvency in irrational markets can be mitigated if the company has loyal shareholders willing to participate in secondary offerings, as was the case with Tesla in 2019.
Market shifts towards benchmark stocks and away from innovation are seen as temporary risk-off periods, which create opportunities to buy disruptive companies at a discount.
fundraising_mentions: Mention of companies doing an IPO or a secondary offering to raise capital, citing Tesla in early 2019 as an example where loyal shareholders would have supported a secondary offering.
quotable: If we're right, we're seeing the total rate of return expectation increase for the next five years so we keep our eye on that prize.
Do you worry that the market can remain irrational longer than companies can remain solvent?
one_liner: Cathie Wood explains how her conviction in ARK's strategy is reinforced by data-driven research during major downturns, leading them to average down and concentrate their portfolio in their highest-conviction innovative companies.

title: Kevin Niparko: Big Mistakes Founders Make When Hiring Product Teams | E1066
key_insights: Analysts can become great product managers because they are forced to think broadly about the business and dive deep into both quantitative and qualitative data.

A powerful model for product team performance is a 2x2 grid of shipping speed (fast/slow) vs. impact (high/low). The goal is to get teams to a state of shipping fast with high impact, which requires high context, high trust, and high talent density.

When hiring product people, avoid two key mistakes: not having a clear understanding of the role archetype you need (e.g., strategy, execution, team building) and overweighting specific domain skills over the generalist craft of product management.
'Product memes'—short, simple, memorable perceptions of your product—are more important than your roadmap for internal alignment because most people will never read your detailed documents.
Always listen to your customers' problems, but rarely listen to their solutions. The most advanced users often build hacky workarounds that provide early signals for major product opportunities.
fundraising_mentions: Segment Series A
quotable: The key learning is go listen to your smartest customers sit next to them really learn what they are doing with your product because that can really inform and give you early signal as to what's going to be big.
Product memes are this concept of really simplifying your thinking down into the shortest simplest most memorable perception of your product and then distributing those ideas through the meme.
one_liner: Segment Product Leader Kevin Niparko discusses common mistakes founders make when hiring product teams, the importance of creating 'product memes' for internal alignment, and frameworks for balancing innovation with core product development.

title: How I came up with a $3 BILLION idea 💰
key_insights: The inspiration for Olo stemmed from early mobile point-of-interest applications on Palm Pilots and observing operational inefficiencies in busy coffee shops.
The core concept was a win-win: consumers could order and pay ahead to save time, while restaurants could increase their throughput and operational capacity.
The business idea was conceived in 2003 but was incubated while the founder was working for a non-profit in South Africa, where he connected with mobile developers.

Early conviction was tested by a key investor, David Frankel, who made his backing conditional on the founder fully committing by quitting his job and forgoing his admission to Harvard Business School.
This 'burn the boats' moment was a critical step in making the venture the founder's sole focus and path forward.
fundraising_mentions: Initial backing was provided by David Frankel, who agreed to invest if the founder quit his job at Endeavor and declined his admission to Harvard Business School.
quotable: If you really believe in this enough to quit your job at endeavor and enough to tell Harvard Business School that you're not coming I'll back you.
That was this beautiful burn the boats kind of moment where it made me make Olo my only path forward.
one_liner: Olo founder Noah Glass shares the origin story of his mobile-ordering platform, from a simple idea inspired by Palm Pilots and coffee shop lines to securing early backing by making a life-changing commitment to his vision.

title: SpaceX Valued at $800BN & Harvey Raises $160M at an $8BN Price & Netflix Acquires Warner Brothers
key_insights: Private market valuations often prove to be inflated when they eventually face public market realities, though this cycle repeats.
The 2026 IPO market could be monumental if mega-cap private companies like SpaceX, Anthropic, and DataBricks go public, potentially returning hundreds of billions to VCs.
AI startups like Harvey are commanding extreme valuations (e.g., over 500x ARR) based on hyper-growth (3-10x YoY), a bet on durable, long-term growth that is still unproven.

LLMs are becoming increasingly swappable (like commodities), forcing model providers to build moats through consumer apps (like ChatGPT) or enterprise integrations, but the underlying technology is still unstable and subject to step-function changes.

Geopolitical factors are creating significant valuation disparities, such as the 'Asia discount' affecting companies like Airwallex, which trade at a fraction of their US counterparts despite similar metrics.
fundraising_mentions: SpaceX pursuing $800 billion valuation through a secondary sale.
Harvey announcing a $160 million round at an $8 billion valuation.
Naveen Rao's new company raising a $500 million seed round at a $5 billion valuation.
Tiger Global raising a new $2.2 billion fund.
Airwallex raising $330 million at an $8 billion valuation.
quotable: Every time that private market valuations came into contact with public market valuations, private market valuations were found wanting.

one_liner: VCs Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll analyze massive private market deals including SpaceX's $800B valuation and Harvey's $8B round, debating the sustainability of AI hype, the future of the IPO market, and the commoditization of LLMs.

title: Hadi Partovi: How I Became an Advisor to Mark Zuckerberg; Lessons from Steve Ballmer | 20VC #961
key_insights: The first 5-10 hires at a startup are critical as they set the cultural and quality bar for the next hundred or thousand employees.
Effective leaders like Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer are deeply involved in the details and expect their teams to be exceptionally prepared.
When conducting layoffs, it's better to cut deep once rather than performing multiple rounds, which destroys morale and credibility.
The focus of education should shift from 'how to teach better' to questioning 'what to teach' to prepare students for a future dominated by technology and AI.
Optimizing for societal impact rather than personal wealth can be a more fulfilling life path, though it requires a deliberate decision to step away from traditional measures of success.
fundraising_mentions: Facebook received a term sheet from Accel at a $100 million valuation.
Hadi Partovi became an advisor to Facebook at a $10 million valuation.
quotable: I feel like the American dream is broken and not everybody has that access and what I'm running towards is really creating a world where that American Dream works for everybody.
Socrates once said that education isn't the filling of a pail, it's the lighting of a fire.
one_liner: Code.org founder Hadi Partovi shares lessons from his journey as an immigrant, entrepreneur, and advisor to tech giants like Mark Zuckerberg, detailing his shift from pursuing wealth to focusing on reforming global education.

title: The Myth That The World is Getting Worse
key_insights: The pervasive narrative that the world is getting worse is a media-driven myth; by most statistical measures (wealth, health, safety), humanity is better off than ever before.
Happiness is a temporary, fleeting emotion and a poor long-term goal; individuals should strive for contentment, a more stable and achievable state of being.
The 'hedonistic treadmill'—the constant human desire for more—is not a flaw but the fundamental engine of progress, driving entrepreneurship, innovation, and ambition.
After a certain threshold of financial comfort is reached, massive material wealth only contributes a small percentage (e.g., 2-5%) to one's daily quality of life.
Societal discontent and political polarization often stem from people feeling left behind, but the actual spectrum of disagreement is much narrower than portrayed.
People derive significant value from well-crafted, quality items they use daily (like a good keyboard or mattress), which can be a more meaningful use of discretionary income than pure luxury.
quotable: Happiness is a temporary thing but it's a terrible goal... it's a goal that's sold to people to keep them miserable. You want contentment, which is very different.
The best things in life are free. The second best things are extremely expensive.
one_liner: Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke argues against the prevailing narrative of global decline, differentiating between the pursuit of happiness and the value of contentment, and explaining how the 'hedonistic treadmill' drives human progress.

title: Ryan Peterson: Why I invest in rebels who want revenge
key_insights: Revenge can be a powerful motivator for entrepreneurial success, driving founders to achieve comeback stories.
Investing in founders with 'messy pasts' can create contrarian opportunities, especially if their past issues were not moral or ethical failings.
Talented founders who have been wrongly dismissed or passed over by other investors can represent a 'perfect storm' for finding great talent.
It's crucial for investors to distinguish between minor rule-breaking and serious harm to innocent people when evaluating such founders.
The case of Parker Conrad building Rippling into a much larger business after being ousted from Zenefits exemplifies this investment philosophy.
quotable: I think revenge is a really powerful motivator. You want people are motivated and driven, and if someone feels like they've been wronged, there's a couple benefits: one, they're going to be incredibly driven to go solve that, you know, to go have a comeback story.
if you can get really comfortable with that and they're really talented and other people aren't willing to invest in them then that's like a perfect storm for finding a great founder
one_liner: Ryan Peterson discusses his investment philosophy of backing driven founders, often with 'messy pasts' and a desire for 'revenge,' exemplified by Parker Conrad's success with Rippling after leaving Zenefits.

title: Airwallex CEO & Co-Founder, Jack Zhang: The Angel That Turned $1M into $1BN
key_insights: Founder resilience, forged through early-life hardship, is a critical predictor of entrepreneurial success. Jack's experience of losing financial support at 16 and working grueling jobs built the toughness needed to navigate multiple startup crises.

Airwallex pivoted multiple times, from a peer-to-peer model to an SME invoicing tool, before finding product-market fit with an API-first platform for large enterprises, demonstrating the importance of iterating until a scalable model is found.

The company faced and survived at least three near-death experiences, including running out of money and having a signed term sheet pulled, highlighting the thin line between failure and success in startups.

Turning down a ~$1.2 billion acquisition offer from Stripe, despite having only $2M in revenue, was a pivotal moment. The decision was driven by a long-term vision to build a generational company, not short-term financial gain.

Airwallex achieved hyper-growth, maintaining over 100% year-over-year growth from 2015 to 2023 by relentlessly focusing on building deep infrastructure and expanding its product from a single API to a full-stack global banking platform.
fundraising_mentions: Initial $1M angel investment from a friend for 20% at a $5M post-money valuation.
Matrix Partners pulled a signed term sheet for a $2M round at a $10M post-money valuation.
Series A of $13M from Sequoia, Tencent, and Mastercard at a $60M valuation with zero revenue.

quotable: We basically never grow below 100% from 2015 to 2023.
I don't know what is financial discipline. So I don't have a budget. I'm just like hire as fast as possible. Just blow it all up. And then I realized at one point that we're running out of money.
one_liner: Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang recounts his journey of building a global payments giant through extreme resilience, surviving multiple near-death experiences, turning down a $1.2B acquisition from Stripe, and achieving over 100% annual growth for eight consecutive years.

title: Mastering SEO Measurement: Insights from Yoast founder - Joost de Valk
key_insights: As a starting point, allocate 10% of your CPC budget to SEO.
Measuring the direct effectiveness of SEO is challenging because modern analytics platforms, influenced by Google, are optimized to track CPC, not organic search.
Attribution systems that rely on last-click often credit 'brand search' for a conversion, even though the initial discovery may have happened through a long and untraceable SEO-driven journey.
Google has intentionally obscured keyword referral data, making it difficult to know which specific terms are driving traffic.
The belief that everything in the 'growth world' is perfectly measurable is a fallacy; like TV advertising, SEO's impact is significant even if it's hard to attribute directly.
fundraising_mentions: Advised for a hypothetical 'angel investment' or 'series B' company.
quotable: Google has very successfully made it impossible for people to track the effect of anything but CPC.
I think actually it's one of the falsities that we have in the in the whole growth world is that we can measure everything I don't think he can.
one_liner: Yoast founder Joost de Valk explains that while measuring SEO's ROI is notoriously difficult due to attribution challenges, a good starting point for budget allocation is 10% of the existing CPC spend.

title: The Inspirational Founding Story of Allbirds
key_insights: Allbirds was born from co-founder Tim Brown's personal frustration with over-branded, non-casual footwear, leading him to launch a Kickstarter.
Co-founder Joey Zwillinger's background in biotechnology revealed that even with viable, high-performance sustainable materials, established brands were too margin-focused to adopt them.
The core insight was to merge consumer-centric design with advanced material science to create a 'no compromise' sustainable product that brands were failing to deliver.
The partnership was a fusion of Tim's design and consumer intuition with Joey's material science and business experience.
The mission was driven by a desire to leverage the private sector for positive environmental impact and build a legacy business.
fundraising_mentions: A Kickstarter campaign was launched in 2014 to test the initial concept.
quotable: I realized that while the technology existed the consumers wanted it this no compromise offering was there for the taking and Brands could not position it correctly.

We could blend his design instinctual sense for the consumer with my Material Science Background and experience in entrepreneurship and we decided that this was a worthwhile Endeavor for leadership for business and for a legacy that we thought our grandkids would be proud of.
one_liner: Allbirds co-founder Joey Zwillinger recounts how his material science background combined with his co-founder's design intuition to create a sustainable footwear company that addressed a gap in the market for stylish, eco-friendly shoes.

title: Is There a Playbook to Become CEO?
topics: Founder CEOs vs. Hired Gun CEOs
key_insights: There is no single formula or playbook for becoming a successful CEO; leaders have vastly different backgrounds, demeanors, and styles.
Founder-CEOs are often 'quirky' and don't fit the stereotypical, 'central casting' image of a CEO.
Authenticity is a key advantage; trying to be someone else has significant overhead and is less effective than being yourself.
CEO peer groups can be incredibly helpful for growth and learning from others' experiences.
Observing and learning from other successful, albeit different, leaders can provide crucial insights for your own journey.
quotable: I tried to look at different CEOs and come up with a rubric of like this is what you look for here's the five questions you should ask a Founder to tell if they can scale as a CEO I haven't come up with that yet.
I'm quirky inside maybe I can just be quirky like these two and so I tried to start being myself after that and it paid off trying to be somebody else has a lot of overhead to it.
one_liner: HubSpot's co-founder explains why there's no single playbook for being a CEO, highlighting the success of authentic, 'quirky' founders over stereotypical leaders and the value of peer groups.

title: Wesley Chan: How I Created Google Analytics; The Founding Story of Gmail & Canva | 20VC #919
key_insights: Look for the '2-gigabyte moment' - a product feature that offers an order-of-magnitude improvement over the competition, rather than just an incremental one.
The best founders have a '100-year plan'; they possess a long-term vision for how their company will change the world, even if the path adapts over time.
While the 'market always wins,' truly visionary founders create or massively expand their markets, rather than just competing in existing ones.
Avoid investment dogma (e.g., strict ownership targets, board seats, geographical limits), as the best deals often defy conventional VC rules.
When you're an expert in a field, you often know too much, which leads to skepticism and passing on great deals; it's better to know just enough to be dangerous and believe in the founder.
fundraising_mentions: FPV Ventures raised a $450 million fund, which was 2-3x oversubscribed.
Wesley Chan's fund typically writes checks from $10-20 million for about 20 core positions.
The Canva investment was done at a pre-launch valuation of over $100 million in 2014, without a board seat or 20% ownership.
Gmail's initial proposal was for 200MB of storage, but Larry Page pushed it to 2GB, a massive increase at the time.
Robin Hood, Plaid, and Gusto were mentioned as companies where he wrote the first check.
quotable: What's your two gigabyte moment? You're telling me something that's incremental and I'm looking for the two gigabyte when everybody else has 25 megabyte moment.
If you have the data, you're right. If you don't have the data, then I'm right. And you don't want me to be right because I'm often wrong. So bring the data.
one_liner: Wesley Chan of FPV Ventures shares his investment framework, honed at Google and through early investments in companies like Canva, focusing on backing product visionaries who create new markets with order-of-magnitude product improvements.

title: Keith Rabois & Eric Glyman: The Tools, Tips, Secrets and Process That Drive Efficiency | E1148
guest_role: Investor at Khosla Ventures & Co-founder/CEO of Ramp
key_insights: CEOs should act as editors, not writers; consistently 'red-lining' one area of the company is a major red flag.
The team you build is the company you build; an intense focus on hiring top-tier talent from the very beginning is crucial.
To drive focus, distill your business into a simple 'business equation' to identify the single most important variable that moves all others (for Ramp, it was purchase volume).
A 'day count' can be a powerful tool to create urgency and force reflection on whether time is being used effectively to maximize output.
Great businesses typically start by deeply understanding customer problems, not by searching for problems to fit a new technology.
Transitioning from a product to a platform risks losing focus; it's critical to ensure the platform strategy unlocks an even bigger, measurable value proposition for customers.
Leadership style should be inconsistent and adapted based on the task-relevant maturity of the employee and the consequences of the task to the business.
fundraising_mentions: Founders Fund preempted the Series A when the company had only ~$30,000 in monthly spend.
The latest funding round valued Ramp at $7.6 billion post-money.
quotable: If you feel like you're using a lot of red lines consistently in the same area of a company that's a really bad signal.
I couldn't imagine people saying, you know, I just wish I was less efficient with my spending. I wish it took longer to close my books.
one_liner: Ramp's CEO Eric Glyman and investor Keith Rabois break down the frameworks for extreme operational efficiency, talent acquisition, and strategic focus that have scaled the company to a $7.6B valuation.

title: Dave CEO, Jason Wilk: The Best Performing Fund Would Only Back YC Founders on Their Second Time
key_insights: Second-time founders with a previous exit are often more successful as they are more willing to 'swing for the fences' on bigger ideas.
The timing of going public is critical; Dave's SPAC in January 2022 was too late, coinciding with a market collapse that saw its value drop 98% from $4B to $50M.
Dave's turnaround was driven by focusing on profitability and leveraging AI, which reduced customer support costs and dramatically improved underwriting loss rates from over 10% to 1.2%.
AI-powered cash flow underwriting, using data from over 12 million connected bank accounts, has been a key competitive advantage, allowing for better credit decisions and lower losses.
The US neo-banking opportunity is in serving the lower-income population that incumbent banks find unprofitable, a massive market that can be addressed with a lean, scalable, digital-first model.
A clear message to investors about the path to profitability (e.g., reaching 2.1 million monthly paying members) was crucial in rebuilding market confidence.
fundraising_mentions: First business raised a $300,000 seed round from Mark Cuban.
Dave raised a $10 million Series A on a roughly $40 million valuation.
Dave only raised $60 million in primary capital before going public.
Dave received a $100 million convertible note from FTX.
quotable: If you were to have a blank check VC fund and you just wrote a check blank not looking at the idea uncapped convertible note into every successful exited YC founder for their second company you'd have probably one of the best VC funds on the planet.
Fintech became a bad word, SPAC became a bad word, unprofitable growth company became a bad word, like we were sitting in the worst possible place of all time.
one_liner: Dave CEO Jason Wilk discusses the extreme volatility of taking a fintech company public via SPAC, the journey from a $4 billion valuation to $50 million and back to over $1 billion, and how leveraging AI for underwriting became their key to profitability and market recovery.

title: Rob Lacher: How I Scaled to $600M AUM; Hiring Tips for VCs; Venture Capital in Europe vs USA | E999
key_insights: To build a contrarian VC firm, hire young, hungry, hyper-intelligent people rather than those with prior VC experience to avoid inheriting an 'average index' of other funds' thinking.

Europe's strength isn't copying Silicon Valley, but leveraging its unique DNA: the 90% of companies that are family-run, which are highly profitable, long-term oriented, and possess deep domain knowledge, collectively acting as Europe's 'Google' for B2B innovation.
A 'barbell' fund strategy (Pre-seed/Seed and a separate Series B/C fund) allows for early conviction and later-stage support, while avoiding the hyper-competitive, 'bloody red ocean' of Series A.

Founders taking seed money from multi-stage funds face significant signaling risk; if the fund doesn't lead the subsequent round, it's often a negative signal to the market, making fundraising harder.

The best VCs act as a 'Devil's Advocate' for founders, not by imposing their own ideas, but by expanding the founder's option space through connections to a network of operators who have solved similar problems.
fundraising_mentions: Visionaries Club has 600 million AUM.
La Familia started as a 40 million Angel fund.
The latest Visionaries seed fund is 150 million.
The seed fund has a 60% reserve for follow-on investments.
The growth fund invests 5 to 10 million in Series B/C rounds.
Biontech raised a 130 million seed round in 2008 from the Strüngmann brothers.
quotable: we always complain that we don't have a Google Facebook Amazon or tencent... but what we have in Europe is 90% of our companies are family businesses... if you take those family businesses together I think this is our Google.
The best thing you can do on your partner in a finding team is take risks with someone that is a totally different ingredient than you have.
one_liner: Rob Lacher of Visionaries Club shares his playbook on building a multi-stage venture firm, detailing his unique 'barbell' strategy, contrarian hiring principles, and the untapped potential of Europe's family businesses to dominate the B2B landscape.

title: Fiverr CEO & Founder, Micha Kaufman: "If You’re Not Adapting to AI, F* You. You’re Done!"
key_insights: Individuals, not employers, bear the ultimate responsibility for upskilling and adapting to new technologies like AI to remain valuable professionals.

AI democratizes capabilities, raising the baseline for everyone but diminishing individual competitive advantages from technology alone, thus amplifying the importance of the team and human ingenuity.
The current AI landscape mirrors the dot-com bubble, with an unsustainable influx of companies, suggesting an impending market correction or consolidation.

AI fundamentally challenges the concept of copyright and fair use, potentially disincentivizing human creativity if creators receive no recognition or value from their work being used to train models.
In an era of rapid change, long-term prediction is futile; leadership must prioritize 'velocity' (speed with direction) and reduce the cost of failure to navigate uncertainty effectively.
Marketing, particularly entry-level roles, is experiencing a more immediate and fundamental disruption from AI than even engineering, as basic content creation tasks are easily automated.
quotable: Why do you think it's my responsibility to make you better as professionals? [ __ ] you. Seriously, if you're not going to take the time to make yourself valuable, to embrace reality, you're doomed. I'm not going to help you.
What's happening with AI is forcing us to rediscover our humanity because in many ways if functions that we do as robots can be automated then there's no reason for a human being to do it.
one_liner: Fiverr CEO Micha Kaufman delivers a blunt wake-up call on the personal responsibility required to adapt to AI, the parallels between the current AI boom and the dot-com bubble, and the profound implications for the future of work and human creativity.

title: Jeff Wang: Sequoia Capital's $9BN Global Equities Fund on The Future for NVIDIA, Google & Meta|E1212
key_insights: Sequoia Capital Global Equities (SCG) employs a long-growth, short-value thematic strategy with low leverage, focusing 70% of its research on identifying the right themes ('sailing to the right island') and 30% on specific companies.
The firm utilizes a crossover model, co-investing in late-stage private companies to gain deeper insights and an edge before they enter public markets.
SCG maintains a concentrated portfolio of 15-20 longs, with the top five positions making up 35-40% of the portfolio, believing the power law still exists in public markets.

Jeff Wang believes AI's initial impact favors incumbent giants with vast data and distribution like Meta, which can immediately monetize through its ad auction model, while the effect on Google's search business is less certain.

While the level of AI-related capex is unprecedented, Wang believes application companies will eventually realize ROI, and SCG's strategy is to invest in these application companies with a call option on AI, like ServiceNow, rather than just the underlying hardware providers.
fundraising_mentions: SCG started with $50 million of internal capital and now manages about $9 billion.

The fund has a '3-3-3' structure: a three-year or more investment horizon, a three-year minimum capital lock-up for LPs, and a three-year incentive (carry) crystallization, which is not standard in the hedge fund industry.
quotable: For us 70% of our research process is actually upfront on the theme and only 30% on the actual company. You have to be a pirate interpreting a treasure map... we need to sail to the right Island. Now if we don't sail to the right Island it doesn't really matter which ship you picked.
I do think there are more threats on Google's business than there have been ever in the company's history.
one_liner: Sequoia's Jeff Wang details the strategy behind their $9B global equities fund, discussing their thematic long/short approach, crossover investing, and outlook on AI's impact on tech giants like NVIDIA, Google, and Meta.

title: Aloe Blacc: The Secret to Songwriting & Storytelling; Working w/ Avicii on “Wake Me Up” | 20VC #979
key_insights: Aloe Blacc's songwriting process often involves turning a single phrase into the nucleus of a song, building a story around it, and using poetic devices to create a 'flow state' for the listener.
He views his career transition as accidental; he only pursued music full-time after being laid off from his corporate consulting job at Ernst & Young.
To maintain privacy and peace, he has strategically worked to make his songs more famous than his face, allowing his voice to precede his personal identity.

The hit song 'Wake Me Up' was created in a single four-hour session with Avicii and Mike Einziger, starting from lyrics Blacc already had in his phone, but it initially received a negative reception at its debut.

After recovering from COVID, he founded 'Genesis', a biotech company aimed at creating a prophylactic to block the ACE2 receptor, and learned firsthand the challenges of fundraising in a specialized sector like biotech.
fundraising_mentions: Learned that biotech is a specific investment sector and not all VCs are amenable to it.
Discovered that for VCs, the team behind the idea is more critical than the idea itself for securing investment.
quotable: I've always looked at rules like good suggestions.
A good story I feel is something that helps the listener forget that the world exists and fall into your paradigm, your that whatever fantasy that you're building in a story.
I need to figure out how to make my songs precede me. I need to figure out how to make sure that people know my voice not my face.
one_liner: Musician Aloe Blacc breaks down his creative process for songwriting and storytelling, shares the story behind the hit 'Wake Me Up' with Avicii, and discusses his entrepreneurial pivot into biotech with his new company, Genesis.

title: How This Australian Company Grew To $40BN Valuation 🤑
key_insights: Canva had strong early signs of product-market fit, including several hundred thousand monthly active users, despite having no revenue.
The company was growing 30-40% month-over-month completely organically.
Early cohort retention was very strong, indicating a sticky and valuable product.
Usage was highly fragmented across various media types (pitch decks, posters, social media), showing broad appeal.
The investment broke many traditional VC rules (Australian-based, pre-revenue, non-traditional founders), emphasizing the need to look beyond a standard checklist.
fundraising_mentions: Raising a convertible note at a $25 million valuation cap.
quotable: it broke a lot of the traditional rules you know we thankfully decided to make that investment but there were all sorts of reasons to let it go.
if you only stared at that [early signs of product market fit], you could see that there was something really special here.
one_liner: A partner at Shasta Ventures discusses the contrarian investment in Canva, highlighting how focusing on strong, organic product-market fit signals can lead to exceptional returns, even when breaking conventional investment rules.

title: Mark Suster: Why Private Equity Will Replace IPOs and M&A as the Exit Path | E1147
key_insights: Private Equity will increasingly replace IPOs and M&A as the primary exit path for venture-backed companies due to a blocked IPO market and regulatory hurdles for strategic acquisitions.
The 2021 market was significantly more overvalued than the dot-com bubble, with a correction that will likely take another five years to play out.
A vast majority (estimated 1,000 of 1,200) of the 'unicorns' created in 2021-2022 will never achieve a billion-dollar exit, leading to a large number of zombie companies.
True investment alpha comes from holding a correct, contrarian belief. Investing in today's hyped trends (like generative AI) is unlikely to produce strong returns due to inflated entry prices.
Discipline on entry valuation and ownership is critical for consistent returns. Upfront Ventures has maintained a median entry pre-money of $11-12M and an ownership target of 18-21%.
fundraising_mentions: Advocates for VCs to do a first close with the minimum amount possible to get 'in business', rather than waiting for a single large close.
Recounts raising a $195M fund where he was stuck at $110M until a crucial $2.5M commitment from Morgan Stanley unlocked the rest of the raise.
Upfront's strategy is to invest ~42% of a fund as first checks and reserve ~58% for follow-on rounds.
The firm's median first check has been $3.2-$3.5M for 18-21% ownership since 2009.
quotable: 1998, '99, 2000 are nothing compared to the overvaluations of 2021. So we're two years into a correction; I think it's going to take another five.
To make money as any investor, you have to believe something that other people don't believe, and you have to be right.
one_liner: Veteran VC Mark Suster argues that private equity will become the dominant exit path, warns that the 2021 market correction is far from over, and makes the case for disciplined, contrarian investing in sectors like space over hyped areas like AI.

title: How to do Layoffs the Right Way | a16z's Martin Casado
key_insights: Companies should conduct scenario planning (bear, median, bull cases) during significant macro-economic shifts.
A comprehensive top-down operating plan, aligned with the current economic environment, is essential before making decisions like layoffs.
The primary goal during a downturn is to ensure company solvency and protect employees where possible.
Layoffs should be a last resort, resulting from strategic planning rather than knee-jerk reactions from investors or boards.
Boards must be aligned on the company's strategic posture and risk profile during challenging times.
fundraising_mentions: we may not be able to raise for you know let's say three years
quotable: I deeply appreciate and I empathize with what Founders are going through on this but I also think a lot of this skill set has been lost because it's been a long time since we've seen them they're reset this large.

I tend to be very top down on these sorts of things you know the goal is to keep the company solvent and and successful you know protect common and as many employees as possible and so I think the right approach is to create an operating plan given the current economic environment and ask the question is like what is the right company in order to do that given whatever risk profile that you're comfortable with as a board
one_liner: Martin Casado of a16z advises founders on navigating economic downturns by emphasizing strategic scenario planning and top-down operating plans over reactive layoff decisions to ensure company solvency.

title: Billionaire Chris Sacca's 5 SIMPLE STEPS to help anyone who is struggling and upset
key_insights: When someone is upset, the first step is to repeat back what they said to show you've heard and are validating their feelings.
After validating, pause and 'wallow in it' with them before jumping to a solution, as people's primary need is to feel heard.
Your next step should always be to ask a question, not make a statement, to guide the person toward finding the solution themselves.
To coach an employee after a failure, express your own feelings of disappointment as part of the team ('we' failed), and then ask them what should be done going forward.
Giving the employee ownership of the solution empowers them and is a more effective management technique than imposing a solution and reprimanding them.
quotable: The one thing we all crave is to be heard and validated.
You may have a solution in mind but you have to let them find it along the way you can't impose it.
one_liner: Chris Sacca explains a five-step framework for managing conflict and coaching employees by validating their emotions and empowering them to find their own solutions, a technique he learned from raising toddlers.

title: a16z GP Martin Casado: How I Went from Engineer to VC; Lessons from Chris Dixon | 20VC #956
key_insights: Venture capital needs to mature and scale to fund innovation throughout a company's entire lifecycle, challenging traditional finance.
The most valuable (and rare) board members are former operators who have empathy from their experience but don't try to backseat drive the company.
Instead of trying to determine if a single company is a good investment, it's more effective to study a space deeply and then identify the most promising company within that cohort.
Category creation is as important and difficult as product development, requiring a long-term process of 'market annealing' that is not well-documented.
The most reliable signal for a promising area is not a VC's thesis, but observing where a critical mass of smart founders is choosing to build.
fundraising_mentions: Started his company Nicira in 2007 and almost went out of business in 2008.
Had to pay salaries out of his own bank account.
Did the Series A for dbt Labs.

If any company walks in I haven't a clue if it's a good investment or not... on the other hand and this is this is this obvious unlock that I've had mentally if I meet five companies I can probably tell you which one of those five has a better chance than the others.
one_liner: a16z General Partner Martin Casado shares his journey from engineer to leading infrastructure investor, arguing for a scaled, more mature venture capital model and detailing his investment strategy of deeply learning spaces to bet on the strongest founders within them.

title: How I got a job in Tech with NO EXPERIENCE — DoorDash VP Brian Hale
key_insights: Brian Hale secured a tech job at 17 with no prior experience.
He creatively described non-technical jobs on his resume to sound technical (e.g., 'marine ceramic technologist' for dishwasher).
His candid and humorous explanation of his resume on a call helped him land the job.
His first role involved working on search engines like Alav Vista and Hotbot in 1999, before Google's dominance.
His early entry into tech at a young age paved his path in growth and technology.
quotable: I called up this guy and I was like you should hire me and he's like how old are you and I was like oh I'm 17 you hired my brother he's like are you an engineer and I said no and he said send me your resume which is Canadian for no right but I didn't know that so this is the beauty of being young and naive
what the heck is a marine ceramic technologist and I was like oh that's a dishwasher and he thought that was hilarious so he gave me a job
one_liner: DoorDash VP Brian Hale recounts his unconventional entry into the tech industry at 17, using ingenuity and humor to land a job working on early search engines.

title: Hero Worshipping CEOs and Founders -- Good or Bad?
key_insights: A CEO's main goal should be to build a team that can succeed without them.
The idea of a 'superhero CEO' who is involved in every decision, including all hires, is not scalable.
If a CEO feels they need to be involved in every hire, it shows a lack of trust in their team.
A company's ability to succeed in the absence of its CEO is a key performance indicator of that CEO's success.
The role of a CEO is to empower their team to make great decisions and hires, rather than being the central point of failure.
quotable: Your biggest kpi at the end of the day is if you've died tomorrow is the company still going to succeed like are you able to build something that succeeds in your absence.
Ultimately your job as a CEO is to build a team that succeeds without you.
one_liner: Miki Kuusi challenges the idolization of 'superhero' CEOs, arguing that a leader's primary measure of success is building a team that can thrive independently.

title: Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO & Founder: Why Agents Do Not Mean RPA is F*** | E1240
key_insights: In the current AI cycle, product experience and ease of use matter more for adoption than pure technological innovation in models.
RPA is ideal for reliable, rule-based tasks, while agentic AI handles non-deterministic, unstructured parts of a process; they are complementary, not competitive.
The future of enterprise automation lies in 'agentic orchestration'—a single platform to manage both rule-based robots (low-skilled employees) and AI agents (high-skilled employees).

Enterprises are adopting agents cautiously, preferring them to make recommendations validated by humans rather than take autonomous actions, due to their unpredictability and the low risk appetite for critical workloads.
The widespread, scaled deployment of agentic AI in the enterprise will be a gradual 5-10 year process, limited by corporate inertia and the current state of LLM reliability.
True AGI for the enterprise requires a new 'giant leap' in technology, as current LLMs are still stochastic engines that lack the predictable reasoning of a human with average IQ.
fundraising_mentions: Bootstrapped the company for 10 years before raising the first capital.
quotable: Agents will make recommendations, agents are not going to take actions directly... they are like idiot savants sometimes they can be extremely smart, sometimes they can be extremely dumb, and you have no idea right now how to distinguish between these two scenarios.
I've wasted my late 20s, a big part of my 30s and 40s, thinking in this way [wanting more material possessions]. It's a totally waste of cycles and energy, man.
one_liner: UiPath CEO Daniel Dines explains why agentic AI complements rather than replaces RPA, arguing for a future where an orchestration layer manages both, and why product experience has become more important than model innovation for enterprise adoption.

Dara Khosrowshahi's assurance that Careem could maintain its purpose, culture, and team was a key factor in the acquisition, framing it as primarily a shareholder replacement.

title: How my side project became a $20B company
key_insights: A side project created to keep an engineering team busy can become a multi-billion dollar company.
The initial idea for Cloudflare (Project Honey Pot) was an anti-spam project to track how spammers harvest emails.
Customer demand to 'not just track the bad guys, but stop them' was initially dismissed as a dumb idea.
A co-founder's perspective can be critical in identifying the true potential of an idea that the originator might overlook.
The 'aha' moment for Cloudflare didn't come from the original creator, but from co-founder Michelle Zatlyn who insisted 'that's the idea we're building'.
quotable: The number one request was can you not just track the bad guys could you actually stop them and to be totally honest like I ignored that and we were like that's a dumb idea.
It wasn't really even my aha moment it was it was actually Michelle's.
one_liner: Cloudflare's co-founder explains how an anti-spam side project evolved into a $20B company, thanks to persistent customer requests and the crucial insight of his co-founder.

title: How to Build Product Like Boeing ✈️
key_insights: To build customer confidence, products should be tested beyond their expected operational limits, similar to how Boeing tests airplane wings.
It is crucial to have an overwhelming amount of confidence in a product before its general release, based on accumulated evidence of success.
A key challenge for entrepreneurs is balancing the desire to move fast with the need to maintain stability and reliability for customers.
To manage the risks of innovation, companies can reduce the 'blast radius' of their experiments to limit the impact of potential failures.
Before a full market launch, it's wise to gather substantial evidence from smaller, controlled experiments to validate the product's success and reliability.
quotable: I want to move really fast but my customers are telling me that I'm breaking their stuff too frequently.

You can find ways of reducing the blast radius of your experimentation such that when it's the time that you bring the product to everybody you've accumulated enough evidence of success that you have an overwhelming amount of confidence in what you're bringing to the market.
one_liner: This episode explores a product development philosophy inspired by Boeing's rigorous testing methods, advocating for controlled experimentation to build confidence and reliability before a full-scale launch.

title: Mark Roberge: The Framework for How Startups Should Scale into the Enterprise -Stage 2 Capital|E1176
key_insights: When making the first sales hire, prioritizing experience with a similar deal size over the same customer category is more critical for success.
Early sales compensation plans should be creative and strategically aligned with the business's 6-12 month goals, rather than adopting a generic model.
For land-and-expand or PLG models, incentivize expansion revenue more heavily than initial ACV to align sales behavior with the company's growth strategy.
Startups should resist the pull to sell to the enterprise too early, as it can distort the product roadmap and company strategy, even if it means turning down large, seemingly company-changing deals.
The right time to scale into the enterprise is when the company is consistently being 'pulled' by larger customers, not by proactively pushing into that market prematurely.

Channel partnerships require significant effort to mobilize; success depends on high-level strategic alignment and creating strong incentives (like quota relief and bonuses) for the partner's sales reps.
Payback period is a critical unit economic metric; for a Series A company, a payback period of 12-15 months is considered very good, while over 20 months is concerning.
A founder's initial sales playbook should focus on defining the buyer journey, ICP, and value proposition, rather than trying to perfect the sales methodology, which a professional hire can refine.
fundraising_mentions: HubSpot raised a $5 million Series A round from General Catalyst.
Salesforce.com was an investor in HubSpot's Series D round.
quotable: The best way to devise a comp plan is to think about what you need the business to do in the next 6 to 12 months strategically. Don't even think about sales.
I have a strong conviction that deal size has a higher weight in correlation to success.
one_liner: Mark Roberge shares his framework for building and scaling a startup's go-to-market engine, covering the first sales hire, compensation plans, unit economics, and knowing when to move into the enterprise.

title: Hiring the Best Product People in Five Steps, Why the Best PMs are Writers
key_insights: A structured, five-interview process is key for hiring great PMs: a recruiter screen, a hiring manager interview focusing on core competencies, an engineering manager interview for technical/domain skills, a hands-on peer interview, and a final case study interview.

The four essential buckets for a PM's skills are: 1) Validation (customer interviews, data gathering), 2) Build (working with engineering, making tradeoffs), 3) Business (understanding KPIs and outcomes), and 4) Communication (with execs, customers, and engineers).
Long-form writing is a critical skill for PMs to drive alignment. Use one-pagers ('Opportunity Canvas') for specific concepts and longer two-to-six-page docs for longer-arc strategy.
Founders should wait until they have repeatable product-market fit before hiring their first product manager to avoid abdicating critical early decisions.

Product management is a blend of art and science. Early-stage startups are more art-driven (80% art, 20% data), while mature companies with product-market fit should instill more scientific rigor and process.
quotable: Listen to customers about their problems and generally ignore their recommendations around solution because they may not be building exactly what they want may not be the most elegant way to solve the problem.
If you're a startup you have very little data at your disposal, you're mostly working on early qualitative feedback... and that might be more like 20 data 80 art.
one_liner: Product leader Scott Williamson shares his frameworks for hiring, managing, and structuring high-performing product teams, emphasizing the importance of written strategy documents and deep customer understanding.

title: Why Jeff Bezos Deserves More Credit
key_insights: Jeff Bezos is credited with creating more jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic than any other individual.
Amazon raised its minimum wage to $15/hour, significantly higher than the federal minimum wage, compelling other corporations to follow suit.
True social contribution from for-profit businesses, like ensuring employees have a livable wage, is often undervalued compared to traditional non-profit charity.
There has been a cultural shift away from glorifying the creation of massive, 'behemoth' businesses.
Despite donating billions to environmental causes, Bezos's most significant societal contributions may lie within his for-profit business practices that directly impact workers' livelihoods.

one_liner: This episode argues that Jeff Bezos deserves more credit for his positive impact on job creation and raising the minimum wage through Amazon, suggesting these for-profit actions are a powerful, underappreciated form of social contribution.

title: The Ultimate Guide for Building a Two-Sided Marketplace
key_insights: Great marketplaces thrive on a fragmented supply side; it's hard to aggregate but creates immense defensibility once achieved (e.g., OpenTable).
Capital efficiency is paramount; marketplaces that get paid in advance (like Airbnb or Incredible Health) have a massive advantage and can scale with less venture funding.
Avoid heavy reliance on paid acquisition channels like Google and Facebook, as CAC tends to rise over time. The best businesses often have a compelling organic growth component.
Market timing is a more significant risk than market size. Many failed ideas were simply too early, and later iterations succeeded with better technology and execution (e.g., Webvan vs. Instacart).
When analyzing cohorts, look for improving trends over time as a potential sign of a network effect, and focus on revenue retention, not just user retention, as engaged users often spend more.
fundraising_mentions: Incredible Health raised a round at a $1.65 billion valuation, after a previous round at $60 million post-money.
When a16z invested in Instacart, the company was losing $20-25 per order.
quotable: There are no bad ideas, only bad timing.
The get paid in advance is very rare but when you see it I've come to Value it heavily.
one_liner: a16z's Jeff Jordan shares his playbook for building defensible, two-sided marketplaces, emphasizing the importance of supply-side fragmentation, capital efficiency, and avoiding over-reliance on paid acquisition.

title: Girish Mathrubootham (HINDI): Biggest Product and Pricing Lessons from Scaling to $597M in ARR
key_insights: It is easier to go from the bottom-up (SMB to Enterprise) than top-down. No major software company has successfully started in Enterprise and won the SMB market.
A low-cost, high-value product can effectively penetrate a crowded market, attracting SMBs and educational institutions initially, before moving upmarket by adding features and increasing prices.

Day-one global strategy is crucial for Indian SaaS startups. It's easier to earn a dollar than a rupee, partly due to Indian customers having a more service-oriented mindset versus a product-centric one.
A 'twin engine' model of inbound PLG and outbound sales is powerful but creates significant challenges in balancing product needs, pricing transparency, and hiring people who understand both motions.

When launching new products, do it when the first product is growing strongly. This allows you to fund the new initiative from a position of strength, as it's nearly impossible to get funding for a second product when you're struggling.
fundraising_mentions: Invested in Chargebee at a ₹2.4 crore (24 million) pre-money valuation with a $25,000 check.
Co-founded Together Fund, an operator-led fund for B2B SaaS and AI startups in India.
quotable: एक डॉलर कमाना एक रुप कमाने से ज्यादा आसान है। (It's easier to earn a dollar than to earn a rupee.)
जब आप नौकरी बदल रहे होते हैं, तो आपकी सोच अपने साथ ले जा सकते हैं, लेकिन प्लेबुक नहीं। (When you are changing jobs, you can take your mindset with you, but not the playbook.)
one_liner: Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham discusses the journey of scaling a multi-product SaaS company globally from India, emphasizing a low-cost entry, product-led growth, and the challenges of moving upmarket.

title: #1 Mistake Early-Stage Startups Need to Avoid -- Ed Baker (Fmr. VP of Growth @ Uber)
key_insights: Startups should find product-market fit before focusing on growth.
Hiring a growth leader too early, before product-market fit, is a common mistake.
Product-market fit is defined as building a product that people love to use.
Achieving product-market fit is the hardest task for an entrepreneur and often involves luck.
Using a drilling for oil analogy, ensure you've hit oil (product-market fit) before investing in growth expertise.
quotable: no matter how how good your drill is if you're Drilling in the wrong place you'll never hit it
you don't want to start growing if you're Drilling in the wrong place you want to make sure you've hit that oil first then you add the growth expertise
one_liner: Ed Baker advises early-stage startups to prioritize achieving product-market fit before investing in growth initiatives, using an analogy of drilling for oil.

title: Nicolai Tangen: Managing the Largest Sovereign Wealth Fund in the World | E1122
key_insights: The next 5-10 years will be difficult for generating returns due to underlying inflationary pressures and geopolitical tensions.
A successful investment strategy involves being long-term, contrarian, and focusing on quality companies that are market share gainers.
Transparency is crucial for building trust, as demonstrated by the fund's public, real-time value ticker, which is the most-watched number in Norway.
Effective leaders must balance stubbornness in their convictions with the agility to change their minds when facts change, and they must admit their own mistakes to foster a safe culture.
Urgency is critical for execution; Tangen keeps a countdown clock in his office for his 5-year term to motivate his team to act quickly.
As a universal owner of 1.5% of all global companies, the fund cannot hide from systemic issues like climate change and must actively engage with companies to drive change.

quotable: I have a countdown clock in my office showing how many days I've got left on my job... when I got somebody in my office who says over the next 3 months we can do it I said Hey listen to that look at this I got 580 days left we need to hurry up.
If you are not happy now, you will never be happy.
one_liner: The CEO of the world's largest sovereign wealth fund discusses his long-term, contrarian investment philosophy, the challenging macroeconomic outlook for the next decade, and the leadership principles of transparency and urgency required to manage a $1.4 trillion fund.

title: The hardest part about releasing a new product
key_insights: The decision to launch a new product versus a paid upgrade often depends on whether it serves a distinct buyer for whom the existing product wouldn't appeal.
A critical test for product vs. feature is to evaluate it from the customer's perspective: would they naturally expect this functionality within their existing workflow?
Investigate how customers are currently solving the problem; if they are using a separate, dedicated platform, it's a strong signal that it can be a standalone product.
Founders and VCs might be tempted to label everything as a 'product' to focus on TAM expansion, but customer expectations should be the primary guide.
If customers are using makeshift solutions like spreadsheets, it's likely the functionality can be integrated as a feature within your existing product.
quotable: I think you have to look at it from the customer's point of view and say for the vast majority of course customers to use our current products would they expect this to be part of a connected workflow within the platform or do they think that this is somewhat exogenous to what they're currently doing here.
I sound like the douche VC when I say I think it's a feature not a product.
one_liner: Des Traynor explains the strategic thinking behind deciding whether a new capability should be launched as a standalone product or an integrated feature, emphasizing customer expectations and existing workflows as the most important criteria.

title: The great product debate: Art vs Science 🎨🔬
key_insights: Many believe product management is an art, often for self-preservation, but true value lies in leaders who can articulate and share their thinking.
Product management is argued to be 100% science and 0% art, despite common perceptions.
The perceived 'art' of product management often stems from the non-replicable innovations of visionaries, rather than an inherent lack of scientific principles.
Great product leaders can introspect, synthesize their thought processes, and scale them into models to improve the entire company, avoiding bottlenecks.
quotable: I actually think product is 100 science and zero percent art

I think really great leaders they are able to introspect themselves synthesize how they think about something and then put that into a model or try to scale it and if you can do that it makes the entire company much better than you bottlenecking the entire company
one_liner: A speaker passionately argues that product management is a quantifiable science rather than an art, emphasizing the importance of structured thought and scalable leadership in driving company-wide success.

title: Mark Cuban's plan to take on Big Pharma 🏥
key_insights: The pharmaceutical industry's status quo is ever-increasing drug prices, which negatively impacts patients and the healthcare system.
Cost Plus Drugs' business model is built on transparent pricing: cost + 15% + $3 labor + $5 shipping.
The company's marketing strategy is driven by adding new drugs and continually lowering prices, which are both unconventional in the industry.
Lowering prices as volume and efficiency increase serves as a key differentiating factor and marketing tool.
Word-of-mouth is a powerful growth driver, as patients with similar conditions share information about affordable medication options.
Focusing on core competencies and understanding why customers choose your business is fundamental to growth.
quotable: The Zeitgeist of the pharmaceutical and slash drug industry is that prices keep on going up and every time prices go up whoever's a patient for that drug their spirit and their potentially their health goes down.

When everybody is so used to prices just going up and we're pushing prices down that becomes our differentiating factor that becomes something that makes it worthwhile for our customers to tell others in similar circumstances.
one_liner: Mark Cuban explains how Cost Plus Drugs is disrupting the pharmaceutical industry with a transparent, low-cost pricing model that uses falling prices as its primary marketing engine.

title: Jason Lemkin’s 2023 Prediction 🔮
key_insights: Economic downturns often feel slow and brutal, but the subsequent recovery can be surprisingly fast.
Despite strong business fundamentals in 2023, SaaS multiples fell to historic lows, even lower than during the 2016 flash crash when companies were shrinking.
A recovery in public market multiples is expected, but they will not return to the peak levels of 2021.
The extreme growth and multiples seen in 2021, such as 80x ARR for public companies, were an anomaly and should not be expected to return.
The hyper-growth experienced by companies like Zoom during the pandemic was a unique, generational event, not a new standard for the market.
quotable: I've never seen multiples this low when businesses were this good.

realized that you lived in insane times they will be better at the end of this year in the start but you will never the world will never work the way it worked before it can't it can't it can't it can't.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin analyzes the 2023 SaaS market downturn, predicting a rebound in valuation multiples but emphasizing that the unprecedented highs of 2021 are a thing of the past.

title: Is Shreyas Doshi right about avoiding "process people"? | Marty Cagan w/ Harry Stebbings
guest_role: Founder at Silicon Valley Product Group
key_insights: Shreyas Doshi's framework identifies three product leader archetypes: the Visionary, the Craftsman, and the Operator.
There's a dangerous trend of 'operator' product leaders who rely on installing processes, which can stifle creativity and slow down execution.
Operational leaders can be divided into two categories: those who scale with rigid processes and those who scale through team coaching.
Leaders like Elon Musk and Steve Jobs have warned that in large companies, 'process becomes a substitute for thinking,' leading to an exodus of talented product people.
The concept of 'think deeply to move quickly,' used by companies like Stripe and Amazon, argues that thorough upfront thinking and debate lead to faster, more effective execution.
quotable: In big companies process becomes a substitute for thinking.
There are two kinds of operational people: there are those that believe in in operation or scale...with process and those that believe in scale with coaching.
one_liner: Marty Cagan analyzes the destructive impact of 'process people' in product organizations and champions a culture of deep thinking and coaching to drive meaningful innovation.

title: Failure in Hollywood vs. Silicon Valley
key_insights: Hollywood's culture brutally punishes failure with public humiliation, unlike Silicon Valley.
Silicon Valley embraces failure as a mechanism for growth, making individuals smarter and stronger.
The failure of Quibi was a humbling experience for the speaker, not a humiliating one.
Quibi achieved a high standard of content quality, with excellent work from Hollywood storytellers.
The primary reason for Quibi's failure was a lack of product-market fit, not the quality of its content.
Quibi's launch strategy was a mistake, designed like a movie opening with a binary outcome of success or failure from day one.
quotable: In Silicon Valley you know you fail you get on to the next thing like failure makes you smarter makes you stronger it's part of how you grow.
I was never humiliated by the failure of it I was humbled by it.
one_liner: A reflection on the cultural differences in handling failure between Hollywood and Silicon Valley, using the experience of Quibi to illustrate how high-quality content can fail due to a lack of product-market fit.

title: dLocal CEO Sebastian Kanovich: The $8BN Company You Might Not Know
key_insights: High performance is characterized by individuals who bring energy, focus on solutions not problems, and take ownership to get things done.
When making decisions, speed is crucial for learning and iteration, but the key is to not fall in love with your mistakes and to own them quickly.
Bootstrapping instills a powerful culture of frugality and customer-centricity, as customers are your primary investors.
A major unlock for growth can be bringing in the right investors who help you dream bigger and provide access to networks and expertise you wouldn't have otherwise.
For global expansion, a hybrid team approach is essential: you need core team members to embed the company culture and local talent to navigate the nuances of the new market.
Prioritize by listening to your enterprise customers; their collective feedback is the most reliable guide for your product and expansion roadmap.
fundraising_mentions: Bootstrapped from 2016 to 2019.
First investment was from General Atlantic in 2019.
The first round was all secondary funds.
Went public in 2021.
quotable: We weren't ambitious enough. We were afraid that we wouldn't be good enough and that was a mistake and it was a very painful one.
I really believe in efficiency of movements... if I'm spending too much time in my own mind, there's something wrong. I'll rather execute in some sort of direction.
one_liner: dLocal CEO Sebastian Kanovich discusses the journey of bootstrapping a global payments powerhouse from Uruguay, the strategic shift after taking on investors, and the cultural challenges of scaling a public company across 35 emerging markets.

title: Predictions for 2026: Top Buy & Biggest Short | Why Salesforce Could Win & NVIDIA’s Challenges
guest_role: Founder of SaaStr and Partner at Scale Venture Partners
key_insights: Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, is highlighted as a potential 'Founder of the Year' for the significant impact of Claude 3.5 and subsequent models on the AI ecosystem.
The venture capital landscape has fundamentally changed, with no apparent ceiling on valuations for top-tier AI companies, which alters investment strategies and return expectations.
DataBricks is named a breakout company for masterfully leveraging the AI wave to accelerate its growth to a $5 billion run rate, surpassing competitors.

Salesforce is identified as a potential top-performing stock for 2026 due to its immense potential to monetize agentic AI products across its vast customer base, which could drive significant revenue uplift.
A major societal risk for 2026 is a 'tech-lash' against AI if unemployment rises for any reason, as tech leaders have already publicly linked AI to job displacement.
fundraising_mentions: Revolut raised at $75 billion.
Hummingbird's $100 million fund returned $800 million.

OpenAI is discussed as raising another $100 billion.
