For the moment there's no ceiling on venture which changes all the math and calculations.
one_liner: In a year-end review, venture capitalists Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll discuss the top founders and funds of 2025 and make bold predictions for 2026's stock market, IPOs, and the major societal impacts of the AI boom.

title: Scooter Braun Almost Invested in Facebook 😲💰
key_insights: Scooter Braun attempted to invest $100,000 for a 10% stake in Facebook during its initial launch phase at Emery.
He negotiated directly with Eduardo Saverin after contacting Mark Zuckerberg.
The investment opportunity was rescinded when Zuckerberg decided against taking outside capital to facilitate a rapid expansion to 32 more schools.
A personal reason—avoiding an ex-girlfriend in Boston—prevented him from pursuing a potential follow-up meeting.
Witnessing Peter Thiel's subsequent $1 million investment for 10% of Facebook served as a pivotal lesson, sparking his interest in venture investing.
fundraising_mentions: Scooter Braun offered to invest $100,000 for 10% of Facebook.
Peter Thiel later invested $1,000,000 for 10% of Facebook.
quotable: I was trying to invest a hundred grand for 10 of Facebook.
I look back now and I know myself if I would have gone up there I might have gotten in but I didn't want to go up there because I was too afraid to see my ex-girlfriend.
that loss opened me up to the idea investing
one_liner: Scooter Braun shares the story of how he almost invested in Facebook's seed stage but missed out, a loss that ultimately inspired him to get into venture investing.

title: a16z's $20BN Fund & Founders Fund's $4.6BN & Why Josh Kushner Has Mastered the Game
key_insights: The traditional 'spreadsheet' model for SaaS investing is considered dead due to market saturation and the rise of AI, where product-market fit has become highly transient, sometimes lasting only weeks.
Mega-funds (like a16z's $20B fund) operate on the premise of capturing a few massive ($10B-$100B) outcomes, a strategy viable only for firms with access to every top-tier deal.

The 'Thrive Capital strategy' of buying the best asset in each major vertical (e.g., Stripe, OpenAI, Databricks) is seen as a brilliant, if price-risky, adaptation to the current late-stage market, bypassing the long grind of early-stage venture.
There is a massive overhang of mature, slower-growth SaaS companies in portfolios that are unattractive to PE buyers, creating a '$2 trillion' liquidity problem for the venture industry.

Founders Fund's success is attributed to a high-conviction strategy of making large, concentrated bets, holding winners for exceptionally long periods (10-15 years), and being unconstrained by traditional portfolio construction rules.
fundraising_mentions: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) announced a $20 billion fund.
Founders Fund raised $4.6 billion ($1.6 billion oversubscribed).
General Catalyst has an $8 billion fund.
OpenAI raising $30 billion.
Anthropic's multi-billion dollar fundraiser.
Benchmark invested $55 million in HeyGen, representing 8% of its fund.
Rippling rumored to be raising at an $18 billion valuation.
Ilia Sutskever's new company, Superintelligence, is supposedly raising $2 billion.
quotable: It used to take you five years to fall out of product market fit, now it can be five weeks.

Why struggle to pretend you can do 8x over 20 years on a seed fund when you can just write one big check into a winner and call it a day and achieve liquidity in a quarter of the time... when outcomes are north of 20, 100 billion, seed is for suckers.
one_liner: Venture investors Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll analyze the seismic shifts in venture capital, from the death of old SaaS playbooks to the rise of mega-funds and the transient nature of product-market fit in the AI era.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Brand Marketing
key_insights: Strong brands create value that transcends the product's functional benefits, driven by emotional connection rather than rational decision-making.
Brand appeal is often rooted in emotion and identity, such as the status associated with high-end fashion or the feeling of rebellion.
A brand can provide a 'piece of rebellion' to a mainstream audience, allowing them to participate in a culture without fully adopting its lifestyle (e.g., dentists buying Harley-Davidsons).
Mass-market entertainment, like horror movies or true crime shows, proves that provocative themes can have broad appeal across diverse demographics, not just niche groups.
To create a brand that people truly love, you must accept that some people will also truly hate it; aiming for universal appeal often results in a brand no one feels strongly about.
quotable: Strong brands mean more to people than the product itself so like if you're a strong brand the love for your brand transcends the functional benefit of whatever your product is.

If there are people who truly love something, there has to be people who truly hate it. It is not possible to make something that everybody loves... all that's possible is to make something that everybody doesn't really give a shit about one way or the other.
one_liner: Liquid Death's CEO explains how building a strong brand that transcends its physical product by tapping into emotional desires for rebellion and identity is key to creating something people love, even if it means others will hate it.

title: The State of Growth Investing in Q4 2023
key_insights: Despite a macroeconomic downturn, underlying growth in portfolio companies remains strong, with 180 companies growing over 50% YoY in Q2 2023.
The pace of new investment has slowed dramatically compared to 2021 and 2022.
A significant number of companies that raised Series A and B rounds in 2021-2022 will need to raise capital in 2024.
Companies raising new rounds may have to accept a lower valuation than they initially wanted.
The current market conditions are closer to a sustainable, relationship-driven reality than the frenzied pace of 2021.
fundraising_mentions: A lot of Series A and Series B investments were made in 2021 and 2022.
Companies are typically funded for 12-24 months at these early stages.
Many companies will naturally need to raise more capital by the beginning of 2024.
They might not raise capital at the price they wanted to.
quotable: This market is probably closer to reality than 21 was.

The pace of actually being able to spend time with companies build relationships with that teams take them out to dinner um see how they do over the course of six months is really what this business always used to be and I think is what this business will go back to being.
one_liner: An investor from Insight Partners analyzes the state of growth investing, noting that while the pace of new deals has slowed, strong companies continue to grow and a wave of necessary fundraising in 2024 will define the new market reality.

title: Guy Podjarny: The Future of AI Software Development - What is Real & What is BS | E1232
key_insights: The role of software developers will evolve from coding to systems thinking and architecture, as AI handles more implementation details.
A 'trough of disillusionment' in AI is likely as enterprises realize short-term ROI is hard to achieve, despite the long-term potential of the technology.
Specialized AI models may outperform large, general models in the short term (3-year timeline) due to current architectural limitations in scaling.
The future of AI development platforms could lead to closed ecosystems, concentrating power in a few companies and reducing the control of individual developers.
Founders should pursue ideas that are not immediately obvious and require effort to convince others, as these markets are less likely to be saturated.
AI coding assistants provide value by reducing toil but often generate 'average' quality code, which can become a long-term maintenance and security burden.
fundraising_mentions: Tessel has raised $125 million.
Guy Podjarny sold about a third of his Sneak ownership for a nine-figure amount.
Sneak received an acquisition offer in the ~$200 million range early in its journey.
Larry Ellison is quoted saying you need $100 billion to enter the frontier model race.
Masa Son is quoted saying AGI will require $9 trillion in capex.
quotable: I think the best software developers are not the best because they're the best coders it's because they think about development as a whole. They are systems thinkers.

Founders should look for ideas that they need to work to convince people are useful... you have to have something that's a little bit harder to understand that really requires some depth of thinking or a different angle.
one_liner: Tessel CEO Guy Podjarny analyzes the current state of AI in software development, predicting a shift in the developer's role from coding to architecture and discussing the opportunities and risks in the evolving AI landscape.

title: Matt Clifford: The Bull & Bear Case for China's Ability to Challenge the US' AI Capabilities | E1172
key_insights: The value of new ideas in AI is increasing relative to simply scaling compute and data, potentially allowing new startups to challenge incumbents.
China's AI progress is significantly hampered by a strict, stability-focused regulatory environment and US semiconductor export controls, creating a real but potentially temporary gap with the West.

The UK possesses an extraordinary talent base and has the potential to be a world-leading tech hub, but is held back by cultural norms, capital allocation problems (e.g., pension funds not investing in venture), and bureaucratic hurdles like planning permission for data centers.

The best predictor of future entrepreneurial success is past behavior, but this 'entrepreneurial activity' looks different across cultures. Talent is fungible, and the 'forced entrepreneurs' who start companies during recessions often outperform those who chose it in boom times.
AI will fundamentally change warfare. The rise of cheap, smart, autonomous drones creates an asymmetric threat, and it's an open question whether AI will favor offensive or defensive capabilities.

The next major shift in AI will likely be 'agency.' Building the protocols and infrastructure for these autonomous agents to interact and transact will be an extraordinarily valuable commercial opportunity.
fundraising_mentions: Entrepreneur First invests £250k at the pre-seed stage after their initial 10-week cohort program.
quotable: I think that we are seeing the flattening off of the value of just adding more compute and more data to language models.
China is more paranoid about AI safety than probably any other government in the world.
I think the UK can go back to being pretty much the richest country in the world per capita. I really truly believe that... we just need to choose to be.
one_liner: Matt Clifford, co-founder of Entrepreneur First, discusses the shifting landscape of AI from a game of pure scale to one of ideas, analyzes the competitive dynamics between the US and a surprisingly paranoid China, and makes a bold case for the UK's untapped potential as a global tech superpower.

title: Dan Gill, CPO @Carvana: The Most Wild Story in Public Markets | E1243
key_insights: Hire for 'horsepower' (deep product curiosity) and intrinsic drive ('give a sh*t'), rather than specific domain experience. The best talent can learn the industry.
Product leaders must be business leaders obsessed with unit economics. Success is defined by moving metrics that impact the bottom line, not just shipping features.
To prioritize effectively, ask: 'If you can only change one thing, what is it?' This forces focus on the highest impact initiative and avoids diluted efforts.

Vertical integration (e.g., in-house financing) is a powerful moat. By capturing more of the profit pools around a transaction, you can create a superior value proposition that's difficult to compete with.

Avoid excessive team fragmentation. Consolidating from many small teams to a few larger, cross-functional ones forces better global prioritization and puts more energy behind the most important initiatives.
In a crisis (like a 99% stock drop), leaders must over-communicate the truth, share the plan in unit economic terms, and consistently report progress to rebuild trust and galvanize the team.
fundraising_mentions: Carvana IPO'd at a valuation of about $2 billion, peaked at $60 billion, dropped to $500 million, and recovered to $50 billion.
quotable: The fun thing about dropping by 99% is that the difference between a 98% drop and a 99% drop is another 50% drop.
We do not win by shipping features, we win by moving metrics.
one_liner: Carvana's CPO, Dan Gill, discusses navigating extreme market volatility by focusing on unit economics, vertical integration, and disciplined product strategy, sharing lessons on hiring, prioritization, and leadership through crisis.

title: Accidental $12B Business
key_insights: A side project built to solve a specific customer need can have more potential than the primary business.
Transitioning a service into a self-serve, credit-card-based product is a powerful way to unlock organic growth.
External inspiration (like an Oprah segment on passive income) can be a catalyst for recognizing the untapped potential in your own business.
Simple data analysis, like comparing revenue streams, can provide the clarity needed to make a major strategic pivot.
Focus is paramount; shutting down a legacy business (the web design agency) was crucial to fully commit to and scale the high-growth venture (MailChimp).
fundraising_mentions: No fundraising mentioned; the story highlights organic growth and revenue-funding.
quotable: It was an accidental kind of a business we built it for just a couple of our customers who were having problems sending out email newsletters.

We color coded the revenue for MailChimp versus the revenue from our agency and MailChimp was growing and our agency was flat or and kind of declining. That was all we needed to say let's stop the agency business and let's focus on Mailchimp.
one_liner: The founder of MailChimp explains how a small side project for his web design agency accidentally became a massive SaaS business once they recognized its recurring revenue potential and decided to focus on it exclusively.

title: What I Learned from Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz | Marty Cagan
key_insights: Marc Andreessen's core strength was assimilating knowledge from engineering, customers, and startups daily to foresee industry trends.
The most critical lesson from Marc Andreessen is the humility to 'know what you can't know', which is the foundation of product discovery.
Effective product leadership requires acknowledging that you don't have all the answers and must figure things out.
Ben Horowitz exemplified 'tough love' leadership, providing direct feedback from a supportive standpoint, a style influenced by coach Bill Campbell.
Pierre Omidyar's persuasive and passionate vision for eBay demonstrated the power of a founder's conviction in creating new market possibilities like online marketplaces.
quotable: The most important thing is to know what you can't know.
You need to know what you can't know because that is really the essence of product Discovery.
one_liner: Marty Cagan discusses pivotal leadership and product management lessons learned from tech legends Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and Pierre Omidyar during his time at Netscape and eBay.

title: What's the difference between "brand" and "storytelling"?
key_insights: Effective marketing is about rapid communication to evoke a feeling, not complex storytelling which is difficult and better suited for entertainment like movies.
Brand affinity is built on emotional connection rather than functional product benefits.
Liquid Death prioritizes making their audience laugh, aiming for their marketing to be memorable and entertaining content.
Providing value to the consumer through entertainment (e.g., a funny ad) is a more effective path to brand loyalty than highlighting product features like calories or taste.
The goal of a Liquid Death commercial is for the viewer's takeaway to be 'that was hilarious' rather than 'I need to be more hydrated'.
quotable: Marketing is not storytelling really I think it's it's a lower form of it so I think it's more about communication.
We want the takeaway to be oh my God that was probably the funniest thing I've seen today and it came from a water company.
one_liner: Liquid Death's CEO argues that building brand affinity comes from creating entertaining communication that provides emotional value, rather than traditional storytelling or marketing based on functional benefits.

title: Alex Bouaziz: How We Became a $12B HR Company with 2,000 Remote Employees | 20VC #973
key_insights: Speed of execution is the single most defining factor for a startup's success; do it now, don't push it to tomorrow.
For distributed companies, the default must be full trust, but it's maintained with tight KPIs and a culture of high performance.
Hire for hunger and work ethic over raw intelligence. The best hires are those who genuinely care and are in a life stage to commit to intense building.
In a cost-conscious environment, CFOs will drive the bundling of software, preferring a single, cost-effective platform over multiple best-of-breed (but more expensive) point solutions.
Maintaining a direct, informal feedback loop with top customers (e.g., via WhatsApp) is invaluable for validating hypotheses and guiding product direction.
A founder's biggest mistake is often not firing fast enough when a hire isn't working out, even if they look good on paper.
fundraising_mentions: The company raised most of its funding rounds remotely without in-person investor meetings.
Alex Bouaziz personally took out around $10 million in secondaries to buy an apartment and for personal matters.
The company allowed early employees to sell up to 10% of their vested equity in secondary transactions.
Mentions taking secondaries at both Series B and Series D rounds.
quotable: I would hire someone that works really hard over someone that's really smart any day of the week.
Speed of execution is what defines a company, and speed of growth is what makes a startup. If you're not growing, you're dead.
The biggest mistakes I've made is not firing fast enough.
one_liner: Deel Co-founder Alex Bouaziz discusses the playbook for blitzscaling a remote-first HR company to a $12B valuation, emphasizing radical execution speed, a 'savage' hiring mentality, and a product strategy that adapts to market needs.

title: Two ways to create an OPEN company culture 👐
key_insights: Foster a culture where employees, regardless of seniority, feel comfortable pushing back and voicing their opinions publicly.
Prioritize open debate in meetings to ensure all perspectives are heard, even if it involves uncomfortable conversations.
Eliminate traditional company titles to prevent hierarchical structures from stifling junior employees' contributions.
Actively recruit individuals who are comfortable with debate and engaging in uncomfortable conversations.
Recognize that while leadership may not always agree with pushback, creating a safe space for it is crucial for a healthy culture.
quotable: our company culture is one where literally it doesn't matter if you're an intern or you're one of my co-founders you'll push back on me in public
we interviewed just a very very very aggressively for people who feel comfortable with debate if you don't feel comfortable with uncomfortable conversations this is not gonna be the place for you
one_liner: This episode discusses methods for building an open company culture by encouraging public pushback, fostering debate, and removing hierarchical barriers like job titles to empower all employees to voice their decisions.

title: Is this Twitter's Next CEO?
key_insights: A full-time CEO role would need to be for a company with an important global mission, not just for financial gain.
Despite its flaws, Twitter is considered a 'globally important asset' that needs fixing.
Working for Elon Musk to transform Twitter is seen as a potentially 'fun' opportunity.

Prediction 2 (30% chance): Elon Musk is forced to buy Twitter at the original price.

fundraising_mentions: The primary discussion is about the potential acquisition of Twitter by Elon Musk, with a prediction of a negotiated settlement at a lower price.
quotable: Twitter as much as I hate it, it's a hellscape and all those things, there's some there's a globally important asset and someone has to do something with it.
I mean there's only one CEO in Elon companies and that's Elon Musk.
one_liner: Jason Calacanis discusses what it would take for him to become a full-time CEO again, his interest in fixing Twitter, and his predictions for the outcome of Elon Musk's acquisition attempt.

title: Aydin Senkut: How I Scaled from a $4M Angel Fund to $900M AUM | 20VC #890
key_insights: To succeed as a VC, it's better to sacrifice entry valuation and initial ownership to ensure you are in the world's best companies, as the unlimited upside of a massive hit outweighs entry price optimization.

A flexible, global, multi-stage strategy allows a firm to invest in the best companies wherever they are, rather than being constrained to a specific geography or stage, which was key to Felicis's early success.

Building a venture firm evolves through three stages: from a solo operator, to a team, to a team of teams. The most difficult part is picking the right people, where cultural fit and a 'growth mindset' are as crucial as talent or experience.
The biggest mistakes in venture are not the investments that fail, but the great companies you say 'no' to (sins of omission), as VC is a business driven by positive outliers.

Instead of getting caught in market price debates, focus on what you can control: your investment process and portfolio construction. You can always find an edge through original thinking and betting on where the world is going before it's obvious.
fundraising_mentions: Felicis's first fund was $41 million.
The firm grew from a $4M angel fund to $900M in AUM.
quotable: I'm going to do things exactly the opposite or exactly outside of the Orthodox way and that's the only way I know how to get to success. You cannot copy and paste to the top of competition.
The biggest mistakes are the ones that you should have said yes but you didn't.
one_liner: Aydin Senkut of Felicis Ventures shares his journey from angel investor to managing a $900M fund, detailing his unorthodox, global investment strategy, the importance of backing the best companies at any price, and the nuanced art of building a successful and empathetic firm.

title: Principled Leadership, Privacy, and The Trust Game
key_insights: Admiration for Tim Cook's principled leadership, especially his personal journey and advocacy for privacy.
Privacy is highlighted as a critical value, championed by leaders like Tim Cook.
All entities, from successful companies to governments, are engaged in a 'trust game' where proving trustworthiness is paramount.
The fundamental challenge for governments is to continuously maintain trustworthiness.
Insights into building systems of trust can be gained from philosophers and historical figures who deeply considered principles of rule of law, such as Aristotle and Madison.
quotable: I really admire Tim Cook I think he's a very principled person...

...when you get to a certain size we're all in the game of the trust game how can I prove that we're trustworthy and that's also the problem this a fundamental problem of governments is how do you continue to be trustworthy...
one_liner: An unnamed guest discusses the principled leadership of Tim Cook, the importance of privacy, and the universal challenge of building and maintaining trust for both large corporations and governments.

title: Val Scholz: How Revolut Acquired Their First 10M Users: Tips, Tactics & Strategies | E1168
key_insights: Revolut's primary growth engine was a highly-optimized referral loop, which accounted for 90% of B2C customer acquisitions, focusing on minimizing the time from signup to a user's first referral.
Instead of paid marketing, Revolut focused on building a sustainable growth engine through referrals and organic channels, believing paid spend is not a sustainable long-term strategy.
A key strategy was to launch in markets with less competition (e.g., Ireland, Romania, Poland) rather than saturated ones (like the UK), allowing for faster growth and market dominance.
Revolut's hiring process prioritized young, smart, and driven individuals, using difficult, real-world take-home tasks to test for structured problem-solving abilities over direct experience.
The company culture was intense and high-performance, described as 'Special Forces,' with frequent, direct feedback loops with leadership (including the CEO) to maintain speed and execution quality.
fundraising_mentions: A lot of the fundraising went directly back into product, engineering, and payment platforms rather than marketing spend.
quotable: You want to go in a market where you don't have competition.
It's a lot better to do one thing but do it really well than doing 10 or 100 things at the same time.

We're like Special Forces. We go in, we don't f*** up. So it had that mentality that every meeting, every design catchup, every marketing campaign, essentially anything you do is perfectly executed at all times at the maximum speed.
one_liner: Revolut's former Head of Growth, Val Scholz, breaks down the strategies behind scaling to 10 million users, emphasizing the power of referral loops, intense hiring standards, and dominating uncontested markets.

title: Homebrew’s Hunter Walk & Satya Patel: Why $100M is Not Enough to Execute a Seed Strategy | 20VC #972
key_insights: For seed funds, a $100M fund is a difficult 'tweener' size; it's better to be larger for significant ownership or smaller for flexibility.
Strong VC partnerships require a shared definition of success, clear roles based on what gives each partner energy, and consensus on the investment thesis from the start.
Switching from institutional LPs to investing personal capital provides maximum flexibility in check size, ownership targets, and strategy, removing the pressure to deploy a fixed fund size.
In a downturn, many companies funded on hype will fail, but it's a great time for new, fundamentally sound companies to be built.
Your fund size dictates your strategy; larger funds implicitly force decisions around ownership and impatience that can sacrifice long-term success for short-term metrics.
fundraising_mentions: Homebrew started pitching their first fund in January 2013.
They decided against raising a larger fund (e.g., $300-400M) which would have required a larger team and different strategy.
They switched to investing their own capital instead of raising a new institutional fund.
Their new model involves check sizes between $100k and $500k without a formal reserve strategy.
The plan is to become self-funding from the carry of their first three funds after an initial two-year period of using personal savings.
Fund I has recycled 117-120% of its capital.
quotable: If it doesn't feel right before you write the check, it definitely doesn't get better after.
Your fund size is your strategy.
one_liner: Homebrew partners Hunter Walk and Satya Patel detail their 10-year journey, the strategic decision to shift from a $100M institutional fund to investing their own capital, and their frameworks for building a lasting partnership and navigating market cycles.

title: DeepSeek Special - How Should OpenAI and the US Government Respond | E1253
key_insights: DeepSeek's model represents a 'Sputnik 2.0' moment, achieving top performance by 'distilling' or scraping data from OpenAI, thus leapfrogging with higher quality data despite lower training costs.

The rise of competitive open-source models like DeepSeek commoditizes the models themselves, shifting the strategic moat for companies like OpenAI towards brand, scale economies, and user trust, rather than just model superiority.
In response to DeepSeek, OpenAI should consider open-sourcing its own models to win user loyalty, as 'open always wins' and the proprietary model advantage is eroding.
The vast majority of future AI compute spend will be on inference, not training (95% vs 5%), a trend explained by Jevons Paradox, where increased efficiency leads to massively increased consumption.
There are significant national security risks with Chinese AI models, as user data can be accessed by the CCP, creating a new, deniable form of international conflict and control.
fundraising_mentions: Groq raised money in late 2024.
OpenAI's rumored $500 billion Stargate project is mentioned as an attempt to build a 'scale economy' moat.
quotable: If I was in [OpenAI's] position, I would be gearing up to open-source my models in response because it's pretty clear you're going to lose that, so you might as well try and win all the users and the love from open sourcing. Open always wins.
The llm is just the printing press of the generative age, it's the start of it.
one_liner: Groq founder Jonathan Ross analyzes the 'Sputnik 2.0' moment of DeepSeek's advanced AI model, discussing its implications for OpenAI, the US-China AI arms race, and why the future of AI competition lies in inference, open-source strategy, and brand.

title: OpenAI Restructuring: Who Wins and Who Loses & Mercor Raises $350M at a $10BN Valuation
guest_role: Partner, Scale Venture Partners & Founder, SaaStr
key_insights: OpenAI's restructuring into a capped-profit entity has resolved major governance issues, paving the way for a potential IPO that could be the most popular retail offering in history, with Microsoft emerging as a significant winner from its early investment.

Venture is increasingly dominated by mega-platforms like Andreessen Horowitz, which leverage scale, media presence, and multi-stage 'optioning' strategies to win deals, shifting the competitive landscape.

The market for human-in-the-loop AI training is experiencing explosive growth, enabling companies like Mercor to achieve hyper-growth, but this success is highly dependent on the continued capex spend of a few concentrated buyers like OpenAI.

For founders of successful late-stage companies like Synthesia, the decision to accept a multi-billion dollar acquisition offer versus aiming for an IPO is a complex choice between a guaranteed outcome and the immense pressure and different skillset required to run a public company.

While headline valuations for late-stage private companies like Ramp are high, the actual returns for early investors can be diluted by frequent, smaller-step-up rounds, highlighting the importance of understanding valuation, dilution, and time (IRR) in assessing fund performance.
fundraising_mentions: OpenAI's post-restructuring raise at valuations ranging from $300B to $500B.
Mercor's $350M raise at a $10B valuation led by Felicis.
Andreessen Horowitz's $10B raise across multiple funds (growth, AI, defense).
Ramp's reported new funding round at a $30B valuation.
Synthesia turned down a $3B acquisition from Adobe to raise a new round at a valuation 'well north of three billion'.
quotable: I just can't think of a retail IPO that would be more popular than OpenAI.
Andre Herds is the red army of the venture industry.
one_liner: A deep dive into OpenAI's landmark restructuring, the dominance of venture mega-funds like a16z, and the strategic dilemmas facing hyper-growth AI companies navigating massive valuations and M&A offers.

title: BIll Ackman wants this CEO to run for President
key_insights: Bill Ackman believes Donald Trump has a strong chance of winning the presidency if he runs against Joe Biden.
Ackman posits that if President Biden runs for re-election, it creates a unique opportunity for a candidate from outside the traditional political system to run on the Democratic ticket.
His preferred candidate is Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, whom he describes as a globally respected and talented business builder who understands economics and geopolitics.
Ackman believes a business leader like Dimon could secure the Democratic nomination and also attract moderate and center-right Republican voters in a general election against Trump.
Ackman expresses a desire for a 'better version of Trump'—a successful business leader—to enter politics and is personally open to the idea himself in the future.
quotable: My favorite version of events is is Jamie Diamond actually.
I'd like a better version of trump A Better Business leader to run for office and and I think they can absolutely get the Democratic nominee.
one_liner: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman advocates for JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon to run for President as a Democrat, arguing that a respected business leader could unite the country and win against Donald Trump.

title: Dave Powers: The Meteoric Rise of Hoka Running | E1098
guest_role: President and CEO of Deckers Brands
key_insights: Hoka's meteoric rise from a $1.1M acquisition in 2012 to a $1.4B brand was fueled by focusing on a niche ultra-runner community first, creating a product they couldn't live without, and letting word-of-mouth drive initial growth.

Ugg's brand decline was caused by over-distribution and losing its 'specialness'; the recovery involved pulling back from the market, repositioning with key influencers, and innovating on the core product to change consumer perception.

The direct-to-consumer (DTC) model is difficult to sustain alone due to high, continuous marketing spend. A healthier model involves a blend with selective wholesale partners who can represent the brand story effectively.
Great brands often originate from solving a specific problem for a niche consumer (e.g., Ugg for surfers, Hoka for ultra-runners). This creates a loyal initial base from which to expand.

Maintaining brand health requires carefully managing the balance between growth and exclusivity. Chasing growth numbers can lead to excess inventory, markdowns, and brand dilution, which is difficult to recover from.
fundraising_mentions: Hoka was acquired for $1.1 million in 2012.
Ugg was acquired for $14.6 million in 1995.
quotable: The DDC model is hard to keep sustained because you're spending so much on marketing the minute you pull that marketing away to make profit your sales lines drops.
Great brands are meaningful and important to their consumer it's almost you want to build a brand that your consumers can't live without.
one_liner: Deckers Brands CEO Dave Powers shares the playbook behind Hoka's explosive growth, the strategic revival of Ugg, and the principles of managing a multi-billion dollar portfolio of iconic consumer brands.

title: Shopify CEO: Remote Work vs In-Person
key_insights: Physical proximity is massively underrated for knowledge transfer (osmosis), especially in small, mentored teams.
The ideal team size is around six people, fostering a collaborative and intellectually diverse environment.
Hybrid work models are often worse than fully remote or fully in-person, as they can create power imbalances and a 'lesser experience' for remote employees.
For scaling companies, going remote can be a strategic necessity to access a global talent pool that cannot be sourced from a single city.
There's a potential 10-20% productivity decline in remote work, but this can be offset by a significant increase in talent density from a wider hiring pool.
In-person work is superior for creative brainstorming and 'wartime' scenarios, while remote work is better for focused, individual 'peacetime' tasks.
quotable: Physical proximity is massively underrated and underappreciated.
Hybrid is worse than remote because hybrid creates concentration concepts... it's actually much more shared experience if everyone's in their own Square on a Zoom call.
If you say yes to something you actually say no to everything else... yeses are way more costly than noes.
one_liner: Shopify's CEO discusses the nuanced trade-offs between in-person and remote work, arguing that while physical proximity is ideal for small, learning-intensive teams, a fully remote setup is superior to hybrid models when scaling a company globally.

title: The Path to Success: Joost de Valk's Story of Turning a Hobby into a Thriving Business
guest_role: Founder of Yoast SEO, SEO Consultant
key_insights: Joost de Valk started the Yoast SEO plugin as a hobby, combining various specific SEO tools he had built.
The plugin addressed a clear user need for a single, comprehensive SEO solution, simplifying technical aspects and providing content feedback.
The transition from hobby to business occurred when the free plugin gained a million users, requiring significant support.
His wife Marika played a pivotal role in the decision to either monetize or stop the project.
Initial monetization through a video SEO add-on quickly surpassed the target of 100K in the first year, demonstrating the business potential.
quotable: "take all the technical stuff away from people and just fix it for them and give them good feedback on their content"
"if I'm gonna make a 100k with this in the first year then it's actually worth continuing doing this"
one_liner: Joost de Valk recounts his journey of transforming the Yoast SEO plugin from a personal hobby into a successful business by focusing on user needs and strategic monetization.

title: Chandra Narayanan: Top 5 Lessons from Leading Analytics at Facebook | E1126
guest_role: Former Head of Analytics at Facebook
key_insights: True impact is defined as moving a key metric, influencing a product decision, or improving a process; anything else is just 'motion' without progress.

A world-class team is built on high 'impact per capita,' hiring slowly to maintain a high talent bar, and ensuring people love what they do, who they work with, learn from their peers, and see the company succeeding.
Effective decision-making requires forming a hypothesis, deeply understanding the story behind the data, and rigorously testing that hypothesis against the data, iterating between the two.
The most critical skill for senior leaders is the ability to simplify complex problems, which demonstrates clarity of thought and a first-principles approach.
In hiring, prioritize 'slope' (a candidate's growth potential) over 'asymptote' (their current level of accomplishment), as compounding growth is more valuable long-term.
fundraising_mentions: Advises Series A companies on when to make their first growth hire (post-product-market fit).
quotable: You never want to be a quitter... set things right, fix things, and then when you're in a better State of Mind, come back to me.

If you think about why anyone comes to work, four different reasons: one is they love what they do, number two they love the people they work with, number three they feel like they can learn from the people that they work with, and four the company is going up and to the right. If one of these four does not work, they will leave.
one_liner: Former Facebook analytics leader Chandra Narayanan shares his frameworks for driving high-impact growth, building world-class teams, and making data-informed decisions by focusing on 'impact over motion'.

title: Aravind Srinivas:Will Foundation Models Commoditise & Diminishing Returns in Model Performance|E1161
key_insights: Model performance improvement now hinges more on meticulous data curation and algorithmic innovation rather than just brute-forcing with more compute, though scale is still a key advantage for a few top labs.
The next major breakthrough in AI will be 'real reasoning,' where models can iterate on their own outputs and explanations, a capital-intensive race likely to be won by a few well-funded companies.
While mid-tier foundation models are becoming commoditized, the frontier of AI is not. The value lies in the teams and machinery that build the next generation of models, not just the current ones.

The biggest beneficiaries of the commoditization of foundation models will be application-layer companies that build great products, own the user relationship, and can leverage cheaper models to offer premium experiences.

Perplexity's strategy is not to compete in building foundation models but to be the best at the application layer, creating a differentiated 'answer engine' and diversifying revenue through consumer subscriptions, enterprise offerings, and advertising.
fundraising_mentions: Fundraising is described as 'brutal,' despite the perception that AI companies can raise easily.

A majority of the capital spent by Perplexity goes towards compute, which includes paying for APIs (like OpenAI, Anthropic), post-training models, and serving models, but not for training large foundation models from scratch.
The difficulty of competing with the capital and free cash flow of giants like Microsoft is highlighted (mentioning Mistral's funding round was equivalent to ~30 hours of Microsoft's free cash flow).
quotable: Today's models are just giving you the output. Tomorrow's models will start with an output, reason, elicit feedback from the world, go back, improve the reasoning... that is the beginning of real reasoning era.
The biggest beneficiaries of the commoditization of foundation models are the application layer companies.
one_liner: Perplexity AI's CEO Aravind Srinivas discusses the nuanced reality of AI progress, arguing that while mid-tier models are commoditizing, the future lies in application-layer companies that can master data, product, and user experience, rather than competing in the capital-intensive race to build foundation models.

title: How Do All Providers Deal with Anthropic Dependency Risk & Figma IPO Breakdown: Where Does it Price?
key_insights: AI agents like Anthropic's Claude are powerful but inherently untrustworthy as they are optimized to satisfy user requests, posing significant safety and security risks when used in production environments without strict guardrails.

The venture capital seed stage is hyper-competitive due to pressure from Y Combinator and large multi-stage funds, forcing smaller funds to find non-obvious markets or invest extremely early to compete.

Thin-wrapper AI applications face existential platform risk from model providers who may compete directly or cut off access, though massive user traction can provide leverage to de-risk by building proprietary models or securing better contracts.
Figma's initial IPO pricing is likely a conservative starting point to build demand, and the small primary offering reflects its profitability and strong cash position.
The market for 'consensus' investments is fully priced, meaning VCs must identify and invest in opportunities before they become widely recognized to achieve outsized returns.
fundraising_mentions: Cursor is raising at a $28 billion valuation.
Perplexity raised another $100 million at an $18 billion valuation.
Figma's IPO is priced at an approximate $16 billion valuation.
Anthropic is reportedly raising at a $100 billion valuation.
A deal mentioned went from a '$30M on $300M' to '$50M on $500M' valuation.
Rippling's seed round was done at a $35 million valuation.
quotable: The market for consensus is fully priced in and fully discovered.
Anti portfolio regret is the psychological price you have to pay for being in the game because it's literally the emotional tax you pay for being in good deal flow.
one_liner: VCs Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll analyze the dependency risk on AI model providers like Anthropic, the challenges facing seed funds, and the dynamics of the Figma IPO and other high-stakes tech deals.

title: What Does it Take to Be Good at Series A and B Today?
guest: Fabrice Grinda, Rory O'Driscoll, Jason Lemkin
guest_role: Founder at FJ Labs, Partner at Scale Venture Partners, Founder at SaaStr
key_insights: The current venture market is in a tough 'low low quadrant': things are expensive to invest in, and it's a hard time to get money back due to a lack of exits.

The AI sector is an intense 'gold rush', attracting massive capital but also creating extreme competition, high valuations for pre-product-market-fit companies, and significant platform risk from incumbents like OpenAI.

For long-term returns, maximizing the fund multiple (e.g., aiming for 3x+) is more critical than optimizing for the highest possible IRR, as long as the IRR remains above a healthy threshold (e.g., 20-25%).

The extended time-to-IPO means the technology lifecycle to obsolescence can be shorter than the private holding period, forcing companies to face an existential 'reinvent itself' crisis before they can exit.

Investing in different geographies carries significant, and changing, geopolitical risks (e.g., China), while also presenting opportunities in talent arbitrage (Europe) and emerging sectors (Ukrainian defense tech).
fundraising_mentions: Manis raised 75 million led by Benchmark.
A quarter of a billion dollar SPV into open AI at 300 billion valuation.
A guest's 2017 fund is at 4.31x with a 32.56 IRR.
An unnamed guest's portfolio company closed a unicorn round on April 7th.
quotable: The problem with series B is if you get it wrong, you end up effectively paying series B prices for series A risk. And it's exactly correct. Now, at the A, you're paying series A prices for seed risk. But the whole point of having to be good at this job is being able to figure out which is which.

My number one fear is that the technology life cycle to obsolescence is now shorter than the holding period of privately held software companies, which means every company at least one time before it gets to go public will have an existential reinvent itself second product crisis.
one_liner: Three veteran venture capitalists—Fabrice Grinda, Rory O'Driscoll, and Jason Lemkin—offer a masterclass on navigating today's tough market, debating the AI gold rush, the tension between IRR and multiples, long liquidity cycles, and the shifting geopolitical landscape for tech investing.

title: Financial analysis of Allbirds, Hims, and Warby Parker
key_insights: Allbirds raised $202M but has a market cap of only $183M.

The speaker suggests that venture capitalists have likely lost significant amounts of money investing in the D2C sector.

Warby Parker raised $530 million.

your question was whether d2c people have lost a lot of money in d2c and I honestly I think so
one_liner: An analysis of the financial performance of major D2C brands like Allbirds, Hims, and Warby Parker, questioning the overall profitability and return on investment for VCs in the sector.

title: 20VC: What is Analytics Debt and How Founders Can Build the Right Data Foundations
key_insights: Analytics debt is defined by the excessive difficulty or cost required to answer basic questions about business performance, such as user cohort retention.
A key indicator of analytics debt is the need for custom, time-consuming queries (e.g., taking several days) to answer straightforward business questions.
Simply implementing a visualization tool like Mixpanel or Google Analytics is not enough; without proper data collection, these tools are ineffective ('garbage in, garbage out').
Poor instrumentation—failing to capture and log key user events within the product (e.g., 'add to cart' in e-commerce)—is a primary cause of unreliable analytics.
Establishing a strong lens on product usage through correct event logging is a prerequisite for a company to begin effectively working on growth.
quotable: A good indicator of analytics debt is if I come in and ask a very basic question... and... they're being a really high cost to go answer those questions, like someone needs to go do a custom query of the database and it takes a few days.
The reality is, you know, garbage in, garbage out. I think poor instrumentation of a product is actually a very common problem here.
one_liner: An expert defines 'analytics debt' as the high cost of answering basic business questions and advises founders that proper product instrumentation is the essential foundation for growth, not just the implementation of visualization tools.

title: Karri Saarinen: How to Grow Capital Efficiently in a World of BS Growth | E1221
key_insights: Prioritize 'quality growth' based on a superior product over artificially juiced hypergrowth, even if it means slower, more sustainable progress.
Achieving profitability early gives founders the ultimate leverage in fundraising, as it removes the need to raise capital.
Founders should remain deeply involved in the product details ('on the field') to maintain high-quality standards, especially in the early stages.
When hiring, look for a deep sense of 'craft' and passion for the work, not just credentials. Hiring slowly and deliberately for the right fit is crucial.
Be skeptical of standard VC playbooks, such as premature leadership hires or creating dishonest competitor comparison charts.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a ~$30M Series B.
Prefers dilution around 10% or less, rather than the standard 20%.
Raised Seed and Series A from Sequoia.
Used a short, curated list of ~5 investors for fundraising processes.
Gives VCs 'homework' with questions to simulate the working relationship.
quotable: The only real protection you can have as a startup founder in your business is to be successful.
The growth is coming from the fact that you go to the gym and that that's more sustainable than than using steroids.
one_liner: Linear founder Karri Saarinen shares his counter-intuitive approach to building a successful SaaS company by focusing on sustainable 'quality growth', achieving profitability, maintaining an exceptionally high bar for product quality, and retaining leverage in fundraising.

title: Mamoon Hamid: AI - Where Value Accrues, Startups vs Incumbents & Scaling Laws | E1217
key_insights: The current AI super cycle is reminiscent of the 1997 internet boom but multiplied by ten, presenting a massive tidal wave of change.
Significant value in AI will be captured at the application layer, particularly by creating 'co-pilots' that supercharge scarce, highly-skilled professionals like doctors, lawyers, and developers.
Despite extreme valuations and market entropy, the fundamentals of venture capital remain unchanged: backing incredible people in the right markets at the right time.
The rapid revenue scaling in AI is driven by software replacing labor, justifying much higher price points ($300-500/month per seat) compared to traditional SaaS.
The most successful companies often create their own markets (e.g., Slack, Figma), allowing them to define the playing field and win the game.

Kleiner Perkins operates as a 'boutique' firm with a small, focused team, believing that the craft of venture capital doesn't scale with more people, even while managing significant capital across early and growth funds.
Founder conviction is paramount in decision-making; Kleiner Perkins avoids formal voting structures, allowing partners to back their individual conviction on deals.
fundraising_mentions: Figma's investment was made at a ~$100M post-money valuation.
Slack's investment was made at a $250M post-money valuation with only $500K in ARR.
Glean's seed round was $15M at a $35M post-money valuation.
Box required multiple bridge rounds at a $25M valuation during the 2008-2009 financial crisis.
A seed investment of $3M for 30% of a company sold for $700M, yielding a 70x multiple but a 15% IRR over 15 years.
A loss of $30M was incurred on the investment in Tally.
quotable: I love products that create markets. Slack created a market, Figma created a market. They get to create the playing field they play on, the playing field and they win the game.
It is the most exciting time to be alive. We're in the midst of a super cycle like none we've seen before, the AI super cycle.
one_liner: Mamoon Hamid of Kleiner Perkins discusses his investment thesis for the AI super cycle, focusing on application-layer companies that create new markets, and shares his insights on venture strategy, valuation, and navigating market shifts from his experience with iconic companies like Figma and Slack.

title: Cohere's Chief AI Officer, Joelle Pineau: Why Scaling Laws Will Continue & Future of Synthetic Data
key_insights: Scaling laws for compute and data have proven remarkably robust, but algorithmic innovations are the source of non-linear, step-function progress.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is fundamentally inefficient due to compounding errors and the need for expensive simulation environments, making it difficult to apply to tasks without clearly defined goals.
The true value of AI in the enterprise is not replacing the workforce, but augmenting employees to be 10x more productive.
The future of AI security will involve tackling agent impersonation, where AI agents illegitimately act on behalf of entities they don't represent.

Synthetic data generation faces the risk of model degradation due to a loss of diversity, similar to a shrinking gene pool, except in structured domains like code where diversity can be artificially injected.
fundraising_mentions: Hypothetical question asked about what the guest would do with a $10 billion investment.
Interviewer mentions a different company (Mistral AI) raising 'two billion out of 10 billion'.
quotable: I don't have a lot of patience as a scientist for people who are predicting the extremist scenarios...the catastrophic risks of AI, you know, AI becomes our overlord kind of scenario.
I used to be quite skeptical that neural networks were necessarily the ultimate solution to machine learning. I'd seen enough cycles... I seem to be quite wrong on this one.
one_liner: Cohere's Chief Scientist Joelle Pineau breaks down why AI scaling laws will continue, the fundamental inefficiencies of reinforcement learning, the future of AI in the enterprise as a productivity tool rather than a replacement, and the challenges of synthetic data and agent security.

title: From Romania to Partner at top VC firm! 😲

Transition from Investment Banking into the European Venture Capital industry.
The significance of working with impactful Founders in shaping the European venture landscape.
Joining Sequoia due to its thoughtful approach to new geographies.

one_liner: This episode details a Romanian immigrant's career journey from securing a scholarship to Georgetown and working in Investment Banking, to becoming a Partner at Sequoia, contributing to the European Venture industry.

title: Tips for Giving Negative Feedback | Peloton CEO Barry McCarthy
key_insights: Delivering tough feedback effectively requires adapting your communication style to the recipient's personality or 'frequency'.
Having a lower EQ can sometimes make it easier to ask direct, hard-hitting questions without being confrontational.
The skill set for giving a CEO negative feedback is the same as an employee needs to communicate effectively with their boss.
To ensure feedback is received well, you must check your ego and intellect at the door.
It's crucial to find a way to communicate with a CEO, especially a founder, in a manner they can absorb and act upon.
quotable: To be interpersonally effective you have to find frequency, you need to find a voice and the way of communicating with the CEO... in a way they're able to take it on board.

Get your like check your ego at the door and your intellect if necessary and you know find the interpersonal skills required to to say it in a way that makes it accessible to the people or the person you're saying it to.
one_liner: Peloton CEO Barry McCarthy shares his framework for delivering difficult feedback, emphasizing the importance of adapting your communication style to the individual you are addressing.

title: How to Hire Salespeople | Sales Tips from Maggie Hott
key_insights: Always hire sellers in groups of 2-4, as it's not much more work to train a group than an individual and they provide mutual support.
The two most important traits for early-stage sales hires are the ability to deal with ambiguity and thrive in chaos.
To test for ambiguity, ask candidates for specific examples of how they handled process changes and what impact they had.
Instead of asking candidates to demo your product in a final interview, have them pitch something they are passionate about to evaluate their enthusiasm and ability to explain concepts.
A mock discovery call is more valuable than a product demo; it allows you to assess a candidate's research, curiosity, and, most importantly, their coachability by providing live feedback.
quotable: If you are not okay with ambiguity meaning things are going to change every day every week every quarter if you need stability this is not the place for you.
A hiring mistake can cost a company to the tune of one million dollars.
one_liner: Maggie Hott shares her framework for hiring early-stage salespeople, emphasizing the importance of hiring in groups, screening for ambiguity tolerance, and using a mock discovery call to assess coachability.

title: The Dark Side of Your Hamburger: Uncovering the Meat Industry's Secrets
key_insights: The modern meat industry is fundamentally broken, causing immense suffering to animals, the environment, and farmers.
While agreeing with vegans on the problem, the solution proposed is to reform the industry for the majority who still eat meat, rather than advocating for universal veganism.
There's a critical lack of oversight for worker welfare in meat processing facilities, unlike other industries where third-party audits (like Fair Trade) are standard.

ButcherBox's brand identity is modeled after Patagonia, aiming to represent a brand that obsesses over every ethical detail in its supply chain, from animal and worker welfare to environmental impact.

The average consumer is highly disconnected from meat production, spending only seconds making a purchase decision and lacking awareness or concern for the systemic issues, including the welfare of workers in the supply chain.
quotable: I call it like the Patagonia of me[at]: like we want you when you buy from butcherbox to know that we obsessed over every detail possible for that piece of meat to make sure I had the best life the farmer was treated the best the environment was treated the best.
If I was creating t-shirts in Bangladesh I could have fair trade in there like again in a very short amount of time and why well because nobody wants to open that door and see what's behind it.
one_liner: ButcherBox Founder Mike Salguero discusses the deep-seated ethical, environmental, and labor issues within the meat industry and explains his mission to build a transparent, high-welfare alternative for consumers.

title: MTV's Origin Story 📖
key_insights: MTV's initial branding strategy was to position itself as a rebellious alternative to traditional TV.
The speaker's personal experience as an outsider, due to losing an eye and frequent moves, cultivated a strong ability to understand and 'read' people.
This 'outsider' perspective was a valuable skill for identifying effective and impactful messages and slogans.
The speaker considers themselves a skilled editor for recognizing powerful phrases.
The slogan 'I Want My MTV' was identified as a highly successful and memorable branding message.
quotable: at MTV we were trying to convey the image of we were not TV we were throwing TV out we were spitting on TV we're the new TV we're the Rebellion

title: Eleanor Dorfman: How We Scaled Retool to $50M ARR; Red Flags for Sales Hires | 20VC #925
key_insights: Founders should generate the inputs for a sales playbook (understanding how customers want to buy) but hire a sales leader to create the actual playbook.
A blend of product-led growth (PLG) and enterprise sales can be effective, especially from $0-100M ARR, before needing to specialize in one motion.
When hiring early sales talent, prioritize adaptable 'street fighters' over those from large incumbents, as they thrive in ambiguity and help build the playbook.
When selling a platform with open-ended use cases and no single buyer, focus on highly personalized, vertical-specific outbound based on problems you solve.
A customer success background provides a massive advantage for sales leadership, fostering a holistic view of the customer lifecycle and enabling you to 'see around corners'.
Invest in foundational roles like sales enablement and RevOps earlier than you think you need them to avoid accumulating significant process debt.
Structure the sales hiring process to test for un-teachable traits you must 'buy' (like IQ, EQ, character, curiosity) versus skills you can 'build' (product knowledge, sales process).

Sales is there to accelerate a healthy machine, but it can’t fix a broken one.
one_liner: Retool's Sales Leader Eleanor Dorfman shares her playbook on scaling a sales organization, blending PLG and enterprise motions, hiring 'street fighter' talent, and the importance of founder-led sales in the early days.

title: The Biggest Mistakes Founders Make When Hiring for Growth
key_insights: When hiring for growth, prioritize senior candidates with a proven track record ('signs of excellence') and use trusted back-channel references.
Standalone growth teams can be highly effective, but their success hinges on a very tight, collaborative relationship with the product and marketing teams.
A key interview question to vet growth candidates is 'Tell me something I don't know about growth,' to assess the depth of their understanding beyond surface-level tactics.
The biggest mistake founders make when hiring growth teams is misjudging talent due to a small talent pool and misleading signals like social media presence.
The ability to move from a high-level vision to granular details is a critical skill for a growth leader, but it must be done in a way that empowers, rather than deflates, the team.

title: 3 Tips for Board Members
key_insights: Effective board members surgically add value on topics they are qualified to opine on, rather than trying to micromanage areas like product design.
Founders should be highly selective when choosing investors and board members, as it's a critical long-term relationship.
The primary misalignment between VCs and founders is that VCs manage a portfolio and can favor riskier, high-upside paths, whereas a founder has only one company.
Great board members, like Alfred Lin, are thoughtful, do their homework, and provide unique insights without dominating the conversation.
New board members should learn by observing how seasoned members add value and model their behavior.

title: The Current State of Venture Capital
key_insights: The venture capital market has significantly tightened, with investors requiring higher performance and capital efficiency from startups.
The 'Postmates effect' (multiple billion-dollar winners in a single category) is less prevalent today, emphasizing the need for competitive differentiation.
Founders must demonstrate strong conviction and a clear strategy for winning against competitors, as 'why will you win' questions are crucial again.
SaaS companies are expected to achieve $100-$200 million in ARR within 7-10 years to be considered IPO-ready.
The total capital a startup can raise has reset to around $100 million, requiring founders to be more capital-efficient than in the peak years.

title: Shopify President, Harley Finkelstein on What is Being a Good Husband | Full Interview
key_insights: Entrepreneurship can be a powerful tool for overcoming personal and financial setbacks, providing a path to survival and independence.
Vulnerability and authenticity, such as discussing anxiety, can make leaders more approachable and foster stronger connections with their team.
The rate of personal learning for a leader must be equal to or greater than the rate of change in their company to remain effective.
In relationships, proactively asking whether your partner needs you to listen or to help solve a problem can dramatically improve communication and dynamics.
Strong professional partnerships, like the one between Harley and Toby, are built on deep mutual respect, complementary skill sets (being 'spiky'), and genuinely enjoying the work together.

key_insights: Raising initial capital for a new fund requires persistence and numerous pitches.
Targeting established wealthy individuals for relatively small investment amounts proved effective for early-stage funds.
A strong personal conviction and 'track record of life success' can outweigh a lack of direct investment experience for convincing early investors.
Demonstrating successful investment ideas independently can persuade reluctant investors to join the fund.

title: #1 Mistake to Avoid When Picking Your Co-Founder
key_insights: Choosing co-founders who are too similar to yourself can lead to destructive infighting over control and responsibilities.
Optimal co-founder relationships are like a Venn diagram with minimal overlap, ensuring each person covers a distinct and large part of the company's problem space.
Complementary skill sets are more critical for a founding team's success than pre-existing deep friendships.
Founders should have deep self-awareness of their own strengths and weaknesses to intentionally select partners who fill their gaps.
Clear separation of roles and responsibilities ('lanes') from the start fosters stability and allows the company to scale effectively.
quotable: The fundamental reason we were fighting is that... we were the same person.

It's like a vend diagram where you want circles that have a tiny bit of overlap so that there's there's some ability for the people involved to relate to one another but ideally each of those circles has a ton of space covering the problem area to do that.

title: Flexport CEO Ryan Peterson debunks the old adage that "speed of execution is everything"
key_insights: Velocity (speed in the right direction) is more important than mere speed for startup success.
Agility and the ability to change direction quickly are critical, especially in chaotic markets like logistics.
Bezos's concept of 'one-way door' (irreversible) vs. 'two-way door' (reversible) decisions guides the speed of action.
Decisions involving significant capital or key hires are often 'one-way doors' requiring careful judgment.
Authentic values are demonstrated by actions, particularly in how a company responds to mistakes and maintains customer relationships.
quotable: I don't think speed is the most important thing, I think it's velocity and if you remember your physics velocity has a vector it's speed in the right direction.
Your values don't really count unless you're willing to give up money for it otherwise it's just word on the wall.
one_liner: Flexport CEO Ryan Peterson redefines startup success by prioritizing velocity and agile decision-making, stressing that true company values are proven by action and navigating irreversible choices with care.

key_insights: Effective storytelling is crucial for successful fundraising and communicating business ideas.
Stories must evoke feeling and empathy, allowing the audience to see themselves in the narrative.
Simplifying complex business concepts into relatable, understandable stories is more impactful than relying solely on numbers.
A good story can make a business idea accessible and clear even to a layperson.
Without an empathetic narrative, quantitative data often fails to capture attention or secure investment.

title: Why Valuations and Fundraising are BS
key_insights: The venture capital 'power law' model creates a fundamental conflict of interest between VCs, who need multi-billion dollar exits, and founders, for whom a smaller outcome can be life-changing.
For enterprise SaaS, high gross retention is the single most important metric, indicating a sticky, durable business that can compound steadily over time, even without hyper-growth.
In vertical SaaS, expanding to a multi-product suite is critical to increase average selling prices (ASPs) and make the economics of an expensive enterprise sales motion viable.
Counter-intuitively, shrinking your Total Addressable Market (TAM) to intensely focus on a specific Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) can accelerate growth by improving focus and ROI.
M&A can be a powerful form of innovation, allowing a company to acquire years of product discovery and subject matter expertise, not just revenue or customers.

The $1.8B deal was structured so that management rolled over a majority of their stake, with defined liquidity options in years 3, 4, and 5.
quotable: Your business runs on a power law. Your business is about finding the next coinbase... OpenGov has been quite successful but it doesn't move the needle. It's a couple billion dollar type exit that's not what you're in the game for.
I got tricked into thinking it was 1999, you're going to sell it for loss and make it up on volume.

title: Jason Lemkin: PluralSight S*** the Bed & The Next IPO Candidates | E1160
key_insights: The SaaS market is bifurcated: B2B to Consumer/non-tech businesses (e.g., Canva, Toast, Samsara) is growing strong, while B2B to tech companies (e.g., Salesforce) is struggling with budget cuts and slowing growth.

Salesforce's drop to single-digit growth is a significant market signal, indicating that even market leaders are struggling with smaller deal sizes and seat reductions, challenging the long-held belief that high NRR would guarantee durable growth.

The massive $3.5B write-down of Pluralsight by Vista Equity signals major stress in the private equity playbook of using heavy debt to acquire SaaS companies, potentially reducing a key liquidity path for startups.
AI spending is currently a substitution game, not a net-new budget. Companies are churning multiple existing applications to fund one new AI tool, creating churn pressure on incumbent SaaS vendors.

There is a severe liquidity crisis in venture capital, with only two major SaaS IPOs since 2021 and public multiples compressing to ~6x ARR, making it difficult for VCs to generate returns on later-stage investments.

I took LP's money too seriously... I genuinely think it's a bad thing.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin discusses the challenging state of the B2B SaaS market, highlighting the fallout from Pluralsight's failure, Salesforce's slowing growth, the illusion of AI budgets, and the resulting liquidity crisis for venture-backed companies.

title: Silicon Valley is Stronger than Ever
key_insights: Contrary to popular belief, Silicon Valley is not dead; it's being revitalized.
Massive tech layoffs are fueling a new generation of entrepreneurs and innovative startups.
There's a cultural reset in the startup world, moving away from entitlement and back to core principles of hard work, customer acquisition, and product development.
A recessionary environment is seen as a necessary corrective for the excesses that developed during the long bull market.
The fundamental drivers of Silicon Valley's network and creative energy remain intact and are adapting to the new economic reality.

key_insights: A CEO's four primary jobs are hiring the management team, setting the company vision, defining the culture, and allocating resources.
The biggest mistakes in a large company are often of omission (not pursuing opportunities aggressively enough) rather than commission (doing the wrong thing).
When fundraising, using a 'one-shot, closed envelope bidding' process can force VCs to offer their best price upfront and avoid collusion, potentially leading to an outlier valuation.
Intentional, periodic in-person gatherings can boost team connectivity by 30% for 4-5 months, suggesting that a fully remote team can maintain high connectedness without daily office attendance.

The decision to shut down a major product (like Stride) becomes easier when framed by the question: 'Can I look my staff in the face and say the next 5 years of their life will have the biggest impact to humanity working on this?'

Luck can be engineered through 'engineered serendipity'—the macro result of thousands of micro-actions that increase your surface area for opportunities.
To grow an audience, you must first create value for people, and in return, you will receive value in the form of their attention.
True high performance as a creative requires taking care of your full self, not just working the maximum number of hours.
Consistency is a powerful advantage; it's very difficult to keep someone down if they just keep showing up relentlessly.

Exploding term sheets are a contentious tactic; building a strong, trusted partnership with a founder is more valuable than forcing a quick decision.

When evaluating founding teams, the 'spikiness' or exceptional, standout quality of the single best founder is often the most critical indicator of success, more so than the combined skills of the whole team.

title: Are VCs to Blame for SVB Collapse? 🏦🧐
key_insights: The VC community is being blamed for the SVB collapse, but the speaker questions the fairness of this singular blame.
Companies, especially public ones, acted reasonably in protecting their assets by pulling capital, as fiduciaries are obligated to make strategic decisions during potential bank failures.
It would be negligent for a public company board to 'do nothing' when facing the risk of a bank failure.
Many companies made significant mistakes in their own risk assessment by concentrating all their capital, including payroll, at SVB without alternative systems.
The situation escalated rapidly once the instability of SVB was perceived, acting as a 'Powder Keg' for mass withdrawals.
quotable: any one person can protect themselves and I can't imagine everyone sitting there saying let's just sit here and do nothing as a risk assessment
a lot of companies made a lot of mistakes about their own assessment of risk
one_liner: This segment discusses whether VCs are solely to blame for the SVB collapse, arguing that companies' defensive capital withdrawals were rational fiduciary actions, while many firms also exhibited poor individual risk assessment by over-relying on SVB.

title: How to Hire for Diversity
key_insights: To hire diverse candidates, you must first get them into your pipeline by making your company and its policies genuinely attractive to them.

Founders should actively combat unconscious bias by diversifying their sourcing channels beyond personal networks, using different recruiters, or leveraging communities focused on underrepresented talent.

Winning over diverse candidates requires more than abstract commitments; it requires having women in leadership and demonstrating concrete inclusive policies like parental leave and mentorship programs.
The experience of being a 'token woman' is discouraging; true inclusion involves actively setting up employees for success and ensuring they can thrive within the company.
Venture capitalists should focus on serving founders and their missions, regardless of the founder's gender or background, rather than serving their own egos.

title: "Man Plans, God Laughs," How to Prepare Your Business for Unpredictability
key_insights: Traditional business plans are often ineffective because the future is unforeseeable and businesses frequently pivot.
Entrepreneurs should instead create a three-year personal vision focusing on their desired lifestyle, and align the business to that vision.
Even if the scale of the business drastically changes from the original vision (e.g., a hobby business becoming a $100M+ company), the core principles of that vision can guide crucial decisions.
The choice between bootstrapping and raising venture capital leads to different strategic decisions, such as outsourcing key functions for bootstrapped companies.
Many aspiring entrepreneurs are fundamentally chasing a desired lifestyle rather than a specific business model.

title: Ryan Petersen: Why Velocity not Speed is Most Important in Company Building | E1081
key_insights: Velocity (speed in the right direction) is more important than raw speed. It's sometimes better to stop and reorient than to move quickly in the wrong direction.
In logistics, almost all inefficiency stems from bad quality. Focusing on quality (e.g., on-time performance, data accuracy) ultimately leads to lower costs and higher efficiency.
Raising too much money can lead to a loss of discipline and imprudent spending. A hiring freeze after a large round can help instill discipline.
Promoting from within is generally lower risk and better for culture than hiring senior executives externally.
A company's culture should be built on purpose, trust, and a willingness to have open, critical conversations, even with leadership.
Trade is an innate human activity that will likely continue to grow globally despite geopolitical tensions, driven by the benefits of specialization.

Venture capital is increasingly characterized by 'kingmaking' through massive, rapid-fire funding rounds for infrastructure companies in obvious, developer-led trends (e.g., Vercel, Supabase).
Late-stage companies with decelerating growth face a tough path to IPO, making PE buyouts or strategic consolidation more likely outcomes, though PE interest is currently muted.

title: Why It Is Harder To Give Money Away Than It Is To Make It 💸
key_insights: Measuring the impact of philanthropy is difficult because, unlike a business, there are only costs and no revenue or profit to create a clear 'report card' of success.
The ambiguity in defining and measuring success in the non-profit world makes it challenging to allocate resources effectively.
While businesses are governed by the clarity of an income statement (P&L), philanthropy lacks equivalent universal metrics, making it hard to determine if efforts are 'enough' or successful.
The challenge lies in establishing measurement points for success, such as determining the necessary scale of impact or the required success rate of portfolio initiatives.

Before committing more resources to philanthropic efforts, one must grapple with the complexities of measuring intangible outcomes, which is a significantly more complicated task than in the for-profit sector.
quotable: When you do a budget for your foundation you only have cost. How do you measure, how do you really measure your impact?

You are ruled by the P&L, by your income statement, and we love that. It's clear, it's your report card. Are you winning? Are you losing? Do you need to change things? In philanthropy, you can change one community... is that enough?
one_liner: Orlando Bravo explains that philanthropy is harder than making money because it lacks the clear financial metrics of a business, making it incredibly difficult to measure impact and define success.
