one_liner: A critical look at the D2C space, questioning the profitability and venture returns of well-funded brands like Allbirds and Warby Parker.

title: Roundtable #7: Spotify, Adobe and Linkedin on How AI Changes The Future of Product & Design | E1097
guest: Scott Belsky, Gustav Söderström, Tomer Cohen
guest_role: Chief Strategy Officer at Adobe, Co-President at Spotify, Chief Product Officer at LinkedIn
topics: Product Leadership in the AI Era
key_insights: AI is fundamentally shifting from being a tool that supports the UI to being the core product itself, with the UI designed to serve the AI and capture better signals.
Product leaders must embrace a shift from deterministic to probabilistic experiences, letting go of complete control over the final user experience, which is a major mindset change.
The future of AI in products will likely consist of many specialized, cost-efficient models rather than a few mega-models, requiring intelligent routing to select the right model for each task.

Data is the most critical asset ('oxygen') for AI. Product leaders must prioritize high-quality data collection and understand its direct impact on the algorithm's performance, rather than delegating it.

AI is set to disrupt traditional business models, moving away from seat-based pricing to value-based models that charge for work done or efficiency created, fundamentally changing how software is bought and sold.
quotable: AI is the product and the UI is there to help the AI to capture better signal.
When you think in an AI first principled kind of way, you're really unleashing the idea of control. What happens basically in AI is you don't control the experience anymore.
one_liner: Product leaders from Adobe, LinkedIn, and Spotify discuss how AI is reshaping product development, from embracing probabilistic UIs and specialized models to the critical need for a data-first mindset and new value-based business models.

title: Why Did SVB Collapse?
key_insights: SVB's collapse was precipitated by its massive investment (over $90B) in long-dated securities at near-zero interest rates, a huge bet on rates staying low.
By classifying these assets as 'held-to-maturity,' SVB avoided mark-to-market accounting, which concealed a $15 billion unrealized loss as interest rates began to rise.
The bank's depositor base was heavily concentrated in the hyper-connected tech and VC community, which enabled a rapid, large-scale, and coordinated withdrawal of funds (a bank run).
A public announcement of an attempt to raise $2B in capital, before the deal was secured, backfired and created widespread panic among depositors, directly triggering the run on the bank.

The situation highlighted a broader systemic risk, with the FDIC reporting $620 billion in unrealized losses across the US banking system in Q4 2022, indicating other banks could be vulnerable to similar pressures.
fundraising_mentions: SVB invested over $90 billion in long-dated securities.
SVB attempted a last-minute $2 billion capital raise that failed.
The capital raise announcement included a $500 million commitment from General Atlantic.
quotable: No one wants to be the last man standing in that bank with your deposits as the FDIC shows up in an illiquid situation.
They should have raised the money, made the announcement that they raised the money and that they were in great position.
one_liner: SVB's collapse was caused by a combination of a massive, risky bet on long-term bonds, rising interest rates that created huge unrealized losses, and a panic-induced bank run from its highly-concentrated tech depositor base following a fumbled capital raise announcement.

title: Jackie Reses & Kris Dickson: What Happened with SVB? Are VCs to Blame? | E988
guest_role: Chairman and CEO of Lead Bank; CFO of Lead Bank
key_insights: SVB's failure was caused by a massive bet on long-dated securities ($90B+ with maturities >10 years) at a time of near-zero interest rates. When the Fed aggressively hiked rates, this created a massive unrealized loss ($15B) that exceeded their market cap.

The bank's deposit base was heavily concentrated in the hyper-connected VC/tech ecosystem. This concentration, combined with modern communication (social media) and electronic banking, enabled an unprecedentedly fast bank run, with $40 billion in withdrawal requests in a single day.

A critical strategic mistake was SVB announcing their need to raise capital ($2B) before it was secured. This signaled distress and triggered panic among depositors, directly causing the run on the bank.

While VCs telling their companies to pull funds accelerated the collapse, it was a rational fiduciary action to protect their investments against a non-zero risk of failure, rather than a malicious attack.

The best-case outcome is a weekend acquisition of SVB by another large bank (like JPM, PNC), which would make all depositors whole and restore confidence. The worst-case involves a protracted FDIC liquidation, where depositors receive their insured $250k plus an 'advance dividend' from liquid assets, but have to wait for the rest.
fundraising_mentions: SVB announced they were doing a $500 million capital raise with General Atlantic and a market offering to fill a $1.5 billion hole.
SVB unsuccessfully tried to fill a capital hole with a last-minute $2 billion capital raise.
quotable: There are tons of rumors out there. There are three groups of people who know what's happening: the FDIC, the folks at svb, and at the banks, the people who are buying and looking at the assets of these companies. I can't imagine any of those three people are sitting on Twitter and WhatsApp rumor mongering about what is happening.
No one wants to be the last man standing in that bank with your deposits as the FDIC shows up in an illiquid situation.
one_liner: Banking experts Jackie Reses and Kris Dickson break down the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, attributing it to a combination of a massive bad bet on interest rates, a hyper-concentrated depositor base, and a fatal PR error that triggered a historic bank run.

title: Bob Pittman: How I Went from Creator of MTV to CEO of iHeartMedia
key_insights: True innovation and market insight come from being wildly observant and curious, and identifying unique epiphanies rather than following groupthink. If everyone agrees on an idea, it's likely a bad one.

Effective leadership involves rapid decision-making and accepting that you'll be wrong most of the time. The key is to quickly change course and kill ideas that are not clear winners, not just the clear losers.

In consumer products and services, convenience is the single most important factor, consistently winning over quality. This principle drove strategies at AOL ('so easy to use') and Six Flags ('closer to home').

A sustainable business must have a clear and simple path to profitability (the 'back of an envelope' test). Metrics like 'eyeballs' or revenue growth are meaningless without a realistic plan for turning them into earnings.

Success and failure are functionally the same; they are both just stepping stones on a continuous journey. Don't keep a ledger of wins and losses, but rather use every outcome as an opportunity to learn and adjust.
quotable: If you're going to get it wrong most of the time, then what goes along with that is quick decisions. Because when you get it wrong, admit it you made it wrong and change it. And change it quickly.
Convenience beats quality... if quality won, everyone would still have a wired line instead of a mobile phone because the quality is a lot better.
one_liner: Bob Pittman, the creator of MTV and CEO of iHeartMedia, shares his core philosophies on building iconic consumer brands through relentless focus, embracing convenience over quality, and a leadership style rooted in rapid decision-making and learning from both successes and failures.

title: How We Scaled Facebook to 1 Billion Users
key_insights: Growth accounting (registrations + resurrections - churn) reveals that reducing churn and increasing resurrections are often larger levers for growth than new user acquisition.
Focusing on user retention over pure acquisition is a critical strategic shift for sustainable growth.
Identifying the core user actions that strongly correlate with long-term retention (like connecting with friends on Facebook or placing a bid on eBay) is key.
Optimize user onboarding to guide new users towards the core actions that lead to retention, even if it means lower initial registration numbers.
A data-inspired growth model is essential for understanding the true drivers of growth and making informed product and marketing decisions.
quotable: Retention is King.
The Churn number and the resurrection number were massively bigger than the registration number and so we hadn't realized how big a lever reducing churn and resurrecting people to the site was.
one_liner: Facebook's former CMO, Alex Schultz, explains the critical shift from an acquisition-focused strategy to a retention-based one, driven by data and growth accounting, which was instrumental in scaling the platform to one billion users.

title: CATHIE WOOD: Is now the time to buy $META?
key_insights: Mark Zuckerberg might be investing in the metaverse before its time.
Zoom can be considered a form of the metaverse.
Facebook (Meta) shows astonishing user engagement with 67% daily over monthly active users.
Facebook (Meta) is becoming a potential value stock.
TikTok is identified as a 'two trillion dollar power course'.
quotable: I think that Mark Zuckerberg probably investing in an idea before it's time.
I think tick tock's the two trillion dollar power course.
one_liner: Cathie Wood analyzes Meta's metaverse strategy, its surprising user engagement, and its potential as a value stock, while also noting TikTok's significant market power.

title: Hussein Kanji, Founder @Hoxton Ventures: Why AI Means London Can Compete with the US | E1248
key_insights: The European venture ecosystem has matured, but many funds still focus on momentum and markups rather than building long-term, category-defining companies.

There is a direct correlation between the amount of capital a company raises and its probability of success, with an average of ~$300M needed to reach unicorn status, making the larger US funding rounds a critical advantage.

When raising a new fund, managers should optimize for time (e.g., a 90-day sprint) rather than a specific fund size; it's better to secure initial capital, start investing, and then go back to the market with proven traction.
AI represents a horizontal, seismic shift where, for the first time, Europe is on par with the US in core technology creation, presenting a massive opportunity for local investors and founders.
As a seed investor, being contrarian is necessary, but the market must recognize your vision within a 1-2 year timeframe for your companies to get follow-on funding and succeed.
fundraising_mentions: Hoxton's Fund 1 ($28M) took 39 months to raise.
Hoxton's Fund 2 ($89M) took 28 months to raise after losing an anchor commitment due to Brexit.
Mike Maples' advice: 'do not do a fund raise for size of the fund do a fund raise for time of the fund'.
Deliveroo's first round was a £3M round led by Index Ventures.
Darktrace raised a $40M Series C at a $400M post-money valuation from KKR.
The average capital raised to get to unicorn status is about $300 million.
quotable: The world does not need yet another fund... there are not that many old-fashioned Venture funds left in this industry. I think most of us become momentum investors... we write the check largely to get the next markup not to build the long-term durable big company of tomorrow.
There is a correlation between how much money goes in to a company and what the probability of success is... your best path to scale from a financing perspective is America.
one_liner: Hoxton Ventures founder Hussein Kanji argues that conviction-led, contrarian investing is lacking in Europe, and explains why the AI revolution and proper capitalization are key for European startups to finally compete with the US.

title: BVP Partner, Byron Deeter: The Future of Venture - Why Chanel vs Walmart is BS
key_insights: The pace of innovation in AI is creating 'supernova' companies that grow from zero to $100M in 1.5 years, making traditional growth metrics like 'treble, treble, double, double' obsolete.

The scale of the AI opportunity, with the potential for multiple trillion-dollar companies, justifies breaking traditional valuation discipline and investing heavily in generational companies, even at high prices.
AI is already moving beyond the technology budget into the human labor budget, supercharging roles and enabling companies to achieve massive growth with a smaller workforce.
While the AI wave gives incumbents advantages (data, distribution), the sheer scale of the market and the power of great products mean high-execution challengers can still build massive businesses.
Underestimating TAM is one of the biggest mistakes in venture; great founders consistently find new horizons (like payments for Vertical SaaS) that dramatically expand their initial markets.
The venture industry is bifurcating into large, multi-stage, global platforms and specialized, boutique firms, making it difficult for undifferentiated firms in the middle to compete.
fundraising_mentions: Anthropic rumored to be raising at $170B.
Top 3 LLMs projected to raise $100B in a six-month period.
Canva's valuation mentioned at $40B+.
Anthropic's valuation mentioned at $70B+.
Cornerstone OnDemand went public with $50M in ARR at a $700M market cap.
Anthropic's growth trajectory: zero, $10M, over $100M, to over $1B in successive years, with a path to $10B.
Bessemer owned 28% of Shopify and Twilio at IPO.
quotable: I thought we understood this next phase we were going into and how big this was going to be and very sincerely we've probably added a zero to everything. I think there's going to be a lot of trillion dollar businesses that are created from this.
We're seeing businesses go from zero to 100 million in 1.5 years. That's the supernova profile.
one_liner: Bessemer's Byron Deeter explains how AI is creating 'supernova' startups with unprecedented growth, forcing a complete recalibration of venture capital rules around valuation, market size, and speed.

title: Arvind Narayanan: AI Scaling Myths, The Core Bottlenecks in AI Today & The Future of Models | E1195
key_insights: AI progress is facing a significant data bottleneck, as models have already trained on most available public text data. This means simply increasing model size and compute is yielding diminishing returns.

The AI industry is shifting towards smaller, more efficient models. This is driven by the high cost of inference (which dominates a model's lifetime cost) and the benefits of on-device processing for privacy and new applications.

Current LLM evaluation is a 'mindfield' because benchmarks don't capture real-world performance ('vibes'), and models are often optimized for or contaminated by benchmark data, creating a misleading picture of their capabilities.

Effective AI regulation should focus on governing harmful activities (e.g., non-consensual deepfakes, fake reviews) regardless of the tool used, rather than attempting to regulate the AI technology itself.

Fears of mass job replacement are currently overblown. AI automates specific tasks, not entire jobs. Historically, technologies that automate tasks have often led to an increase in related jobs by making services cheaper and more accessible.
fundraising_mentions: Meta (Zack) has committed $50 billion over the next three years to AI development.
quotable: Every exponential is a sigmoid in disguise.
Jobs are bundles of tasks and AI automates tasks not jobs.
one_liner: A computer science professor debunks common AI scaling myths, arguing that data, not compute, is the new bottleneck, and explores the societal implications of a future dominated by smaller, more specialized models rather than a race to AGI.

title: Peter Singlehurst: Lessons from Turning Down Stripe, Coinbase and Losing Money on Northvalt
key_insights: Building a better business is possible by staying private for longer, allowing for more focus and avoiding the pressures of public markets.
A distinction exists between bad investments (known risks materializing) and mistakes (analytical errors, like underestimating execution risk in Northvolt).
The most enduring competitive advantages are often found in a company's business model, culture, and integration strategy, rather than a single product (e.g., Bending Spoons' M&A playbook).
True investment discipline isn't about avoiding high valuations, but being highly selective and judicious about when to pay a high price for an exceptional company.
The growth stage market is professionalizing, favoring long-term, institutional investors who understand how to own companies at scale, not just early-stage venture investors.
The quality of a business should be judged on its long-run return on equity, a concept often overlooked in the venture world's focus on over-capitalization and growth at all costs.
fundraising_mentions: First invested in Stripe at a ~$30 billion valuation.
Passed on a subsequent Stripe round at a ~$50 billion valuation.
First invested in DataBricks at ~$30 billion and did a pro-rata in a $60 billion round.
Mentioned Bending Spoons' $5 billion valuation.
Invested in Anduril in a round where the only new investors were from public market backgrounds.
Invested in Tesla in 2013 at a $3 billion market cap.
quotable: I think what people realize today is that you can build a Better Business by staying private for longer.

Not all of our bad Investments are necessarily mistakes... There are then other kinds of Investments where they are mistakes because there's something you should have seen... and those are mistakes. Northvolt has been a very bad investment for us... what we got wrong was the team's ability to execute.
one_liner: Peter Singlehurst of Baillie Gifford shares his firm's framework for global growth-stage investing, emphasizing long-term value, business model quality over product specifics, and the lessons learned from both successful and failed investments in companies like Stripe, Northvolt, and Bending Spoons.

title: Hiring Tips for Sales Reps | Frank FIllmann with Harry Stebbings
key_insights: Hiring sales reps requires assessing 'fit' based on the specific account and sales spectrum (SMB to strategic).
An effective sales team benefits from a mix of profiles: closers, visionaries who can build a future, and hunters who aggressively pursue deals.
Team chemistry is vital; avoid having too many 'Alphas' who might clash.
Interview questions should probe a candidate's passion for creating demand and their natural inclination towards different sales roles.

Creating demand that doesn't exist means identifying and solving customer problems they haven't articulated, often by tailoring existing products or visions to their needs, rather than leading with technology.
quotable: It's like how do you how do you buy a suit it doesn't really matter like the color the fat it's like does it fit you was it bespoke was it made for your frame right so for me it depends on the account and so you look at a spectrum of like SMB to strategic sales the answer is going to be wildly different.

for me it's like every conversation starts with through the lens of the customer and great empathy what are they trying to do and then how do we reverse engineer the product to fit it it never starts with product
one_liner: Frank Fillmann shares insights on building a high-performing sales team by identifying diverse sales profiles, fostering team chemistry, and emphasizing the crucial skill of creating demand through deep customer empathy.

title: What happens if the Fed keeps raising rates -Bill Ackman
key_insights: The Federal Reserve may not need to raise interest rates significantly more, as current short rates are near or above underlying inflation.
Full employment and rising wages are identified as contributors to inflation.

Increasing the supply of workers through immigration is proposed as a superior solution to temper wage increases and inflation, rather than deliberately slowing the economy and forcing people out of work.
quotable: Why force people out of work to slow the economy to get rid of inflation? Why not increase the supply of workers so that um you know we temper the increases of wages? I just think it's a better answer.
one_liner: Bill Ackman suggests that instead of further interest rate hikes to curb inflation, increasing immigration to boost the labor supply is a more effective and humane approach to temper wage growth.

title: Bill Ackman: SVB Collapse; Biden vs Trump; How I Lost $400M on Netflix; Bill's 10-Year Long | E991
guest_role: Founder & CEO, Pershing Square Capital Management
key_insights: Ackman strongly advocated for a temporary, system-wide deposit guarantee to prevent a run on regional banks after the SVB collapse, arguing financial stability must be the top priority.
The Fed should pause interest rate hikes until the banking system is stabilized to avoid causing further 'cracks' in the economy.

On losing $400M on Netflix, he exited the long-term investment within months because new data emerged that fundamentally contradicted his original thesis, showing the importance of admitting when you're wrong.

He believes the most important lesson from early business failure (Gotham Partners) was the danger of an asset-liability mismatch, leading him to structure Pershing Square to only invest in liquid public companies.
To address wealth inequality, he proposes a 'Birthright' savings account for every child born in America, giving them a stake in the country's economic success through compounding.
When selecting partners in business or marriage, finding someone you can completely trust and whose core values align with yours is 98% of the battle.
fundraising_mentions: Raised $3.1 million for his first fund, Gotham Partners, from six investors after meeting with over 100 people.
Four of the six initial investors were from the Forbes 400 list, asking them for relatively small amounts like $500k.
His partner David made raising a minimum of $3 million a condition for starting the fund.
quotable: Don't let the past disrupt the future. Don't be upset that you double faulted... just focus on... a blank sheet of paper. It's a new set, new opportunity and rebuild from here.

The problem with the wealth tax... the Biden wealth tax which is like 25 percent of the appreciation of things that you own privately it's going to bankrupt every startup no one will ever start a business in America anymore.
one_liner: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman provides a masterclass on the SVB collapse, interest rate policy, and risk management, while sharing candid lessons from losing $400M on Netflix, his views on politics, and the principles behind building successful partnerships.

title: Kieran Flanagan: Hiring Tips for Growth; North Star Metrics; Hubspot's Mistake | 20VC #916
key_insights: Growth can be applied pre-product-market-fit by building acquisition and retention mechanisms directly into the product roadmap, rather than treating it as an afterthought.

The ideal structure for a growth team depends on the company's go-to-market motion; for PLG companies, a central team in product is effective, while for sales-led businesses, it often resembles a performance marketing function.
When hiring for growth, a case study with a theoretical model is effective for evaluating a candidate's ability to prioritize metrics, design experiments, and defend their strategic choices.
Founders must act as the primary sponsor for a new growth team in its first year to navigate organizational friction and ensure cross-functional buy-in.

Mistakes in hiring for growth often stem from being swayed by a candidate's strong personal brand rather than their actual work, or misjudging their fit for an early-stage environment when they come from a large, established company.

To build a truly big company, leaders must invest in brand and creativity, which are often hard to measure with direct attribution, rather than focusing solely on easily quantifiable, short-term revenue metrics.
fundraising_mentions: Advises that a proper growth function is typically for 'Series A and beyond'.
quotable: In the beginner's mind there is endless possibilities, in the expert mind there are very few.
I think creativity and brand is how you build a big company in the future... If we tie everything to revenue, then we're all going to do the same stuff.
one_liner: Hubspot's SVP of Marketing, Kieran Flanagan, offers a masterclass on building and scaling modern growth engines, covering hiring frameworks, the shift to product-led models, and why investing in brand is the ultimate long-term differentiator.

title: So Many Investors Are Missing This Trend | Bill Ackman with Harry Stebbings
key_insights: Most investors are ignoring the trend of persistent inflation.
The world is structurally different than the last 20 years, leading to persistent inflation.
Expect three to four percent inflation for the foreseeable future.
The current pricing of long-term bonds (3.6% yield) is illogical given the expected inflation rates of 3.5%.
quotable: the world is a structurally different place than it was uh for the last 20 odd years and you're going to see persistent levels of inflation you know three to four percent inflation for the foreseeable future

a 3.6 yield for committing to the government you know the government's only gonna it's gonna if our money governments borrow money for 30 years at 3.6 that can't make sense in a world where inflation's three and a half percent
one_liner: Bill Ackman warns that investors are missing the trend of persistent inflation, rendering current long-term bond yields nonsensical.

title: Outbound Sales Tips from Maggie Hott, Director of Sales at Webflow
topics: Annual Contract Value (ACV) considerations for targeting
key_insights: Outbound sales should be initiated early in a company's lifecycle, as it's crucial for market awareness and shouldn't be delayed.
The main goal of cold outbound is to educate potential buyers about the product and its solutions, building brand awareness for future conversions rather than immediate sales.
The '10-80-10' rule for outbound emails (10% personalization, 80% core content, 10% personalized call to action) enables scaled personalization.
Sales and marketing, though distinct, are interdependent; marketing builds broad awareness, while sales provides hyper-targeted, personalized outreach.

Founders should avoid trying to sell to 'everyone' and instead focus on their Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) and securing initial customer logos to build reputation, rather than chasing large, complex deals prematurely.
quotable: cold outbound your single biggest objective there is to build a marketing machine and build build your brand awareness
I actually think it is so important to not try to be everything to everyone and this is a mistake that I see Founders make all the time
one_liner: Maggie Hott, Director of Sales at Webflow, shares practical insights on building effective outbound sales motions, emphasizing early implementation, brand awareness through education, scaled personalization, and strategic ICP focus for founders.

title: Steve Goldberg: Core Questions All CFOs Ask Today When Buying | E1094
key_insights: The market has shifted from a 'nurturing' to a 'performance-driven' environment, demanding more rigor and accountability in sales.
Budgets have consolidated under the CFO, who now scrutinizes every deal, asking 'what if you didn't have it?', effectively making every renewal a new sale.
To identify true champions, find people 'on their way up, not on their way out' by understanding their personal and professional motivations for driving change.
In crowded markets, differentiation comes from the 'how' (customer journey, success, and outcomes) not just the 'what' (product features).

RevOps is a highly valuable function that provides data-driven insights to uncover blind spots, such as identifying churn patterns that necessitate changes in sales models (e.g., shifting from Hunter-Farmer to Hunter-Hunter).
quotable: The market has changed from a nurturing Market to a performance-driven market and that's happened probably over the last 6 to 9 months.
Every renewal is a new deal. The first question my CFO ask me is what if you didn't have it and that's what every CFO is asking.
one_liner: SalesLoft CRO Steve Goldberg shares insights on navigating the modern performance-driven sales landscape where CFOs control budgets, every renewal is a new deal, and success hinges on proving tangible business outcomes.

title: FOUNDER ADVICE: Downrounds Incoming
key_insights: Despite being damaging and complicated, a wave of down rounds is expected as the market corrects from 2021 highs.
VC psychology naturally resists down rounds, preferring clean, up-and-to-the-right deals, which means fewer happen than probably should.
Private market software valuations are correcting to pre-COVID 'normal' multiples, around 10-15x forward ARR.
Companies that raised at massive valuations in 2021/2022 face a reckoning: they must either grow into their valuation or risk becoming 'zombie' companies.
Startups are aggressively cutting costs to extend runway, but many will still be forced to raise in a difficult 2023-2024 market.
fundraising_mentions: IVP invests post-product-market fit at Series B and C.
IVP priced deals in 2022 at 10-15x forward ARR.
The guest's firm saw two potential down rounds in the week of the interview.
There is a noticeable uptick in deal flow from Q4 2022.
quotable: Fewer down rounds happen than probably should happen because VCS don't like them.
At some point you need growth to become a real company and not a zombie.
one_liner: IVP's Tom Loverro predicts an unavoidable wave of down rounds as the market corrects, discussing how VC psychology impacts fundraising and what will happen to the cohort of companies that raised at inflated valuations in 2021.

title: How to Pick Which Startup to Work For
key_insights: Prioritize joining a high-growth 'rocket ship' company over chasing a specific job title, as career growth will follow.
When evaluating a job offer, look beyond the On-Target Earnings (OTE) and ask about the sales quota and historical team attainment rates.
A high OTE is meaningless if the associated quota is unattainable.
The value of equity is highly contextual; equity in an established, successful company is far more valuable than a similar amount in an unproven startup.
Candidates should ask detailed questions about equity, including fair market value, strike price, and the number of outstanding options, not just the total value offered.
quotable: Choose the company not the role.
You could have a 300K OTE but if you have a five million dollar quota and nobody is bringing in more than two million dollars, you're not going to get anywhere close to hitting your number.
one_liner: Maggie Hott provides advice for job seekers on how to select the right startup, emphasizing the importance of choosing a high-growth company over a specific title and critically evaluating the details of compensation packages beyond face value.

title: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong Doesn't Know How to Vacation
key_insights: Many entrepreneurs start their careers motivated by negative emotions like fear, shame, or anger, which often fades after achieving initial success.
Successful entrepreneurs may face an existential crisis when their initial motivators disappear, requiring a shift towards finding intrinsic joy and passion in their work.
Fulfillment can come from the process of building and scaling at a massive level, rather than from celebrating the achievement of specific goals.
The concept of 'work-life harmony' can be more fulfilling than 'work-life balance' for those who are passionate about their work, integrating it with travel and personal interests.
An intense drive to build can be viewed as a positive addiction, channeling that energy into creating impactful products and services for the world.
fundraising_mentions: Mentions reaching a 'billion dollar valuation' as a past goal.
quotable: I'm going to [...] go do something great here or die trying.
I happen to be addicted to building things and scaling them.
It's not work life balance it's work life Harmony.
one_liner: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong shares his personal journey from being driven by a fear of insignificance to finding fulfillment in the 'addiction' of building and scaling, and why he prefers work-life harmony over traditional vacations.

title: How to Fix US’s Broken Meat Industry
topics: Food safety vs. worker welfare audits
key_insights: The US meat industry is profoundly broken and requires significant transformation to produce guilt-free products.
ButcherBox aims to be the 'Patagonia of meat,' obsessing over animal welfare, farmer treatment, environmental impact, and worker conditions.
There is a critical lack of third-party auditing for worker welfare in US meat processing facilities, unlike the ease of food safety audits.
Consumers primarily prioritize their own benefit, then the animal and environment, with farmer and worker welfare being low considerations.
Real change in the meat industry demands a long-term vision and consumer dollars directed towards companies actively trying to disrupt the existing system.
quotable: I call it like the Patagonia of meat like we want you when you buy from butcher box to know that we obsessed over every detail possible for that piece of meat to make sure I had the best life the farmer was treated the best the environment was treated the best the workers in the supply train that we've actually thought about it we've tried to move it forward.

there's nobody in this country that I can hire to go in and third party audit these facilities it's crazy I mean if I was creating t-shirts in Bangladesh I could have fair trade in there in a very short amount of time why well because nobody wants to open that door and see what's behind it
one_liner: A ButcherBox representative discusses the broken US meat industry, their company's mission for ethical sourcing, and the challenges of consumer apathy and lack of worker welfare oversight.

title: Marc Benioff: How to raise your kids when you’re a billionaire
key_insights: Many wealthy individuals find it challenging to raise children with the same hunger and tenacity they had.
Attentive parenting is crucial for instilling values in children, regardless of financial status.
Marc Benioff credits his parents and grandparents for his own upbringing and values.
The guest implies that spending quality time as a parent is a key factor, referencing Matthew McConaughey's perspective.
Benioff feels that he resolved fundamental questions about his own happiness long ago, thanks to his upbringing.
quotable: The single biggest challenge that they have is how do you bring up children with the same tenacity hunger work ethic when brought up in very different Financial environments.
Fortunately some of these questions about happiness aren't things that I have to wrestle with because I was able to cross those bridges so many decades ago.
one_liner: Marc Benioff shares his perspective on raising children amidst wealth, emphasizing the foundational importance of attentive parenting in building character and work ethic.

title: 20VC: Tom Loverro on The Calm Before the Storm, Why The Fundraising Market Will Get Worse Before It Gets Better & The Survival Guide for Founders Navigating The Downturn
key_insights: A wave of companies will be fundraising simultaneously, leading to a highly competitive environment for founders.
Investors will become more selective, triaging their time towards the most promising companies.
Founders should fundraise proactively, starting the process with at least 12 months of runway, rather than waiting until the last minute.
Down rounds are likely to become more common as companies that raised at inflated 2021 valuations face a market correction.
During a downturn, founders should prioritize survival and strong unit economics over valuation, and be decisive in cutting costs.

Sequoia Capital's enduring success is partly attributed to its culture of fostering debate between partners with opposing viewpoints, which polishes ideas into 'diamonds'.

title: How much further will startup valuations drop?
key_insights: Founders are still asking for high valuations ($20-25M) despite a cooling market.
It's potentially better for founders to pitch a lower valuation ($12.5-15M) to create investor competition and possibly achieve a higher final valuation.
Fundraising involves a trade-off between three variables: amount of money raised, valuation (price), and the quality of the investor ('who').
If a compromise must be made, it should be on price, not on the amount of capital or the quality of the investors.
The most important factor in a fundraise is who you partner with, followed by securing enough capital to make meaningful progress.
fundraising_mentions: Founders asking for $20-25M valuations.
Advice for founders to start with a $12.5M or $15M valuation.

title: The Greatest Myth in the Investing World 🤑
key_insights: Diversification is effective for preserving wealth but detrimental to creating it.
Risk mitigation is not synonymous with diversification, as all assets can become correlated during market crises (e.g., 2008).
Generating 'alpha' (excess returns) stems from intellectual capacity, strong networks, and unwavering conviction in investment opportunities.
Investors should allocate maximum capital to their strongest convictions rather than spreading it across many less compelling ideas.
In venture capital, 'slugging percentage' (the impact of big wins) is more crucial than 'batting average' (the number of successful deals).
Significant returns are generated by having early conviction and investing substantially, not by token participation in late-stage rounds.

quotable: diversification is a great way to preserve wealth but a terrible way to create it
the gross profit dollars come from having conviction before the rest of the world does and putting sufficient money behind it
one_liner: The speaker challenges the conventional wisdom of diversification, arguing that significant wealth creation in investing, particularly in venture capital, hinges on concentrated high-conviction bets rather than widespread portfolio allocation.

title: Mark Goldberg: Why Politics is Rife & Decision-Making is Broken in Large VCs | E1219
key_insights: Large multi-stage VC firms suffer from a paradox where the most experienced partners have the least time for new deals due to bureaucracy and portfolio management.
Portfolio services teams at large VCs are often built to make the VC's job scalable, not primarily for the founder's direct benefit, leading to disintermediation.
A smaller, focused fund with a 'light reserve model' can offer better alignment with early-stage founders by ensuring experienced partners dedicate more time to them.

Consensus-based investment decisions at the early stage can filter out outlier opportunities; a model where a single partner can lead a deal is preferable for capturing high-risk, high-reward investments.
The venture landscape is in a dynamic transition, with a 'New Guard' of smaller, specialized funds challenging the 'Old Guard' of large, industrialized asset managers.
fundraising_mentions: Chemistry raised a $350 million fund for seed and series A.

quotable: I think one of the dirty secrets of multi-stage investing is that Portfolio Services teams are not for Founders they're for the VCS they are a way to make something unscalable scale.
The biggest mistake is when you try to make consensus decisions at the early stage I think you end up with consensus funds.
one_liner: Mark Goldberg discusses the founding of his new VC firm, Chemistry, as a deliberate move away from the misaligned incentives and bureaucracy of large, multi-stage funds to a smaller, more founder-focused model.

title: How Index Makes Decisions & Why Benchmarks & Averages in VC are BS
key_insights: The sins of omission (missing a huge company) are far greater than the sins of commission (making a bad investment).
The three primary lessons from missed opportunities are: don't be cute on price, don't overthink it, and don't pass on generational founders.
TAM (Total Addressable Market) is often a trap; the best founders find and expand market opportunities beyond initial estimates.
The power law, not averages, dominates venture returns, making it critical to invest in outliers rather than seeking 'good deals' or 'safe 2x returns'.
Conviction for follow-on investments should be built by creating a net-new investment case each time, not by simply averaging down or incrementally increasing ownership.
fundraising_mentions: Invested in DataDog at a high price in every round.
Invested in Wiz at a very high price in every round.
Invested in DataDog at the Series A.
Suggests splitting seed rounds into three sleeves: one for the multi-stage fund, one for a seed fund, and one for angel operators.

We are in the business of finding fund returners the power law dominates our business not being in a 10 20 50 hundred billion doll company is actually painful.
one_liner: Index Ventures Partner Shardul Shah shares his investment philosophy, focusing on the power law, building conviction in exceptional founders, why TAM is a trap, and the art of multi-stage investing.

key_insights: Going the extra mile in a competitive funding round can make a significant difference.
Unconventional and creative approaches, like a meme-based pitch deck, can effectively capture a founder's attention.
Demonstrating genuine product vision and excitement is as important as the content of the pitch.
Perseverance and hustle, even in difficult circumstances (like being sick with COVID), can be a powerful signal to founders.
Smaller or lesser-known funds can win against top-tier funds through creativity and personalized effort.

title: Eventbrite Sold for $500M, Databricks $5B Raise at $134B Valuation & Why SaaS is Like Japan
guest: Harry Stebbings, Jason Lemkin, Rory O'Driscoll
key_insights: Venture capital is a power-law game where VCs focus on deepening relationships and investment in their biggest winners, like Thrive with OpenAI.

High-growth, accelerating companies like Databricks can command significant valuation multiples (32x revenue) compared to slower-growing public counterparts (Snowflake at 20x), as extra growth compounds immense value.

Many established public SaaS companies are in a 'TAM trap,' struggling with slow growth due to market saturation, making them vulnerable to acquisitions at low multiples, as seen with PagerDuty and Eventbrite.
The rise of AI threatens traditional seat-based pricing models, as companies become more efficient and employee headcount shrinks, a concern highlighted by Workday and former Twilio CEO Jeff Lawson.

There's a debate in venture between investing in hot, fast-growing AI deals (e.g., coding assistants) and slower-compounding businesses that use AI to disrupt large, inefficient traditional markets (e.g., wealth management).

Security and data residency are becoming critical concerns as AI agents proliferate, potentially benefiting incumbents who can provide secure platforms, highlighted by Salesforce's actions against Gainsight and Drift after security breaches.

one_liner: Three venture capitalists discuss the stark contrast between hyper-growth AI companies like Databricks and stagnating SaaS players, exploring the implications for valuations, the 'TAM trap,' and the future of seat-based pricing in the age of AI.

title: Matt Fitzpatrick: Who Wins the Data Labelling Race & Why Al Needs Forward-Deployed Engineers
key_insights: There is a major gap between the exponential improvement in AI model performance and the slow pace of enterprise adoption, which is hindered by challenges in data infrastructure, workflow redesign, trust, and observability.

Externally driven AI builds are twice as effective as internal team builds. Successful enterprise deployment requires ROI-focused initiatives led by business units, not just isolated tech 'science projects'.

The traditional SaaS model is less effective for complex AI implementations. A 'prove it works first' approach, utilizing forward-deployed engineers and solution sprints at no initial cost, is key to winning enterprise trust.

Human feedback (RLHF) will remain indispensable for the next decade, especially for complex reasoning tasks and fine-tuning models for specific enterprise contexts like legal or healthcare, countering the narrative that synthetic data will become all-sufficient.

The future of enterprise software is moving away from rigid, out-of-the-box SaaS towards hyper-personalized 'systems of agility' that are custom-built and fine-tuned for a specific customer's data and workflows.
fundraising_mentions: Invisible historically raised only $7 million in primary capital over 9 years.

quotable: MIT just released this report that 5% of geni deployments are working in any form. You've seen Gartner saying 40% of enterprise projects will likely be canceled by 2027.

one_liner: Invisible CEO Matt Fitzpatrick explains why enterprise AI adoption is slow despite model advancements, advocating for a service-heavy, 'prove-it-first' approach with forward-deployed engineers to build trust and deliver real value beyond the hype.

title: Jordan Van Horn: 3 Reasons Salespeople Fail; How to Make a Sales Playbook | 20VC #918
guest_role: Head of Revenue at Monte Carlo
key_insights: A founder's initial (v0) sales playbook must clearly define: the problem you solve, who you solve it for (and who you don't), the key points of resonance with customers, and the top reasons for a customer to buy now.

Startups should not hire a salesperson to solve a product-market fit problem; instead, they should hire when they want to amplify learning, increase revenue per lead, or when the founder's time is too constrained by managing sales.

Salespeople typically fail for three reasons: they don't fit the company culture, they lack the motivation for the startup environment, or their skills don't align with the role's actual needs. The interview process must screen for all three.

When evaluating sales candidates, dig deep into their past experiences by asking multi-level questions about their achievements (e.g., 'How did you get to that number?', 'What was hard about it?') to separate individual contribution from just being on a 'rocket ship' company.

A sales leader should create a 'user guide' for their team, documenting their work style, boundaries, and what they care about to shortcut the trust-building process, especially in a remote environment.

In long enterprise sales cycles, assess new reps based on leading indicators and discrete, measurable events in the sales process (like setting next steps or getting introductions), not just the lagging indicator of revenue.
Early on, a company's success is determined by how quickly it learns, not just revenue. Conduct post-mortems on everything—wins, losses, and POCs—to extract learnings and iterate quickly.

Caring is not being nice they're not the same thing. You can be like very uncaring and very nice.

title: Eran Zinman, Co-Founder & Co-CEO @Monday.com: Going Upmarket, International and Multi-Product |E1247

A successful transition from SMB to Enterprise happens when you are pulled upmarket by customer demand, not by prematurely pivoting your entire business model.

Horizontal platforms can successfully verticalize (e.g., into CRM, Service Desk) by building on a flexible core architecture, allowing them to package solutions for specific use cases that emerge from their user base.

When scaling, don't just focus on acquiring new customers; a significant portion of growth must come from expanding within your existing customer base, which necessitates adding functions like sales and customer success.

title: Mike Salguero: How I Grew ButcherBox to $600M/year in Revenue; Tips for Influencer Marketing | E998
key_insights: Bootstrapping forces a focus on operational efficiency and profitability from day one, which can be a significant competitive advantage over heavily funded competitors.
For subscription box companies, focusing on 'dollars per box' (aiming for $30+) is more critical than gross margin percentage, as it directly impacts payback period.
Early growth can be achieved by dominating a single, fertile marketing channel (like influencer marketing for ButcherBox) before diversifying, allowing for deep expertise and efficiency.
Customer acquisition costs (CPAs) inevitably rise over time as a company saturates its core audience and must expand into broader, more expensive markets.
Outsourcing non-core functions (like distribution, farming, and customer service) can enable rapid scale without the massive capital expenditure and operational debt of building everything in-house.

title: The Next Wave of Social Media | Instagram Founders Kevin Systrom & Mike Krieger
key_insights: The future of social media is moving away from a reliance on the social graph towards machine learning-directed content discovery, similar to TikTok's model.
The core thesis that your friends share your interests is flawed; an interest graph is a much better filter for relevant content than a social graph.
Social networks need to become 'less social' in terms of discovery, but the desire to discuss content with people you care about remains a crucial component.
Algorithms can be designed to work for the user's benefit, enhancing their experience, rather than solely for the company's metrics.
When evaluating investments, the quality and skill set of the founding team is far more important than the perceived attractiveness of a market vertical.

key_insights: Founder burnout can manifest subtly, such as losing interest in your company and personality changes, before escalating to severe health crises.
The decision for a founder to step away from their company is incredibly difficult, and the primary feeling can be immense relief, which is a strong indicator of severe burnout.
VCs and founders often have misaligned timelines and incentives, and conversations about founder mental health are almost non-existent in late-stage growth environments.
The extreme 'hustle culture' in startups comes at a high personal cost, including health and relationships, and the mantra of 'never giving up' can be toxic.

The future of enterprise software is moving away from traditional applications and UIs towards an AI-first, human-centric experience that automates tedious work, which is the thesis behind Lanng's new company, Beyond Work.

title: Hugo Barra: How I Built Hardware for Android, Xiaomi, and Oculus | 20VC #947
key_insights: Hardware development requires immense conviction upfront; unlike software, a failed V1 can be fatal for a startup due to inventory costs, so the initial product must be delightful, not a 'minimum viable product'.

Successful consumer hardware products must clearly be either 'Feature King' (premium price, best features) or 'Budget King' (value-focused, cost-constrained); falling in the middle fails to satisfy any customer segment.
Price is a critical feature that can define a brand's success or failure; engineering a product to a specific, aggressive price point ('Budget King') is a powerful strategy.
Resilience is a critical leadership trait built by putting oneself through real struggle and stepping far outside one's comfort zone, such as working in a drastically different cultural environment.
Storytelling is the soul of product marketing; start by writing a press release that speaks to customers' emotional needs to create a compelling narrative before the product is even built.

key_insights: Speed is critical once you have a signal of product-market fit; it's better to get a product out and iterate based on user feedback than to over-analyze.
Transitioning from a team of generalists to bringing in specialists is crucial for scaling. This should happen when you have clarity and are ready to 'put the pedal down' on growth.

For a platform play, it's acceptable for initial products to be less feature-rich than point solutions, as the value comes from the integrated, bundled offering that solves multiple customer problems.
A key founder transition is moving from 'doing' to 'coaching and teaching'. Underestimating the value of management and leadership early on can be a significant mistake.
The go-to-market flywheel can be hyper-local; achieving density in a specific geographic area creates strong word-of-mouth referrals and improves sales efficiency.

For seed rounds of $3-4M, establishing a board can be a good preparation for future governance, even if meetings are informal.
The communication cadence between founders and investors should be flexible and founder-driven, not based on a rigid schedule.
The best founders are proactive, reaching out to investors with specific asks when they need help.
Early-stage board interactions should be lightweight, focusing on quarterly text updates rather than onerous, slide-heavy meetings.

title: Samir Vasavada: The Real Story of Vise: The Regrets, Mistakes and Mis-Hires | E1171
key_insights: Raising excessive capital too quickly can lead to a loss of discipline, poor spending habits, and hiring mercenaries instead of missionaries.

Hiring senior executives from big tech companies into an early-stage startup can be detrimental, as their 'playbooks' are often misaligned with the first-principles thinking required to find product-market fit.
A high valuation creates intense pressure for unrealistic growth and can attract the wrong type of employees who are focused on a quick win rather than long-term building.
Founders must learn to filter advice from investors and stakeholders, as most advice is bad or contradictory, and ultimately, they must learn lessons for themselves.
The transition from being an underdog proving people wrong to a 'foregone conclusion' proving people right can be a deeply uncomfortable and demotivating psychological shift for a founder.
