quotable: Microsoft will stand by customers for copyright data because Enterprises are worried about if they incorporate gen AI into any of the products or services in a way that they truly depend on it and at some point lawsuits start to fly everywhere they're exposed and because of those concerns it has held back Enterprises
I think they standing by folks from a copyright effective is a step forward
one_liner: Microsoft is taking a proactive step to boost enterprise AI adoption by offering copyright protection to its customers, addressing a key concern that has slowed widespread integration of generative AI.

title: Jason Lemkin: Why Pricing is Worse Than Ever and There is More Funding Than Ever | E1157
key_insights: The best investments grow from $1M to $10M in ARR in 5 quarters or less, and you can't IPO without a 'triple, triple, double, double' growth trajectory.

A key diligence step is a deep-dive with the CTO early in the process to find a 'binary pair' of co-founders; great CTOs are hyper-transparent and can demonstrate 'surprise and delight' in their product.
When a company approaches 10% market share in its core ICP, it must have a plan to expand (new product, geography, or ICP) to avoid growth deceleration.
For SMB SaaS, monthly churn over 3-4% is a critical red flag, indicating it might not be a true recurring revenue business.
When the original founders leave a company, it's often a strong signal for an investor to sell their position, as the company may lose its competitive agility and founder-led DNA.
fundraising_mentions: SalesLoft sold for $2.5 billion at ~100 million in ARR.
PipeDrive sold for $1.5 billion at ~100 million in ARR.
Logical sold for $300 million.
Jason's seed investment in PipeDrive was at a $16 million valuation when it had $1 million in ARR.
Jason's first investment in RevenueCat was pre-YC at a $7-8 million valuation when it had $30/month in revenue.
quotable: You can't IPO unless you triple triple double double.
I have never met a great CTO that isn't at the edge of hyper transparent. Never met one. If I did, I would run for the door.
one_liner: Veteran SaaS investor Jason Lemkin discusses his best and worst investments, sharing crucial lessons on evaluating CTOs, navigating competitive markets, identifying sustainable growth metrics, and knowing when to sell.

title: How Ring Almost Died
key_insights: Rapid growth in a hardware business is incredibly cash-intensive and risky, requiring inventory orders far in advance of revenue.
A single external event, like a lawsuit, can cause a nine-figure funding round to evaporate days before closing, plunging the company into immediate crisis.
In extreme crisis situations, a leader's ability to remain calm and methodical ('like a pilot with a checklist') is a critical asset.
Radical transparency with your team during a crisis, rather than causing them to flee, can unite them and create an 'arm-in-arm' mentality to save the company.
A company's fate can turn dramatically in a short period, going from the brink of bankruptcy to signing an acquisition term sheet with a major corporation in just 45 days.
fundraising_mentions: Series A from True Ventures was delayed, causing a cash crunch.
A $100 million investment was pulled days before the wire transfer due to a lawsuit and injunction.
quotable: When things get to the most extreme I actually get very calm... like a pilot I get my checklist out like the wings could be ripped off the plane and I'm like calm and like reading the checklist.
People are always scared that when you say this like everyone will leave your business it's exactly the opposite they literally are arm in arm with you like immediately.
one_liner: Ring's founder recounts a period where a lawsuit caused a $100M investment to be pulled, forcing the company to the brink of bankruptcy before the team rallied to achieve record-breaking sales and secure an acquisition by Amazon just 45 days later.

title: Anthropic Inference Costs Skyrocket |TikTok Deal Closes |The IPO Market:Wealthfront & EquipmentShare
guest: Harry Stebbings, Jason Calacanis, Rory O'Driscoll
topics: Competitive dynamics in Fintech (Ramp vs. Brex)
The IPO market and company scale
Future of SaaS and AI integration
Andreessen Horowitz's dominance in AI investing
key_insights: The $5.1B acquisition of Brex is a strong outcome but highlights the risks of 'hubristic financing' at peak valuations, setting up weird feelings even in a success.

Skyrocketing AI inference costs are becoming a major competitive hurdle, where even profitable SaaS companies may struggle to fund the necessary AI features to compete with heavily capitalized startups.
The IPO market is open but selective, favoring scaled, profitable companies like EquipmentShare, while sub-scale firms like Wealthfront face significant post-IPO challenges.
Underlying demand for compute remains massive, as indicated by TSMC's capex plans, suggesting the AI investment cycle is not slowing in the near term despite bubble concerns.

Firms like Andreessen Horowitz are achieving institutional dominance in venture, capturing a majority of private AI revenue, and raising questions about whether venture is becoming a more traditional asset class.
fundraising_mentions: Brex acquired by Capital One for $5.15 billion.
Brex's prior valuation of $12 billion in 2021.
Ramp's valuation of $32 billion.
Capital One's acquisition of Discover for $35 billion.
Open Evidence raises at a $12 billion valuation.
EquipmentShare IPO'd at an $8 billion market cap.
Wealthfront IPO'd at a $1.3 billion market cap, down from a $2.7 billion private valuation.
Ethos going public at a $1.3 billion valuation, down from a $2.7 billion private valuation.
Andreessen Horowitz invested $8 billion in 2025.
quotable: The bad feelings last for a day and the 5 billion lasts forever, right? So, you'll get over it.
SAS is not dead. And now SAS has an army.
one_liner: The 20VC panel analyzes the week's major tech news, debating the implications of the Brex acquisition, rising AI costs, a selective IPO market, and venture capital's changing landscape.

title: a16z, Anish Acharya on Is SaaS Dead? | Why We Are Not in an AI Bubble | Cursor vs Claude Code
key_insights: The narrative that AI will completely replace all SaaS ('SaaSacre') is overblown; software spend is only 8-12% of enterprise spend, and the real opportunity for AI is to optimize the other 90%.
AI coding agents will dramatically decrease the switching costs between major enterprise systems (e.g., SAP to Oracle), turning 'hostages' into true 'customers' and increasing competition.
Startups are most likely to win in new, AI-native categories (e.g., 'AI movie making'), while capable incumbents will use AI to improve their existing products.
The application layer is poised to create significant value by acting as an aggregation point for multiple specialized foundation models, which are becoming fragmented substitutes and specialists.
The high costs associated with AI products force better business model discipline from day one, ending the 'build a free product and figure out monetization later' era.
fundraising_mentions: Discussion of Series A pricing: 'sub 100 million, like 50, 70, 100, even 120, the main way that price shows up is it may impair your ability to raise the next round'.
Example Series A terms: '12 on 60', '15 on 75'.
a16z is 'very elastic on price' but 'not very elastic on ownership'.
Belief that a16z must 'see 100% of the deals in our domain and that we win 100% of the deals that we go after'.
quotable: You have this innovation bazooka with these models. Why would you point it at rebuilding payroll or ERP or CRM?
The general story that we're going to vibe code everything is flat wrong and the whole market is oversold software.
one_liner: a16z GP Anish Acharya discusses why SaaS is not dead, how startups can win against incumbents in the AI era, and why the application layer is a significant investment opportunity.

title: Maria Angelidou: Product Lessons Leading Facebook App Monetisation Team to Billions in Revenue | E1210
key_insights: Promotions should be 'trailing indicators,' given only after an individual has consistently demonstrated they can operate successfully at the next level for a long period.

To foster IC career growth and retain top talent, establish distinct PM archetypes (e.g., Captain for complex projects, Entrepreneur for 0-to-1, Specialist for deep expertise) that allow progression to senior levels without forcing a move into management.
Effective product reviews are structured into four distinct types: Strategy (the 'what'), Roadmap (the 'how'), Launch (readiness and quality check), and Business Review (financial performance).

A rigorous hiring process is crucial; a multi-phase approach including screening, functional loops (product sense, execution), a practical case study, and a leadership/values interview ensures you hire the right talent.

Allocate resources intentionally across three horizons: 30-40% on existing products, 30-40% on new products (with at least 5-10% of that for 'planting new seeds'), and the remainder on maintenance (KLO) and internal productivity.
quotable: You only promote people to the next level when they consistently already demonstrated they can operate successfully at that level for a long period of time because at that next level they will be calibrated compared to the group of people the whole cohort of people who already operating really well in the next level and if you promote them prematurely it's actually going to be really bad for them.
If product was all science then you wouldn't see so much diversity in outcomes of all these companies that trying to get to product Market fit.
one_liner: Maria Angelidou shares her product leadership playbook, honed at Facebook and Personio, covering everything from hiring and promoting talent to structuring product reviews and allocating resources for sustainable growth.

title: Duolingo Co-Founder, Severin Hacker: How AI Impacts the Future of Work and Education
key_insights: AI is transforming Duolingo in three main ways: accelerating content creation (building 148 courses in one year vs. 100 in the first 12), enabling new interactive features like AI conversation partners, and improving overall company productivity.

The hardest part of learning a language isn't the learning itself, but the motivation. Duolingo's success comes from being a 'motivation engine' through gamification, which is their key differentiator.
Duolingo intentionally does not have an office in Silicon Valley after other founders warned it creates an internal funnel for your best employees to get recruited away by hot local companies.
The two biggest mistakes in the early days were waiting too long (five years) to figure out monetization and waiting too long to hire senior managers for their flat organization.

For M&A, the best predictor of success is having a prior working relationship with the company, similar to how having worked with a co-founder before is the best predictor of a successful founding team.
fundraising_mentions: The Series A was $3 million at a $15 million valuation, led by Union Square Ventures (USV), and it was the only offer they received.
quotable: I can guarantee you Dualingo would not have been able to raise any money in Europe. You know, we had 0 revenue for the first 5 years.
The hardest part about learning a language is the actual motivation... Duolingo is a motivation engine. And it really gets you to do this.
one_liner: Duolingo's Co-Founder, Severin Hacker, discusses how AI is revolutionizing education through personalized learning and accelerated content creation, the critical role of motivation in user retention, and the strategic decisions behind their product, hiring, and fundraising.

title: Billionaire's Unbelievable PRODUCTIVITY HACK
key_insights: Happier teams and individuals significantly outperform unhappy ones.
Happiness is presented as the single most significant advantage for productivity in business.
Practicing gratitude journaling for just three minutes a day over 21 days can rewire your brain.
The exercise involves writing down three specific, key moments from the previous day for which you are thankful, rather than generic statements.
This practice trains the brain to create a 'background screening application,' enabling real-time recognition and appreciation of positive moments, which leads to increased happiness.
quotable: Happiness is actually the biggest Advantage for a productivity perspective in business.
After 21 days your brain created an application that just notices it in real time and all of a sudden you're much happier because in the moment you're appreciating those moments of gratitude.
one_liner: Henry Schuck, Founder and CEO of ZoomInfo, reveals how a 21-day gratitude journaling practice can fundamentally rewire your brain for happiness, leading to a significant and often underestimated productivity advantage in business.

title: How I Raised $230M; ChatGPT vs. Google; How LLMs Work; Trump vs DeSantis | E1004
key_insights: VC fundraising in a tough market requires treating it like a software sales process, with a large funnel and a realistic close rate (e.g., 15%).
Thesis-driven, concentrated investing (12-15 companies with 40-50% of the fund in the top 3) can be an optimal strategy for a solo GP.
The future of AI isn't a single dominant model but a dual ecosystem: large, closed, integrated models and a fragmented world of open-source models, similar to the Apple vs. Linux/Windows dynamic.

Incumbents like Google face a classic innovator's dilemma, hesitating to disrupt their profitable core business (search) with a new, initially less economical technology (generative AI), creating an opening for startups.
The primary moat for AI startups against incumbents isn't just data, but superior execution, product development, and go-to-market strategy.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a $230M fund for Theory Ventures.
It took approximately 150 LP meetings to close the fund.
Operated with a 15% close rate assumption.
About 50% of the capital came from new LP relationships.
The largest LP is no more than 12% of the fund.
The fund strategy is a concentrated portfolio of 12-15 companies, with initial check sizes of $8-12M.
quotable: Anytime we talk about machine learning there's always this question around like what is the moat I think the answer is the one that's always been which is better execution is the mode.

If you're a venture capitalist or if you're a startup founder you have to believe that it's in your fabric that no matter how big the incumbent is or the advantages that they have that if you have really great execution you can still win and you can win big.
one_liner: Tomasz Tunguz breaks down the process of raising his $230M fund, Theory Ventures, and shares his perspective on why execution is the ultimate moat for startups competing with incumbents in the new era of AI.

title: Larry Aschebrook, Founder & MP @GSquared: How We Lost Money on Uber and Made Millions on Lyft
topics: Deal Stories (Spotify, Uber, Lyft, Palantir, Theranos)
key_insights: G Squared's core strategy involves secondary direct buying in late-stage private companies, often starting with small checks to gain information before making large, concentrated bets.
The firm made a significant return on Lyft by selling before its IPO, while losing money on Uber, highlighting the critical importance of exit timing and avoiding public market volatility.

A pivotal moment was securing a $150 million allocation in Spotify by flying to Stockholm without an appointment and then raising the capital in 60 days, which became a foundational investment for the firm.
The 2020-2021 market bubble led to overpaying for assets, forcing a pivot to structured equity deals to protect the vintage and a painful internal restructuring.
Aschebrook emphasizes DPI (Distributed to Paid-In Capital) as the most important metric, arguing that TVPI is a 'fake number' and real cash returns are all that matter for LPs.
fundraising_mentions: First fund was $35 million raised over 3 years (2010-2013).
Raised $125 million in 60 days for a $150 million co-investment in Spotify.
The 2020 vintage fund was $1.4 billion.
The 2022 vintage fund was $1.2 billion.
quotable: I mean, we made ridiculous sums of money for LPS in that period. We were the largest shareholder of Corsera. $800 million back to LPS on Corsera. We made a ton of money on Lyft and we lost money on Uber.
I went back to our LPs and said, 'Listen, we [ __ ] up. We need to pivot. We need another 300 million bucks because I need to protect this thing.' The next 3 years were some of the worst of my life.
one_liner: G Squared Founder Larry Aschebrook shares candid stories of building a multi-billion dollar secondary investment firm, detailing massive wins like Spotify and Lyft, painful losses on Uber and Getir, and the lessons learned from navigating extreme market cycles.

title: Google's Brutal Hiring Process
key_insights: Google's hiring process was extremely credential-driven, requiring SAT scores and college transcripts years after graduation.
This credentialism contributed to talent density but also created significant blind spots.
A computer science degree requirement for product managers at Google excluded talented individuals like Kevin Systrom.
Such strict requirements inadvertently led to excluded individuals going on to found successful companies, as seen with Kevin Systrom and Instagram.
quotable: I what 12 years after graduating college had to provide my SAT scores to Google I had to go find them

Google I was one of the last product managers hired into Google who did not have a computer science degree and because of that computer science requirement to be a product manager people like Kevin's sister weren't allowed to be product managers at Google right so he went off and found it at a little company called Instagram
one_liner: A former Google product manager discusses Google's highly credential-focused hiring process, highlighting its role in fostering talent density while also creating blind spots that inadvertently propelled excluded talent, like Kevin Systrom, to found companies such as Instagram.

title: From Romania to NASA to Silicon Valley 🇷🇴😲
guest_role: Machine Learning Engineer / Software Engineer (formerly at SAP)
key_insights: Guest's humble beginnings in a Romanian village until age 18.
A NASA contest win at 18 led to the first trip to the US and a revelation about a career in software.
Pursued computer science and machine learning studies in Germany independently.
Worked for SAP, facilitating a transfer to their Palo Alto office in the Bay Area.
Experienced a quintessential Silicon Valley arrival, including living with a prominent Atari executive.
quotable: I was mesmerized by the amount of intelligent system work they're doing I knew I have to be in software
I wasn't still am a die-hard Atari fan so I was Starstruck when I met Mr Robert Brown and that's when I felt like I truly arrived to to the valley
one_liner: A Romanian individual recounts their journey from a rural upbringing to becoming a software and machine learning professional in Silicon Valley, influenced by a NASA contest, German education, and experience at SAP.

title: Robinhood Founder & CEO, Vlad Tenev: Robinhood’s $85BN Resurgence & Tokenizing SpaceX & OpenAI
key_insights: Tokenization of private assets like SpaceX and OpenAI can democratize access to high-growth, illiquid companies for retail investors, and the mechanism is designed to work without the company's explicit opt-in.

Robinhood has achieved significant operational efficiency by building its own internal AI systems, which now write the majority of new software engineering code and power a 'best-in-class' customer support experience.
A key driver of Robinhood's business turnaround was a strategic shift to focus on serving 'digitally native active traders,' a resilient customer segment that remains active in volatile markets.
The future of finance will see crypto evolve from a speculative asset class into a foundational infrastructure layer that enables features like 24/7 settlement and innovative DeFi products.

Robinhood's long-term vision is to become an all-encompassing financial platform, expanding into services like digital private banking with unique offerings such as on-demand cash delivery to eliminate reasons for customers to move money out of the ecosystem.
fundraising_mentions: Vlad mentions his other company, Harmonic, raised a Series B.
Robinhood raised $6 billion in cash in 2021, including $4 billion during the GameStop event and $1.5-2 billion in its IPO.
quotable: I think it's important for the tokenization mechanism to work without the opt-in of the companies that are being tokenized.
I've shared this viewpoint with uh Patrick and John and they give me some variant of, 'Oh, well, we're just a small Irish family company. Please don't tokenize my shares.'
one_liner: Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev discusses the company's resurgence driven by AI-powered efficiency and a focus on active traders, while detailing his ambitious plan to tokenize private companies like SpaceX and OpenAI to democratize finance.

title: The least talked about climate change solution 🌎
topics: global warming impact on vulnerable populations
key_insights: Research into sunlight reflection (geoengineering) is an absolute necessity for addressing climate change.
Natural events like volcanic eruptions demonstrate the planet-cooling potential of stratospheric aerosols.
Exploring methods like aerosols, cloud brightening, and cloud creation in the Pacific is crucial to buy time.
Delaying these interventions will lead to the loss of hundreds of millions of lives, especially among vulnerable populations.
The topic of geoengineering is underfunded and must be prioritized to prevent uncontrolled interventions by rogue states.
quotable: the one thing we absolutely have to do is research sunlight reflection we have no way out of this without reflecting sunlight back into the solar system
I think the ultimate privilege right now the ultimate Ivory Tower is to sit there and say hey that's scary — I do think it's scary that's why we have to research it
one_liner: The speaker passionately argues for immediate and extensive research into sunlight reflection and geoengineering as a vital, yet overlooked, climate change solution to protect vulnerable communities and prevent chaotic unilateral interventions.

title: Why VC Today is Worse than 2021
guest: Harry Stebbings, Jason Lemkin, Rory O'Driscoll
topics: Talent compensation in Tech vs. VC
Private market valuations and the Revolut fundraise
The role of founders in expanding TAM
Capital intensity in the AI industry
OpenAI's strategy with Oracle and Microsoft
The future of software development with AI tools like Replit
key_insights: The current VC landscape is characterized by a fear of TAM (Total Addressable Market) exhaustion, especially in vertical AI, where high expectations and valuations may not be sustainable long-term.

A temporary surge where 'everyone is in-market' for AI tools is inflating growth metrics, creating a risk that investors are over-extrapolating short-term adoption into long-term growth, similar to mistakes made during the COVID-19 boom.

Building competitive AI now requires immense capital intensity, pushing companies like Poolside to build their own data centers out of necessity, which dramatically raises the stakes for new entrants.

There is a growing concern that while it feels easy to invest now due to the high volume of entrepreneurs and technological change, actual fund returns may be 40-50% lower because of high entry valuations, diluted ownership, and unproven gross margins.

The venture market is bifurcating between making early-stage bets and participating in large, public-style growth rounds for 'anointed winners,' making the middle ground increasingly difficult to navigate.
fundraising_mentions: Revolut's $3 billion fundraise at a $75 billion valuation.
Sierra's funding at a $10 billion valuation on $50 million ARR.
Salesforce's venture arm has invested $850 million of its new $1 billion AI fund.
quotable: My gut tells me we're overromanticizing verticals in the age of AI. Like we're going to hit the same TAM exhaustion and it's going to be worse because expectations are so high.
In a bull market, the most aggressive person will look the smartest just before the crash because the more risk you've taken, the more money you've made.
one_liner: Venture capitalists analyze the current AI investment climate, expressing concerns over TAM exhaustion, inflated valuations from a temporary market rush, and the escalating capital required to compete.

title: David Clark: Lessons from 32 Years of Fund Investing - Why Exits Will Be Larger | E1131
key_insights: To accurately assess fund potential, you must compare today's fund sizes with the projected exit sizes of 10-15 years in the future, not today's exit market.
The venture industry is governed by a power law where ~1% of exits generate the majority of returns, making access to the few managers who can consistently find these companies critical.
An LP doesn't need to invest in every great manager; they just need to ensure that every manager they *do* back is great, emphasizing focus over breadth.
The best time to invest in a new manager is often at Fund III, as Fund I provides enough data to see if they can identify a top 1% company, which is the key indicator of future success.
Despite the perception of large funds being unable to generate high returns, data shows 45 investments that have returned over a billion dollars to a single fund, validating the large fund model.
fundraising_mentions: Vancap missed the opportunity to invest in Benchmark's first fund because their client, a UK pension fund, would only approve a $4 million investment when the required amount was $5 million.
quotable: What you need to do is to compare fund sizes today with the exit sizes in 10 to 15 years because that's when those companies are ultimately going to become liquid.
You don't have to do every great manager out there you just have to make sure all the managers you do are great.
one_liner: Vancap LP David Clark shares lessons from his 32-year career, arguing that future exit sizes will justify today's large funds and detailing his focused strategy on backing a select group of elite, proven VC managers.

title: Is DPI The Only Thing That Matters? with Sam Lessin, Jason Lemkin & Rory O’Driscoll
guest: Sam Lessin, Jason Lemkin & Rory O’Driscoll
guest_role: Seed Investor; Founder @ SaaStr; Partner @ Scale Venture Partners
key_insights: DPI (Distributions to Paid-in Capital) is argued to be the only metric that truly matters for LPs, as it represents real returns, unlike TVPI which can be a 'vanity metric'.
The venture capital market is hollowing out in the middle, favoring very large, asset-gathering funds and small, specialized seed funds.
The massive capital expenditure by hyperscalers on AI infrastructure is unprecedented, creating a dynamic where the application layer revenue is currently lagging far behind the investment.
The cost of AI is collapsing, making aggressive AI integration a necessity for survival in B2B SaaS; failing to do so (the 'AI slow roll') is seen as a fatal mistake.
Agentic interfaces (MCPs) and new user behaviors pose an existential threat to traditional SaaS applications by abstracting the system of record and changing how users interact with software.
fundraising_mentions: Tomo Bravo raised a $34 billion fund.
Chime's last private round was at a $25 billion valuation.
Circle filed for an IPO at an $8 billion valuation.
Snowflake acquired Crunchy Data for $250 million.
Data Bricks acquired Neon for $1 billion.
ClickHouse raised a late-stage round at approximately a $6 billion valuation.
YC's new deals are pushing for $50-60 million post-money valuations for pre-revenue AI startups.
quotable: Public company investors are just mean VCs on steroids. We turn on a dime from I can't believe you're not spending more to what the freak do you mean you're spending so much money.
Every company's market share is up for grabs when there's a platform shift.
one_liner: Venture capitalists Sam Lessin, Jason Lemkin, and Rory O’Driscoll debate the primacy of DPI in venture returns, the hollowing out of mid-tier VC, and the existential opportunities and threats presented by the AI platform shift.

title: Tom Hulme & Stan Boland: Lessons from Jensen Huang & How to Fix the UK Tech Ecosystem
key_insights: The UK has a significant venture capital shortfall (raising $3.7B vs. a pro-rata equivalent of $15.4B in the US), which crimps founder ambition and leads to talent drain.

There is a critical talent problem, not just in engineering but in the supply of world-class operators needed to scale companies; a proposed solution is to 5x the number of computer science graduates and staple visas to their graduation certificates.
The UK should focus on its unfair advantages, such as semiconductor design and fintech, rather than trying to compete across all sectors.
Current government policies like R&D tax credits may be creating 'zombie companies' that limp on, whereas reallocating that capital to active venture funds could foster more global winners.
The London Stock Exchange suffers from a supply and sentiment problem, but the priority should be building valuable companies with IP and employees in the UK, regardless of the listing venue.
fundraising_mentions: Stan Boland raised $30M for his first chip company, which sold to Broadcom for ~$640M.
Stan Boland has raised ~$330M in venture capital in total.
Wordware, a Cambridge-founded company, raised $30M on a $220M post-money valuation in San Francisco.
UK venture funds raised $3.7B last year, compared to an estimated pro-rata need of $15.4B based on US figures.
The British Business Bank (BBB) invests ~$424M a year into funds.
Whiz was acquired for $32B.
OpenAI is at a $12B run rate.
quotable: We need to flood the UK with venture capital.
If you graduate in an engineering or computer science or something here you you should have stapled to your graduation certificate a tier 2 visa ready to go.
one_liner: GV's Tom Hulme and serial entrepreneur Stan Boland diagnose the key problems holding back UK tech—from a massive capital deficit to talent drain—and propose radical solutions to build a globally competitive ecosystem.

title: Career Advice for Women
key_insights: The perception of women in the workplace often unfairly changes after they have children, suggesting they are less committed.
Women should not apologize for their family responsibilities and must define their own narrative, rejecting the idea that motherhood is a career trade-off.
Being open and honest about personal life, including parenting, fosters a more thoughtful, interesting, and diverse team environment.
To build an inclusive culture, leaders must genuinely care about their employees as complete human beings and show interest in their lives beyond work.
Inclusivity is not about specific grand actions, but about making people feel seen, heard, and accepted for who they are.
quotable: Don't apologize. Don't accept this narrative that it's a balance or a trade-off or you're giving something up somehow. It's up to you to Define your own narrative and you don't have to accept that idea.

It's really just people just want to be seen... people want to be heard they want to know they can be themselves and if you just open the door you don't have to understand you don't have to do anything very specific other than see them as a full human being in everything they're dealing with in life.
one_liner: Vanta CRO Stevie Case discusses the perceptual challenges working mothers face and advises women to own their narrative, while urging leaders to build inclusive cultures by genuinely caring for their employees as whole people.

title: Eoghan McCabe, CEO @Intercom: Freedom of Speech, Censorship and Government Control | E1213
key_insights: Building domain-specific AI applications on top of LLMs requires immense, specialized work, creating a defensible moat against both base model providers and in-house solutions.
The adoption of revolutionary technology like AI is far slower than predicted; there's a decade-plus window for specialized applications to thrive before potential AGI disruption.
True startup defensibility lies not in patents but in the speed and quality of execution and the ability to ride successive growth cycles and reinvent.
A return to an intense, unapologetic, founder-led culture (vs. professional CEO consensus) was critical for Intercom's turnaround and growth acceleration.
Freedom of speech is a critical principle for a healthy society, and governments should not have the power to censor what can be said, as it's a hallmark of totalitarianism.
fundraising_mentions: Intercom nearly went public in June 2022 but pulled back when the markets collapsed.
The average time for an AI company to reach $30M ARR is less than two years, compared to four-five years for traditional SaaS.
Ilia Fushman and Mamoon Hamid from Kleiner Perkins are mentioned as respected VCs, with Mamoon having invested in Intercom's Series A.
quotable: I think it's deeply evil to to decide what can or cannot be spoken about.
I think that building your own AI agent platforms is going to be as smart as in a previous generation building your own SAS workflow tools that's a terrible fucking idea.
one_liner: Intercom CEO Eoghan McCabe discusses the practical realities of building defensible AI in customer service, the necessity of a hard-charging founder mindset for turnarounds, and makes a strong case for absolute freedom of speech.

title: Jackie Reses: The Most Powerful Woman in Finance; Making $50BN for Yahoo on Alibaba | E996
key_insights: Hiring should focus on a person's innate skills, grit, and judgment rather than just their resume or specific domain knowledge.
Successful deal-making is not a zero-sum game but about creatively understanding and meeting the other party's core needs, even if it means giving up on less critical points.
The next decade of fintech innovation will focus on solving the complexities of expense management and underlying infrastructure, moving beyond the well-optimized revenue collection space.

To foster innovation within a company, it's crucial to reward high-performing individual contributors (ICs) and incentivize leaders to start new projects, breaking the cultural link between power and headcount.
Building a high-performance culture from the start is essential; it requires setting a tone of intensity and focus, and weeding out entitlement to inspire a mission-driven team.
fundraising_mentions: When raising for Lead Bank, Jackie Reses was willing to give investors favorable terms because her primary goal was to bring on their expertise and discipline, prioritizing speed and a strong regulatory structure over maximizing economic terms for herself.
quotable: We built the bank we wanted to see in the world full stop. We built the bank we wanted to see.

I would rather focus on things like raw intelligence, judgment, curiosity, grit, ability to manage ambiguity rather than looking for things like domain knowledge or operators with prior scale experience.
one_liner: Jackie Reses discusses her career in finance and tech, sharing powerful lessons on hiring for innate skills over resumes, non-zero-sum deal-making, and her vision for reinventing banking infrastructure with her company, Lead Bank.

title: Product Tips from Steve Jobs and Elon Musk | Marty Cagan
key_insights: When gathering customer feedback, don't ask what they want or what they would build, as they don't know what is technically possible.

To get truthful feedback and determine if a customer is serious, use value tests like asking for payment, a non-binding letter of intent, or a time commitment.
Product development is a blend of art and science; the 'art' is the judgment in deciding when to rely on the 'science' of statistically significant data.
Qualitative feedback is not about counting the number of people with an issue; it's about deeply understanding the reasons for potential non-adoption from every user.

title: How ButcherBox scaled to $1 BILLION
key_insights: Precise control over product weight (e.g., a 3lb pack of chicken being exactly 3lb) can add significant margin (e.g., 50 bips) directly to the bottom line.
Financial constraints from bootstrapping force a rigorous focus on eliminating operational waste that well-funded competitors might overlook.
At scale, negotiating the cost of seemingly minor items, like the tape for boxes, becomes a significant financial lever.
Optimizing logistics, such as ensuring trucks are fully loaded, is a key area for cost savings in a shipping-intensive business.
Hyper-growth, often fueled by large funding rounds, can distract companies from the crucial, detail-oriented work of cost management.
fundraising_mentions: The company was constrained at the beginning by not raising money.
Mentions that overfunded companies often don't have time to focus on operational details.
quotable: If the 3 lb of chicken is actually 3.3 lb well now my chicken cost just went up 10% and if you're able to reduce that it's literally like 50 bips of of margin to the bottom line.
We were constrained at the beginning by not raising money how do you squeeze every bit of operational like waste out of this thing.
There's a ton of money to be made in the details.
one_liner: The founder of ButcherBox explains how a relentless focus on operational efficiency and cost-cutting in the details, born from the constraints of not raising money, was key to scaling the company to a billion dollars.

title: How Box Subscriptions Work
key_insights: Partnering with established experts in areas like distribution can be more effective than attempting to build all functions in-house, especially when competing with heavily funded companies.
Bootstrapping forces a relentless focus on operational efficiency and squeezing margin out of every detail, which can become a significant long-term advantage.

Margin expansion doesn't solely come from large-scale vertical integration; it can be driven by meticulous details like optimizing product weight, negotiating prices on consumables, and reducing logistical waste.
For a physical goods business, controlling critical, non-core components of the supply chain (like manufacturing their own dry ice) can be a strategic move to de-risk operations.
Growth at all costs can mask operational inefficiencies, whereas a constrained, bootstrapped approach necessitates a dual focus on both marketing and deep operational optimization.
fundraising_mentions: The business was started as a 'hobby business' and was constrained at the beginning by not raising money.

one_liner: ButcherBox founder Mike Salguero details how bootstrapping and strategic partnerships, rather than full vertical integration, forced a culture of extreme operational efficiency and margin optimization from day one.

key_insights: Outworking competitors, even if they are more intelligent, is a direct path to outperforming them.
A strong work ethic can be deeply rooted in family examples of hard work and sacrifice.
The modern expectation of large rewards without commensurate effort is a flawed mindset.
The regret of knowing you could have succeeded if you had just worked harder is a powerful motivator to always give maximum effort.
One should take personal responsibility for their success by removing 'not working hard enough' as a possible reason for failure.

title: How We Scaled Reddit to 55M Users; Lessons from Zynga
key_insights: Growth should be seen as 'value connection'—connecting users to existing value—rather than 'value creation,' which is the core product team's role.
The first senior growth hire should be made post-product-market fit and should be an experienced product leader who can execute immediately, not just listen and learn for the first 60 days.
To avoid burning out channels like push notifications, set guardrail metrics (e.g., minimum CTR) to force a focus on quality and relevance over volume.
Validate ideas cheaply before investing heavy engineering time, using methods like simple user dialogues asking if they'd want a new feature.
Deeply understanding your user persona (e.g., 'Mary from Ohio' for Words With Friends) is critical for making correct product decisions and avoiding personal biases.
The interview process for a head of growth should test their ability to break down an ambiguous problem (e.g., 'How would you grow Reddit?') into a clear, structured process.
When a team is floundering, foster a culture of ownership where every member feels responsible for finding a solution, rather than waiting for leadership to solve it.
quotable: Growth really should be renamed to something like value connection... there's value that exists in your product and you need to make sure that that value gets connected to each and every single user.
The right candidate just wants to get going... I mean get going as in they want to launch something their second week there or even their first week there should just be itching to execute.
one_liner: Reddit's Head of Growth, Vaibhav Sahgal, shares his playbook on building and scaling growth teams, defining growth as 'value connection', and the hard lessons learned from his time at Zynga and Reddit.

Early-stage AI startups should prioritize speed and user adoption over premature margin optimization. The focus should be on 'flapping faster than the other chickens shot out of a cannon.'

The future of software development will shift from detailed, step-by-step processes to a more unified, AI-driven experience where users provide high-level direction and the AI handles the implementation, design, and even marketing.

title: What is the time to value of B2B Mandate Products? ⏳
key_insights: Mandate products are solutions that new executives make a company-wide priority to implement upon joining, often to drive efficiency or cost savings.
Examples include Workday for HR VPs and Netsuite for CFOs, signifying their established credibility and industry standard status.
These products typically have a long 'time to value' (e.g., 6 months to a year) due to extensive rollout, training, and integration processes.
Despite the long time to value, implementing a mandate product is a 'safe' decision for executives, often leading to promotion rather than termination.
Strong product positioning and branding can allow for a longer time to value, as the product's perceived necessity and benefit are high.

"when your positioning is very unique and very strong you can have a much longer time to Value as well"

title: How To Stay Positive When You're Down 90%?

A downturn of 80-90% in stock prices is viewed as an opportunity, as the five-year expected rate of return increases if the initial research is correct.
During risk-off periods, the strategy is to average down on holdings rather than selling them.
Concentrating portfolios towards the highest conviction names is a key strategy during market downturns, as seen by the ARKK fund reducing its holdings from 58 to 32 names.
External factors like inflation and interest rates can cause a temporary shift away from innovative stocks towards benchmarks, creating buying opportunities for those with long-term conviction.

title: David Lieb on The Contrasting Launch Philosophies of Google Photos vs. Startups
key_insights: The required quality and polish for a product launch is highly contextual; big companies like Google must have a high bar, especially for products handling sensitive user data.

To build trust, the Google Photos team decided the core photo grid had to be exceptionally fast, reliable, and work in all network conditions, a technical challenge that took months to solve.
In contrast to a big company launch, most startups should prioritize shipping a product quickly to learn from users, even if the initial version is embarrassing or imperfect.

Founders must understand their context and the risks they are willing to take; for startups, the biggest risk is often not learning, whereas for large companies, it can be damaging the brand with a poor experience.

title: Zico Kolter: OpenAI's Newest Board Member on The Biggest Questions and Concerns in AI Safety
guest_role: Professor and Head of the Machine Learning Department at Carnegie Mellon / Board Member at OpenAI
key_insights: The ability of word-predictor models to generate intelligent, coherent, long-form responses is one of the most notable scientific discoveries of the last 20 years.

We are not close to hitting the limits of available data for training models; vast amounts of multimodal data (video, audio) exist, with compute power being the primary bottleneck, not data availability.

The biggest immediate AI safety concern is the inability to make models reliably follow specifications, leading to vulnerabilities like prompt injection and jailbreaking, which amplifies all other downstream risks.
The real negative outcome of AI-driven misinformation is not that people will believe fake content, but that they will stop believing anything they see, eroding the concept of objective fact.
We are entering a 'post-architecture' phase in AI, where specific model architectures (like Transformers) matter less than scale, data, and compute.
Cybersecurity is a more clear and present threat from AI than biological or chemical risks, as models can significantly lower the bar for finding and creating exploits in software.
quotable: The real negative outcome is that people are not going to believe anything that they see... it didn't even need AI to get there but AI is absolutely an accelerant for this process.
I think basically models don't matter, architectures don't matter and that that applies to Transformers too... we are arguably in a post-architecture phase.
one_liner: OpenAI board member Zico Kolter discusses the fundamental mechanics of modern AI, breaks down his hierarchy of AI safety concerns, and argues that we are in a 'post-architecture' era where data and compute have eclipsed the importance of specific model designs.

Using frozen meat significantly reduces food waste, as it can be stored for years in a freezer without substantial quality degradation.
Consumer perception often associates tenderness in meat with a healthier, higher-quality product.

title: ButcherBox CEO: What Blue Apron did wrong
key_insights: Blue Apron's major mistake was insisting on building custom software for their fulfillment operations instead of using proven, existing solutions, which led to significant and costly failures.
Founders often err by trying to 'boil the ocean' and control every aspect of the business themselves, which can be a major red flag and is often unsustainable.
For many D2C businesses, unspent marketing dollars translate directly into profit, allowing bootstrapped companies the flexibility to grow at a slower, more sustainable pace.
Out-of-home advertising (billboards, bus wraps) was the worst-performing marketing channel for ButcherBox.

Bootstrapped companies have the luxury of time and are not beholden to investor pressure for rapid growth, enabling them to pursue long-term strategies that venture-backed companies might not have the patience for.
fundraising_mentions: The guest has consistently turned down venture capital for the past five or six years due to a traumatizing fundraising experience with his first company.
quotable: The story I heard about Blue Apron when they opened their New Jersey facility and they insisted that like all the software that runs like all the machines is custom like we're gonna build it ourselves... it's just this big freaking mess.

A lot of Founders try to boil the ocean really fast by worrying about everything at the same time and that just is not conducive in my opinion to... building something that you know people want to support.
one_liner: The CEO of ButcherBox analyzes the operational missteps of competitors like Blue Apron, discusses the challenges of marketing attribution in a bootstrapped D2C business, and explains his rationale for consistently rejecting venture capital.

title: Cerebras CEO, Andrew Feldman on Why Raise $1BN and Delay the IPO & Why NVIDIA’s Worried About Growth
key_insights: In a rapidly moving, uncertain market, large capital commitments should be viewed as 'options on the future' rather than guaranteed purchases.
The primary depreciation driver for AI chips is the performance improvement of future generations; if new chips aren't significantly better, older generations remain viable for longer.
Cerebras's core innovation is using wafer-scale chips to overcome the traditional low-capacity limitation of fast on-chip SRAM, creating a competitive advantage for large model inference.
The major bottlenecks in the AI industry are not just chip supply, but also a shortage of AI expertise, data center capacity, and the slow pace of building new fabrication plants.

True productivity gains from AI will come from fundamentally reorganizing workflows around it, much like the factory floor was reorganized for electricity, rather than just using AI to replace existing tasks like search.
fundraising_mentions: Cerebras raised $1 billion in a pre-IPO round, described as the largest raise in its category.

Risk comes in financial markets where people fundamentally underestimate risk. When risk is priced properly, then what happens is your outcomes are not surprising.
one_liner: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman discusses his company's $1B fundraise, the competitive landscape with NVIDIA, the bottlenecks facing the AI industry, and why their unique wafer-scale chip architecture is built to handle the explosive growth of AI.

title: How much of SUCCESS is based on LUCK? 🍀
key_insights: Success is a combination of circumstantial luck (e.g., birth country, timing of geopolitical events) and deliberate, sustained hard work.
The guest's entire life trajectory was altered by a lucky opportunity to emigrate from the Soviet Union in 1978, which would not have been possible otherwise.
Proactive effort, such as continuous learning, saving money diligently, and strategic networking, is what allows one to capitalize on lucky breaks.
A decade of disciplined saving and hard work enabled the high-conviction decision to invest heavily in Facebook, Twitter, and Tumblr.
Building genuine relationships and providing value is key to positioning oneself for opportunities, moving beyond mere luck.
fundraising_mentions: The guest mentions saving all his money in his 20s and spending it all in a one-year period to invest in Facebook, Twitter, and Tumblr.

saving my money in my 20s and then deciding to spend all of it in a one year period on Facebook Twitter and Tumblr based on at that point 10 years of very hard work diligence... doesn't feel as oriented towards luck as it does towards being thoughtful with the gifts I was given
one_liner: Gary Vaynerchuk reflects on how his success is a product of both immense luck—emigrating from the Soviet Union as a child—and intense, deliberate hard work, culminating in his early, strategic investments in social media.

title: Miro CRO Zhenya Loginov: Hiring Tips for Sales; Why Dropbox Lost Enterprise | 20VC #900
key_insights: If your market includes the enterprise, it's a segment you must win, which requires a company-wide commitment starting from the CEO, not just a GTM-led effort.
The ideal long-term business model is a combination of Product-Led Growth (PLG) and a direct Enterprise sales motion.
Founders should hire a Head of Sales to create the first sales playbook, rather than creating it themselves and hiring junior reps to execute it.
When hiring leaders, look for candidates who have 70% of the required experience and are passionate about learning the other 30%, as this motivation leads to incredible results.
A structured hiring process for leaders should involve the hiring manager spending 4-5 hours with a candidate to deeply vet them before they meet a broader, hand-picked interview panel.

To avoid conflict between PLG and sales-led motions, align incentives by giving one leader responsibility for all revenue (both self-serve and high-touch), even if the teams are structured separately.

The first month for a new leadership hire should be dedicated to learning and building relationships across the company, especially with functions they'll need to partner with a year from now, not just their immediate team.
quotable: I think the biggest one for me from Dropbox was that you have to win the Enterprise Market if your Market kind of includes the Enterprise you you have to figure out as a company how to win the Enterprise Market.

I'm a big believer in enablement and empowerment and I think if the founder hires sales people who he gives the Playbook to that the founder developed, it's going to be less effective and less efficient than if the founder brings in the person and lets them create something that they would feel ownership over.
one_liner: Miro CRO Zhenya Loginov shares his framework for building a dual PLG and enterprise go-to-market machine, including why Dropbox failed to win the enterprise, how to structure sales playbooks, and a detailed process for hiring and onboarding senior sales leaders.

title: Mercor CEO & Co-Founder, Brendan Foody: How They Grew from $1M to $500M in 17 Months
key_insights: Mercor scaled from $1M to $500M in ARR in 17 months, claiming it's the fastest revenue growth of all time.
The AI data market is shifting from low-skill crowdsourcing (pioneered by Scale and Surge) to high-caliber, expert-driven data sourcing for complex RL environments.
Mercor's average marketplace pay rate is $95/hour, significantly higher than competitors, reflecting their focus on quality.
The majority of AI model improvement comes from the top 10-20% of data contributors, making the ability to source and match top-tier talent a key differentiator.

Current AI model evaluations (academic benchmarks like Olympiad math) are disconnected from real-world enterprise needs. The future lies in evals that measure performance on practical, specific tasks.
The company raised its Series B at a 100x revenue multiple ($20M ARR for a $2B valuation), justifying it by the immense market potential and rapid growth trajectory.
Despite being profitable, Mercor is supply-constrained and turns down projects daily, indicating massive unmet demand for high-quality data.
fundraising_mentions: Scaled from $1M to $500M in revenue run rate in 17 months.
Raised a seed/Series A round at a ~$250M valuation on a ~$2M revenue run rate.
Raised a Series B at a $2B valuation on a $20M revenue run rate (a 100x multiple).
Discusses rumors of a potential new round at a $10B valuation.
quotable: We scaled the business from 1 to 500 million in the last 17 months, which is the fastest revenue growth of all time.

I think that one of the largest inefficiencies in all of AI research is that the evals that people have been going on of humanity's last exam and PhD level reasoning or Olympiad math are wholly disconnected from the outcomes that consumers and enterprises actually care about.
one_liner: Mercor's CEO Brendan Foody details the company's unprecedented growth to $500M ARR in 17 months by capitalizing on the market shift towards high-quality, expert-driven data for training advanced AI models and critiques the current state of AI evaluations.

title: Sheel Mohnot: Lessons from Investing in Flexport and Missing on Robinhood | 20VC #917
key_insights: The power law is a tangible force in venture; a single outlier investment can generate returns that dwarf the rest of the portfolio, making small exits relatively insignificant.
Maintaining strict price discipline on initial, pre-seed/seed investments is critical. It's better to negotiate hard for ownership upfront and then be fully supportive, rather than overpaying early.

Capital efficiency is a key determinant of investor returns. A lower exit valuation in a capital-efficient business can yield more profit than a much higher exit in a capital-intensive one due to less dilution.

In a risk-off macro environment, capital retreats from emerging and frontier markets, posing significant fundraising challenges for companies in regions like Africa and Pakistan that lack a mature, self-sustaining local venture ecosystem.

Don't let the failure of one company in a specific category (e.g., Simple in neobanking) create a mental block against investing in that category again; a different team or approach (e.g., Chime) can unlock success.
fundraising_mentions: BTV Fund 1 had 50% reserves; Fund 2 has 60% reserves.
BTV's new fund is $60 million, with a strategy of writing $2 million initial checks for 7-10% ownership in rounds of $3-4 million.
Flexport investment: invested at $0.15/share, sold at $25.40/share.
Chipper Cash investment: first invested at a $2.5 million valuation, with the last round over $2 billion.
A company exited for $230M after an initial investment at a $2.5M valuation.
Top BTV Fund 1 company invested at $12.5M is now valued at $1.2B.
Another top BTV company invested at $2M is now valued at $600M.
quotable: I realized that there are very few monetary things that make me happy. Like I just don't need any material things to be happy.

You can read about the power law, but actually seeing it for me was a big game changer. And you realize actually like, even though I invested in 70 plus companies, there's only a handful of them that really matter.
one_liner: Sheel Mohnot of Better Tomorrow Ventures discusses the critical importance of entry price discipline, the visceral reality of the power law, and lessons from major fintech wins like Flexport and misses like Robinhood.

title: Fighter Pilots & Founders Both Need This ONE SKILL 🛩️
guest_role: Air Force instructor pilot, military strategist
key_insights: Agility and faster decision-making are more crucial than initial correctness, as it allows for rapid adjustment based on feedback.
Taking the initiative and moving quickly disorients opponents and provides an advantage in competitive situations.
The F-16 fighter jet's design prioritized agility (changing direction faster) over straight-line speed, demonstrating the power of rapid adaptation.
The concept of 'getting inside the enemy's decision loop' involves processing information and acting faster than the opposition.
Founders should pre-emptively establish systems and strategies to enable quick, decisive action when facing business crises.
quotable: The best pilot was the most agile pilot.
If I'm moving at twice the rate that you're moving I can adjust to make my next move before you make your first move.
one_liner: This episode delves into the strategic importance of agility and rapid decision-making, as exemplified by fighter pilot John Boyd's philosophy, for both military success and effective entrepreneurial crisis management.

title: Sam Altman & Brad Lightcap: Which Companies Will Be Steamrolled by OpenAI? | E1140
key_insights: There are two strategies for building on AI: one assumes models are static, the other assumes rapid, continuous improvement. 95% of startups should bet on the latter.

Companies building on GPT-4 in a way that will be made obsolete by a more capable GPT-5 will likely be 'steamrolled' by OpenAI's progress, not out of malice, but as a byproduct of its core mission to advance AI.
The long-term differentiation for AI will not be the base model, but the model that is most personalized, has full life context, and is deeply integrated into a user's life.

Enterprises often focus on quantifiable ROI by inserting AI into specific business processes, but criminally underrate the value of giving employees broad access to the technology to improve general productivity in unquantifiable ways.
OpenAI's strategy of 'iterative deployment' is crucial for allowing society to adapt to, react to, and co-develop AI, preventing the shock of a sudden AGI release.
quotable: There are two strategies to build on AI right now there's one strategy which is assume the model is not going to get better and then you kind of like build all these little things on top of it there's another strategy which is build assuming that open air is going to stay on the same rate of trajectory and the models are going to keep getting better at the same Pace it would seem to me that 95% of the world should be betting on the latter category but a lot of the startups have been built in the former category.

If you're building something on open on GPT 4 that a reasonable Observer would say if gp5 is as much better as gp4 over gpt3 was not because we don't like you but just because we like have a mission we're going to steamroll you.
one_liner: OpenAI's Sam Altman and Brad Lightcap discuss the company's rapid scaling, their strategy for AI development, why most AI startups will be 'steamrolled' by progress, and how enterprises should think about adopting the technology.

title: 3 Reasons Bain Capital is Successful
key_insights: Bain Capital's success was initially driven by applying the analytical skills of their consulting practice (Bain & Company) to the businesses they acquired.

A crucial second element is the high degree of alignment with investors, maintained by firm partners personally investing a significant amount of capital (over a billion dollars in a recent $12B fund) alongside LPs.

The firm's global network is a major competitive advantage, allowing them to share expertise across geographies, such as applying European industrial chemical knowledge to a US company or helping an Asian company enter the US market.

One of the biggest challenges in scaling a large investment firm is maintaining investment discipline and a high-performance culture, rather than becoming an 'asset gatherer' focused on deploying capital.

To avoid bottlenecks, Bain's investment committee (IC) operates with extreme responsiveness, convening at any time, and relies on deals being thoroughly vetted through regional processes before reaching the final IC stage.
fundraising_mentions: A $12 billion fund where over $1 billion of capital came from people within the company.

We've never lost a deal because of an IC bottleneck. We have a culture of being extremely responsive, extremely creative, and if we need to have an IC at two in the morning on Monday morning or Sunday night, we will.
one_liner: A Bain Capital partner breaks down the firm's success into three pillars: applying consulting skills, ensuring high investor alignment, and leveraging a global team network, while discussing the challenges of scaling and maintaining investment discipline.

His immigrant experience in the U.S. as a child, sharing one bed with his family, fueled his ambition to achieve economic stability.
Partovi believes the 'American Dream' is broken and strives to create a world where opportunity is available to everyone, specifically through his work at Code.org.
Growing up poor, despite his family's previous wealth, gave him significant grit, hunger, and ambition.
He felt a motivation to 'win back' what was lost by his family due to government actions, framing his success as rectifying an injustice.

"Absolutely growing up with a poor family gave me grit and hunger and ambition."
one_liner: Hadi Partovi, co-founder of Code.org, shares his journey from war-torn Iran to Silicon Valley, explaining how his early struggles as an immigrant fueled his ambition to achieve financial security and his current mission to make the American Dream accessible to all by fixing the opportunity system.

One can live a luxurious lifestyle by renting experiences (like vacation homes) instead of owning them, avoiding the responsibilities of ownership.
When coming into money, it's crucial to seek advice not only from those who handled it well but also from those whose lives were negatively impacted by wealth to learn what pitfalls to avoid.
Inspired by Evan Williams, proactively interviewing other wealthy individuals for practical advice is a valuable strategy for managing new-found fortune.

key_insights: Emerging managers often fail at fundraising because they lack a clear 'North Star' or compelling reason for their fund's existence.
It is critical to articulate why 'now' is the specific right time for your fund's strategy to exist.
Getting 'in the chatter zone' and being discussed by institutional LPs is more important for raising capital than a polished pitch deck.
Pitch decks for emerging managers should be concise, around 5-10 slides, and avoid pontification.
A common mistake is having a disconnect between an operator's prior experience (e.g., late-stage) and their proposed fund strategy (e.g., seed).
Elaborate 'advisor pages' in decks are generally considered useless and make no real difference to LPs.

title: Only 15% of Founders Listen to their VCs
key_insights: Only about 15% of venture-backed founders can truly take and act on difficult feedback, while 25% tolerate it and 60% will resent the person who gave it.

The board member-CEO relationship is complex; many VCs avoid directness, preferring to hint at issues over months, which can be too slow.
A founder's inability to take critical feedback from investors might be a sign of a poor leader who also can't handle feedback from customers or employees.
While it's ideal for a founder to reach a conclusion independently, the infrequent nature of board meetings makes it hard to guide them there without being direct.

True brand building is the result of a thousand authentic actions that create an immediate, trusted feeling for the customer upon seeing your logo.
Directly listen to customer 'ground truth' through channels like email, as it provides more valuable insights than surveys and can inspire major product innovations like the car camera.
Fear can be a powerful motivator; instead of causing paralysis, it can be channeled into over-executing and meticulously planning to avoid failure.
The stress and constraints of near-death business experiences, while painful, can force innovation and lead to a stronger, more resilient company, much like stressed grapes make the best wine.
For a successful acquisition, the founder must fully commit to the new parent company's culture and vision, while the acquirer must respect the acquired company's mission and team.

title: Why Adobe couldn't copy Figma
key_insights: True defensibility does not exist on day one for most startups; it is built over time.
Some exceptional products, like Figma, launch with such high-end engineering and craft that the 'road to the starting line' for competitors is exceptionally long.
A startup's defensibility lies in its ability to innovate and progress faster than a large incumbent can copy its initial product.
Even with immense resources, a large company like Adobe would struggle to catch up to a rapidly evolving startup like Figma, which would not remain static.
Venture capitalists were initially skeptical of Figma's potential, underestimating its long-term defensibility.

title: STARTUP ADVICE: It's Time To Go On Offense
key_insights: To justify a risky, cash-burning business to investors, you must demonstrate a massive addressable market.
Show investors a clear trend of improving unit economics over time, even if they are currently negative.
Provide concrete data and examples for why unit economics will improve, not just 'hopes and prayers'.
A company should only 'go on offense' (e.g., aggressive hiring, marketing spend) after it has secured its survival with sufficient cash reserves.
Downturns can be an opportune time to hire great talent that was previously out of reach.
fundraising_mentions: The guest outlines a strategy for pitching investors when unit economics are poor, focusing on market size and the trajectory of profitability.
quotable: If you have enough cash that you're not worried about survival, then you can think about how to go on offense.
You have to show just how amazing the addressable Market size is and that it's a risk, but it's a risk worth taking because if you win the market it's just worth so much money.
one_liner: A guide for founders on securing investment with challenging unit economics and knowing when to strategically shift from a defensive survival mode to an offensive growth phase.

title: Where Will Value Be Created in an AI World?
key_insights: Lasting value in AI will come from differentiated go-to-market strategies, specialized industry knowledge, and unique data access, rather than from the foundation models alone.
AI models will likely become more differentiated over time, each developing unique characteristics and excelling in specific verticals like coding or creative writing.
The biggest barrier to AI progress is creating evaluation environments that mirror complex, real-world challenges, as current benchmarks don't capture the full scope of professional work.
Designing products around AI requires a new UX paradigm that embraces non-determinism, where model quality, prompting, and evaluation are integral parts of the product design itself.

For AI to become truly indispensable, it must move beyond simple Q&A and unlock significant productivity gains, which requires deep integration into professional workflows and solving complex, multi-step problems.
fundraising_mentions: A mention of 'ad dason from MC recently who obviously raised that big new round'
quotable: I still think we are in like day one around is AI an indispensable part of most people's work and I think the answer is no.

one_liner: Anthropic CPO Mike Krieger discusses where future value will be created in the AI landscape, emphasizing the importance of differentiated data and go-to-market strategies over the models themselves, and how product development must adapt to non-deterministic systems.

title: Beezer Clarkson: Are LPs Open for Business & Why Do LP Incentive Mechanisms Need to Change? | E1073
key_insights: Outperforming early-stage funds (returning 3x or more) almost always have a company that has returned at least the size of the fund; you can't achieve top-tier returns with just singles and doubles.

There's a significant misalignment between LPs and GPs when LP compensation is based on TVPI (Total Value to Paid-In) rather than DPI (Distributions to Paid-In), which can disincentivize taking profits and realizing gains.

The manager selection process is tightening, with a flight to quality and a focus on managers who can demonstrate a path to DPI. The bar is higher for emerging managers to secure institutional capital for Fund II and beyond.

The graduation rate for emerging managers is brutal, with an average 50% breakage between Fund I and Fund II, and a 71% breakage between Fund I and Fund IV, often due to performance, team breakdowns, or an inability to scale their LP base.

Discussion of seed funds needing to be over $100M to lead rounds effectively.

quotable: LPS are not in the same business of risk-taking the way that GPS are you're trying to preserve Capital at some level for all the various reasons.
I appreciate cuz tvpi looked bonkers the last few years people thought it looked different but I think maybe this is the value of being old.
one_liner: Beezer Clarkson of Sapphire Partners provides an LP's perspective on the current venture market, highlighting the growing chasm between paper returns (TVPI) and actual cash distributions (DPI), the critical importance of the power law for fund performance, and the changing dynamics of GP/LP alignment in a more disciplined investing environment.

title: Manufacturing is moving away but China still has one massive advantage
key_insights: China is no longer the cheapest manufacturing location due to rising labor costs, but it remains the world's best and most competent for sophisticated products like electronics.
The average hourly wage in Mexico is now lower than in China, shifting manufacturing for simpler products.
Despite current debates about nationalism vs. globalization, global trade has grown at an average of 4% annually for the last 800 years.
Trade is a uniquely human activity that enables specialization and wealth creation, which is a fundamental driver of its persistence.
Governments may create barriers, but the innate human desire to trade will likely ensure the continued growth of globalization in the long term.
quotable: China is no longer the cheapest manufacturing site in the world but it's the best manufacturing like they're the highest quality highest competency in manufacturing.
I've never seen a dog trade a bone with another dog.
one_liner: Flexport CEO Ryan Peterson explains why China's high-quality manufacturing ecosystem gives it a durable advantage and argues that the fundamental human drive for specialization and trade will overcome current geopolitical headwinds to globalization.

Proactively seeking mentorship from industry leaders can provide invaluable guidance and open doors.
Startups can effectively compete with large corporations for top talent, especially from elite universities.
Personal relationships and direct communication can bypass corporate bureaucracy in high-stakes negotiations like acquisitions.

The liquidation process for a bank's assets can be lengthy, as seen with the Lehman Brothers case, though SVB's more conservative assets should allow for a quicker resolution.
The most favorable outcome is for another financial institution to acquire the failed bank, which would ensure a continuation of operations and immediate access to deposits for the client base.

The common password reset flow that prevents users from reusing their old password creates unnecessary friction for users who are just trying to regain access, not change their password.
The goal should be to get the user logged in with minimum friction, as they are often just trying to access the product, not perform a security update.
