key_insights: Rishi Sunak wakes up between 6 and 7 AM, noting he gets up later due to increased tiredness from his job.
He practices intermittent fasting on some days.
His typical weekday breakfast consists of Greek yogurt and blueberries, with a mid-morning sweet pastry (like a Gail's cinnamon morning bun or pain au chocolat) as a regular indulgence.
Weekend breakfasts are more elaborate, featuring a full cooked breakfast on Saturdays and alternating American-style pancakes or waffles (with crispy bacon, blueberries, and strawberries) on Sundays.
His exercise routine, though impacted by his job, includes Peloton, treadmill sessions, and a Sunday morning HIIT class when possible.
quotable: I get up later than I used to because I'm I'm more tired sadly than I used to be.
I have this problem with uh yeah I need to have this sugary pastry thing uh most mid-mornings.
one_liner: Prime Minister Rishi Sunak discusses his personal morning routine, revealing his breakfast preferences, intermittent fasting habits, and how his demanding job has altered his exercise regimen.

title: Product-Led Growth Tips
key_insights: Combining PLG and traditional hands-on sales simultaneously is not recommended; instead, use the PLG motion to amplify and build out the outbound sales motion.
A common pitfall for PLG companies is having a self-serve product that is too good, which cannibalizes the potential for a future, higher-priced enterprise product.

Effective product differentiation for enterprise tiers must go beyond just SSO and security, including features like legal term negotiation (MSA/DPA), dedicated 24/7 customer support, advanced roles and permissions, and security features like DLP and eDiscovery.
Layering a traditional, expensive sales team on top of a low-priced PLG product is an unsustainable business model.

The right time to build an enterprise sales team is after achieving 1-2 million dollars in ARR, proving product-market fit, being able to quantify the pain you solve, and demonstrating you can sell to customers outside your immediate network.
fundraising_mentions: Advises that a company should have $1-2 million in ARR before starting to build an enterprise sales team.
quotable: If you make your self-serve product too good then it cannibalizes your sales team's revenue and it's really hard to Go reverse.
If you can't be successful as a Founder selling your product, how can you ever expect someone else to be successful?
one_liner: Maggie Hott explains how to strategically layer enterprise sales on top of a product-led growth motion, stressing the importance of early product differentiation and waiting for clear market signals before hiring a sales team.

title: Oren Zeev: 50% of Funds Will Go Out of Business & Why GPs Shouldn't Tell LPs Their Strategy
key_insights: The notion that only growth matters is a dangerous one; it's crucial to build businesses with healthy, sustainable economics rather than pursuing growth at all costs.
The best investment outcomes often look wrong or weird at the outset, as this lack of initial consensus provides a window to build a real moat without intense competition.
In the current era, every investment must be evaluated on whether it's a likely beneficiary of AI; if the answer is neutral or negative, it's a pass.
The venture capital market is bifurcating, with success favoring either massive platforms or specialized boutiques, leaving traditionally sized funds in a 'messy middle' in trouble.

True GP-LP alignment is critical. Zeev practices 'radical alignment' by being the largest LP in every fund, reinvesting all management fees, and taking no salary, ensuring he only makes money when his LPs do.
fundraising_mentions: Zeev's Fund 10 is around $250M.
Zeev's Fund 11 is targeted to be less than $250M.
Discussion of market conditions making it harder to raise funds, with potentially 50% of funds going out of business.
A portfolio company, Decart, raised on an uncapped SAFE that Zeev got converted to a capped note.
quotable: We humans are not truth seekers. We are self- validation machines.
I tell LPS I only have one rule and that rule is that I have no rules.
one_liner: Prominent solo capitalist Oren Zeev shares his contrarian investment philosophy, emphasizing the importance of healthy growth over hype, radical alignment with LPs, and why he believes the best opportunities often look wrong at the start.

title: Adam Fisher: Why Small Markets are Better Than Big Markets | E1106
key_insights: Investing in smaller, niche markets is often better than large, competitive ones as it allows you to become a leader with less competition.
A VC's role is to be a partner who grounds entrepreneurs when they are too optimistic and supports them when they are struggling.
Second-time founders are not always better; avoid those blinded by previous success and prefer those who remain rational and open to feedback.
The ability for a founder to fundraise with ease, even when not meeting their plan, is a critical and often overlooked skill.
The best exits are often engineered by selling just before a company or market reaches its peak, requiring foresight and a close partnership with the CEO.
Don't concentrate capital based on early predictions of winners; it's impossible to know which companies will be massive outcomes, so focus on getting 'base hits' and let winners emerge.
The amount of money a startup is raising is a more important signal than the valuation itself; raising too much money at the seed stage distorts everything.
A great storyteller, in the context of a founder, is one who can effectively communicate with customers and investors in one-on-one settings, not just perform on a stage.
fundraising_mentions: Invested in a tiny fund of $15-20M in 1996.
Was the first institutional investor in both Wix and Fiverr.
Warns against raising too much money, citing entrepreneurs asking for $25M in a first round or AI companies raising $20M seeds.
Mentions the problem of a company raising $50 million at an early stage as inappropriate.
quotable: I see my role as of VC as picking up an entrepreneur when they're like on the ground but also pulling them down when their head's in the clouds.
I don't think that the way you build a big company or the way you get a big exit is by investing in the most ambitious companies growing the fastest; those are also the companies that crash and burn.
one_liner: Bessemer's Adam Fisher shares his contrarian investment philosophy, advocating for patience, strong founder partnerships, and the strategic advantages of targeting smaller markets to achieve significant exits.

title: Donald Tang: How SHEIN Got So Big So Fast - The Fastest Growing Company in History | E1208
topics: Personal philosophy on success and life
key_insights: SHEIN's core is an on-demand business model, producing very small batches (100-200 units) to test market demand before scaling, which reduces unsold inventory to a low single-digit percentage compared to the industry's 25-35%.
The business philosophy is to 'do good first, then do well,' by listening to consumer desires for choice and self-expression, which leads to efficiency gains that are passed back as lower prices.

A proprietary supply chain management software is mandatory for all factory partners, creating a networked system that allows for real-time order allocation and production adjustments based on customer signals.
The company's global expansion strategy is 'glocal' (global-local), aiming to become part of the local community fabric in each of its 150+ markets rather than acting as a foreign entity.
The decision to IPO is driven by a desire to embrace public diligence and scrutiny, making transparency and accountability a formal requirement for the company at its current scale.
fundraising_mentions: The discussion centers on a future IPO as a mechanism for liquidity and to embrace public diligence, rather than specific past fundraising rounds.
quotable: If you want your business to thrive on a global scale you have to become a local community business in Great Britain you want to be a UK company you want to be part of the fabric you don't want to be a some company parachuting in just making money that's not the kind of trend anymore.
Traditional apparel model would be Mass producing the Styles a few designers want you to wear and we literally micro producing the styles that you want us to make.
one_liner: SHEIN's Executive Chairman, Donald Tang, explains the on-demand, technology-driven business model that revolutionized retail by testing trends with small batches, drastically reducing waste, and focusing on hyper-localization to become the fastest-growing fashion company in history.

title: Sam Taylor: How I Became VP of Sales at Loom; Lessons from Dropbox | 20VC #908
key_insights: Early sales hires should act as 'workflow therapists,' focusing on gathering customer insights to inform product and go-to-market strategy, rather than just closing deals.
Founders are the first salespeople and should document their early customer conversations and wins to create the initial sales frameworks for new hires.
When building an early sales team, hire for authentic curiosity and cross-functional collaboration skills, not just a traditional sales background.
Product-led growth (PLG) and enterprise sales are distinct motions; layering on outbound is a 12-18 month process that should be started before it's urgently needed.
Avoid standard variable compensation for the first few sales hires due to a lack of data; instead, use a higher base salary with incentives tied to learning and input metrics.
quotable: I refer to our early sales team as workflow therapists: lay on the couch, tell me all your problems.
I don't love 'playbook' as a term because it sounds rigid... I refer to it as frameworks.
one_liner: Loom's VP of Sales, Sam Taylor, breaks down his frameworks for building early-stage sales teams, from the founder's first sale to balancing product-led growth with an enterprise motion and hiring the right talent.

title: The most under appreciated breakthrough in crypto
key_insights: A private key, which grants ownership of digital assets, is simply a set of ones and zeros originating from code.
Code can be written to generate and hold a private key without ever revealing it to a human.
A smart contract is a piece of code that can custody money, effectively becoming the owner of those assets.
This creates an entirely new type of entity that is non-human, not a corporation, and does not exist within a traditional legal jurisdiction.
These non-jurisdictional, code-based entities can custody billions of dollars, which has massive, yet underappreciated, implications.
quotable: What that means is you could send money to the smart contract and you don't own the money anymore now a piece of code owns the money.

Now you have a non-human non-business entity that doesn't have a Social Security number or tin it like doesn't exist as far as the government is concerned and it doesn't live in a jurisdiction and it can custody billions of dollars and you look at that you're like wow that's kind of crazy what are the implications of that.
one_liner: Smart contracts are an underappreciated breakthrough because they create a new type of non-human, non-jurisdictional entity that can custody billions of dollars, fundamentally changing the nature of ownership.

title: Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's Favourite Book
guest_role: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
key_insights: Rishi Sunak's favorite author is Roald Dahl.
His favorite books by Roald Dahl are the autobiographical works 'Going Solo' and 'Boy'.
He also admires 'A Suitable Boy' by Vikram Seth.
He lists 'The Count of Monte Cristo' as a favorite.
He includes 'To Kill a Mockingbird' by Harper Lee among his favorite books.
quotable: I absolutely loved all Roald Dahl books, 'Going Solo' is one of my all-time favorite books.
one_liner: Prime Minister Rishi Sunak shares his all-time favorite author, Roald Dahl, and lists 'Going Solo', 'A Suitable Boy', and 'The Count of Monte Cristo' as some of his most-loved books.

title: The time Steve Jobs tried to buy Dropbox
key_insights: Steve Jobs personally tried to acquire Dropbox in a private meeting.
Jobs pitched Apple as a 'startup with unlimited resources' to persuade the founders.
When the acquisition offer was declined, Jobs' tone shifted from charming to threatening.
Jobs famously dismissed Dropbox as 'a feature, not a product' and vowed to 'kill' it with a competing Apple service.
The guest's primary goal during the meeting was to de-escalate the situation and avoid provoking a more aggressive competitive response from Apple.
fundraising_mentions: An acquisition offer from Apple was discussed, but no specific financial numbers were mentioned in the transcript.
quotable: You guys are a feature, not a product.
I wanted to leave that meeting with no action items.
one_liner: Dropbox co-founder Drew Houston recounts his intimidating meeting with Steve Jobs, who went from attempting to acquire Dropbox to threatening to destroy it after the offer was declined.

title: Facebook beat their competitor in Japan by changing ONE WORD in their registration process
key_insights: Cultural nuances significantly impact user conversion and growth in different markets.
A seemingly minor change in wording ('invites' to 'announcements') can have a dramatic positive effect on user adoption.
Direct invitations were perceived as rude in Japanese culture, hindering Facebook's initial growth.
By reframing the action as an 'announcement,' Facebook aligned with cultural expectations, encouraging user engagement.
This linguistic adaptation transformed Japan from one of Facebook's slowest to fastest-growing countries, leading to market leadership.
quotable: it's just a cultural thing it's rude it's considered rude to invite people to a new thing like this

just by changing the wording it was more cultural accepted and Japan went from one of our slowest growing countries to one of our fastest growing countries and shortly after that we surpassed our our local competitor in Japan
one_liner: Facebook achieved rapid growth and surpassed its local competitor in Japan by culturally adapting its user invitation process, changing 'invites' to 'announcements' to align with local customs.

title: VC ADVICE: How to Know When To Sell
key_insights: Deciding when to sell is one of the most difficult aspects of venture capital.
The best strategy is not to perfectly time the market, but to sell in stages to de-risk over time.
Selling decisions depend on two main factors: the fundamentals of the specific company and the broader macro-economic environment.
There should be a bias towards selling when you believe both the company and the market are overvalued.
In fairly valued markets, the decision to sell should be based on your conviction in the individual company.
quotable: It's probably the hardest part of venture capital is deciding when to sell.
If you really think a company's overvalued and the Market's overvalued you know then you're going to have a bias to action and a bias to sell.
one_liner: A venture capitalist shares his strategy on when to sell portfolio companies, emphasizing a staged approach based on company fundamentals and macro conditions rather than trying to perfectly time the market.

title: Roger Ehrenberg: Why VC Returns Will Get Worse & Why LP Incentive Structures are so Broken | E1117
key_insights: VC returns are expected to compress due to a massive influx of capital from new sources like sovereign wealth funds, making the asset class more institutionalized.
Traditional LP incentive structures are broken, often enabling managers to raise successive funds without returning capital (DPI), though new, large LPs are more focused on after-fee returns.

The venture industry is bifurcating into large, multi-stage asset management corporations and specialized, boutique early-stage firms, with the latter remaining a non-commoditized, high-touch business.
In the current environment of closed IPO and M&A markets, continuation funds are emerging as a critical mechanism for providing liquidity to LPs and GPs.

The ability to withstand short-term pain for long-term gain is a superpower in venture, and managing the psychology of when to exit (distribute vs. hold) is one of the hardest challenges for a fund manager.
fundraising_mentions: IA Ventures Fund 1 was a $50 million fund.
IA Ventures Fund 2 was a $105 million fund.
The sale of Simple to BBVA for $117M provided recycling capital for Fund 1.
A secondary sale of Wise shares returned half of Fund 2.
The investment in The Trade Desk returned 5-6x net on a single trade for a ~$250-300 million DPI from a $5.2 million investment.
quotable: Venture is never going to be commoditized... I think incubation, pre-seed, and Seed will always occupy a different place in the universe.

The ability to withstand short-term pain for long-term gain is a superpower. So being able to manage your own internal stress and to let a thesis play out even if it's unpopular and unconventional can lead to amazing compound returns.
one_liner: Veteran investor Roger Ehrenberg discusses the structural shifts in venture capital, arguing that while massive capital inflows will compress overall returns and commoditize later stages, the early-stage boutique model will persist, forcing LPs and GPs to navigate broken incentives and scarce liquidity through new mechanisms like continuation funds.

title: Windsurf CEO & Co-Founder, Varun Mohan: AI's Biggest Acquisition to Date!
key_insights: Startups succeed by picking non-conventional ideas but must be humble enough to pivot quickly when a weird idea proves to be a bad one.
Being first to market provides a learning advantage, allowing a company to discover dead ends and be first to the next idea.
A startup's only real moat is speed and the ability to learn and iterate faster than competitors, as compounding knowledge is hard to replicate.
When developing new products, start with a small team; if even the 'crappy version' of the idea is amazing, it has legs and is worth resourcing further.
Startups don't fail because they are messy internally; they fail because they don't do the one right thing well enough.
The future of software development will see a spectrum of 'engineers,' from those using natural language abstractions to those who can go deep into critical, complex systems.
Asynchronous AI agents will likely handle simple, well-defined tasks first, as user expectations for quality are incredibly high for long-running, complex tasks.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a Series A for the previous company idea (GPU virtualization) led by Greenoaks.
Greenoaks also led their seed round.
quotable: One of the weird things about startups is that you don't win an award for doing the same wrong thing for longer.
When you have a new great idea, even the crappy version of that idea is already amazing.
one_liner: Windsurf CEO Varun Mohan discusses the journey of pivoting from GPU virtualization to a leading AI code agent, emphasizing the importance of speed, focus, and radical realism in building a successful startup in the fast-evolving AI landscape.

title: Why Offering Discounts is a Mistake
key_insights: Exploding discounts create a horrible customer experience.
For early-stage companies, the focus should be on learning and acquiring good-fit customers who will improve the product, not on the initial contract value.
Aligning price to the value delivered is more important than the discount offered.
As a company matures, pricing discipline becomes crucial because customers value fairness and transparency over just a low price.
To create a compelling event for a sale, you must demonstrate how your product will help the customer make money, save money, reduce risk, or go to market faster.
quotable: Early days I think the only thing that matters is that you're learning and that you have good customers who are good fits that are going to drive your product forward.
Customers don't want to not pay a lot of money... they want to know that you're not fleecing them, right? They want to know they're getting a fair price.
one_liner: A sales leader explains why early-stage startups should prioritize customer learning over revenue and how to strategically approach pricing and discounts as the company scales.

title: What does the future of work look like when AI is writing code?
key_insights: 41% of code is now generated by AI, indicating a major shift in software development.
Coding has been progressively getting easier, and generative AI is the next leap, moving towards natural language-based instructions.
Computer science education must adapt to this change, focusing on higher-level concepts rather than low-level skills that are becoming automated.
Just as you would review an AI-written essay, developers will need to understand and verify AI-generated code, making computer science fundamentals still relevant.
While reskilling the current workforce is important, properly educating the 1.5 billion students currently in the education system for a digital future is a critical priority.
Automation will not just destroy jobs but change them, potentially alleviating shortages in essential fields like teaching and nursing.
quotable: The future of code and the past of code have all had this Progressive it gets easier and easier to code.
If you use generative AI to write an essay you still need to read that essay... you want to read it and confirm that the AI did the thing that you wanted.
one_liner: Hadi Partovi discusses how AI is rapidly making coding more accessible through higher-level, natural language commands, forcing a necessary evolution in computer science education and the reskilling of the global workforce.

title: The Dangers of Holding Last Round Valuation
key_insights: Holding onto a previous, inflated valuation is detrimental to a startup.
It creates an artificial valuation that doesn't align with current market realities.
This makes it difficult to accurately determine 409a valuations for employee stock options.
It is not being intellectually honest with employees who know the valuation is not accurate.
Public companies' valuations are dynamic and reflect their operating performance, a practice private companies should emulate.
fundraising_mentions: raising some heavily structured security to preserve value
quotable: I actually think that's the most dangerous thing the company can do because then you do create a a challenge because you create an artificially High valuation that's not consistent with where current values are.
you're also not just being intellectually honest like in a public company you know when Facebook stock goes down they take action the stock goes up right
one_liner: A discussion on the perils for startups of clinging to high valuations from previous funding rounds in a down market.

title: Should Startups Hire Advisors & How much should they be paid?
key_insights: The most powerful business lever is aligning incentives between the company's business model and customer value, a key to success in marketplaces like Yelp and consumer products like Chime.
Founders should never delegate the strategy for their primary growth lever; they must own it, even while leveraging expert advisors for guidance.

A successful framework for company focus involves categorizing all activities as either 'Offense' (a few high-leverage bets to push the business to the next level) or 'Defense' (protecting against downside risk, done up to a point of diminishing returns).
To incubate a 'zero to one' product within a larger company, it's crucial to create a carved-out, autonomous unit where the leader has full P&L responsibility, treating it like an internal startup.
The role of a startup advisor is evolving from high-level, infrequent meetings to a 'hands-on' model involving weekly, deep engagement where the advisor acts as a thought partner.

When evaluating advisor compensation, fractional roles can be benchmarked against a scaled-down full-time salary, while hands-on advisors who can 'bend the curve' of the business can command a mix of cash and month-to-month vesting equity.
Focusing product teams on 'churn' is a mistake; the focus should be on retention, which is most effectively driven by improving new user activation and habit formation around the core product value.
fundraising_mentions: Advises companies from Seed to Series C.
Discusses incubating internal 'startups' that would go through funding-like stages (Seed, Series A) internally.
quotable: The whole point of strategy is to say no to most things and focus in on a small number of really high leverage things.
Incentive alignment is the most powerful lever you have in a business.
If you're trying to do true zero to one inside of a later Stage Company... trying to do it inside of the sort of Legacy product product org vastly reduces your chances of success.
one_liner: Product and growth expert Eli Lerner breaks down the role of startup advisors, detailing how to structure engagements, determine compensation, and apply his 'offense vs. defense' framework to drive focused growth.

title: Mac the VC on the Journey from Homeless To Becoming A VC
topics: Breaking into venture capital without a traditional background
Raising a venture fund publicly on Twitter
Critiques of the traditional VC industry, including fundraising and diversity
Pre-seed investment strategy and portfolio construction
The structure of rolling funds vs. traditional funds with modern features
Advice for emerging managers on being bold and creating their own rules
The importance of LP and allocator diversity for systemic change
key_insights: It's possible to break into venture capital through non-traditional paths by leveraging unique experiences and being resourceful.
The 'rules' of venture capital, from fundraising structures to GP commits, are often just conventions that can be re-written.
Leveraging public platforms like Twitter combined with a 506(c) designation can be a powerful strategy for emerging managers to raise a fund.
A 'hot deal' backed by top-tier funds is not necessarily a 'good deal' that will return capital; focus should be on fundamental business quality.
Systemic change in VC diversity requires more than superficial hires; it must start with the LPs and allocators at the top of the capital stack.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a $10M fund (Rare Breed Fund I).
Used Twitter to source LPs, conducting over 1100 meetings to soft-circle the first $2M.
Structured the fund using 506(c) to publicly solicit investors.
Had no GP commit.
Offered LPs flexible capital call options (100% upfront, or spread over 2 or 3 years).
Minimum check size from LPs was $10k per year.
Executed 'rolling closes' every three weeks to access capital quickly.
quotable: [F--k] the rules like these are all just legal structures they can be changed.
A hot deal does not mean a good deal... why are you qualifying my returns based on somebody else's previous success? Stupid.
one_liner: Mac the VC details his unconventional journey to raising a $10 million venture fund on Twitter, challenging the industry's established rules on fundraising, diversity, and what defines a successful investor.

title: UK vs. France vs. California: Who has the lowest capital gains taxes?
key_insights: The UK is introducing an unsponsored, points-based visa not linked to a specific job to attract top talent.
A new 'scale-up' visa is being launched to help high-growth companies hire talent, expanding on a recommendation from the fintech sector.
The Global Talent Visa's eligibility criteria will be broadened to include a wider range of accomplishments.
Reforms to the Innovator Visa are planned to make it easier for entrepreneurs to found businesses in the UK.
The Global Entrepreneur Program will be expanded to proactively recruit top talent from international universities.
quotable: I want this to be the best place for people to come I want us to be able to attract the best and the brightest.

My vision is we you know we have a UK person who's at Stanford trying to figure out who the best and brightest are over there and and come and attract them to the UK whilst they're actually doing their MBA or their computer science degree or whatever it might be.
one_liner: UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak details a series of far-reaching visa and immigration reforms aimed at making the UK the world's most supportive country for attracting and retaining high-skilled talent for growing companies.

title: Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone: The Yahoo Turnaround Plan | 20VC #911
key_insights: High-performing teams are built on four pillars: domain expertise, high EQ, natural ambition, and a genuine 'love of the game' for the specific company or industry.
Effective leadership in a downturn involves protecting the balance sheet, viewing the crisis as an opportunity, and being a source of optimism while remaining grounded and adaptable.
Successful turnarounds are possible when a company has 'good bones': significant traffic, a well-known brand, underdeveloped but sticky products, and an organization ripe for optimization.

To maintain execution speed at scale, leaders should focus on unblocking talented teams and creating a 'federal and state' model where general managers are empowered as CEOs of their own business units.
Prioritization is a balanced breakfast of short, medium, and long-term goals, all centered on the ROI for growth, which encompasses user experience, retention, and monetization in harmony.
fundraising_mentions: Raised $50 million for his first Web 1.0 startup which later crashed.
Mentioned his second startup, Clicker, was funded by Bill Gurley and Jeff Yang right before the 2008 crash, and he offered to give the money back.
quotable: Never mistake activity for achievement.
I truly believe your company values are the people you hire. Like that is 90% of it.
one_liner: Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone discusses his playbook for executing corporate turnarounds, building high-performing teams, and navigating economic crises, drawing on his extensive experience at companies like Ask Jeeves, CBS Interactive, and Tinder.

title: Raman Malik: Inside Perplexity’s Growth Machine: What Worked, What Did Not Work | E1226
key_insights: Growth is an independent function bridging product (optimizing the user funnel) and marketing (using channels and campaigns to drive the funnel).
Perplexity's growth is ~80% organic word-of-mouth, supplemented by aggressive partnership deals which are more effective for distribution than direct advertising.
A key activation metric for Perplexity is getting a user to three queries in their first session, as this strongly correlates with long-term retention.
Micro-optimizations in retention are underrated and can raise the entire active user base, but taking big, high-risk swings quarterly is crucial for breakthrough growth.
Paid acquisition is used sparingly for testing specific audiences (e.g., 18-24 year olds on TikTok) rather than broad acquisition, to avoid cannibalizing strong organic growth.
When hiring for growth, look for a 'taste' for what good looks like and a founder's mentality of being comfortable with taking big swings and failing.
quotable: You need someone to hear about your product three to seven times before they're going to give it an honest trial.
There's no middle ground if you're not first it literally just means you're only other option is to just be a lot better than everyone else.
one_liner: Perplexity's Head of Growth shares their strategy of focusing on organic growth, strategic partnerships, and a key activation metric (three queries in the first session) over paid acquisition to build a sustainable growth machine.

title: Bill Ackman wants to give $7000 to every baby
key_insights: Wealth inequality is a significant societal problem that poses a risk of social unrest.
The key to addressing wealth inequality is to ensure everyone has ownership in the growth of the economy, not just through wages but through asset appreciation.
A proposed solution is to create a government-funded, tax-exempt investment account for every newborn (e.g., $7,000), which could grow to $1 million by retirement through compounding.
Specific tax loopholes, such as like-kind exchanges in real estate and borrowing against stock appreciation without taxation, exacerbate wealth inequality and should be closed.
Taxing loans taken against appreciated assets (beyond the original cost basis) would be a logical and fair reform, unlike a general wealth tax which could stifle entrepreneurship.
quotable: My idea was you give every baby that's born in America you know whatever like a seven thousand dollar account... when they're born and they can't remove money from that account and it's tax exempt and it compounds... by the time you're 65 it's a million dollars.

If you're borrowing five billion dollars against your Tesla stock and you've borrowed more than your basis in the Tesla stock I think the distribution from that kind of borrowing should be taxable because it's really tantamount to a sale.
one_liner: Bill Ackman argues for giving every newborn a government-funded investment account to combat wealth inequality and suggests specific tax reforms to make the system fairer for all Americans.

title: Anthropic Raises $13BN & OpenAI Buys Statsig for $1.1BN All Stock
key_insights: Hyper-growth AI companies like Anthropic command massive valuations because their extreme revenue acceleration can justify the price on a forward-looking basis, despite the high absolute numbers.

Established SaaS leaders are experiencing re-accelerated growth by integrating AI 'workhorses' rather than 'gimmicks' into their core products, with AI contributing significantly but not being the sole driver.

The cost of AI is substantial, with large software companies budgeting up to 10% of revenue for compute and model usage, viewing it as a near-term marketing and R&D cost that will be optimized over time.
For highly profitable, late-stage private companies like Canva, the primary motivation to IPO shifts from capital raising to providing structured liquidity for employees and early investors.

In venture capital, passing on a company early doesn't preclude future investment; seeing a team execute on their promises over time is a powerful signal that can justify investing in a later, more expensive round.
The rise of LLMs is shifting content discovery, creating a new field of 'LLM SEO' where having a strong brand and valuable product can lead to being a top referral source from platforms like ChatGPT.
fundraising_mentions: Anthropic raised $13 billion at a $183 billion valuation.
OpenAI acquired Statsig for $1.1 billion in an all-stock deal.
Canva's valuation is discussed at $42 billion, with a past valuation of $40 billion and a dip to $26 billion. Their current round is a secondary.
Lovable raised a round at a $4 billion valuation, up from $1.8 billion just months prior.
Versel is reportedly working on a $9 billion round.
Figma's successful IPO is used as a benchmark for private company valuations and IPO strategy.
quotable: We're all about creating workh horses, not gimmicks, into Canva.
The markets will do what they're going to do, but as a company, we can compound growth. We can compound margins and increase margins and we can deliver value to our customers first and foremost.
one_liner: Canva's COO discusses the massive valuations of AI leaders, the strategic decisions behind staying private versus pursuing an IPO, and how established SaaS companies are leveraging AI for growth while managing its significant costs.

title: EXPLAINED: Public Market CEO vs Private Market CEO
key_insights: Transitioning from a private to a public CEO role involves a massive shift from managing a small, trusting board to a large, impersonal investor base that requires constant, political-style communication.
Public company validation and access to a larger investor pool are significant upsides, despite the communication overhead.
Employees often misunderstand stock market fluctuations, attributing broad market trends to company-specific issues, which requires proactive education from leadership.
It is critical to distinguish between general market/peer group stock movements and company-specific performance, especially around earnings announcements.

For top-tier software companies, the market's expectation is perfection; delivering strong results (e.g., 46% growth with 41% margins) can still lead to a stock drop if it's not perceived as flawless.
fundraising_mentions: The company went public after having private equity investors for several years.
quotable: It is a pain in the ass being a public market CEO in this environment... if it was Private you're like guys, it's [__] but we're gonna get through it in this way. Now you have to be the politician.
We grew 46% with 41% operating margins... so look we showed up good we just didn't show up perfect and in moments where you don't show up perfect and perfect is the expectation this is what happens.
one_liner: A public company CEO contrasts the intense communication and political challenges of managing a public entity with the trust-based relationships of a private one, especially in a volatile market.

title: Andrew Feldman, Cerebras Co-Founder and CEO: The AI Chip Wars & The Plan to Break Nvidia's Dominance
key_insights: The fundamental architecture of GPUs, with off-chip memory (HBM), is a significant bottleneck for inference workloads due to slow data movement. Cerebras' wafer-scale approach allows for massive on-chip SRAM, providing superior memory bandwidth and speed for inference.

The AI industry is far from mature; there is immense room for improvement in algorithms (moving beyond Transformers), data (shifting towards synthetic data for targeted training), and compute efficiency (current GPU utilization in inference is only 5-7%).
Nvidia's moat is less about 'Cuda lock-in' (which is non-existent for inference) and more about their dominant market-share leader status, making them the default choice.

The cost of inference will decrease as a result of more efficient algorithms, better data center infrastructure, and improved chip performance, unlocking new applications and accelerating the diffusion of AI into everyday life.

To succeed as a hardware challenger, building large strategic partnerships (like the one with g42) is crucial to prove scalability, harden software on large clusters, and build the organizational muscle required for massive growth.
fundraising_mentions: The g42 deal was estimated at north of a billion dollars.
Nvidia was worth $10 billion in 2014.
The host mentions his '$400 million fund'.
quotable: The fundamental architecture of the GPU with off-chip memory is not great for inference. Now they will continue to do well in inference, but it can be beaten and I think they know it.
Our AI algorithms today are not particularly efficient. In a GPU most of the time it's doing inference, it's 5 or 7% utilized. That means it's 95 or 93% wasted.
one_liner: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman explains why the fundamental architecture of GPUs is ill-suited for the coming wave of AI inference and how his company's wafer-scale chip design offers a faster, more efficient alternative to challenge Nvidia's dominance.

title: Is a $4.5BN Exit Enough in VC? & Harvey Raises $150M & Why Google is a Buy and Amazon is a Sell
guest_role: Founder @ SaaStr & Partner @ Scale Venture Partners
key_insights: The benchmark for a successful VC exit has dramatically increased, where even a $4.5 billion IPO like Navan's is considered potentially insufficient for large venture funds.

The age of AI is bifurcating the market: hyper-growth AI-native companies are commanding massive valuations, while even successful pre-AI SaaS companies must demonstrate AI-driven re-acceleration to remain relevant and avoid low-multiple PE buyouts.

VC ownership targets are under pressure; both highly capital-efficient startups and massively capital-intensive AI companies are leading to lower equity stakes for investors, challenging traditional fund models.
There is immense pressure on established tech companies and their leadership teams to leverage AI for growth; failing to show re-acceleration from AI initiatives is seen as a major failure.
A founder's optimized, incremental fundraising strategy often directly conflicts with a VC's goal of achieving a target ownership percentage, a central tension in the current market.

The massive, multi-trillion dollar capex commitments for AI by companies like OpenAI and Meta are met with significant market skepticism regarding the unproven revenue models to support such spending.

OpenAI's plan to fund a trillion dollars in capex.
Andreessen Horowitz investing in Harvey's $150M round.
Benchmark accepting a 10% ownership stake in a deal, down from their traditional 20% target.

For me, it's like I don't even want to take meetings with mortal founders.
one_liner: VCs Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll debate whether a $4.5B IPO is a meaningful exit in the current climate, analyze Harvey's massive AI-driven valuation, and discuss the immense pressure on all companies to adapt or become irrelevant in the age of AI.

title: Brian Singerman: How I Became a Partner at Founders Fund, Why We Put $400M into Anduril | 20VC #943
key_insights: Venture capital is a game of upside maximization, not downside minimization; focus on finding the best companies and don't get bogged down by protective terms.
The core investment strategy is to put the most money possible into the best companies possible at the best price possible.
Do not try to predict macroeconomic cycles. Instead, focus on fundamentals you can assess, like founder and company quality.
A successful venture firm should be built by hiring partners with unique, differentiated strengths and 'moats', rather than hiring clones.
When starting out, raise as small of a fund as possible to maximize the chances of delivering exceptional returns, which builds the track record for future, larger funds.
Meeting founders in person is critical for assessing quality, a process that cannot be replicated over Zoom.
fundraising_mentions: Founders Fund invested $200 million into Anduril in 2022, for a total of $400 million invested in the company.
Founders Fund invested $150 million into Airbnb at a $1.5 billion valuation.
quotable: I don't pontificate. I invest.
I have no dogmas about how the world should be, how the world will be, how the world is. I'm open to unique angles of any type.
one_liner: Founders Fund Partner Brian Singerman details his investment philosophy focused on maximizing upside through large, concentrated bets in the best companies, highlighting their $400M investment in Anduril and the importance of ignoring macroeconomic predictions.

title: Why SVB is Actually the Safest Bank in America
key_insights: SVB and Signature Bank now have an explicit, unlimited US government guarantee on all deposits, making them ironically the safest banks.

A three-tier banking system has been created: explicitly guaranteed banks (SVB, Signature), implicitly guaranteed systemically important banks (JPM, BofA, Citi), and the rest with the standard $250,000 FDIC limit.
This new tiered system is confusing for consumers and businesses.
The loss of general confidence in the banking system is a major problem, as nuances get lost in headlines, leading to bank runs.
Large, systemically important banks are perceived as safer, causing a flow of capital towards them from smaller regional banks.
quotable: The irony is... there's sort of two banks that now have an explicit guarantee regardless of how much money you put in those Banks right that's signature and Silicon Valley Bank.
We've created this now three tier uh guarantee system which is very confusing to Consumers.
one_liner: David Sacks discusses the ironic outcome of the 2023 banking crisis, where government intervention made SVB and Signature the safest banks, creating a confusing three-tiered system for depositors.

title: How I Got Sanctioned by Russia -- Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince
key_insights: Cloudflare detected Russia's probing activities in late 2021, similar to patterns seen before other military actions in Georgia and Crimea.
The company provided its services at no cost to Ukrainian government and infrastructure companies to ensure they remained online during the invasion.
Keeping Ukrainian infrastructure online was crucial for President Zelenskyy's communication and for documenting atrocities during the war.
As a result of these actions, Matthew Prince was personally sanctioned by the Russian government, alongside other tech executives like Marc Benioff and Mark Zuckerberg.
Cloudflare's technology is also used by activists, such as women organizing protests in Iran, for private and secure communication.
quotable: I've been personally sanctioned by the Russian government which is somewhat surreal but like I'm super proud of that and I'm proud of the fact that we um helped are continuing to help um Ukraine win win the war.
I think that that success and anonymity is like the best possible thing.
one_liner: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince discusses how his company helped keep Ukraine's internet infrastructure online during the Russian invasion, leading to him being personally sanctioned by the Russian government.

title: Why did Snap shut down Zenly?
key_insights: Incumbent social media companies are moving away from reliance on the social graph.
The social graph is no longer a defensible moat and is becoming commoditized.
Distributing content through the social graph is not an efficient means of generating user engagement.
Guaranteed content distribution via the social graph creates significant and expensive content moderation burdens.
The business model of providing free, guaranteed distribution is inefficient for driving return on investment (ROI).
quotable: It [the social graph] is not defensible anymore it's actually very easily commoditized.

What these platforms were doing was they were effectively giving away free distribution that was more or less guaranteed potentially very expensive for them in terms of content moderation and maybe not really that efficient in terms of engagement.
one_liner: An analysis of why large social media platforms are shifting away from the social graph as a core distribution model because it has become a commoditized, inefficient, and costly strategy.

title: Larry Shurtz: How to Hire, Train & Retain the Best Vertical Teams | E1151
key_insights: Effective sales leadership hinges on ruthless prioritization, focusing only on people, executing the number, and customer success, as trying to do too much leads to burnout and team dysfunction.
The most critical aspect of scaling a sales team is hiring the right talent; avoid rushing the process for 'hot candidates' as hiring mistakes are incredibly costly and time-consuming to fix.
A successful vertical sales playbook requires specialization across the entire customer-facing organization (AEs, SEs, CS, Services), not just the sales reps, to deliver true value.
Accurate sales forecasting is a non-negotiable part of a sales leader's brand and requires deep business understanding, customer diligence, and speaking to the right people.
Empathy is a core, difficult-to-train leadership trait that is more critical for retaining top talent than compensation; a lack of it leads to poor culture and high attrition.
quotable: If you can't forecast accurately either you don't truly understand your business, you aren't truly doing the amount of diligence with customers and opportunities, you don't have enough opportunities to be able to balance out some of the riskier things with some of the things that look better and we might not even be asking the right questions and we're likely not talking to the right people.
Bad decisions are made when you compress timelines and don't know people.
one_liner: A seasoned CRO shares his comprehensive playbook on hiring, training, and retaining elite vertical sales teams, emphasizing the importance of ruthless prioritization, deep customer empathy, and building a robust, full-funnel sales process.

title: How to Build Anti-Fragile Venture Portfolios Today
key_insights: To assess a company's fundamental value during a downturn, ask: 'Would you put a single dollar into this company at a zero valuation?' This separates real businesses from market momentum plays.
Build an 'anti-fragile' portfolio not through a high number of investments, but by diversifying the types of risks across different end markets, go-to-market motions, and capital requirements.
Solo VCs provide a specific 'product' for entrepreneurs: high-impact advice and support without dominating the cap table, allowing founders to craft their ideal syndicate.
Embrace uncertainty, which is inherent in VC, but use a consistent framework for decision-making to reduce anxiety and systematically evaluate opportunities.
Effective board participation, especially at the early stage, involves a high-cadence of problem-solving outside of formal meetings, rather than using boards as a reporting forum.
fundraising_mentions: Day one investment can be $1-3 million.
Series A investments can be up to $8 million from his funds.
Chalfen Ventures funds are sub-$100 million.
quotable: The first question is would you put a single dollar into each of these companies at a zero valuation and what he was asking was is this a fundamentally good business or was were you just playing the market were you just playing the dot-com boom and that has always stayed with me.
You're not looking for proof of unit economics but you've got to imagine all the levers clicking into place so that good unit economics emerge.
one_liner: Veteran solo GP Mike Chalfen discusses his framework for building concentrated, anti-fragile venture portfolios by focusing on fundamental business value, navigating market cycles with discipline, and providing high-impact support to founders.

title: Wayne Ting, CEO @Lime: From Losing $3 on Every $1 to $90M in EBITDA | E1252
key_insights: Lime's turnaround was driven by a relentless focus on unit economics and operational efficiency, fixing a model that initially lost $3 for every $1 of revenue with a 3% daily hardware decay rate.
Investing in proprietary, differentiated hardware was crucial for improving vehicle lifespan from 30 days to over 5 years, which was key to achieving profitability.
The introduction of swappable batteries cut operational costs by half and, combined with software to optimize tasks, dramatically improved the business's core economics.
Achieving free cash flow positivity was a critical turning point, allowing the company to fund its own growth and capital expenditures without relying on the VC fundraising treadmill.

Leadership requires a hands-on, data-driven approach ('game of inches'); the quality of local general managers who were physically present and accountable was the biggest differentiator between profitable and unprofitable markets.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a $140 million emergency funding round during COVID.
The COVID round was led by Uber, who also sold their Jump micro-mobility business to Lime as part of the deal.
The deal that included acquiring Jump was a 'down round' for previous investors.
quotable: When I first joined line we were losing $3 for every dollar of Revenue the daily Decay rate was 3% so in the course of 30 days your entire fleet was gone so the business was completely upside down.
It's doing a thousand little things right. It is a true game of inches and when you do a thousand little things better than your competitor then you have a different business model.
one_liner: Lime CEO Wayne Ting shares the story of the company's incredible turnaround, from near bankruptcy with unsustainable unit economics to achieving $90 million in EBITDA through a relentless focus on operational improvements, proprietary hardware, and data-driven decision making.

title: Three reasons why you need a co-founder 🧐
key_insights: A co-founder should have skills that are complementary to your own.
Founders need a trusted partner to discuss sensitive topics they can't share with the board, management, or their family.
A co-founder can provide crucial support and carry the company's load during a founder's personal or family issues.
When a founder is feeling down, a co-founder can lift them up and offer different perspectives.
The argument that the most successful tech leaders (Zuckerberg, Jobs, Musk) were lone founders is debatable, as they often had pivotal partners (Wozniak, Sergey Brin, Gwynne Shotwell).
quotable: You need a partner who you can share all the things you can't talk to the board about or you can't talk to the management team about.
You need somebody who when you're down can lift you up or can see things that you don't see.
one_liner: A debate on the necessity of a co-founder, highlighting the need for complementary skills and emotional support versus the examples of historically successful solo founders.

title: Dan Fougere, CRO @Datadog: Why Discounting is Dangerous and Contract Sizes are Misleading | E1229
key_insights: Sales qualification requires intellectual honesty to find weaknesses ('the dirt') in a deal, using frameworks like MEDDIC to probe metrics, economic buyers, and decision criteria.
Sales leaders should focus on the front of the sales process (pipeline generation) rather than just the end (closing), as having a ton of pipeline is more critical than a high close rate.

A bottoms-up sales motion, starting with practitioners (like at Datadog), can be more effective in certain markets than a traditional top-down executive approach, by building groundswell and earning your way up.
Discounting must be tightly controlled by leadership (CRO/CPO level) to protect long-term unit prices and valuation. Reps given autonomy will almost always default to the maximum discount.

Great sales cultures are built by setting a clear vision for greatness, holding people accountable, removing underperformers quickly, and leaders being 'in the boat' with their team, especially during tough times.
fundraising_mentions: Datadog was at $60 million ARR and doubling year-over-year when Dan joined.
Medallia had a $5 billion exit.
Datadog's early fundraising rounds were unpopular and difficult to raise.
Dan had to find $2 million in cash to exercise his Medallia stock options after leaving.
quotable: You will learn more and become better at your job working on my team than you would have at any other team during that same amount of time and you will never have to look for a job again because the Halo of our success will be over your head for the rest of your career and people will seek you out.
Asking somebody else to do PG [pipeline generation] for you is like asking them to go to the gym for you.
one_liner: Datadog's former CRO, Dan Fougere, breaks down his playbook for building legendary enterprise sales teams, covering rigorous qualification, the two types of sales motions, and why leaders must control discounting and own pipeline generation.

title: Miles Dieffenbach: Inside Carnegie Mellon’s $4BN Endowment & The Math Behind DPI, TVPI, Illiquidity
guest_role: Investor at Carnegie Mellon University Endowment
key_insights: The vast majority of LPs are not adequately compensated for the risk in venture capital, as median returns (around 8% net IRR) do not consistently outperform public market equivalents (PME) unless they access top-decile managers.

Large, multi-stage funds face a mathematical challenge to deliver traditional venture multiples (e.g., 4x net), requiring hundreds of billions in enterprise value from exits, a scale that is historically unprecedented for a single manager.

The venture industry is suffering from a severe liquidity drought, which is the primary driver of the difficult fundraising market. One good year of IPOs will not solve the problem; multiple years are needed.

There is a growing misalignment between LPs and GPs at scaled funds, where high management fees on massive AUM create immense wealth for GPs regardless of performance, breaking the traditional risk/reward partnership.
The five pillars of venture are sourcing, picking, winning, helping, and selling, with selling being a muscle that many managers failed to exercise effectively during the 2021-2022 market peak.
fundraising_mentions: A manager targeted a $7 billion fundraise, split across early-stage, growth, and opportunity funds.
A manager was holding OpenSea at a $13 billion valuation during a 2023 fundraising process.
The guest notes CMU's typical commitment size starts at $10 million into funds ranging from $80M to $1B.
Discussion of why $50-100M seed funds can be mathematically challenging due to check size, ownership, and diversification requirements.
quotable: My question to any new allocator or investor is do you think you're going to have access to top decile managers cuz at that point top desile you are achieving returns above the PME consistently but below that even top quartile you're not.
So my message here to all venture capitalists, now is the time. Please take your companies public.
one_liner: Miles Dieffenbach from Carnegie Mellon's endowment provides a data-driven LP critique of the venture capital asset class, questioning fund sizes, fee structures, and whether LPs are truly being paid for the risk they take.

title: IAC CEO Joey Levin: Why Value Investing is BS; The Most Insane Element of SPACs | 20VC #982
key_insights: True 'value investing' is not just buying assets at low multiples, but can also mean paying high multiples for companies where you see significant future growth potential.
Simplification is the most powerful tool for value creation; it's what entitles a business to its margin by making things easier for customers.
The most insane flaw of the SPAC model was companies giving a third party, who didn't know their business, a free, multi-month option to sell their company to the public.

In market downturns, private market valuations lag public markets because the entire ecosystem (investors, LPs, companies) is incentivized to maintain pretend valuations until they are forced to raise new capital.
Company values are only effective if they are unique and force uncomfortable decisions, rather than being generic platitudes like 'integrity' or 'customer first'.
fundraising_mentions: IAC has over a billion in cash and no debt at the parent level.
Sequoia's investment in Figma at a $400 million valuation, which was 100 times revenue at the time.
quotable: The way this back works you build a company for as long as it takes you to build a company you get it to a position where you think it can maybe endure the public markets and then in that critical moment you give somebody else who doesn't know your company at all a free option on effectively selling that company to the public for three months that is completely insane.
Simplifying is our margin in all of our business that's what entitles you to margin.
one_liner: IAC CEO Joey Levin discusses his contrarian take on value investing, deconstructs the fundamental flaws of SPACs, and shares his core belief that simplification is the ultimate driver of business margin and value creation.

key_insights: Impatience during a negotiation can be a costly mistake.
Posturing without a strong basis can be easily detected and can backfire.
The tone of voice and specific wording can make or break a deal.
Over-eagerness to negotiate can lead to unfavorable outcomes.
It's crucial to know when to stop talking and let a deal unfold.

quotable: Steve I think we're worth three times that... actually I know we're worth three times that.
at that instant with that one word difference the deal had fallen apart and I have relived that experience so many times since then

title: Life Inside Alphabet's $7BN Growth Fund
key_insights: The best investors combine past insights with an open mind, as relying solely on historical patterns is insufficient in a fast-moving market.

When evaluating investments, underwrite what exists today. Be skeptical of a company's 'second and third acts' unless there is concrete evidence of execution, as most companies struggle to expand beyond their core business.
Predictability and disciplined execution are more critical for a successful public market transition than revenue scale alone; a company must be able to 'do what they say they're going to do'.
While founder-led companies are powerful, successful non-founder-led CEOs exist; as a company scales, building a strong executive team becomes a team sport and is crucial for long-term success.
A true test of leadership and company culture is the ability to maintain 'followership' during difficult periods, not just during times of rapid success and valuation growth.
fundraising_mentions: Led the Series B in Gusto over 10 years ago.
Invested in Stripe in 2017.
Invested in UiPath in the Series B.
Led an investment in Whatnot a couple of years ago.
CapitalG underwrites for 3-5x money-on-money returns on its growth investments.
CapitalG typically writes a $100-150 million check when partnering with private equity firms on larger buyouts.
quotable: If you feel nervous and like you're advocating for something so hard and others are telling you no... to the point that it almost makes you doubt it yourself, you're exactly where you should be.
I wish I knew just how important getting the really big things right would be. Venture is a business of, you know, 80/20 outsize returns so you have to make a few big, big decisions, bold bets right.
one_liner: Laela Sturdy of CapitalG shares her framework for growth-stage investing, detailing her skepticism of multi-product stories, the importance of predictable execution for public markets, and the nuances of leadership required to scale generational companies.

title: Shyam Sankar: The Broken Incentive Structure of How Governments Buy Defence | E1104
key_insights: The US government's procurement process, based on a cost-plus, labor-based model, stifles innovation and is misaligned with modern software development, where Palantir pioneered a product-first, license-based approach.
The defense industrial base has a 'problem' due to post-Cold War consolidation (from 51 primes to 5), leading to a lack of competition and a culture that favors conformity over Maverick founders.

To foster a healthy defense tech ecosystem, the Department of Defense (DoD) needs to abandon 'peanut butter spreading' of funds and start 'picking winners' to create large-scale successes that attract more capital and talent.

Effective talent management mirrors an 'artist colony,' not a 'factory,' by crafting roles around unique individuals, embracing non-linear career paths, and prioritizing talent spotting over rigid organizational structures.

The value in the AI stack will accrue to the application and infrastructure layers, not the models themselves which are becoming commoditized; true value is in owning the user-facing application and integrating AI with deterministic code and human workflows.
fundraising_mentions: Roughly a hundred billion dollars of venture investment has entered defense tech recently.
quotable: In an effort to have a perception of Fair competition, we have created so much process that we neither have Fair competition nor speed.
Smart people cannot be taught anything; they can learn. And that's the environment you're trying to set up.
one_liner: Palantir's CTO, Shyam Sankar, breaks down the broken incentive structures in government defense procurement, the need for a new innovation model, and his 'artist colony' approach to hiring and managing elite talent.

title: Des Traynor: How to Survive and Thrive in a World of OpenAI
key_insights: AI disruption is creating a new wave of winners and losers, where companies that fundamentally reimagine entire workflows ('thick wrappers') will thrive, while those merely adding superficial AI features ('thin wrappers') will be vulnerable to platform shifts from players like OpenAI.

The value in the AI stack will likely shift from the infrastructure layer (which will become commoditized over time) to the application layer, where true differentiation and end-to-end problem-solving for users will command pricing power.

Incumbents may have an advantage in the AI race if the core technology can be layered onto their existing stack and distribution, whereas startups have an edge when a market needs to be rebuilt from the ground up with a completely new AI-native architecture.

Most startup advice expires within 5-6 years due to evolving market dynamics; however, timeless skills like hiring executives, building culture, and maintaining a clear vision are perpetually valuable for serial entrepreneurs.

In the AI era, go-to-market and product strategy must be tightly aligned. It's crucial to identify a niche, build a product that offers unique value not easily replicated by incumbents, and relentlessly communicate that value to a focused audience.
fundraising_mentions: Discussion of OpenAI's potential $90 billion valuation on $1 billion in revenue.
Mention of the 'weird Capital Market' history where companies like Hopin raised billions at 'ridiculous valuations'.
quotable: You're never going to make money filling in the gaps in a platform. The thing they haven't got around yet... you're on a train tracks picking up dollar coins... there's a train coming it's going to hit you at some stage.

The disruption comes when you would build the entire thing differently in a world post-AI. If you actually wish you could borrow all their servers and their sender reputation... then I think you're at best looking you're trying to add a thin layer on top of what is ultimately a surviving incumbent.
one_liner: Intercom Co-founder Des Traynor analyzes the massive disruption AI is causing for startups and incumbents, breaking down where value will accrue, how to build a defensible AI product, and why most companies are approaching it wrong.

title: Why Your First Growth Hire Should Be a Former Founder | E1088
key_insights: Your first growth hire should be a former founder who is scrappy and revenue-focused, not a senior executive who is unlikely to 'get their hands dirty'.
Truly effective outreach provides direct value or creates a sense of human reciprocity, like scraping for negative comments on a prospect's Instagram posts and alerting them.
Marketing KPIs must be tied to revenue; reject vanity metrics and instead use a weighted pipeline dollar figure based on lead scores and close rates.
A successful growth process is about high-velocity experimentation, where the primary goal is learning, and the ability to test a channel's depth is critical for scaling.
Most startups attempting both PLG and Enterprise motions land somewhere in the middle; it's rare to perfect one, let alone both, from the start.
Don't hire a growth team too early; wait until you have enough data (e.g., after a couple million in revenue) for them to run statistically significant experiments and learn effectively.
fundraising_mentions: The '33222' framework for top-decile startups: grow 3x, 3x, 2x, 2x, 2x year-over-year past the first million to reach $100M+ in 5 years.
quotable: If you can drive value about mistakes problems of the business you have discovered that your audience does not know you will get engagement guaranteed.

I'm French I know how to cheat 10 times out of 10... you give me anything as a goal that is not revenue and you incentivize me strongly for that be warned you're going to get that kpi but you're not going to get the revenue.
one_liner: Growth leader Guillaume Cabane breaks down why your first growth hire should be a founder, how to tie marketing KPIs directly to revenue, and the creative experiments that drive low-CAC customer acquisition.

title: Billionaire explains how he hacked his brain to be happier and more productive (it actually works)
key_insights: Happier teams and individuals significantly outperform their unhappy counterparts in a business context.
Happiness is presented as the single most substantial advantage for boosting productivity in the business world.
The practice of gratitude journaling for just three minutes a day over 21 days can fundamentally change your brain.
Instead of general gratitude, the method requires recalling and writing down three specific, key moments from the previous day for which you are thankful.
This practice trains the brain to create a 'background screening application' that learns to recognize and appreciate moments of gratitude in real-time, leading to a sustained increase in happiness.
quotable: If you tell me to gratitude Journal you might as well also tell me to drink kumacha every like uh couple of hours and sing kumaya Melodies it was just BS 100.
It turns out happiness is the thing that drives the biggest advantage in business and an Out product of it is that you're happy.
one_liner: A skeptical entrepreneur reveals how a 21-day gratitude journaling exercise, based on research from Harvard's happiness lab, rewired his brain to appreciate positive moments in real-time, ultimately boosting both his happiness and productivity.

title: From OpenTable to eBay to a16z -- The Unbelievable Career of Jeff Jordan
key_insights: Transitioning from established corporations like Disney to the tech world during the early internet era was driven by a sense of necessity and opportunity.
Being early to a market, like with video-on-demand at Hollywood Entertainment, can be just as fatal as being wrong about the idea itself.
Deep, hands-on operational experience in a pioneering company like eBay, where the playbook was written as they went, provides an unparalleled understanding of business fundamentals.
Understanding a network effect business at an 'anatomical' level from building it is a key advantage for an investor.
A core investment thesis can be successfully built around a single, powerful concept, such as identifying and backing businesses with strong potential for network effects.
quotable: Doing eBay early uh meant there was no Playbook we had to write the Playbook and you get you get to know a business at such an atomical you know uh way you're just building it from the ground up.
Largely as an investor I'm a kind of a one-trick pony everything I would like to talk about as an operator and an investor typically involves a network effect.
one_liner: Jeff Jordan shares how his formative operational experience building network effects at eBay became the cornerstone of his 'one-trick pony' investment strategy focused on marketplaces.

title: What happened to HubSpot's Website Grader?
key_insights: Free tools can be a massive lead generation engine, especially when they catch a wave of market interest.
The effectiveness of a marketing channel or tool can significantly decline as the broader ecosystem evolves (e.g., diversification of the web, rise of social media).
A critical strategic mistake is trying to recapture the 'peak' of a declining asset or channel instead of optimizing for its new, lower steady-state.
Resources (time, energy, capital) spent trying to revive a declining channel are often better invested in conquering a new, emerging channel.
Recognizing that a tool or strategy had a specific 'point in time' efficacy is crucial for making forward-looking decisions.
quotable: The mistake that we made there is thinking oh you can salvage that and get back to that Peak... we spent a while like a couple years trying to do that.

I would have been much much better off if I had a time machine I would say no no our job is to like get the best steady run rate and we should go and Conquer a new Channel with that same time energy and capital.
one_liner: A HubSpot co-founder recounts the decline of their viral 'Website Grader' tool as a lesson in recognizing when a growth channel has matured and the strategic imperative to re-invest resources into new opportunities rather than chasing past peaks.

title: Ian Lee: Why DAOs Will Replace Venture Capital; Biggest Threat to Web3 | 20VC #893
key_insights: DAOs are the technological culmination of a multi-decade trend towards decentralized, community-based investing, poised to challenge the traditional venture capital model.

Web3's core promise is to shift the internet's business model from value capture by centralized companies (Web2) to value creation and capture by decentralized, community-owned protocols and networks.
The transition from Web2 to Web3 requires investors to develop new, native capabilities like on-chain governance, staking, and active network participation to remain competitive.
The consumerization of Web3—making complex technologies like wallets and dApps accessible and user-friendly for a mass audience—is the largest opportunity for growth and societal impact.

The biggest threat to Web3 achieving its positive potential is the prevalence of short-term, profit-seeking behavior that leads to exploits, rug pulls, and a loss of trust, which can set the industry back years.
Web3 has the dual potential to either dramatically centralize or decentralize wealth; the outcome depends entirely on how founders, investors, and communities design and govern these new networks.
fundraising_mentions: Syndicate's seed round included 9 funds and 18 angels.
Syndicate conducted a 100-person community raise with operators and founders.
Syndicate's Series A was led by Andreessen Horowitz and included 150 other people and funds.

quotable: I was always bothered by how the traditional venture capital model was actually centralizing wealth and control and ownership of these networks... and I always was wondering why isn't there a more network native or community based model to invest in these technologies and networks that want to fundamentally be community owned.
Web3 has a chance... at enabling more people in the world and the users of the internet... to become co-owners of that internet and of the services that are built on that internet.
one_liner: Syndicate founder Ian Lee explains why community-owned DAOs represent the future of investing and how Web3 could fundamentally restructure the internet's economics away from centralized corporations.

title: Does Money Make This Billionaire Happy?
key_insights: Below a certain income threshold, lack of money is a significant source of unhappiness, but the marginal value of each additional dollar diminishes greatly after basic needs and securities are met.
Material possessions like expensive cars and houses do not fundamentally increase happiness once a certain level of comfort is achieved.
True motivation can be found in purpose-driven goals, such as making the world better, rather than using wealth as a competitive scorecard.
A key value of wealth is ensuring the well-being and future of one's family, such as providing for children's education.
A fulfilling entrepreneurial goal is to generate wealth and opportunity for the entire team that embarks on the company's journey.
quotable: I think not having money sucks.
Do I feel like we're making the world better?
one_liner: A billionaire entrepreneur discusses why happiness doesn't scale with wealth after a certain point, and how purpose and positive impact become the primary motivators.

key_insights: Successful, long-term founder partnerships are built on a foundation of deep trust, complementary skills, and a shared ability to evolve viewpoints without ego.
The future of social products is shifting from social-graph-based discovery to machine-learning-powered interest graphs, serving users highly personalized, 'unconnected' content.
Building a second company after a major success comes with immense pressure and expectations, but also the advantage of leveraging a strong reputation to bootstrap initial growth and data collection.

Startups must be ruthless in identifying and removing 'brilliant jerks' or team members who aren't the right fit, as moving quickly on personnel changes is more compassionate in the long run than letting a bad fit linger.

Artifact's strategy is to start with news to build a powerful recommendation engine, with the long-term vision of creating a system where algorithms transparently serve user interests, not just company metrics.
Early-stage startups cannot afford to 'play'; the focus must be on execution. The culture is fundamentally different from large tech companies where exploration can be funded.

Social networks made a mistake by assuming a user's friend group is the best filter for content; individual interests are far more diverse and nuanced, which is the opportunity for ML-driven platforms.

one_liner: Instagram founders Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger detail the launch of their new venture, Artifact, and share their thesis that machine learning-driven interest graphs, not social graphs, represent the future of content consumption and social interaction.

title: Tristan Handy: Why The CEO Should Make As Few Decisions As Possible | 20VC #937
key_insights: Use time as a strategic weapon by delaying monetization to build a beloved, standard-setting open-source product and a strong community before getting on the VC-funded growth treadmill.
When hiring, look for the feeling of a 'locked-in' conversation and clear thinking over specific role experience, as many jobs are not as hard as they seem if the person has the right core traits.
The CEO's role should be to make as few decisions as possible, instead empowering the team and focusing on balancing the long-term interests of all stakeholders (community, employees, investors).
Embrace radical transparency with the team, even around fundraising timelines, to build trust, while drawing a firm line at protecting individual employee privacy.

A distributed, asynchronous company is amazing, but fully remote work can be lonely and dehumanizing; solve this by providing budgets for out-of-home work and opening small satellite offices for community, not for in-person collaboration.

Working remotely is terrible but distributed companies are amazing.

title: Lessons from SVB; Crisis Management Tips; USD's Status as the Reserve Currency
key_insights: In a crisis, the best founders use scenario planning to map their choices against different uncertain outcomes, focusing on what they can control.

Startups should practice 'financial agility' by having at least three bank accounts with runway in each and pre-established pathways to move money quickly, rather than trying to become part-time financial experts.
Crisis communication requires over-communicating, being radically transparent about what you know and don't know, being human and empathetic, and maintaining forward momentum.
True product-market fit is the single most important determinant of a startup's success; companies that achieve it almost never fail.
The constant printing of money by Western governments is unsustainable and will inevitably lead to the US dollar losing its reserve currency status if stewardship doesn't improve.
Time diversification in fund deployment (e.g., investing a fund over 5 years instead of 18 months) is a crucial, underappreciated strategy for mitigating risk in early-stage investing.

Some AI companies may require $100 million in mass compute resources, representing a return to 'Big T' technical risk.

Startups start out dead and have to prove they're alive and they have one job to do which is get product Market fit and that means answering one very specific question which is what can we uniquely do that people are desperate for.
