key_insights: The true value of any company is its future cash flows, not abstract revenue multiples or speculative technology promises.

A private equity buyout acts as a powerful catalyst for change, allowing a company to break from past inefficiencies and realign its strategy, incentives, and operations around a singular goal of maximizing cash flow growth.
Great innovators become great companies by breaking down large problems into measurable component parts, prioritizing them, and delegating ownership to the responsible individuals.

The most successful private equity strategy involves partnering with management teams who are open-minded and care about profitability to transform inefficient but high-quality businesses into cash-flow-positive market leaders.

Price is critical in investing; valuation should be based on the predictable earnings that can be generated post-acquisition through operational improvements, not on market sentiment or buying high to sell higher.
quotable: We believe every company in the world is worth its future cash flows. We don't believe in multiples of revenue.
Any business problem can be solved, health is another matter.
one_liner: Thoma Bravo founder Orlando Bravo shares his framework for successful software private equity, emphasizing value investing based on future cash flow, operational excellence, and the art of turning great innovators into highly profitable companies.

title: Where will Liquid Death be in 5 years?
key_insights: Liquid Death aims to become a multi-billion dollar beverage company.
The brand seeks to blur the lines between being an entertainment company and a beverage brand.
Liquid Death compares its growth aspirations to established brands like Monster and Red Bull.
The company differentiates itself from Red Bull by focusing on comedy and irreverence in its entertainment.
The goal is to create entertainment that people would consume independently of the beverage.
quotable: how can we become a multi-billion dollar beverage company that is also in service of creating really great entertainment that people would consume even if they didn't consume the beverage
we're all about being funny and comedy and irreverence and all of that
one_liner: Liquid Death CEO Mike Cessario outlines the company's five-year vision to become a multi-billion dollar beverage brand by uniquely blending beverage sales with comedy-focused entertainment.

title: Scooter Braun's Self Care Advice
key_insights: Prioritize dedicated time for self-work annually, completely disconnected from work (no phone, no emails).
The Hoffman Process is an intense, week-long program for self-work that can be life-changing.
Reaching a point of extreme pain or 'rock bottom' can be a catalyst for profound personal change.
Making a conscious choice to change your path, even when it conflicts with major professional commitments, is crucial for long-term well-being.
Support from your team and clients is essential when you need to step away for personal reasons.
quotable: I was being given a choice: choose the path that I've been on of success that had me hitting that Rock Bottom moment, or do something new and different.
I thought my phone would be off for a week and as you know my phone stayed off for two and a half months.
one_liner: Music executive Scooter Braun recounts his decision to attend a week-long, disconnected self-work retreat during a major album release, a choice that put him on a different path and saved him from burnout.

title: This Clever Engineering Hack Could Save Us From Global Warming -- Billionaire Chris Sacca
key_insights: Sunlight reflection is presented as a necessary, urgent solution to mitigate global warming and prevent catastrophic loss of life.
The cooling effect of volcanic aerosols, like from Mount Pinatubo, serves as a natural precedent for engineered sunlight reflection.
Potential methods for geoengineering include introducing aerosols into the stratosphere, brightening clouds, or creating new clouds over the ocean.
There is a significant risk of rogue states unilaterally attempting geoengineering, making controlled, scientific research even more critical.
Delaying action on sunlight reflection while waiting for a transition to a net-zero economy will disproportionately harm the world's most vulnerable populations.
quotable: We have no way out of this without reflecting sunlight back into the solar system.
The ultimate privilege right now the ultimate Ivory Tower is to sit there and say hey that's scary... that's why we have to research it.
one_liner: Billionaire investor Chris Sacca makes an urgent case for prioritizing research into sunlight reflection technology as the most critical and underfunded strategy to combat the immediate existential threat of global warming.

title: Second-Time Founders Are More Investable & Why Not To Hire People Out of College
key_insights: Second-time founders are more investable because they've learned painful lessons, have better networks, and have proven their perseverance.
True focus is a superpower; serial founders recognize that only a few key decisions determine a company's success, unlike first-time founders who often mistake activity for progress.

When fundraising, don't automatically answer 'how much are you raising' with a number; it's often a proxy for valuation. Instead, state the percentage of the company you're willing to sell and let the market set the price.
Founders should avoid hiring people straight out of college to maintain a small, senior, and high-velocity team, as junior hires can slow down a project.
Always taking the highest valuation is a mistake; it's better to choose the right partner and a valuation that allows for future growth, rather than optimizing for the highest price.
Founders should trust their gut instinct. The biggest regrets often come from ignoring your intuition and following the advice of others, even smart people you've hired.
To do launches well, focus intensely on the problem you're solving so that customers immediately understand how your product helps their life.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a total of $280 million across two companies.
Optimizely's Series A in 2013 with Benchmark involved ~8% dilution.
Limitless's Series A was led by NEA at a $350M valuation, turning down offers at a $1B valuation.
Allowed employees to sell up to 25% of their vested stock during the Series A round.
Advocates for a public or semi-public fundraising process to cast a wide net and create competition, similar to a dating app.
quotable: First-time Founders brag about how many employees they have. Second time Founders brag about how few employees they have.
When an investor asks how much are you raising, more often than not they're actually asking how much do you think you're worth. Let's start the negotiation on valuation right now.
The biggest mistakes I made were not following my gut.
one_liner: Dan Siroker, founder of Limitless and Optimizely, shares hard-won lessons on why second-time founders are more effective, how to run a fundraising process that avoids common traps, and the importance of trusting your gut.

title: ZoomInfo CEO Henry Schuck: Sales Cycle Elongation; Gratitude Journaling; Sales Layoffs | E964
key_insights: A resource-constrained business forces disciplined and essential investments, which can be a long-term advantage.
The journey of bootstrapping allows a leader to mature and grow with the business, potentially avoiding major mistakes that could come with large, early funding.
Performance is what ultimately creates job safety in a high-performance culture; trust is granted, but safety is earned through results.
Current market conditions have significantly elongated sales cycles, requiring more layers of approval (up to the CFO) and hurting go-to-market velocity.
Happiness can be a significant productivity advantage, and practices like gratitude journaling can retrain the brain to recognize positive moments, leading to a happier and more effective state.
True success isn't just about outworking others, but also about building the right team and executing well over a long period.
As a public company CEO, a significant challenge is managing a large constituency of investors who don't have the same deep, trusting relationship as long-term private equity partners.
fundraising_mentions: Started with $25,000 on a credit card in 2006.
Bootstrapped the business to $30 million of ARR by 2014.
Brought in TA Associates as the first private equity investor in 2014.
quotable: I like a business that's resource constrained because it ensures that the next investment you make is always the most important investment you can be making.
Performance is what creates safety... your safety is in your performance. That's it.
one_liner: ZoomInfo CEO Henry Schuck shares his journey of bootstrapping a SaaS giant, the mindset required to navigate market downturns and elongated sales cycles, and why he believes happiness is the ultimate productivity advantage.

title: Ashley Kelly: The Playbook to Start and Scale Your SDR Team | E1162
guest_role: Head of Sales Development at Rippling
key_insights: An SDR org can function as a 'third pillar' in the go-to-market function, acting as a bridge between marketing and sales rather than reporting to either.
When hiring SDRs, focus on intangible traits like coachability, motivation, and organization. Test for these using role-plays and email writing assessments.
A successful SDR hiring profile is often someone with ~6 months of experience in roles like recruiting or call centers, as they possess organization and phone confidence.
Effective onboarding gets SDRs on the phone by week two, with ramping quotas over four months to build momentum and master the inputs (KPIs) before focusing on outputs (demos).
SDR compensation should be tied to transactional goals like held demos (Stage 2 opportunities), not revenue, to ensure AEs have enough at-bats, especially in companies with longer sales cycles.
quotable: I actually am very bullish on sales development I think it's the third pillar within the go to market function and I think that it can stand alone.
If you're still doing the same thing that you were six months ago you're not going to be successful. So to say that like outbound or SDR is dead is like a little dramatic.
one_liner: Ashley Kelly provides a masterclass on building and scaling high-performing SDR teams, covering her playbook on hiring, onboarding, compensation, and why she believes SDRs are the third pillar of a go-to-market organization.

title: Matt Grimm, Co-Founder @Anduril: How a Trump Administration Changes the Defence Industry | E1224
key_insights: The US defense procurement system's reliance on 'Cost Plus' contracts incentivizes incumbent primes to increase costs rather than innovate efficiently, creating an opportunity for Anduril's 'firm-fixed price' model.
China is the most significant and complex adversary for the West due to its control over critical supply chains, its antithetical stance on human rights, and its global ambitions.
The future of warfare is defined by the economics of mass-produced, low-cost autonomous systems, where the ability to out-produce an adversary at a lower cost-per-unit is paramount for deterrence.
Anduril's success stems from unlocking latent patriotism within the tech talent pool and aligning it with venture capital, attracting top engineers to work on national security problems.

To succeed in the defense sector, startups must navigate not only technology development but also the immense complexities of government appropriations, compliance, security clearances, and logistics, areas where many new entrants fail.
fundraising_mentions: Anduril has raised approximately $4 billion in equity and $1 billion in debt.
The last funding round valued the company at $14 billion post-money.
Founders Fund is a key investor.
The company has conducted multiple secondary offerings for employees, with a relatively low participation rate of around 30%.
quotable: Everyone including Russia and China have given up on communism except Cuba and the DOD.
We are willingly letting a strategic adversary control the knobs on what gets mainlined into the psyche of our youth.
one_liner: Anduril Co-Founder Matt Grimm discusses how his company is disrupting the defense industry with a software-first approach, the geopolitical challenges posed by China, and the unique dynamics of building and funding a patriotic tech company at scale.

title: Roundtable #6 with Rebecca Kaden, Nicole Quinn, Eurie Kim, Harry Stebbings | E1083
guest_role: Managing Partner at Union Square Ventures
key_insights: Seed valuations have remained surprisingly high due to market lag and abundant capital, but a correction is expected as larger funds may retreat and capital dynamics shift.
The Series A market is a tale of two worlds: companies with momentum and seasoned teams command high multiples, while others with complicated stories or in complex markets struggle to raise.
Down rounds are becoming a necessary reality to fix overpriced cap tables from 2021, and are considered preferable to taking on structured/dirty terms.

AI is viewed as a transformative 'lottery of time' that will create immense value, particularly in the application layer by solving real-world problems more efficiently, rather than just in foundational models.

There's a return to collaborative investing, where multi-stage funds will work more closely with seed funds and other investors across different stages, moving away from a winner-take-all approach on cap tables.
fundraising_mentions: Seed rounds at 'six on 30' (6M on 30M valuation) and 'three on 15'.
Series A average valuation is around $35M, similar to 2021 levels.
Series D average valuation dropped from a peak of $740M in 2021 to $340M.
Hot AI seed rounds are priced at '8 on 40' or '8 on 50'.
Klarna did a 90% down round.
quotable: AI is akin to winning the lottery... it is the lottery of time.
The myth of a hot deal is a myth... over time most of those are not going to be worth very much at all.
one_liner: A roundtable of top VCs from Union Square Ventures, Lightspeed, and Forerunner dissect the current state of venture, debating seed valuations, the bifurcation of the Series A market, the necessity of down rounds, and the transformative potential of AI applications.

title: Adarsh Hiremath @ Mercor: The Fastest Growing Startup in Silicon Valley | E1261
key_insights: Human data and talent assessment are converging; high-quality human experts are crucial for training the next generation of AI models.
The future of work will be more specialized, with AI handling a significant portion of tasks but requiring human oversight for the last mile.
As software development becomes commoditized by AI, defensible businesses will be built on strong network effects rather than proprietary code.
Mercor's intense '996' work culture is a side effect of hiring people deeply committed to the mission, which they see as a key driver of their rapid growth.
Scaling company culture is more challenging than scaling software, especially during hyper-growth phases.
fundraising_mentions: Seed round was over $3 million, led by General Catalyst.
Raised a round from Benchmark, initiated after a helicopter ride with Peter Fenton.
Raised a $100 million round at a $2 billion valuation, led by Felicis Ventures, approximately 6 months after the Benchmark round.
quotable: The businesses that succeed in a world where software costs approach zero will be built on network effects.
I think being a recruiter is the highest Prestige position in any company... you can gather all you need to know about a company from seeing the talent inflows and outflows.
one_liner: Adarsh Hiremath, co-founder of Mercor, discusses building a global labor marketplace using AI to vet talent, the critical role of human experts in training foundation models, and the strategies behind their rapid scaling and recent $100M fundraise.

title: This billionaire's fintech startup is going to fix the Money Supply Chain Problem
key_insights: The 'Money Supply Chain Problem' is the complex web of archaic middleware providers and intermediary vendors that developers must navigate to build financial products on top of old-school banks.
True innovation in financial services requires fixing the fundamental problem: the financial institution itself. Building on top of existing banks just adds more layers.
Column's strategy is to be a regulated bank that offers direct API access to developers, collapsing the entire 'money supply chain' into a single layer and going straight to the Fed.

By operating within the regulatory perimeter, Column enables developers to build new financial products quickly and safely, avoiding the risks and consumer harm associated with unregulated entities like offshore crypto exchanges.

The goal is not to build the next killer consumer app, but to provide the fundamental plumbing (infrastructure) that allows other innovators to build the next generation of financial services faster, better, and cheaper.
quotable: No matter how many times you rethink or you rebuild the technology into something slightly better you actually aren't fixing the fundamental problem which is the financial institution itself the bank.

What we are doing is we're simply just solving the supply chain we're saying there's 20 things to solve this one very basic problem which is building on top of the fed and we're just going to collapse all that in one and we're going to go straight to the fed and do it ourselves.
one_liner: Will Hockey explains how his startup, Column, is solving the 'money supply chain problem' by becoming a chartered bank to offer direct API access for developers, collapsing the layers of intermediaries to enable faster and safer innovation in financial services.

title: Do VCs need to meet the Founder in person?
key_insights: The transition to Zoom-first investing since March 2020 has made building trust and genuine relationships with founders significantly harder.
Jason Lemkin believes he has become a 'worse investor' because the lack of initial in-person meetings removes a key element of socialization and trust-building.
Founders have become increasingly transactional and often don't prioritize in-person meetings, focusing instead on securing investment quickly.
While face-to-face meetings aren't a perfect method for judging character, they are crucial for establishing the trust needed to navigate the high-risk, difficult times in a startup's journey.
Although some firms like Point Nine have perfected remote investing, it requires a specific strategy to counteract the increased risk of not knowing the founding team on a personal level.
fundraising_mentions: First check into Pipedrive
quotable: I'm a worse investor for it. I have not figured out the answer to your question.
Investing has gotten so transactional that even if they want you on the cap table, they don't care. They just want to check the boxes and move on.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin argues that the shift to remote investing has made him a 'worse investor' because it erodes the essential trust built through in-person meetings, even as founders become more transactional.

title: David Meyer: Why You Should Hire People Who Aren’t In Product Already | E1076
key_insights: The best product managers often exhibit product management behaviors before they hold the title, showing a natural inclination for the role.
A successful product manager isn't the 'CEO of the product', but rather a 'roadie' who finds impossible compromises to move the vision forward while managing stakeholder friction.
True data-driven product management is about 'truth-seeking' to uncover blind spots and ask better questions, not just hitting metrics, which can be gamed.
To hire great product people, look for demonstrated impact and a deep-seated curiosity by interrogating their past experiences until you could hypothetically do their job.

The relationship between a CPO and CEO is crucial; the CEO is the ultimate product owner, and the product leader's role is to support and execute that vision, requiring high-bandwidth, ego-less communication.
fundraising_mentions: Plum Tree tried to acquire Atlassian in 1998.
quotable: If you're rocking it as a product manager everybody thinks you suck. If sales loves you engineering hates you because you're chasing deals... if engineering loves you sales hates you because you're just doing long-term stuff.
People often think I want to be a product manager I'm the CEO of the product... that's not what the job is. It's finding these impossible compromises.
one_liner: Databricks SVP of Product David Meyer shares his counterintuitive philosophies on hiring non-product managers into product roles, the thankless reality of the job, and why true data-driven culture is about truth-seeking, not just metrics.

title: Adam Fishman: Takeaways from Lyft and Patreon; How to Build Viral Loops | 20VC #897
key_insights: A growth model should be built around 'growth loops' – self-contained cycles where the inputs generate outputs that feed back in (e.g., Lyft's referral program).
When hiring your first growth leader, seek a mid-level 'player-coach' who can both execute and build a team, rather than someone too junior or too senior.
The interview process for a growth role should simulate the job with quantitative exercises, prioritization challenges, and a take-home assignment to test communication.
Growth leaders must be immune to failure and adept at learning from experiments that don't work, blending quantitative data with qualitative customer feedback to avoid costly mistakes.
A successful rebrand requires more than just new visuals; it involves repositioning the product to deliver on the new brand promise and bringing the entire company along on the journey.
fundraising_mentions: The original Series A investor in Zimride (which became Lyft) was Raj Kapoor at Mayfield.
quotable: I think a growth person has to be almost immune to failure because you get so many things wrong in your career.

If you don't have product market fit throwing a growth person into the mix is disastrous for your product because the last thing you want to do is put your product in the hands of more people when it sucks.
one_liner: Adam Fishman shares lessons from his time leading growth at Lyft and Patreon, covering how to build viral loops, hire and onboard growth teams, and execute a successful rebrand.

title: Anchor Founder: Why I like NFTs 👍🏻🎨
key_insights: NFTs revolutionized art monetization by enabling artists, particularly digital artists, to sell their work online, overcoming previous challenges.
A personal anecdote illustrates how an artist friend, John Januzzi, achieved significant financial success and renewed creative motivation through NFTs, giving half to charity.
The speaker's primary appreciation for NFTs stems from their capacity to empower creators and facilitate direct monetization of their work.
The speaker expresses skepticism about the long-term scalability and value of NFTs used primarily for social capital (e.g., displaying ownership of a 'board ape').
quotable: NFTs enabled artists who had never been able to monetize their work to all of a sudden have a very willing potential customer base that might be willing to pay them lots of money for their for their work.
that's the aspect of nfts I really like I like the the ability to empower creators
one_liner: An Anchor Founder explains their positive view on NFTs as a powerful tool for empowering artists to monetize their work, prioritizing creator empowerment over social capital.

title: Base44’s Founder, Maor Shlomo on How Vibe Coding Will Kill SaaS
key_insights: Vibe coding will enable highly customized software, potentially disrupting traditional SaaS by making it easier for users to build bespoke solutions.
The LLM market features rapid switching between providers, creating volatile market dynamics; businesses should adopt multi-model strategies.
Future LLM models are expected to drive down costs significantly, influencing strategic decisions for AI-native companies.
Sustainable moats in the AI application building space derive from deep vertical integration and addressing complex, functional problems.
There are significant untapped angel investing opportunities in AI-native solutions for 'unsexy' but essential industries like law, healthcare, and finance.
fundraising_mentions: Base44 sold to Wix for $80 million.
quotable: It might be in a few months, it might be in a few years where it will be easier to build your own Salesforce type of CRM than to actually buy a license to something off the shelf.
From all things in the industry, I think the margins are the least thing that I'm worried about.
one_liner: Maor Shlomo, founder of Base44, discusses how 'vibe coding' is poised to revolutionize software development, emphasizing the importance of vertical integration, agile adaptation to LLM market dynamics, and the future of AI-driven entrepreneurship.

title: Justin Ishbia: The Three Traits Required to Succeed in Private Equity | E1119
guest_role: Founder & Managing Partner at Shore Capital
key_insights: When a great management team meets a bad industry, the industry maintains its reputation. Picking the right industry is paramount.
The 'Trust but Verify' principle is crucial. As a business owner, you need systems to ensure operational integrity, like watching the cash register.
Private equity can act as a 'huge flashlight' in a dark room, illuminating areas for improvement. This excites high-performers and exposes under-performers.
Don't do things you don't understand. Sticking to your circle of competence, even when others are chasing trends (like subprime mortgages), leads to long-term survival and success.
To assess a local service business (like a doctor's practice), ask their direct competitors who they would send their own mother to for care.
A key competitive advantage is building a system where scale creates value, such as negotiating lower costs from vendors (e.g., 'light switch' savings) that are immediately accretive to acquisitions.
Young, hungry, first-time CEOs can outperform experienced ones if placed within a strong system with a supportive board and clear processes.
Small, thoughtful gestures that show you care about employees' families (like sending flowers on a spouse's birthday) build immense loyalty and are more impactful than grand, impersonal perks.
A manager's job is to understand what uniquely motivates each top performer and provide it to them, whether it's public praise, responsibility, or a competitive challenge.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a first fund of $100 million.
Raised a second fund of $250 million.
Commented on the difficulty for individuals spinning out of large funds to raise a first-time $200 million fund.
quotable: When a great management team meets a bad industry the industry maintains reputation. That always sticks with me.

I be a private equity in the following way we're a huge flashlight walk into a room that may be dark I'm shining the light everywhere in the corners in the crevices what I found is those who are really good at their job they're super excited and those who are maybe less than good at their job curl up and kind of hide from that light.
one_liner: Shore Capital Founder Justin Ishbia shares his playbook for success in micro-cap private equity, focusing on deep industry expertise, creating value through scale, and building a resilient, people-first company culture.

title: Cathie Wood: Elon & Twitter; Why Facebook is a Value Stock Now; ARK's Performance | 20VC #949
guest_role: Founder, CEO, and CIO of ARK Invest
key_insights: ARK's strategy is to focus exclusively on disruptive innovation across five platforms: genomic sequencing, robotics, energy storage, AI, and blockchain technology.
The firm believes passive, benchmark-based investing is increasingly risky because it overlooks transformative technologies that will disrupt the traditional world order.
During market downturns ('risk-off periods'), ARK's strategy is to concentrate its portfolio into its highest-conviction names, averaging down on stocks they believe are undervalued.
The new ARK Venture Fund is structured as an interval fund to provide retail investors access to private markets, challenging the traditional accredited investor model.

Cathie Wood views Elon Musk's acquisition of Twitter as a major opportunity for innovation, potentially including subscription models, vertical integration to compete with Apple, and creating an 'everything app' integrated with digital wallets.
fundraising_mentions: ARK launched a public-private crossover venture fund structured as an interval fund for retail investors.
The fund has a minimum investment of $500.
The fee structure is a 2.75% management fee with a 0% carry, which was chosen to allow non-accredited investors to participate.
The fund is not limited to 20% secondaries and can use convertibles, initially focusing on Series B and later stages.
quotable: I've been very clear that one of the things that I've been running from in the traditional Asset Management world is index based investing... we actually think that is becoming a very dangerous way to invest.

If you don't have that long-term investment time Horizon and and a real and real conviction that the Innovation that we're seeing today is going to create massive investment opportunities... then you shouldn't be involved.
one_liner: Cathie Wood discusses ARK Invest's high-conviction strategy focused on disruptive innovation, their contrarian approach to market volatility, and the launch of a new venture fund aimed at democratizing access to private companies for retail investors.

title: Chris Sacca's True Unfiltered Opinion on Facebook and Softbank | Full Interview
key_insights: True success in venture capital requires obsession; when Sacca lost that obsession for general tech, he stepped back, fearing he'd become a 'B-teamer.'
Parenting privileged children requires intentionally exposing them to hard work ('shitty jobs') and the concept of failure to build resilience and gratitude.
Effective management and relationship-building involve validating the other person's feelings first before jumping to a solution, a technique learned from parenting toddlers.

The investment thesis for climate tech is now purely economic: it's cheaper to power the world with clean energy than by 'digging up old dinosaur bones,' creating the largest addressable markets in history.

Sacca is critical of Facebook for its negative societal impact and Softbank for its destructive, bullying investment tactics, contrasting them with a more collaborative approach he sees in climate investing.
fundraising_mentions: First check was $50,000 into Photobucket using credit card checks.
Invested $25,000 into Twitter.
Raised a fund for Lowercarbon Capital, offering a no-fee, no-carry allocation to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).
quotable: When things are going up you tend to think it's correlated with your genius and talent and when things are going down you tend to think it's unlucky. You learn over time to invert that curve.
I just have no time in my life for b teamers let alone c teamers or d teamers... it's always a lack of effort and ownership.
one_liner: Legendary investor Chris Sacca shares unfiltered insights on his career from early bets on Twitter to his new climate fund, detailing his frameworks for investing, parenting, and why he believes climate tech is the biggest financial opportunity in history.

title: The Secret to Storytelling 🤫
key_insights: To successfully pitch your business, you must tell a simple, relatable story that your audience can emotionally connect with and feel, rather than just presenting data and processes.
A powerful story is one that can be easily understood and retold by anyone, even someone without industry knowledge, like an investor's mother.
Authenticity and passion are crucial in storytelling; people are more likely to care if they can sense that you genuinely believe in and feel the story you're telling.
Effective communication involves constant repetition of a memorable story with clear, concise sound bites, as people have limited capacity to retain information.
Founders should not be afraid to create and refine a narrative on the spot until it resonates emotionally, as this is more effective than sticking to a script that lacks feeling.
fundraising_mentions: The guest was raising a Series B after having completed a Series A.
quotable: If you do not tell someone a story that they can see themselves in and they can like empathize with you can say all the numbers in the world you can describe all the processes and Analysis in the world no one gives a [ __ ].
You only get to choose like maybe three words you can Lodge in someone's brain at any given point in time and you really need to choose what they are.
one_liner: Handshake's CEO shares a pivotal lesson on the existential threat of poor storytelling in fundraising, revealing how an investor forced him to craft an emotionally resonant narrative that became the key to making his complex B2B business understandable and compelling.

title: Bryan Johnson: Why Humans are No Longer Qualified to Manage Our Own Affairs | E1130
key_insights: Humans are becoming increasingly unqualified to manage their own affairs due to inherent self-destructive tendencies; algorithmic systems can make superior decisions for personal well-being.
The primary goal for intelligence should be 'Don't Die'—prioritizing continued conscious existence above all else, which challenges all existing societal and personal frameworks.
By measuring hundreds of biomarkers and adhering to a data-driven protocol, it's possible to reverse biological age and significantly improve physiological function beyond typical human potential.

To process new ideas, one must resist the knee-jerk reaction to reject them, and instead observe one's own internal threat response to understand personal biases and allow the new concept space to breathe.

From the perspective of the 25th century, current human behaviors that shorten lifespan will be seen as primitive and ridiculous, as we are on the cusp of an era where we can engineer our own biology.

The future will likely involve an 'autonomous man,' where individuals are run by a computational mesh of goal-aligned algorithms that manage biology and decisions far more efficiently than the conscious mind.
quotable: I'm fundamentally proposing that the human race is no longer qualified to manage our Affairs.
I made an algorithm that takes better care of me than I can myself.
The game I'm trying to play in life is how to be respected by the 25th Century.
one_liner: Bryan Johnson explains his controversial 'Blueprint' project, where he has submitted his life to an algorithm to reverse aging, arguing that humanity must adopt a 'Don't Die' philosophy and algorithmic governance to survive the transition to superintelligence.

title: Groq Founder, Jonathan Ross: OpenAI & Anthropic Will Build Their Own Chips & Will NVIDIA Hit $10TRN
key_insights: The demand for AI compute is insatiable, and the primary bottleneck for revenue growth at major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic is the lack of available inference compute.
Major AI companies and hyperscalers will inevitably build their own chips, not necessarily to outperform Nvidia, but to gain control over their supply chain and destiny.
The countries that control energy will control AI, as compute is fundamentally limited by energy availability, creating a significant geopolitical challenge.
Groq's main value proposition is its supply chain advantage, with the ability to deliver its LPUs in 6 months compared to the 2+ year lead time for GPUs.
AI will cause massive deflationary pressure and labor shortages, not mass unemployment, by creating new industries and allowing people to opt out of the traditional workforce.
Nvidia's CUDA software moat is primarily for training, not inference, opening the door for competitors in the rapidly growing inference market.
fundraising_mentions: Groq raised $750 million at an almost $7 billion valuation.
The round was 4x oversubscribed.
quotable: The countries that control compute will control AI. And you cannot have compute without energy.

I think over time we're going to realize that LLMs are the telescope of the mind. That right now they're making us feel really, really small. But in a hundred years, we're going to realize that intelligence is more vast than we could have ever have imagined and we're going to think that's beautiful.
one_liner: Groq Founder Jonathan Ross explains why the insatiable demand for compute and its energy requirements are the defining challenges of the AI era, and how Groq's unique chip architecture and supply chain are positioned to address them.

title: FOUNDER ADVICE: How to Create a Category
key_insights: Category creation is a complex, under-documented field, often learned through one-on-one mentorship rather than established resources.
Successfully creating a category requires a persistent, long-term effort likened to 'market annealing'—continuously hammering at the market until it becomes receptive.
Working against a negative macro trend is extremely difficult; aligning with market trends is crucial for success.
Effective storytelling is vital not only for educating the market but also for aligning and motivating the internal team around a clear, deeply believed-in vision.
In a market contraction, companies must right-size to the new reality through a full operational replan, rather than simply freezing hiring, to remain viable and continue building.
fundraising_mentions: The discussion addresses how a changing funding environment impacts category-creating companies, with advice to 'cut burn' and 'right-size the company' to match the market opportunity and capital availability.
quotable: I was very very heavily involved in the creation of software-defined network and network virtualization like you know I spent 10 years like I call it Market annealing just hammering the [...] out of a market just [...] beating on the market for years until it comes around.
I believe you can death march to a public company without the market ever actually unlocking.
one_liner: a16z's Martin Casado breaks down the art and science of category creation, highlighting the importance of relentless market development, strategic storytelling, and adapting company operations to the macroeconomic environment.

title: Why You Should Hire a Former Founder
key_insights: Former founders are ideal for leading growth teams due to their resilience, long-term focus, and revenue orientation, even if their previous startup failed.
If a former founder isn't available, seek candidates from consulting backgrounds who are strong in data, process, and hypothesis testing, as growth is fundamentally about running a process.
An initial growth team should be a 'startup within the startup' comprising a head of growth (the ex-founder), at least one engineer to build and ship, and a marketer/copywriter.
A key interview tactic is to provide a take-home data assignment with hidden 'Easter eggs' (outliers or anomalies) to see if the candidate can spot and question inconsistencies.

To assess a candidate's approach to risk and strategy, ask them about how they win at video games or board games to understand if they can think outside the box and make calculated, risk-adjusted bets.
quotable: Growth is about running a process not about like being super like smart it's running a process.
That is growth is understanding the rules thinking outside the box and making interesting valuable bets risk adjusted bets.
one_liner: HyperGrowth Partners Founder Guillaume Cabane makes the case for hiring former founders to lead growth teams, outlining their unique advantages and a specific hiring process to identify candidates who are aggressive, data-driven, and strategic risk-takers.

title: Top Two Lessons from 27 Years in Venture Capital
key_insights: Too much cash, even for disciplined startups, can be detrimental and lead to a 'death spiral' if performance falters.
Hypergrowth phases can create pressure for new hires if the company misses targets, impacting morale.
Ownership in investments is crucial, but it must be carefully balanced against the company's valuation.
Frequent preemptive fundraising rounds can lead to investments made without adequate de-risking or performance validation between rounds.
A less competitive fundraising environment allows for more thorough evaluation and strategic increases in ownership.
fundraising_mentions: too much cash can kill startups right at any stage
so many preemptive rounds happening over the last few years where every 6 months people are raising rounds
shouldn't have gotten into every single one of those rounds because maybe it wasn't risked enough between the time you closed around and the next round
less retive rounds there is more time to understand has this been der risked enough is this an appropriate time to lean in even more to actually do your prata or get more ownership
ownership always Matters by the way on these exits particularly in a world of lower multiples
quotable: no matter how disciplined you are... too much cash can kill startups right at any stage
ownership matters always but also you have to balance that out with valuation as well
one_liner: A venture capitalist shares two key lessons: the perils of too much cash for startups and the delicate balance between ownership and valuation, especially concerning preemptive fundraising rounds and exits in a lower-multiple market.

title: Why We Need to Fix Climate Change NOW
key_insights: A massive resource reallocation, potentially up to 50% of GDP, is necessary and possible to fight climate change, but it requires political leadership that can frame it as a winning proposition and a societal mission.
Incremental approaches to the climate crisis are failing; what's needed is a dramatic, transformational change across the board, moving beyond the mindset of small fixes to the industrial age.
Developing nations have a unique opportunity to 'leapfrog' legacy fossil fuel infrastructure by directly implementing decentralized, renewable energy systems, much like they did with mobile banking.
The public misunderstands the sheer scale of the climate crisis; the excess heat being trapped in the atmosphere is equivalent to the energy of 4-7 Hiroshima-sized nuclear bombs every second.

Civil disobedience is a compulsory and historically proven tactic for forcing significant societal change, serving the crucial role of keeping the climate crisis in the news and applying pressure on the political system.
quotable: Of every second of every minute of every hour of every day, it's like four to seven Hiroshima size nuclear bombs worth of heat. Now I wanted to imagine for a moment... alien spaceships hovering above Earth and throwing four to seven Hiroshima size nuclear bombs into our atmosphere every second. What will we do? We would drop everything.

As long as you're caught in this idea that this is an incremental transition, your approach to the climate crisis will also be incremental. But it's not a problem that can be solved with incremental approaches.
one_liner: Albert Wenger argues for a radical, non-incremental, leadership-driven transformation of the global economy to address the climate crisis, viewing it as both the greatest threat and biggest opportunity of our time.

title: Amjad Masad: How I Founded Replit; Zuck's Famous Saying; Will TikTok be banned? | E987
key_insights: Great startups are like 'conspiracies to change the world,' started by a small group with a secret or unique insight.
Hiring for 'early signs of exceptionalism' and 'misfits' can be a competitive advantage, though it comes with management challenges.
A core value is to 'seek pain,' meaning proactively facing difficult problems and truths to avoid larger issues down the line.
AI is creating the next major productivity S-curve in software development, with models writing up to 80% of code for some engineers, allowing them to focus on higher-level business logic.

The rise of AI will likely increase wealth inequality as small, highly-leveraged teams can create billion-dollar companies, but it may decrease knowledge inequality by providing universal access to powerful tools.
quotable: Great startups are examples of conspiracies to change the world.
The idea of being normal is just or Normie as we call an internet culture is like very scary to me and undifferentiated is is is something that I really don't like to be.
one_liner: Replit founder Amjad Masad shares his journey and contrarian views on building startups, hiring 'misfits,' and how AI will fundamentally reshape software development and wealth distribution.

title: How Helium uses tokens to boost network effects 🤔 - Part 2/2
key_insights: Early network participants take on more risk and should be compensated with greater financial upside.
Helium's model issues a fixed amount of tokens per unit of time, meaning fewer early participants split more tokens among themselves.
This token incentive structure directly couples the financial risk of being an early adopter with a higher potential reward.
Participants in the Helium network create tangible economic value by building a physical wireless network that competes with established players like Verizon and AT&T.
Token-based incentives represent a breakthrough in capital formation, enabling the bootstrapping of physical infrastructure networks in a way that was previously not possible.
quotable: This is I think like the textbook example of using token incentives to bootstrapping network where you actually are both able to assign risk and reward and couple those things in in a real meaningful way.
This is like I think like a real breakthrough in capital formation and just wasn't possible before.
one_liner: This episode explains how Helium's token model incentivizes early adopters with higher rewards to compensate for greater risk, effectively bootstrapping a decentralized wireless network to compete with incumbents.

title: Trae Stephens: Why No Company is Successful Because of their VC | E1135
guest_role: Partner at Founders Fund & Co-Founder of Anduril
key_insights: The worst deals are the most competitive, consensus-driven ones, as they indicate mimetic contagion in the market.
Founders Fund's unstructured, conviction-driven investment process is intentionally difficult to prevent 'gaming the system' and force high-conviction bets.
A company's success stems from the founder and their team, not the VCs. The best a VC can do is ride along and not be annoying.
To succeed in the defense sector, a company must be excellent at government relations and lobbying from day one; a great product alone is insufficient.
Successful hard tech companies require a founding team that pairs technical genius with equally brilliant business acumen.
If you have a thesis about a market (e.g., Space Tech) but aren't invested in the monopoly winner (e.g., SpaceX), you are probably too late and will lose money.
fundraising_mentions: Founders Fund raising its first billion-dollar fund in 2013.

quotable: Any company that's successful is not successful because their VCs are really smart. That's not how this industry works.
Competition is for losers and it will always be for losers. I don't care if it's venture capital or startups or anything, competition is for losers.
one_liner: Founders Fund Partner and Anduril Co-founder Trae Stephens shares his contrarian investing philosophy, arguing that VCs don't make companies successful, competitive deals are the worst deals, and winning in defense requires mastering both technology and politics.

title: Fivetran's Lauren Schwartz: Must-Ask Questions to Identify Potential Sales Talent | 20VC #939
key_insights: To get past rehearsed interview answers, ask a sales candidate for the 'second' deal they are most proud of, not the first.
Create urgency by working backward from the customer's desired outcome date, building a mutual action plan that demonstrates the need to start immediately.
When hiring initial reps, hire two at once to distinguish signal from noise and ensure you're testing the market, not just one person's ability.
A key interview question is about a lost deal; it reveals if the candidate has an internal locus of control (accountability) or an external one (blaming others).
Effective deal reviews should focus on two key questions: 'What did we learn?' and 'What would we do differently next time?' to ensure they are learning opportunities, not just victory laps.
quotable: It ends up being that you're not selling, you're helping them participate in their own rescue.
The best skill you can develop in sales is an insatiable curiosity about what's possible.
one_liner: Fivetran's sales leader Lauren Schwartz shares her playbook on hiring elite enterprise sales reps, creating genuine urgency, and running effective deal reviews to build a high-performing team.

title: How Venture Capital differs in the EU vs US
key_insights: The European venture market has matured to a point where founders no longer need to go to the US for capital, giving them more control over who they choose as partners.
Venture is described as a 'transparently competitive sport' where founders' choices determine which VCs succeed.
US multi-stage VCs are increasingly competing and winning hot seed-stage deals in Europe against local European VCs.
European VCs are perceived as having an 'image problem' and are less effective at storytelling and selling themselves compared to their US counterparts.
Despite the prestige of US firms, European VCs have historically been the ones to support future European unicorns at the crucial seed and Series A stages.
fundraising_mentions: US multi-stage VCs are winning 'supremely hot deals' at seed stage in Europe.
Three deals in the last three months were won by US multi-stage VCs against European seed VCs.
quotable: Venture is a very transparently competitive sport where the founders ultimately choose who deserves to be in the ring.

European VCS suck at telling stories I know often people like oh why didn't you have more European VCS honestly they they really do not articulate stories well and they're not inspiring exciting they don't resonate in a way that us VCS absolutely do.

title: Bill Ackman: Why I Post on Twitter
guest_role: Hedge Fund Manager, CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management
key_insights: Twitter serves as a powerful platform for influencing large companies and corralling shareholders.
Financial independence is crucial for exercising free speech without fear of professional repercussions.
The ability to speak freely is perceived as being suppressed, making platforms like Twitter vital.
Twitter is an effective tool to reach influential figures in policy-making, even if direct calls are not taken.
Public advocacy on Twitter during financial crises, like the Silicon Valley Bank situation, is critical for addressing systemic risks.
quotable: I would say Independence was always one of the uh I did not like the fact that my parents could control me.
it's an effective way to reach the people that matter in DC and otherwise uh about important policy things.

title: How To Create and Execute a World-Class Sales Playbook
key_insights: Founders must create the initial sales playbook, which focuses on identifying the right customer persona, the value proposition, and the best way to reach them.
A scalable, repeatable sales playbook isn't feasible until a company has at least 20 ramped Account Executives; before that, the focus should be on agility and learning.
When hiring initial customer-facing roles, prioritize smart, hungry individuals to gather market insights, not necessarily pure salespeople focused only on revenue.
Early sales hires should be onboarded with a focus on product knowledge first (often through support tickets), then market context, and finally sales process.

Transitioning from a product-led growth (PLG) model to an outbound sales motion is a company-wide initiative that requires new messaging, product augmentation, and marketing alignment for a more senior buyer persona.
Early-stage variable compensation should be flexible (e.g., bonuses, team comps) rather than a rigid commission plan, as targets are hard to set and likely to be wrong.
A key responsibility of a sales leader is to provide structured feedback and insights to the CEO to aid in strategic decision-making, not just to bring in revenue.
When a sales champion leaves a deal, the 'five whys' analysis often reveals a failure to build a multi-threaded relationship within the account, not just bad luck.
fundraising_mentions: Founders have gotten enough traction to raise a Seed or Series A round.
Today's seed rounds and Series A rounds are 'massive'.
Asana had $20 million in revenue, primarily from self-serve, when a formal sales deck had not yet been created.
quotable: If you're going to operate you either build product or resell product everything else is supporting one of those two.
I don't think you create that playbook until you have at least 20 ramped aes where you can where you have the right to say this is a playbook.
one_liner: Sales leader Oliver Jay breaks down the process of building a world-class sales playbook, detailing when and how to hire the first sales reps, structure compensation, and scale from a product-led motion to an enterprise sales organization.

title: We're Gonna Need a Bigger Yacht | Billionaire Founder of Mailchimp, Ben Chestnut
key_insights: Even after immense success, founders can feel inadequate when comparing themselves to others, exemplified by the 'bigger yacht' anecdote.
A significant post-exit challenge for founders is learning to be content with their achievements rather than perpetually wanting more.
The guest's personal ambition has shifted from external exploration (space, ocean) to internal exploration of his own mind and motivations.
The desire 'to not want' is framed as the ultimate form of contentment and freedom from the cycle of desire.
The guest reflects on the freedom of not taking VC money, which allowed him to operate on his own timeline without external pressures.

one_liner: Mailchimp founder Ben Chestnut discusses the psychological shift after selling his company, the trap of constant comparison, and his personal journey toward finding contentment by wanting less.

title: Clubhouse CEO Paul Davison: What does Clubhouse do now to regain mindshare? | | 20VC #929
key_insights: The best communication products don't invent new behaviors; they take what humans are already wired to do and make it easier to do instantly with anyone.
Clubhouse's core value proposition is not content consumption but creating a space for authentic conversation and friendship ('hanging out'), differentiating it from broadcast-focused platforms.
The 'why now' for Clubhouse was a convergence of AirPods, Alexa, and accelerated remote living, creating a window for a new social audio experience to emerge.
Managing hypergrowth is a double-edged sword; while it brings massive attention, it can severely stress the product and community, leading to a poor user experience if not managed well.
Davison believes the company that wins in a new medium (like social audio) will be the one that is 100% focused on it, rather than a larger incumbent adding it as a secondary feature.
fundraising_mentions: The company was just two founders at the time of the Series A.

quotable: My fundamental belief is that the best communication products they don't invent new behaviors they take what we are wired to do as humans what we love doing and they make it easier to do it instantly with anyone.

I feel personally that I really admire entrepreneurs I really admire people who take a swing and it's so easy to try to dunk on people... but I get personally really inspired by the people that they're out there trying.
one_liner: Clubhouse CEO Paul Davison reflects on the company's founding, the challenges of navigating hypergrowth and public perception, and his vision for the future of social audio centered on friendship and authentic conversation.

title: Sanjit Biswas: Samsara's $18BN Market Cap & $1BN in ARR in 8 Years | E1092
key_insights: Product-market fit shouldn't be forced; listen for the 'wow' moment from beta customers who will literally pull the product out of your hands.
A practical capital allocation strategy is the 70-20-10 rule for R&D: 70% on scaling existing products, 20% on new products for the 1-3 year horizon, and 10% on long-term bets.
Second-time founders have a key advantage in pattern matching, knowing what product-market fit feels like and having a network of trusted people to hire quickly.
Founder-led sales are powerful because founders have deep product knowledge and the ability to shape the roadmap, which customers value highly.
Regularly 'rehire yourself' by writing a new job description for your role based on the company's needs 1-2 years in the future, and adjust how you spend your time accordingly.
fundraising_mentions: Meraki (first company) was bootstrapped to nearly $1M in revenue before taking venture capital.
Samsara's seed round was self-funded by the co-founders, allowing them to move much faster without a formal fundraising process.
quotable: Companies pay to have their problem solved and so when we talk about things like revenue and revenue growth for me it's actually impact and problem solving growth.
I think product Market fit is something you don't want to force... get out there with customers with beta testers and listen for the wow.
one_liner: Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas discusses the lessons learned from building his second billion-dollar company, focusing on achieving product-market fit, strategic capital allocation, and the unique advantages of being a second-time founder.

title: Benchmark vs a16z: Why Stage Specific Firms Win

The venture market is polarizing between specialized, single-stage firms and large, multi-stage 'mega funds' that can offer capital from pre-seed to pre-IPO, creating a 'bundled' product that is difficult for smaller firms to compete with.

There's a significant debate on whether AI will cause mass, rapid unemployment in knowledge worker roles within 24 months, or if its impact will be a more gradual productivity increase akin to previous technological shifts like the PC and the internet.

While momentum can create a temporary moat for new AI companies, the extreme pace of innovation and competition means long-term durability is a major risk; today's leader could be 'maimed' by a competitor tomorrow, impacting their ability to IPO.

The return to 2021-style valuations for some AI companies (e.g., Decagon's 100x ARR multiple) is driven by VCs betting on the 'option value' of unbounded future growth, rather than the 'intrinsic value' of a more mature, stable business.

We are missing the fact that no one wants to work. No one wants to work. And this is an honesty that people are not like... if you squint it with these emails that what they're really saying is no one wants to work. So, you're out of a job.

title: Will there be more bank runs?
key_insights: The likelihood of subsequent bank runs depends more on depositor psychology and customer base concentration (e.g., tech or digital assets) than on universal mark-to-market asset values.
Even financially strong banks are at risk if panic spreads, as individual depositors act to protect themselves, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy of a bank run.
The FDIC's most critical task is to instill confidence, ideally by finding a buyer for the failed bank who can guarantee all deposits at par to ensure immediate liquidity and quell panic.

The SVB collapse is not a 'one percenter' problem; its impact extends broadly across the economy to industries like agriculture (wine growers) and affects employees of small companies who lack complex multi-bank relationships.
The worst-case scenario is the FDIC failing to find a buyer, leading to companies being unable to make payroll, causing layoffs, and triggering wider economic disruption.
fundraising_mentions: VCS are trying to line up payroll financing for their portfolio companies.
quotable: No one wants to be the last man standing... if everyone else jumps ship you're still sunk too if the ship goes down. I think that that psychology impact is massive.

It's not a one percenter problem there are employees at those companies that do all kinds of jobs and those companies it's the wine industry so Farm Growers across Northern California and so as much as we want to think of svb and its clients and then its clients clients as being impacted that is a broad swath of the economy right there.
one_liner: A financial expert analyzes the causes and potential fallout of the SVB collapse, emphasizing the power of market psychology in driving bank runs and the broad economic consequences beyond the tech industry.

title: Brian Tolkin, Head of Product @Opendoor: How to Hire the Best Product Teams | E1257
key_insights: The core PM job of understanding user needs and business viability remains, but AI will collapse the development cycle by making prototyping faster and more accessible.
A key product skill is simplification: distilling the 'kernel of truth' from the 'cacophony' of user feedback, executive pressure, and data to focus on what truly matters.
When expanding from a single to a multi-product company, you must leverage an existing competitive advantage (customers or capabilities) without degrading the core product experience.
'Hire your strategy': The type of PM you hire dictates the product's direction, so it's crucial to match their specific skills (e.g., technical, design, business) to the team's and problem's needs.
For early-stage companies, prioritizing growth and new features to 'earn the right to exist' is often more critical than paying down technical debt.

To avoid getting stuck on a bad decision versus a user adjustment period, set up experiments to evaluate behavior over a longer timeframe (e.g., weeks 5-8, not 1-4) to see if user behavior normalizes or improves.
Disagree and commit works for short-term velocity, but if you find yourself disagreeing and committing too often, it's a sign of fundamental misalignment and you might be in the wrong place.
fundraising_mentions: Hypothetical Series A company trying to go from $2 million to $8 million in ARR.
quotable: You hire your strategy. The person you pick to play that role will dictate how that person defines the success of that product.
Computers are deterministic, humans in the real world are not. And so you have real world entropy and you have to think about how your product adapts to that real world entropy.
one_liner: Opendoor's Head of Product, Brian Tolkin, shares lessons from scaling Uber and Opendoor, covering how to hire strategic product teams, the impact of AI on development, and the art of prioritizing in high-growth environments.

title: Matt Plank, Rippling's CRO: How to Build an Enterprise Sales Machine | E1241
key_insights: Founders should hire go-to-market leaders earlier than they think and should not be the ones to create the sales playbook.
Outbound sales are not dead but are critical for scaling; success requires a deep, credit-agnostic partnership with marketing and specialized SDR teams.
Win rates of 60-70% are a negative signal, indicating your price is too low. Companies should raise prices until they encounter friction to maximize revenue.
The biggest reason for losing a deal is often customer indecision, not competitors. The best reps build a pipeline of 'lost' deals that often circle back when the timing is right.
Time kills all deals; sales leaders must distinguish between deals that genuinely 'push' and those that 'poof' (disappear), often due to a failure to manage processes like legal review in parallel.
To scale as a leader within a high-growth company, you must be able to hire people better than you and make tough decisions about layering homegrown talent that has hit its scaling limit.
fundraising_mentions: No specific fundraising details were mentioned, but the context is a high-growth company aiming to be in the 'top 1% of SaaS companies' and growing at '60, 70, 80, 90% year-over-year at hundreds of millions of dollars'.
quotable: I think Founders wait too long to hire a go to market and I think they do that because they feel like they can't hire a good salesperson potentially without a bunch of traction.
You got to be able to know how to lose an opportunity and come back and bounce back... you got to be okay with accepting a lot of rejection if you're in sales.
Did it push or did it poof?
one_liner: Rippling's CRO Matt Plank discusses the essential strategies for building a high-growth enterprise sales machine, covering the importance of outbound, pricing until friction is met, and the mindset required for sales leaders to scale effectively with their company.

title: Bill Ackman's Biggest Loss of All-Time
key_insights: True success is measured by how you handle failure; focus on making small, consistent progress every day to overcome challenges.
A critical lesson from the failure of Gotham Partners was the danger of asset-liability mismatch: avoid holding illiquid assets in an open-ended fund structure where capital can be redeemed.
During dark periods, prioritize fundamental well-being: adequate sleep, proper nutrition, and exercise provide a significant psychological boost.
Post-mortems should analyze not only direct losses but also 'mistakes of omission'—missed opportunities that you should have capitalized on.
In moments of pressure, like being down in a tennis match, it's crucial to not let past errors disrupt future performance; reset and focus on the present opportunity.

Don't let the past disrupt the future... just you know start with a blank sheet of paper it's a new set new opportunity and rebuild from here.

key_insights: The current model of online platforms is broken because consumers and creators do not own the data or the value they generate.
Platforms like Twitter and LinkedIn capture nearly 100% of the direct economic value from user-generated content and data.
While users receive indirect benefits like distribution and personal branding, the share of value is heavily skewed towards the intermediary platform.
The future will see a shift towards a more direct model where creators and data owners receive a larger, more equitable share of the economic value they create.
This new model questions the fundamental structure of how value is captured and distributed in the digital economy.
quotable: The way buyers and sellers connect is fundamentally broken because you don't own your data.

title: Bob Pittman: The Unlikely Story of How I Created MTV (Part 1)
