Technological limitations in the past, such as the lack of syndicated signals in radio, created unique job opportunities.
Rapid career advancement is often dependent on key mentors who believe in you and provide opportunities.
A perceived career setback, like a mentor leaving a company, can unexpectedly open doors to new and transformative ventures.
Career decisions that seem illogical to others, like leaving an established giant for a nascent industry, can be the result of 'dumb luck' and lead to massive success.
quotable: how did I go from being a 15-year-old disc jockey in Brook Haven Mississippi to programming the NBC station in Chicago where I was 20 years old
I went to MTV because my great mentor at NBC at the time herb schaser who is the president of NBC got kicked upstairs and I thought my trajectory is over.
one_liner: Bob Pittman shares his unlikely journey from a 15-year-old radio DJ in Mississippi to programming major NBC stations by 23 and then co-founding MTV, emphasizing the role of mentorship and seizing unexpected opportunities.

title: How to engineer your own luck 🍀
key_insights: Perceived luck is the result of thousands of consistent micro-actions over time.
Putting yourself in a consistent situation, even without a specific goal, can lead to serendipitous opportunities.
The speaker's habit of going to the gym at 5 am daily led to a chance, consistent interaction with Tim Cook.
This consistent, informal interaction blossomed into one of the most important mentor relationships in the speaker's life.
True luck can be created by the actions you take and the routines you follow, rather than being a purely random event.
fundraising_mentions: Tim Cook is a backer of the speaker.
quotable: a lot of what we perceive as luck is just the macro result of thousands of micro actions
it was luck that was created by the fact that I was showing up day in day out with no intentions of having some you know some end to it it was just the natural byproduct of actions on my end
one_liner: The speaker illustrates how consistent daily actions, like an early morning gym routine, can lead to life-changing opportunities and mentorship, as exemplified by their relationship with Tim Cook.

title: Emil Michael: How I Negotiated the $4B Uber-China Deal, Why DoorDash Caught Up to Uber | 20VC #941
guest_role: Former SVP of Business at Uber
key_insights: The most critical element in negotiation is to outwork your counterpart by knowing everything about them, their company, and their motivations.
Effective negotiation requires being a 'shock absorber' to the other party's emotions, maintaining composure to gain a strategic advantage.
The 2022 investment climate shifted from 'FOMO' (Fear Of Missing Out) to 'JOMO' (Joy Of Missing Out), where investors are happy to pass on deals, demanding a return to entrepreneurial humility.
The Uber-China deal, valued at $7B, was achieved through building personal trust and rapport with the counterpart at Didi, even amidst intense competition and suspicion.
Benchmark's push to oust Travis Kalanick was driven by 'loss aversion'—prioritizing the protection of their massive paper gains over the potential for future growth.
Uber missed a significant opportunity by not winning the food delivery market against DoorDash, a mistake estimated to be worth tens of billions of dollars.
fundraising_mentions: TellMe raised $150 million over four rounds in 12 months in the late 90s.
TellMe was acquired by Microsoft for approximately $800 million.
Uber raised $3.5 billion from the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF).
The Uber China entity was acquired by Didi in a deal that valued it at $7 billion.
During a 2014 fundraising, an initial $8 billion valuation offer was turned down, leading to a $17 billion valuation two weeks later, followed by subsequent rounds at $40B, $50B, and $62B.
quotable: Number one thing in negotiations is outwork whoever you're negotiating with.
Last year was fomo Juan square fomo with investors... this here is Jomo. Joy of missing out. They are happy to miss out on whatever deadline you put on them for whatever round.
one_liner: Former Uber SVP Emil Michael provides a masterclass in high-stakes deal-making, detailing the intense negotiations behind the Uber-China deal and offering a candid take on Uber's past, present, and the venture market's shift.

title: Why Creatives Will Always Win: The Limitations of Artificial Intelligence in Content Creation
key_insights: There is a critical need for transparency and regulation regarding the training data used in large language models.
AI is a fundamental platform shift, comparable to electricity or the steam engine, with a far greater societal impact than crypto.
AI will cause a massive step-change in productivity, but threatens to dramatically worsen wealth inequality by enabling billion-dollar companies with very few employees.
In the near future (5 years), 60-80% of code could be AI-generated, allowing developers to focus more on high-level business logic rather than boilerplate code.
Efficiently prompting AI is a difficult but crucial new skill that users and developers need to learn to leverage the technology effectively.
Content creators and publishers have a right to know and control if their content is used for training commercial AI models, raising complex licensing and SEO-like challenges.
fundraising_mentions: The funding hype around AI is overhyped, but it's a necessary part of the innovation cycle to discover what works.
quotable: If it doesn't mean a step change in your productivity, then you're using it wrong.
I think this has a bigger impact on society than than crypto will because this has the the type of impact that uh that electricity and and the steam engine had in terms of productivity changes.
one_liner: Joost de Valk discusses the profound societal and economic impacts of AI, from demanding transparency in LLMs and fearing unprecedented wealth inequality to embracing the massive productivity gains that will reshape content creation and software development.

title: UK Prime Minister's First Job as a Waiter 🍴
key_insights: Having a job, regardless of its glamour, is crucial for personal development.
Early work experience teaches valuable skills like teamwork and responsibility.
The hospitality industry is vital for the economy and provides many first job opportunities for young people.
The hospitality sector has faced significant challenges, requiring government support.
Work provides a sense of fulfillment and contributes to the vitality of local communities.
quotable: having a job whatever the job is is really important
it was amazing to go to a place for the first time to do something fulfilling
one_liner: Keir Starmer, the UK Prime Minister, reflects on his foundational experience as a waiter, emphasizing the profound importance of first jobs for young people, the value of learning essential skills like teamwork, and the critical role and resilience of the hospitality industry, which his government has actively supported.

title: Jason Lemkin: Predictions for 2024 - What Does a Trump Administration do for Startups? | E1099
key_insights: The SaaS market may be reaching a saturation point where it can no longer grow faster than GDP, with 2023 showing the slowest growth rates ever for public SaaS companies.
Venture capital has permanently shifted from 'unicorn hunting' to 'decacorn hunting' for all post-seed investments, raising the bar for what is considered a fundable company.
2024 is expected to be the year many mature, late-stage companies (like Stripe and ServiceTitan) 'might as well go public,' regardless of lower market multiples, simply because it's time to mature.

Founders taking massive secondary exits (e.g., Hopin) before the company is self-sustaining is viewed as unethical and a major red flag indicating they are not truly committed to a long-term, outlier outcome.
The best investors only back founders who are demonstrably better than themselves and will never invest in 'pretty good' founders, regardless of traction, as only outliers generate venture returns.
fundraising_mentions: OpenAI ended 2023 at a $1.4 billion run rate after raising at valuations from $20B to $100B.
Pipedrive, Jason's first investment at $16M pre-money, eventually sold for $1.5B.
ServiceTitan is at over $500M in revenue and was valued at $9.5B in its last private round.
The Hopin founder took out $140M in a secondary sale.
A multi-billion dollar fund declined to do their pro-rata in a good company, signaling a new level of conservatism from VCs.
quotable: I have changed my mind that there is any chance on planet Earth... that a pretty good founder can produce good Venture returns. I will never again invest in pretty good Founders no matter what the traction is.
I think we are Deca-corn Hunters Forever, series a and Beyond. I think the industry has permanently changed and it may be under-discussed that we're Deca-corn Hunters.
one_liner: SaaStr CEO Jason Lemkin analyzes the 2023 venture landscape, predicting a challenging 2024 for SaaS growth that will push mature companies to IPO while VCs focus exclusively on hunting for decacorn-level outliers.

title: Andrew Bialecki: Is Klaviyo the Most Under-Priced Public Company? | E1170
key_insights: Bootstrapping and capital constraints foster creativity and force a deep connection with customer problems, leading to a stronger product.
A successful long-tail SMB strategy requires a product that is so good it markets itself, lowering customer acquisition costs.
Strategic partnerships, like the one with Shopify, are most effective when they are a 'win-win-win' for both companies and the customer, aligning product, go-to-market, and financial incentives.
Pricing changes, even when justified by added value, require transparent communication with customers about the long-term pricing philosophy to maintain trust.
The journey to IPO should be viewed as a milestone for a ready business, not the end goal, with the focus remaining on long-term growth and operational efficiency.
fundraising_mentions: Applied to $20,000 no-equity programs early on and was rejected by all.
Raised a $1.5 million seed round at a 20x ARR multiple when they hit ~$1 million in ARR.
Added $5 million more from the same investor a year or two later.
Raised over $100 million at an ~$800 million valuation when the company was at $50-60 million in ARR.
quotable: You could build the best product but the best product doesn't always win. In some sense we built claviyo to say like well gosh darn it like we're going to level the playing field... and now the best products can win.
I've always subscribed to like you will get the investors that you deserve.
one_liner: Klaviyo Co-founder Andrew Bialecki discusses the journey of bootstrapping a product-led SaaS company, the strategic partnership with Shopify, and the decision to go public while maintaining a focus on customer value and long-term growth.

title: Why 75% of Active Investors Will Disappear in the Next Few Years
key_insights: A significant portion (50-75%) of 'so-so' venture firms are predicted to disappear due to a lack of clear differentiation, as founders increasingly seek distinct characteristics in their investors.
Power in venture is shifting from monolithic firms to individual partners, with personal brands and deep, authentic relationships becoming more critical for winning deals.
Markets matter more than founders. A great founder in a bad market is likely to fail, whereas a sufficient founder in a great market has a high chance of success.
The market correction has not yet led to a full reality check on valuations. Many founders still expect high valuations, while investors struggle to price deals, creating a disconnect.

Successful community building in venture is not an afterthought or a deal flow mechanism (like many scout programs), but a core product focused on providing continuous value to people throughout their careers.
fundraising_mentions: Passed on Coinbase at a $1.5 billion valuation.
Led an investment in Pave from Index Ventures and then invested again from Contrary in the same round.
Discussion on the relative ease of raising a $2 billion fund versus a $200 million fund due to large LP allocation needs.
quotable: If a good manager meets a bad business, it's the reputation of the business that remains intact. I think the same way about a market.

I wish there was a better way to de-risk those earliest days of starting a company. I think that there are a lot of ambitious people sort of trapped in a systemic risk intolerance because of their circumstances.
one_liner: A GP at Contrary analyzes the venture capital landscape, predicting a mass extinction of undifferentiated firms and explaining why power is shifting from firms to individual partners with strong personal brands and deep community ties.

title: Adam Gross: Why Startups Doing Paid Under $100M ARR are not PLG | E1145
guest_role: Former CEO at Vimeo, Angel Investor
key_insights: PLG is a holistic business model, not just a go-to-market motion. It requires architecting the entire product, business, and organization around it.
Authentic PLG businesses below $100M ARR should not rely on paid acquisition; they need a specialized, organic customer acquisition channel.
The PLG journey involves distinct value propositions for different stages: Creation (for individuals), Collaboration (for teams), and Compliance (for enterprises).
When hiring, it's crucial to distinguish whether you need a 'poet' (a domain/content expert) or a 'librarian' (a process/systems expert) for a given role.
A true 'growth mindset' involves intentionally owning and forging your company's growth, rather than passively experiencing viral growth.
Founders should avoid layering on an enterprise motion too early (before $10M ARR) as it distracts from perfecting the core PLG engine.
Building an 'emotive brand' is critical for developer tools and PLG companies to connect with individual users, combining emotional connection with strategic impact.
fundraising_mentions: Saw the Twilio seed round but didn't invest.
Had visibility into the Stripe seed round and might have been able to get in.
Was the first check into Docker's first round, but got recapped.
quotable: PLG is not a go to market motion plg is a business model.
If you are doing plg and you're doing paid acquisition sub 100 million in Revenue I'm not sure you're really plg.
Are you hiring a poet or are you hiring a librarian?
one_liner: Adam Gross explains why true Product-Led Growth is a complete business model, not a GTM tactic, detailing the necessary stages from individual creation to enterprise compliance and the importance of avoiding paid acquisition in the early days.

title: Delian Asparouhov: Inside the Walls of Founders Fund: What the World Does Not See | E1183
guest_role: Principal at Founders Fund & Co-founder of Varda
key_insights: The United States enables both extreme risk and extreme reward (e.g., homelessness and Elon Musk), arguing you can't have one without the other.
Generational companies are built with a strong, pre-conceived vision ('Hollywood analogy'), not by iterating based on early customer feedback.
Founders Fund maintains a contrarian, founder-friendly ethos, believing that founder-led companies are the only path to the highest-beta venture outcomes.

The most successful junior VCs differentiate themselves by doing the things senior partners won't or can't, like deep-diving on niche science or taking last-minute international flights for diligence.
The venture industry is reverting to its deep-tech, capex-intensive roots, and funds that are too specialized in areas like SaaS will struggle as those sectors fall out of favor.
fundraising_mentions: Had the opportunity to invest in Sword at a $100 million post-money valuation ($10 million check).
Ramp's seed round was hot with five or six other offers, priced around a $25 or $30 million post-money valuation.
Varda has intentionally not taken the highest-priced offer in its funding rounds.
quotable: People love software because you know sort of the marginal distribution costs are zero, perhaps what people need to realize is also that the marginal returns are zero as well because there is no moat.
Extraordinary careers when you're junior in venture do not get built sitting behind a desk in an office.
one_liner: Founders Fund Principal Delian Asparouhov shares his contrarian views on venture capital, the importance of founder-led vision, the decline of Western Europe, and why the future of tech belongs to capital-intensive, deep-tech industries.

title: 99% of Startups FAIL Because of this ONE Mistake 🙅‍♂️
key_insights: A company that achieves genuine product-market fit will almost inevitably become massively successful, regardless of how well-run it is.
A primary mistake startups make is hiring too many people before achieving product-market fit, in an attempt to find it.
Operating with 'N-1' resources (being under-resourced) creates a forcing function to focus on achieving product-market fit and eliminate all other distractions.
Having 'N+1' resources (being over-resourced) allows startups to pursue losing ideas for far too long.
It's better to have a small, focused team discovering product-market fit through intense customer interaction, and then scale resources as certainty increases.
fundraising_mentions: The tendency to spend available capital ('I have the money, I might as well spend it') leads to premature scaling of the team.
quotable: What I think people are doing is they're hiring ahead of product Market fit to get product Market fit.
Having too few resources forces you to say get product Market fit eliminate distractions and you don't need that many people to do that.
one_liner: Keith Rabois argues that the most common fatal mistake for startups is hiring too aggressively before achieving product-market fit, whereas staying lean and resource-constrained forces the focus required for success.

title: Sales Lessons from George Hu
key_insights: A strong, respected sales leader can fundamentally pivot a company's strategy by effectively making the case for go-to-market investment, as George Hu did at Twilio.
The 'revenue game' is won not by hope, but by a deep understanding of the underlying math and a predictable operating model that can be controlled to drive growth.
Effective mentorship involves providing challenging, sometimes cryptic, guidance ('haikus') that empowers the mentee to learn and solve problems independently, rather than simply being given answers.
A non-traditional career path, like George Hu's rise from intern to COO at Salesforce, demonstrates that navigating a company internally can lead to immense success.
Scaling from a large run rate (e.g., $200M) to a billion-dollar goal requires implementing a rigorous operating model and mathematical mechanics, moving beyond just product and self-service.
fundraising_mentions: The speaker joined Twilio as the last hire pre-IPO.
quotable: He challenged me through almost like haikus he would give me these like here's a couple of lines about the thing you need to learn next go figure it out and he would certainly not do it for me.

It's about winning that Revenue generating game and how do you continue to make things go up and to the right in a predictable way not on Hope but something that you can control that's going to drive Revenue up into the right.
one_liner: A sales leader from Twilio shares instrumental lessons from mentor George Hu on building a predictable revenue engine through a mathematical and operational approach to sales, and the power of challenging mentorship.

title: The 5 Pillars of Venture Capital & Why Co-Pilot is an Incumbent Strategy
key_insights: Co-pilot strategies for AI are an incumbent's game; the real disruption for startups lies in a new architecture of 'selling the work, not the software', moving from a 'co-pilot' to a 'control center' model.
The five pillars of venture capital are Sourcing, Selecting, Signing, Supporting, and Summiting (achieving an exit/distribution).
Great investors operate with a 'biologist' mindset (curious about new adaptations and variants) rather than a 'physicist' mindset (applying fixed playbooks).
The diligence process should feel like 'planning an adventure, not a colonoscopy,' focusing on collaborative future-planning with the founder rather than an examination.
Kindness and competitiveness are not mutually exclusive; they can and should coexist in harmony within business and investing.

Benchmark's investment in LangChain after a three-month relationship-building period.
Missed opportunities in Figma (Kleiner Perkins, Index Ventures), Plaid, and Scale AI.
Monzo's crowdfunding rounds.
50-60% of Benchmark's investments are as the first institutional partner.
quotable: It should feel like planning an adventure, not a colonoscopy.
The very best entrepreneurs are always making mistakes; the really great ones are just making new mistakes each time.
one_liner: Benchmark Partner Miles Grimshaw discusses his investment philosophy, the five pillars of venture capital, and argues that the future of AI for startups is not in co-pilot features but in a new architectural model of 'selling the work, not the software'.

title: Saam Motamedi: Why Series B Won’t Make Money & Why $1M ARR is a BS Milestone for Series A | E1177
key_insights: The current AI market is in an 'exuberant bubble,' with valuations (100-200x revenue) disconnected from public market multiples (15-20x), making it even 'crazier' than the 2021 peak.

The Series B market is frothier now than in 2021, and the asset class as a whole may not make money in this vintage due to extreme pricing unless growth durability is far greater than historical precedent.

$1M ARR is a poor filtering mechanism for Series A investments; it's more important to prioritize iconic founders and massive market potential, as many companies hit early ARR milestones but fail to scale.

Now is the best time to build new, large horizontal SaaS companies because generative AI enables fundamental disruption to the data models, delivery models (pricing), and interfaces of incumbent systems of record like Salesforce.

For truly iconic, category-defining companies, investors shouldn't pass on a deal over valuation differences in the seed stage (e.g., $20M vs $30M post-money), as the outcome potential dwarfs the entry price sensitivity.
Signaling risk from a prestigious seed investor not leading the Series A is 'total bullshit'; great companies will always get funded on their own merits.
fundraising_mentions: Seed rounds for AI companies are being priced in the 'many tens of millions of dollars even hundred million dollar plus post money ranges.'
Typical high-quality seed rounds are priced between $20M to $40M post-money.
Typical high-quality Series A rounds are priced between $80M to $200M post-money.
Whiz raised its Series A at a $500M valuation with zero ARR.
Upwind raised a $26M seed round led by Greylock.
Greylock invested $5M in BrainTrust's first round.
quotable: I think the series B market may be even frothier than it was in 21. I really wonder if the series B asset class as a whole is positioned to make money this vintage.

It drives me crazy when I hear, you know, investors write these blog posts, 'your checklist for the series a, number one, a million dollars of ARR'. Why does that drive me crazy? Because for you to make money on a series a... you've got to get into a business that gets into the hundreds of millions of ARR.
one_liner: Greylock Partner Saam Motamedi discusses why he believes the current AI bubble is making Series B unprofitable, why $1M ARR is a flawed metric for Series A, and why now is the best time to build new enterprise systems of record.

title: Q-Commerce in Emerging Markets with the CEOs of Airlift, JOKR, & Zepto | 20VC #892
key_insights: Emerging markets offer a faster path to profitability for q-commerce due to lower wage costs and the ability to offer a broader assortment, leading to higher AOV.
High population density in emerging markets ('density is destiny') enables dark stores to achieve thousands of orders per day, dramatically lowering fixed costs like rent as a percentage of revenue.

Unlike Western markets, consumers in emerging markets are already accustomed to frequent, ad-hoc grocery shopping, which makes the q-commerce model a natural extension of existing behavior rather than a forced change.

A primary challenge is the underdeveloped infrastructure and fragmented supply chains, forcing companies to build their own vertically integrated procurement systems, especially for high-margin fresh produce.
Successful q-commerce players in these markets function as a full 'one-stop-shop' supermarket, not just a convenience service, with fresh products being a key driver of retention and margin.

Retail media and advertising present a massive, largely untapped revenue stream (potentially 5-15% of total revenue) as CPG brands have historically lacked targeted, point-of-purchase advertising channels in these regions.

There are two emerging models: ultra-fast (10-15 min) delivery with lower AOV, which requires immense order density, and fast (30 min) delivery with higher AOV, which may have a quicker path to profitability with less capital.

Focusing on 'gross profit per order' is a more nuanced North Star metric than AOV alone, as high-margin categories like fresh produce can have lower average selling prices but contribute more to the bottom line.
fundraising_mentions: One model requires raising 'multiple hundreds of millions of dollars if not billions of dollars' to achieve the necessary order density.
Generating cash from operations (like advertising) allows them to 'raise less money' and reinvest it back into the business.
quotable: In q commerce, density is destiny.
The thing that I want to or would like to change most about the world of quick commerce is to give it a different name because it's not only about quick commerce, it is e-commerce 3.0.
one_liner: The CEOs of Airlift, JOKR, and Zepto break down the unique unit economics, operational challenges, and massive opportunities of building q-commerce businesses in emerging markets, arguing it's a fundamentally different and potentially more profitable model than its Western counterparts.

title: Scooter Braun: How I Discovered Justin Bieber
key_insights: A catalytic moment, often perceived as a crisis or negative event, can be leveraged to create massive public awareness and success.
Having a long-term strategic 'blueprint' or vision for a talent's career from the very beginning is crucial for guiding them to massive success.
Utilizing platforms like YouTube with consistent content can create a binge-watching effect, rapidly growing an audience and making a new artist a platform-native star.
A single breakout piece of content can act as a tipping point, causing an audience to discover and consume an entire back-catalog of work.
Reacting to moments of tragedy or chaos with a strategic mindset can change the entire trajectory of a situation, turning a negative into a significant positive.
fundraising_mentions: The host mentions 'the fundraise' as an example of a catalytic moment, but no specific fundraising details from the guest are discussed.
quotable: When I saw Justin... I was like this kid's gonna be the biggest artist in the world I know exactly what to do to help them become that.
Almost every single time I something bad happens or you would assume it's a bad situation I always say okay there's there's a there's something in this for us.
one_liner: Scooter Braun discusses discovering Justin Bieber and turning potentially negative events, like getting arrested for an over-crowded mall appearance, into a catalytic moment that created a household name.

title: How I Bought 12% of Google for $12M; How VC is Fixing Climate Change | John Doerr Full Interview
key_insights: The climate crisis represents the greatest economic opportunity of the 21st century, involving the wholesale transition of every industry from a fossil fuel-based system to a clean, renewable one.

Using the OKR (Objectives and Key Results) framework, the 'Speed & Scale' plan outlines measurable, time-bound goals for decarbonization across six key areas: electrifying transport, decarbonizing the grid, fixing food, protecting nature, cleaning industry, and removing carbon.

While technology and investment are advancing, the biggest obstacle to climate action is the lack of government urgency; making climate a top-two voting issue in major economies is a critical key result.

The story of the Google investment (the 18th search engine) demonstrates that you can be successful even in a crowded market if you have a dramatically superior innovation and a clear vision for its scale.

VCs don't need to be climate scientists to invest in the space; they can apply their domain expertise (e.g., SaaS, enterprise) to climate-related problems, such as carbon accounting software like Watershed.
fundraising_mentions: Invested $12 million for 12% of Google at a $100 million valuation.
Kleiner Perkins invested about a billion dollars across 70 climate-related companies in its first wave, which is now worth about $3 billion.
Kleiner invested $29 million in Enphase, which is now worth a billion dollars.
quotable: You can only lose one times your money in venture capital, you can make many times that over.
I may not be optimistic but I'm hopeful.
one_liner: Legendary investor John Doerr discusses his OKR-based plan to solve the climate crisis, drawing parallels from his iconic investments in Google and Amazon to frame climate action as the greatest economic opportunity of our lifetime.

title: ButcherBox vs Supermarkets: CEO Mike Sagluero Breaks Down the Cost of Meat
key_insights: Efficiency in the meat supply chain is heavily dependent on the scale of operations, with larger runs and fuller trucks significantly reducing costs.
Logistics, including moving products, and pick-pack-ship operations, represents a massive cost factor in the meat industry.
Operating at scale can lead to dramatic cost reductions, exemplified by ButcherBox reducing organic chicken costs by 70%.
Hiring experienced personnel, like a knowledgeable meat buyer, is crucial for optimizing procurement and avoiding overpayments.
Understanding and leveraging supply chain dynamics is key to competitive pricing in the meat market.
quotable: it costs the same to run a truck half empty as it does to run it fully full
I can get three pounds [of organic chicken] for the same price you want to do that and we're like uh yeah we should do that.
one_liner: ButcherBox CEO Mike Sagluero explains how optimizing efficiency, logistics, and scale in the meat supply chain drastically reduces costs compared to traditional supermarkets.

title: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All?

one_liner: Legora CEO Max Junestrand discusses the intense, winner-takes-all competition in the legal AI space, detailing their explosive growth, strategic shift to Anthropic models, and vision for the future consolidation of AI-powered law firms.

title: Why AI is a 💩 place to invest

The improving capabilities of foundational LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) threaten the viability and retention of application layers built on top of them, leading to churn.
Current 'enterprise buying' of AI often represents small-scale testing (e.g., 10K trials with a few designers) rather than widespread, enterprise-wide rollouts.

one_liner: A venture investor expresses skepticism about current 'AI first' investment opportunities due to excessive hype, high valuations, competitive noise, the potential for foundational LLMs to supersede application layers, and limited deep enterprise adoption.

title: We Accidentally Hired a Sandwich Thief
key_insights: Running background checks on potential hires is a crucial and non-negotiable step in the hiring process.
Early-stage and 'scrappy' startups often overlook essential HR processes like background checks, exposing them to significant risks.
A bad hire can introduce unforeseen and extreme liabilities, including legal and reputational damage.
Terminating a problematic employee can be complex, especially if they try to use leverage or threats.
Founders often learn critical business lessons, like the importance of due diligence in hiring, through difficult and costly experiences.
quotable: It turns out that when you hire people, it's a really good practice to run a background check on them.
I'm gonna let everyone know that you hired a level three sex offender.
one_liner: A founder of CustomMade recounts a shocking early-stage hiring mistake involving a sandwich-stealing employee who turned out to be a level three sex offender, underscoring the critical importance of conducting background checks.

title: We Turned Our Yearbook Company into $40B
key_insights: Traditional graphic design tools were complex and difficult to learn, paving the way for easier online solutions.
The future of creation involves online, collaborative, and user-friendly platforms.
Starting with a specific niche (school yearbooks) can provide valuable experience and validate a broader market need.
Geographic isolation and a lack of early venture capital did not prevent the development of a successful global company.
Observing how users repurpose a product beyond its initial intent can reveal significant market opportunities for scaling.
fundraising_mentions: there's no such thing as Venture Capital there and we had no idea we didn't know what a startup was
quotable: in the future creation is going to be totally different it's going to be online it's going to be collaborative and it's going to be easy
people are using our yearbook software for all kinds of different things they're creating newsletters they're creating posters the world needs this maybe we can scale this idea
one_liner: A co-founder of Canva shares the story of how their initial school yearbook company evolved into a multi-billion dollar global design platform by focusing on accessible online creation.

title: Phin Barnes: The Services Model of Venture Capital is Broken, The Best Founders Do Need Help | E1067
key_insights: The traditional VC services model is broken because services act as a cost center, leading to junior staff providing fractionalized, generic support. An alternative is to unbundle services from capital, offering them for equity, thus aligning incentives and making it a revenue center.
The best founders consistently need and seek out help, but they require deep, one-on-one domain expertise, which is often not what traditional VC platforms provide.
Founder evaluation should focus on understanding priorities and operating styles. A key question to reveal this is, 'What's the best thing that happened at your company this week?'

Investment mistakes often stem from being overwhelmed by a founder's strengths while missing the critical impact of a weakness. A key weakness can act as a 'zero in a multiplication problem,' negating all strengths.

Experienced, second-time founders often prefer specialized, high-impact help over brand-name, multi-stage funds because they understand the difference between perceived value and actual operational support.

VCs should focus on a niche. Expanding beyond what made you successful (e.g., from seed to later stages) is challenging because it can erode the very focus and product that created the initial success.
fundraising_mentions: a five on 25 or six on 40 pre-seed or seed round
a three on 15 vs five or six on 30 or 40 round
five on 50
a $7 million seed round after already raising two
quotable: Every great founder needs help they just don't need it from VCs.
The result of that work to optimize for the GP business model is you end up with increasingly Junior people paying increasingly fractionalized attention to a Founder's most critical needs.
one_liner: Phin Barnes explains why the traditional venture capital services model is broken, detailing his new firm's approach of providing elite, hands-on support in exchange for equity to give founders a genuine execution advantage.

title: Adi Levanon on the Never Again movement
key_insights: The core idea of the 'Never Again' movement is a universal responsibility to prevent atrocities, not just for one group.
Being a passive bystander to hate and injustice is a form of complicity and a moral failure.
There is a shared, fundamental human desire for peace and a good life for one's children, which exists among both Israelis and Palestinians.
Online speech and social media activity have real-world consequences, and inaction in the face of hate is as damaging as the problem itself.
It is crucial to stand up and condemn horrific acts, even if one is afraid to take a specific political side.
quotable: if you see it if you're aware of it you are responsible to stop it that is the immorality that we're fighting against.
if you're out there and you're part of these groups or you're aware of them and you're not doing anything to stop them you're just as bad as the problem itself.
one_liner: Adi Levanon argues that the 'Never Again' movement mandates a universal responsibility to actively combat hate and injustice wherever it appears, emphasizing that passivity is a moral failure.

title: Keith Rabois: The End of Woke Capitalism; Time Allocation Tips; Silicon Valley vs Miami | 20VC #891
topics: The role and value of VCs
key_insights: The 'buy low, sell high' mantra is ineffective in early-stage venture; you are definitionally buying low, and success depends on identifying companies with 100x+ potential from the outset.
Market downturns and crises are healthy because they eliminate distractions like 'woke capitalism' and force companies to focus intensely on performance and survival.

The most successful investors can often identify the massive upside case (e.g., a $50-100B company) within the first few minutes of meeting a founder, a skill derived from experience rather than just metrics.

Silicon Valley has shifted from being an advantage to a disadvantage for building companies, due to an exodus of top talent, network erosion, and safety/quality of life issues that distract from productivity.

Investors should rationally allocate their time to their best-performing companies where they can have high leverage, as these drive returns, rather than being consumed by struggling companies that won't impact the fund.
For early-stage investing (Seed/Series A), the entry valuation is largely irrelevant ('a trap'); the focus should be on the ultimate upside potential, not the initial price.
An investor's biggest mistakes are often not passing on companies they met, but declining to meet founders of what later became highly successful companies.
fundraising_mentions: Airbnb seed round was at a $3.5 million post-money valuation.
Stripe Series C co-led with Founders Fund.
Fair Series C led by Founders Fund.
Founders Fund invested in later-stage rounds (e.g., Airbnb, Stripe) at valuations around $1 billion rather than $3-4 billion.
Khosla Ventures' KV-5 is a $1.3 billion fund.
quotable: I think wokeness is a function of entitlement... when people are under stress when they have to perform when there is no possibility of future finances unless you get your act together it will concentrate people's minds.
The price and valuation just doesn't matter in traditional ventures even series a it's kind of the peter fenton line... valuation is always a trap.
one_liner: Keith Rabois discusses why traditional investment axioms fail in venture, how market downturns enforce focus and kill corporate 'wokeness', and why Silicon Valley is now a disadvantage for building startups.

title: This BILLIONAIRE invented a new kind of debt (but it's not what you think)
key_insights: Culture debt is created by making suboptimal hiring decisions, such as hiring non-diverse teams or individuals who are a poor cultural fit.
Culture debt is considered the most insidious form of debt because its 'interest rate' is unknown and it can never be fully 'paid off'.
A single bad hire in a company's early stages can have a lasting toxic impact on the culture, influencing many subsequent hires.

Unlike financial debt, which is settled with money, or technical debt, which is resolved by refactoring code, the negative effects of culture debt can persist for years, even after the problematic employee has left.
The behavior of early employees establishes a precedent for what is deemed acceptable within the company's culture.
quotable: Culture debt is when you hire um either non diverse teams or you hire people that are jerks that don't really fit and no one wants to be around.
It is the most Insidious form of debt and the reason I say that is number one you don't really know what the interest rate is... you never really can fully pay it off because it's so toxic.
one_liner: Dharmesh Shah explains the concept of 'culture debt,' the long-lasting negative impact of poor hiring decisions, which, unlike financial or technical debt, can be impossible to fully repay.

title: Ultimate Guide to Interviewing a Growth Candidate
key_insights: Before hiring a growth person, founders must first understand their own growth model and initial growth loops to define the required profile.
The job description for a growth hire should detail initial KPIs and focus areas (e.g., onboarding, activation) to attract the right expertise.
A take-home assignment based on the company's actual business is crucial to assess a candidate's thought process, data analysis skills, and ability to generate experiment ideas.
Ask candidates for their most 'unexpected' experiment result; a lack of one is a red flag, as it suggests inexperience with the high failure rate of A/B tests.
Key red flags in a growth candidate include a large ego, a lack of self-awareness, and a rigid mindset that relies on outdated playbooks.
quotable: What is the most unexpected experiment result you saw and what do you do after it?
If I hear them look no I don't have any unexpected experiments everything works as I planned that's a red flag because that's not possible like 60% of a b testing fail.
one_liner: A growth advisor provides a comprehensive framework for founders to structure the hiring process for their first growth leader, from writing the job description to identifying critical red flags during interviews.

title: Shervin Pishevar: What Really Happened in the Firing of Travis Kalanick | E1245
key_insights: Shervin Pishevar alleges that VC firm Benchmark, led by Bill Gurley, orchestrated a deliberate campaign to oust Uber's founder, Travis Kalanick, starting months before public controversies.
The ousting of Kalanick was timed to exploit his vulnerability following the tragic death of his mother, according to Pishevar.
Pishevar claims he was personally targeted with a fabricated police report by Fusion GPS to silence his opposition to Kalanick's removal.

He believes Uber would be a trillion-dollar company today if Kalanick and his right-hand man, Emil Michael, had not been forced out, calling it one of the greatest value destructions in tech history, similar to Steve Jobs' firing from Apple.
Pishevar argues that the traditional venture capital model is 'dead,' having become a commoditized, low-margin industry, and that a new era of founder support and alternative financing is needed.
fundraising_mentions: Menlo Ventures' Series B investment in Uber at a $290 million valuation.
Benchmark's Series A investment at a $50 million pre-money valuation.
Series C led by Google and TPG at a $3 billion valuation.
Series D raise at a $17 billion valuation.
SoftBank's $12 billion investment.
TPG's $83 million secondary purchase using a 'Waverly loan'.
quotable: I believe if Travis and Emil had stayed at Uber Uber would be a trillion dollar Company by now.
The Venture Capital that we grew up with and that we looked up to is that model is gone... venture capital is dead.
one_liner: Investor Shervin Pishevar provides his explosive inside account of the power struggle at Uber, alleging a coordinated effort by VC firm Benchmark to remove founder Travis Kalanick, which he believes cost the company nearly a trillion dollars in potential value.

title: Nick Jones: How I Founded Soho House; Brand Marketing Tips; Hiring Advice | 20VC #898
key_insights: Experiencing and learning from early business failures is an invaluable asset for long-term success.
True brand building is about creating a 'way of living' rather than just a product; simplicity in all aspects is key to this.
Global expansion can be de-risked by first building a membership community in target cities ('Cities Without Houses') to validate demand and build local connections.
Effective hiring involves a mix of internal promotion and external talent, with a core principle of being brutally honest about the challenges of the role during the interview process.
Strong leadership requires admitting your own mistakes to create a culture of psychological safety where team members feel comfortable owning up to their errors.
fundraising_mentions: Mentioned having to raise money to open the New York location, which was incredibly challenging as banks weren't lending at the time.
quotable: I don't really like the word brand... I like to think that it's what we're doing at sour house and and and ultimately... is just a way of living really.
When you do make a mistake is put your hand up admit it, admit it to the team, you know don't try and think you're always getting it right and and I think people really respect that.
one_liner: Soho House Founder Nick Jones discusses the importance of learning from early failures, building a brand as a 'way of living', his strategies for global expansion, and his leadership philosophy on hiring and creating a culture of honesty.

title: Nabeel Hyatt, GP @ Spark Capital: To Win in AI, Investors Need to Change Their Approach | E1255
key_insights: Venture capital must shift from a 'puzzle-solving' mindset (e.g., predictable SaaS metrics) to a 'mystery-navigating' approach for the unpredictable AI landscape, emphasizing first-principles and subjective bets over rigid frameworks.
The current VC industry is often driven by misaligned incentives, where junior partners and principals optimize for short-term markups for promotion rather than long-term company building.

In AI, founder 'taste' and judgment are becoming more important than raw execution speed, as the underlying technology can make execution easier, placing a premium on unique product and user experience insights.

The best way to evaluate founders is to analyze their product as a manifestation of their thought process, decisions, and taste, asking 'why' they made certain choices to understand the humans behind the product.

Sustainable value in AI will come less from temporary moats and more from a founder's ability to continually innovate, learn, and reinvent, as technological shifts can quickly erode existing advantages.

AI startups can be categorized as Adaptation (incumbents adding AI), Evolution (new native workflows), and Revolution (entirely new platforms), with the most disruptive and valuable opportunities lying in the latter two.
fundraising_mentions: Spark's early-stage fund is a little over $700 million.
Spark's growth fund is double the early-stage fund.
An example investment negotiation was mentioned: 'we put down like 10 on 60 and the founders like I want 100'.
Sequoia's seed fund is mentioned as $190 million, and their growth funds as 'a billion and a half or two'.
quotable: We are in the industrialization of startups Playbook land where everybody's trying to churn out some piece of ridiculous Arbitrage every week in order to get through the end of their incubator and raise their seed round.

If you are always the shoot first ask questions later person you probably are not really deeply introspective about the choices that you're making... and if you are deeply deeply deeply full of taste you didn't ship anything.
one_liner: Spark Capital's Nabeel Hyatt argues that to win in the new era of AI, venture capitalists must abandon the industrialized, metric-driven playbook of the last decade and return to a first-principles, taste-driven, and founder-centric approach focused on navigating 'mysteries' over solving 'puzzles'.

title: Uber's $150BN mistake 💰❌
key_insights: Uber's acquisitions of Kareem, Postmates, and Jump Bike are viewed as significant strategic errors that will likely result in complete write-downs.
The acquisition of Postmates for nearly $3 billion is singled out as one of the worst tech acquisitions in recent years, providing no gain in market share from a company on the brink of failure.
Internal conviction that Uber was positioned to win against DoorDash before the departure of CEO Travis Kalanick.
A belief that Uber missed the opportunity to build a global grocery delivery competitor to Instacart, potentially surpassing them.
By winning in its core ride-sharing and food delivery markets, Uber's potential valuation could have been around $200 billion, significantly higher than its current state.
quotable: Postmates may be the worst acquisition done in Tech in the last five years so it's for three billion dollar company that was like going to be a zero within three months.
You're talking about a 200 billion dollar business without any creativity this is just weaning where we should have won and beating instacart when we should have beat instacart.
one_liner: An analysis of Uber's costly acquisition mistakes and missed opportunities that could have valued the company at over $200 billion.

title: SALES TIP: Should you offer discounts to close deals?
key_insights: Discounting should not be the only sales strategy to create urgency.
Strategic discounting can be a powerful tool to close deals, especially at the end of a quarter.
Bundling new features without a pre-existing price and then offering a discount can be an effective tactic.
Procurement departments are often motivated by deadlines and cost savings, which can be leveraged in negotiations.
There are multiple levers to create urgency beyond pricing, including contract terms and highlighting the risks of inaction.
quotable: if discounting is your only strategy then you're in trouble
it's free money that package didn't even exist before
one_liner: A sales leader shares a story from his time at Twilio about strategically using a discount on a bundled product to close a major deal with an airline on the last day of the year.

title: Celtics Owner is Optimistic About Gen-Z
guest_role: Co-owner of Boston Celtics & Co-chairman of Bain Capital
key_insights: The current generation (Gen-Z) entering the workforce has a stronger sense of purpose compared to previous generations, who were more focused on basic security.
Gen-Z is actively demanding and driving positive changes in the workplace, such as increased diversity and a focus on social and environmental issues.
While some view this generation as 'entitled' and lacking a 'grind' mentality, they work just as hard but are more judicious and efficient with their time.
This new generation prioritizes a more balanced life, which can lead to better judgment and decision-making in business and investment.
The push from younger employees is forcing industries like private equity to evolve and address long-standing issues like diversity and climate change, ultimately making organizations better.
quotable: I'm really optimistic about this current generation... they really have a more of a sense of purpose that we have maybe because we came out as depression mentality that all we had to do is feed the family.

I think these people work as hard as ever but they've made it a priority to be more balanced and I said I think that balance would be a good thing for for making judgment and investment decisions and and having a great life.
one_liner: Bain Capital's Co-chairman and Boston Celtics' Co-owner, Steve Pagliuca, expresses his optimism for Gen-Z's purpose-driven approach to work and life, arguing it will lead to better organizations and a healthier society despite challenges to the traditional 'grind' culture.

title: The Art of the Board Meeting
key_insights: Board meetings are valuable for giving functional leaders a voice and providing the board with insight into the founder's team-building capabilities.
Effective board members are low-ego, action-oriented, and act in service of the founders, focusing on adding value rather than dominating the conversation.
A common mistake young investors make on boards is talking too much and not listening enough.

Founders should prepare for board meetings by communicating with members beforehand to set the agenda, sending a pre-read document (preferably not a Google Doc to encourage independent thought), and focusing the meeting on meaty, discussion-worthy topics.

Founders are in control of their board meetings and should manage dominant personalities, either by asking an ally on the board for help or by politely redirecting the conversation back to the agenda.
Post-meeting debriefs between board members (to get aligned) and individually between board members and the founder (to give feedback) are crucial for success.
quotable: As a younger investor you tend to talk to more too much and not listen so I think that's the biggest mistake.
You control the board meeting and it's on you to give everybody room.
one_liner: Oana Olteanu provides a masterclass on running effective board meetings, offering actionable advice for both founders on preparation and execution, and for investors on how to be truly valuable board members.

title: Three Signs of a Bull Market and How to Stay Disciplined
guest_role: Co-President and Chairman of the Global Technology Group
key_insights: The venture and growth communities often lose discipline during bull markets due to excitement, FOMO, and misaligned incentives, leading to over-investment at peak valuations.
A key sign of a market top is when everyone, including the least talented investors, is making money.
When traditional valuation metrics like EBITDA are disregarded in favor of creative new metrics (e.g., growth-adjusted ARR multiples), it signals a frothy market.
A dramatic spike in deal velocity, with deals closing in weeks instead of months, is a third sign that the end of a bull market is near.
To protect against market downturns, GA advised its portfolio companies to secure fully funded plans in 2021, resulting in them raising $20 billion in primary capital.
fundraising_mentions: In 2021, our portfolio raised 20 billion dollars of primary Capital.
Today we have 200 companies 97 of them fully funded plants.
quotable: We drink our own Kool-Aid, we over-invest in the peak of the bull market and we lose all discipline, and it happens time and time again.
When everyone's making money, even the least talented people in the market, that's a clear warning signal.
one_liner: A leader from General Atlantic outlines the three key indicators of a bull market peak and shares the disciplined strategy they employed to prepare their portfolio for the inevitable correction.

title: How Should LPs Price Their Books Today?
key_insights: Many Limited Partners (LPs) are uncertain about the true value of their venture capital portfolios.
A common practice for LPs is to discount their fund managers' reported valuations by an additional 20-25% to account for unknown variables.
Major technological shifts, such as the rise of AI, can cause rapid and dramatic changes in company valuations, creating 'rocket ships' or making others obsolete.
Customer buying behavior is shifting as AI-driven products change the competitive landscape.
There is a significant difference in how transparently and aggressively various fund managers value the companies in their portfolios.
quotable: I know a lot of LPS that will ask their managers and then go back home and take another 20 to 25% off the top because there's things that nobody knows.
AI happens and some companies become rocket ships because they've managed to do something with AI that the works in the market and other companies not right.
one_liner: A discussion on the challenges LPs face in valuing their venture portfolios amid market ambiguity and the disruptive impact of AI, highlighting the common practice of significantly discounting manager-provided valuations.

title: GetYourGuide CEO & Founder, Johannes Reck: The Wild Story Raising $450M From Masa and Softbank
key_insights: Early on, stay narrowly focused on the core product and customer segment; avoid premature expansion and hiring senior people before you have strong product-market fit.
During a crisis (like COVID), it can be better to retain core talent and invest in the product, even at a high cash burn, to be prepared for the rebound.
Founders gain more respect from their board by having a strong, opinionated strategy rather than simply following VC suggestions, which led to significant mistakes after their Series A.
Having a prominent US VC like Spark Capital on the cap table made subsequent fundraising rounds significantly easier due to signaling and network effects.
The journey of a successful company is measured in decades, not years. It's crucial to build sustainable work habits and personal balance to maintain energy for the long run.
fundraising_mentions: Seed: $1 million at a $5-6 million pre-money valuation from Brent Hoberman and Profounders.
Series A (2013): $14 million at a $30-35 million pre-money valuation, led by Spark Capital.
Series B: $25 million at a valuation around $90-100 million, co-led by Spark Capital and Highland Europe.
Softbank Round (2019): $450 million from SoftBank Vision Fund and Temasek at a $1.5-1.6 billion valuation.
Convertible Debt (during COVID): $100 million from existing and new investors.
Post-COVID Equity Round (2023): $100 million at an up-round valuation compared to the Softbank round.
quotable: When you go and race right you look at the road you don't look at the wall because if you look at the wall as a race car driver you're going to hit the wall... stay focused on the road. And I think that's very much what it what it felt like at the time, like we're even considering failing. Like for me, like failure was nonoptional.
The biggest trees grow because they have the nutrient-rich soil after wildfire and they have full exposure to the sun. And I said, I want to be that sequoia after the COVID crisis.
one_liner: GetYourGuide CEO Johannes Reck recounts the tumultuous journey of building a global travel marketplace, detailing the pivots, critical fundraising rounds, navigating the COVID-19 collapse, and the key lessons learned from scaling a European startup to a multi-billion dollar valuation.

title: Jason Lemkin: Cold Email Tips; Why Only 15% of Founders Listen to their VCs | 20VC #954
key_insights: A detailed, high-quality cold email that shows deep understanding and traction is the most effective way to get an investor's attention; it can make them want to invest before the meeting even happens.
As an operator-turned-VC, you should invest in founders who are demonstrably better than you were. This is a key indicator of a startup's potential for success.
Don't be deterred by a small initial Total Addressable Market (TAM). Hyper-growth, even from a small revenue base, is a powerful indicator that the market is much larger than it appears.

Competing with free or open-source products can be a strong positive signal. If you're gaining significant traction against a free alternative, your product must be magical on at least one critical axis.
Nearly every successful company hits a growth plateau. This is almost always a management team problem, caused by waiting too long to hire or refresh the executive team.
fundraising_mentions: Invested $500k in Algolia at a $12M pre-money valuation, with an alternative option of $1M at $15M pre-money.
Pipedrive sold for $1.5 billion.
Salesloft exited for $2.5 billion.
quotable: I like a cold email that's so good that I already want to invest before the meeting.
You have to invest in CEOs that were better than you.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin details his contrarian approach to venture capital, using his investment in Algolia as a case study to explain his preference for inbound deals from 'SaaStr superfans', the importance of backing founders who are better than him, and why early hyper-growth is the best indicator of a large market.

title: The Story Behind Amazon’s $1B Acquisition of Ring
key_insights: The acquisition by Amazon was the result of a multi-year partnership focused on building trust and understanding each other's culture, not an abrupt transaction.
The founder was driven by an intense fear of failure, which he used as motivation to 'over-execute' rather than being paralyzed by it.
Successful post-acquisition integration was heavily dependent on the founder's full and authentic commitment to becoming part of the acquiring company's culture ('I'm an Amazonian now').
Amazon facilitated a successful integration by respecting Ring's autonomy and allowing the team to voluntarily adopt Amazon's resources and processes, rather than forcing a rigid playbook.
Building trust within a team requires a willingness to continuously take risks on people, even if you've been burned in the past, because the leverage from a great team is worth the risk.
fundraising_mentions: The acquisition by Amazon was for $1 billion.
The company was 45 days away from a 'fire sale' before the acquisition, indicating a near-death experience.
quotable: I'm so in fear of everything that I overcompensate on the other side.
I'm not crippled by fear, I over execute because of fear.
I would rather keep getting hurt and find a few great people than never be with great people.
one_liner: Ring founder Jamie Siminoff discusses the emotional journey leading to the $1B Amazon acquisition, how he channels fear into a driving force for execution, and the key principles for a successful post-acquisition integration.

title: Fmr. Uber Exec Grades Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi's Performance - Emil Michael
key_insights: Uber's valuation has declined under Dara Khosrowshahi's leadership, underperforming the broader NASDAQ market.
Uber lost its significant lead in the food delivery market to DoorDash, which is framed as a multi-billion dollar strategic failure.
Acquisitions like Postmates, Kareem, and Jump bike are considered poor strategic moves and likely write-downs, with Postmates being called 'the worst acquisition done in Tech in the last five years'.
Uber missed a major opportunity to build a global competitor to Instacart in the grocery delivery space.

There's a perceived shift from an 'aggressive Barbarians' culture that was necessary for initial growth to a softer, less effective 'kombucha' culture, with a suggestion that a reversion to a more aggressive mindset is needed in tough economic times.
quotable: By all objective measures it hasn't succeeded from a financial standpoint... it's an F.
We were aggressive Barbarians at the gate trying to make a ride sharing work because we had to.
one_liner: Former Uber executive Emil Michael gives CEO Dara Khosrowshahi a failing grade, citing a decreased valuation, the loss of the food delivery market to DoorDash, and a series of poor acquisitions.

title: David Lieb: How I Founded Google Photos & Bump; Why I Left Google | 20VC #927
key_insights: If you have to ask whether you have product-market fit, you don't. It's an unmistakable feeling of being overwhelmed by customer demand.

A clear, focused mission is critical for team alignment and product success. Google Photos' mission was to be 'the home of the world's memories,' which guided decisions on what *not* to build (e.g., a social network).
Your gut is the world's most sophisticated machine learning model. Feed it with as much data and customer interaction as possible, then trust its output for making creative, non-obvious decisions.
Founders often hire senior leaders like a CPO too early. The founder should not delegate the most important problem for the company's success, which is often figuring out the product.

When hiring product leaders, don't over-index on tenure or managing large teams. Look for ambition, a 'chip on their shoulder,' and a craftsman or visionary mindset, as B-players will hire C-players and degrade the team.
The best product hires often come from non-traditional backgrounds with no domain experience, as they bring ambition and a drive to prove themselves.
fundraising_mentions: Mentioned raising money for his startup, Bump, and having a meeting with Sequoia.
quotable: If you don't know if you've got it or not, you don't.
I think your gut is the world's most sophisticated machine learning model ever created.
one_liner: David Lieb, founder of Bump and former head of Google Photos, shares his journey and deep insights into product development, the importance of mission, trusting your gut, and the nuances of hiring and scaling product teams.

title: David Schneider: Why the Worst VCs are "Seagull VCs" & VC Value Add - Is it Real? | E1200
key_insights: Customers buy products for one of three reasons: it helps them make money, it saves them money, or it keeps them out of trouble (off the front page of a newspaper).
The Customer Success function can often be redundant, as its core responsibilities (support, up-sells, implementation) should belong to Support, Sales, and Professional Services respectively.
The worst VCs are 'Seagulls' who fly into a meeting, make a lot of noise, create distracting work for the team, and fly away without adding real value.
When hiring go-to-market leaders, look for people with a 'chip on their shoulder' and something to prove, as hunger is a key driver of success.
Instead of creating new budget categories, it's often easier to win deals by unlocking dollars from existing, known spending areas with a more efficient solution.
fundraising_mentions: Data Domain was acquired by EMC for around $2.2 billion in a hostile takeover.
ServiceNow went public at $18 per share, valuing it at a 'couple billion dollars'.
As a growth investor, Schneider typically writes a $75 million check for a board seat.
quotable: There are VCS that are seagulls fly into a meeting fly into a location they basically take a and they fly away.

People buy product for three reasons they either buy it because it's going to help them make money they buy product because it's going to save them money or it's going to keep them off the front page of a newspaper.
one_liner: Legendary operator David Schneider discusses his playbook for scaling ServiceNow from $80M to $5B, the problem with 'seagull VCs', and why he dismantled the customer success team.

title: Sequoia Partner, David Cahn on Who Wins in AI, Defence & The New $0–$100M Playbook
key_insights: We are in an AI bubble, but the interesting question is who survives. Consumers of compute will benefit as the overproduction of compute drives down prices and improves their gross margins.
The physicality of AI (data centers, power, steel) is a critical, underestimated factor. The ability to build and manage this infrastructure is becoming a competitive moat.

The new playbook for top AI companies is the 'zero to 100 club,' characterized by extremely rapid growth from $0 to $100 million in revenue, which serves as the strongest indicator of product-market fit in the current environment.

The lesson that punches you in the stomach in venture is you can't 'king-make' a company to succeed with capital alone; success is fundamentally driven by the founder, the team, and real product-market fit.

Defense is the 'next AI.' The sector is in its early stages, similar to AI a few years after the Transformer paper, and is poised for a massive digital transformation with a few concentrated, national champions set to win.
fundraising_mentions: Weights and Biases' Series A
Runway ML's investment before Stable Diffusion
Hugging Face's early investment
Clay's Series A in 2019 and a later growth investment at over $1 billion
Juicebox's investment
Sequoia's two rounds in Stark (defense)
Investment in Kella (defense)
Investment in Sesame (AI voice company)
quotable: The lesson that punches you in the stomach in venture is you can't make a company succeed.
Consumers of compute benefit from a bubble because if we overproduce compute, prices go down, your COGS goes down, and your gross margin goes up.
one_liner: Sequoia Partner David Cahn analyzes the current AI bubble, detailing who will win and lose, the new $0-$100M growth playbook for startups, and why he believes defense is the next major technological wave to watch.

title: Sean Murray: Why Discovery Today is F***** & How to Scale Into Enterprise Effectively | E1107
key_insights: The three biggest challenges when moving into the enterprise market are lack of credibility, achieving true product-market fit for large, complex organizations, and proving financial stability.

Modern sales 'discovery' is broken; instead of asking questions they could find answers to online, sellers should focus on 'teaching' the buyer by reframing their problems and introducing new perspectives.

Sales and marketing must be deeply integrated, with the CRO acting as a marketer and the CMO as a seller. This blend is critical because buyers complete most of their evaluation before ever speaking to a sales rep.

To effectively scale into the enterprise, companies must be prepared for a full organizational effort, not just a sales and marketing motion. It requires significant investment and a longer time to see returns.
When hiring sales reps, use a structured, data-driven process based on competencies (like intellectual curiosity and drive for results) to eliminate bias and increase the probability of success.
fundraising_mentions: Mentions the over-inflated valuations of companies raising in 2020-2021 but no specific details about his company's fundraising.
quotable: Discovery as we know it is f*****.
The worst deal is the one that takes too long. Drop your price and go get the f****** deal and move on. Just move on. Go get the next deal.
one_liner: Greenhouse CRO Sean Murray breaks down why traditional sales discovery is obsolete and shares his playbook on how startups can overcome the credibility, product, and financial hurdles to effectively scale into the enterprise market.

title: People who think this recession is bad have NO LIFE EXPERIENCE
key_insights: The current economic downturn is not evenly distributed; certain sectors like healthcare and B2B e-commerce are still performing well.
Founders should identify and target customer segments that are winning in the current market instead of adopting a pessimistic outlook.
B2B e-commerce experienced a downturn but started rebounding in the second half of 2022, indicating resilience in some markets.
Companies selling to overfunded startups are disproportionately affected by the recession.
Being a private company is an advantage during market downturns as it shields the team from the morale-crushing effects of public market stock volatility.
fundraising_mentions: Discussion of the impact of down rounds on private companies.
quotable: These folks who are saying this is the world's worst recession since the Tulip age in Holland are out of their minds they haven't they have no life experiences.
I kind of quit on Founders that say the world's ended.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin argues that the current recession's impact is overstated and unevenly distributed, urging founders to seek out thriving market segments rather than succumbing to pessimism.

title: Pedro Franceschi: What Brex Needs to do to be a Public Company | E1178
key_insights: Founder mental health, particularly managing anxiety, is 50% of the challenge in building a company.
The highest leverage activity for a CEO is to identify the single bottleneck limiting the company's growth and focus disproportionate resources on solving it.
As a company scales, it's crucial to maintain a small company mentality and keep leadership close to the customer, resisting the urge to become overly corporate.
True value and pricing power come from solving deep customer problems with a superior product and service, not just from offering savings or being the cheapest.
Initial conditions are highly underestimated; finding the right idea and the right co-founders is 50% of the company-building journey and is critical for long-term success.
fundraising_mentions: Brex has conducted three tender offers (secondaries) for its team.
Raised $300k for his first company in Brazil.
quotable: If I were to write a book about how to build a company there would be two parts... one takes 6 months part two takes 10 years and the part one is just finding what you're going to do and and with who you're going to do it with. I think the initial conditions are like highly underestimated.

I think when you're deep in the weeds in a problem you're in this state which I call like high stress low anxiety which is like you know you're working on a problem it's really complicated you don't know quite know the solution but there's no anxiety because like you know that this is the thing that matters.
one_liner: Brex CEO Pedro Franceschi discusses the intense mental pressures of founder life, the importance of focusing on the single biggest business bottleneck, and the strategic pivots required to scale a fintech company for an eventual IPO.

title: Why Trader Joe’s is the Most Underrated Brand
key_insights: Trader Joe's is considered one of the most underrated brands due to its unique approach and strong customer loyalty.
During the pandemic, people waited in long lines for Trader Joe's, demonstrating exceptional brand devotion.
Trader Joe's successfully implemented a strategy where all products are their own brand, differentiating it from typical grocery stores.
Consumers associate Trader Joe's with healthier ingredients, good taste, and excellent value, along with a quirky, fun design vibe.
Unlike most private label brands (e.g., Whole Foods' 365), Trader Joe's has built genuine brand belief and loyalty beyond just being a cheaper alternative.
quotable: Trader Joe's is the first time a grocery store all the products in the grocery store are Trader Joe's brand.

people just believe in this brand because when people see Trader Joe's they've established in people's minds oh when it's Trader Joe's it's going to be healthier type ingredients like not a bunch of artificial stuff it's going to be really good tasting and it's going to be really good value
one_liner: This episode explores why Trader Joe's stands out as an underrated brand, attributing its success to its unique private label model, strong customer loyalty, and successful positioning as a source of healthy, tasty, and value-driven products.

title: Adam Grenier: The Inside Story to Uber’s Hypergrowth; How We Spent $1B/mo in China | E989
guest_role: Angel Investor & Former Head of Growth at Uber
key_insights: Most companies don't need a standalone growth team; growth should be a mindset infused throughout the business, especially in product and marketing.
Hiring a Head of Growth is often a mistake for early-stage companies that haven't yet found product-market fit. A lack of growth is usually a product problem, not a growth-hire problem.
A 'Growth CMO' is a full-stack marketer who applies data, experimentation, and technology to all aspects of marketing, from performance to brand.
When building a marketplace, the North Star Metric should force a focus on the health of both sides; for Uber, 'trips' was effective because a trip cannot happen without both a rider and a driver.
Purely relying on CAC is flawed because perfect attribution is impossible. It should be used as one input into a broader media mix model to optimize for confidence, not unattainable perfection.
fundraising_mentions: Uber got funding from Google.
quotable: Most companies actually don't think need a standalone growth team.

The core of growth really dives into user psychology and understanding customers and making sure that you're actually connecting with people when the perceived value of your your product or your offering is at its ultimate highest and then Building Technology and Building Systems around that to soak it up and actually be able to manipulate it and do it over and over and over and over and over again.
one_liner: Adam Grenier shares his experience leading growth at Uber, arguing that growth is a mindset, not a team, and discusses the nuances of scaling marketplaces, hiring, and why most companies don't need a dedicated growth team.

title: The Best Sales Playbook
key_insights: A sales playbook should be repeatable and relevant, focusing on the client's metrics and problems, not the seller's product.
Effective go-to-market strategy starts with the Total Addressable Market (TAM) and works backward to ensure sales efforts are focused on the right areas.
Deal prioritization can be categorized along three axes: near vs. far (sales cycle length), big vs. small (deal size), and known vs. unknown (customer problem awareness).
The most powerful position is to identify and solve 'unknown' problems for customers—issues they have but don't know how to solve, similar to how the iPhone created a need.
By uncovering latent needs and creating a vision for the customer, you differentiate from competitors and align with a much larger budget.
quotable: Clients don't care about you your gear your product your organization they care about them their metrics they're firm and so it's got to be client oriented.
It's about identifying problems a customer has that they don't know how to solve creating a vision and then encouraging them that you have an opportunity to solve that problem for them.
one_liner: Frank Fillman breaks down how to build a repeatable and relevant sales playbook by starting with the market, prioritizing deals effectively, and creating new opportunities by uncovering a customer's unknown problems.

title: Shopify CEO: Why Micromanaging is Actually Good
key_insights: The popular notion that all micromanagement is bad is a destructive idea that has cost immense business value; strategic intervention is crucial.
Leaders must distinguish between reversible mistakes their team can learn from and irreversible, critical errors where they must intervene.
Effective leadership is not about dictating tasks but fostering an 'idea lab' where people with deep context and broad perspective collaborate.
A leader can never abdicate responsibility, they can only share it; accountability for all outcomes ultimately remains with them.
Great products should feel cohesive and logically consistent, as if written by a single author, which is achieved through coordination tools like design systems (e.g., Shopify's Polaris).
Trust with team members must be actively built and verified, not blindly given based on a role or title.
The best companies operate with a structure where everyone supports the people on the front lines, similar to how a military supports deployed personnel.
quotable: There's probably no singular idea that has destroyed more business value on cloud Earth than the idea that micromanagement is a bad thing.
A great company is looks how great products look to the users as if they come like they are a book written by a single author.
one_liner: Shopify's CEO argues that strategic micromanagement is a necessary and valuable leadership tool for ensuring product quality, cohesion, and avoiding catastrophic, irreversible mistakes.

title: What makes the best startups?
