one_liner: Jason Lemkin argues that while many venture fund managers will face a reckoning, established LPs will remain committed to the venture asset class because its top-tier returns, like the historically rare 3x net, consistently outperform other investment categories.

title: Zaria Parvez: How Duolingo Scaled to 8M TikTok Followers & How to Create Viral Content | E1105
key_insights: The most successful content creators are native users of the platform, understanding its nuances, trends, and humor instinctively.
Hiring 'troublemakers' and people from intersectional backgrounds who are willing to push boundaries leads to breakthrough creative work.
A lack of budget is a feature, not a bug; it forces scrappiness and creativity that often results in more authentic and successful content.
Brand accounts on social media should act like a 'sitcom,' with ongoing storylines and characters that build a dedicated following, rather than just chasing one-off viral hits.
Internal teams that are deeply connected to the company's mission will outperform agencies because you can't buy passion and authentic brand advocacy.
quotable: I would say you have to hire troublemakers... troublemakers are the ones that are causing seismic cultural shifts.
I genuinely believe that lack of money is what inspires creativity.
one_liner: Zaria Parvez shares the inside story of how she grew Duolingo's TikTok to over 8 million followers by embracing authenticity, hiring 'troublemakers', and leveraging a deep, native understanding of the platform's culture to create viral content on a shoestring budget.

title: Rujul Zaparde: Why Hiring Inexperienced People is Better | E1144
key_insights: Hiring high-potential, inexperienced people often leads to more original ideas as they approach problems from first principles, rather than relying on a pre-existing playbook.
Speed is a startup's greatest advantage; it's better to iterate and learn quickly from mistakes than to over-plan, as the initial strategy is almost never perfectly correct.

Founders should avoid offering their product for free to 'design partners' and instead charge real money from the first customers, even if they are sourced cold, to truly validate the problem and willingness to pay.
The transition from founder-led sales should happen when the founder is no longer learning anything new from initial customer calls and the process becomes purely about closing the deal.
Product-market fit is not a binary achievement but a continuous process that must be re-validated for every new product, vertical, and customer persona a company pursues.

To maintain speed and creativity at scale, leaders should empower their teams, reward first-principles thinking, and be selective about what they micromanage, focusing on areas that are core to the company's values.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a lot of money in 2021 but maintained discipline by holding back on hiring until product-market fit was clearly established, even becoming cash-flow positive at one point.
quotable: I would much rather invest in the person that has potential that maybe hasn't done the job before... they're going to first principle the problem and so they're just generally more likely to have more original ideas.
You're not going to be right, so you might as well just learn quickly and move on.
one_liner: Zip Co-Founder Rujul Zaparde discusses his counterintuitive approach to building an enterprise SaaS company, from hiring inexperienced talent and embracing speed over perfection to his disciplined go-to-market and fundraising strategies.

title: Jeff Seibert: Why OpenAI Will Become an Infrastructure Play | E1085
key_insights: Pivoting a startup requires decisive, all-in conviction from the entire team, not treating it as a side experiment. A founder must have at least a year of cash to see a pivot through.

Most managers are ineffective because they are promoted from IC roles based on past performance, not their aptitude or passion for management. This is especially true for CEOs who lack a direct feedback loop.
The AI adoption curve will be radically faster than previous tech waves like mobile because there are no new hardware or UX patterns for users to adopt.
Startups building thin wrappers on top of models like GPT are not defensible. True value lies in solving a core market problem where AI is a tool, not the entire product.
OpenAI will likely evolve into an infrastructure company like AWS, with LLMs becoming commoditized. An open-source equivalent, an 'Android to OpenAI's iOS', will emerge as a close second.

Google is the most vulnerable incumbent to the AI shift because its core search business is directly threatened, while Apple is a dark horse with its control over silicon and on-device processing capabilities.
fundraising_mentions: Jeff has angel invested in 97 startups since 2014. Of those, about a third have failed, 19 are at 1x, and the portfolio's success depends on about 10 companies.
His most successful angel investment was in Alchemy, which he exited on the secondary market for a 200x return on his initial 10k investment.
He advises being disciplined with angel check sizes after losing money on larger, high-conviction bets that went to zero.
quotable: What kills companies is uncertainty. And if you sort of muddle your priorities and have one team try this and another team try this, no one's heart is in it and both are going to be mediocre.
I view open AI probably evolving more into an infrastructure company like AWS.
one_liner: Digits founder Jeff Seibert shares his playbook on startup pivots, why OpenAI will become the next AWS, and hard-won lessons from angel investing in nearly 100 companies.

title: Bastian Lehmann: How the Uber Deal Went Down and How a $2.65BN Deal Turned into $5BN | E1137
key_insights: The Postmates acquisition by Uber, initially announced at $2.65B, closed at nearly $5B because the deal was negotiated with no collar on the stock exchange ratio, allowing Postmates to benefit from Uber's rising stock price.
Postmates was not running out of cash at the time of the acquisition; they had just under $100 million and were a few quarters away from profitability.
Lehmann believes determination, grit, and refusing to give up are more critical to a startup's success than luck, stating that most companies fail simply because the founders give up.
The best VCs are humble enough to realize they can't change a company's outcome and provide capital without trying to operate the business.
Lehmann predicts a future need for dedicated, in-home 'inference computers' for personal AI, arguing it's more efficient and private than cloud-based solutions.
He believes the smartphone is 'dead' and will be replaced by new interfaces, possibly voice-based, for interacting with AI.
fundraising_mentions: Postmates raised around $900 million in total.
The Uber acquisition was valued at $2.65 billion at announcement but closed at almost $5 billion.
Founders Fund (Brian Singerman and Peter Thiel) invested in Postmates' Series A.
His new company, Tiptop, raised a Series A from Andreessen Horowitz (Mark Andreessen).
quotable: Most companies fail because the founders give up and we refuse to give up.
We negotiated the deal so well there was no collar on the deal by the time the deal closed it was almost $5 billion.
one_liner: Postmates founder Bastian Lehmann shares the inside story of the $5B Uber acquisition, lessons on grit and negotiating with VCs, and his contrarian takes on the future of AI and personal computing.

title: Kyle Samani: Why Bitcoin is Not a Hedge Against Inflation | 20VC #909
key_insights: Tokens serve as a mechanism to bootstrap network effects by rewarding early participants but also reduce the power of those network effects by making it easier for competitors to bootstrap their own networks.
For most projects, value should accrue to either tokens or equity, but not both, as their value accrual mechanisms are almost always in conflict.
A successful crypto investment strategy can ignore short-term price volatility by focusing on a long-term, indefinite holding period based on deep, thesis-driven conviction.
A rigorous investment process requires intense, systematic, and written debate to identify logical fallacies and false assumptions, prioritizing truth-seeking over comfort.
The primary customer of a Layer 1 blockchain is developers, who require a clear, credible, and specific long-term scaling plan to build with confidence.
fundraising_mentions: Launched a liquid fund on October 1st, 2017.
Added their first venture fund in July of 2018.
Currently on their third venture fund.
Mentioned they raised their latest fund just before the market downturn.
quotable: Prices don't matter if you don't look at them.
Bitcoin is nonsense.
one_liner: Multicoin Capital's Kyle Samani explains his firm's thesis-driven investment strategy, the role of tokens in bootstrapping network effects, why he is bearish on Bitcoin, and the importance of a rigorous, debate-oriented culture for making high-conviction crypto investments.

title: The Shocking Story of How Cloudflare Lost Their 3rd Co-Founder
key_insights: Cloudflare's third co-founder, Lee Holloway, was fired for what was perceived as disruptive and jerky behavior.
The behavior change was later discovered to be a symptom of frontotemporal dementia, a rare neurological condition.
The speaker, a fellow co-founder, expresses deep regret over his anger and the decision to fire him without understanding the underlying health issue.
The frontal lobe of the brain, which was affected, is responsible for empathy and processing human relations, explaining the drastic personality shift.
This experience taught the speaker a valuable lesson: when an individual's behavior changes dramatically, it's crucial to inquire about potential personal or health issues before passing judgment.
quotable: I try now when when people you know their behavior changes dramatically to to ask you know is there something going on in their personal life is there is there something going on with their health is there something else that's that's out there.
The frontal lobe of your brain is the thing that is what helps you process and have empathy and and have human relations and he if you look at the brain scans sees they were missing those.
one_liner: A Cloudflare co-founder recounts the tragic story of having to fire his third co-founder, Lee Holloway, whose disruptive behavior was later revealed to be caused by a rare neurological disease, offering a profound lesson on empathy in leadership.

title: Barry McCarthy: From Netflix CFO to Peloton CEO; How Netflix Beat Blockbuster | 20VC #962
key_insights: In a turnaround, a CEO's most critical and surprising challenge is the immense emotional resilience required to constantly firefight and lead a team through a stream of problems.
A high-performance culture should be viewed as a professional sports team, not a family. Talent density is paramount, and the team must be willing to replace players who aren't performing to win.

The 'one-way vs. two-way door' framework (from Jeff Bezos) is crucial for decision-making. Reversible (two-way) decisions can be made quickly, while irreversible (one-way) decisions require more deliberation.

Demand Creation Theory: The entity that understands and can shift consumer demand (like Netflix did with its recommendation engine for catalog content) ultimately controls the gross margin in the ecosystem.
The best board members are often operators who act as strategic partners, helping management see around corners, rather than trying to manage the company themselves.
Covid acted as a massive, unaffordable marketing campaign for Peloton, propelling it to a scale no competitor achieved, which created lasting advantages despite the subsequent challenges.
Founder-led companies have a fundamentally different board dynamic than those with professional managers; founders often hold immense sway, and boards are more enabling than challenging.
fundraising_mentions: Spotify's direct listing was used because the company had billions on its balance sheet and didn't need to raise more capital, avoiding dilution for existing investors.
Netflix was running out of money after the dot-com bust, and Jay Hoag (VC) 'stepped up in a moment of immense bravery' to provide capital.
quotable: We are not a family, we are a professional sports team.
My job is to advocate for what I think is best for the business. Your job is to keep me from running us into the ditch in your area of expertise. Like you own it. I'll advocate, but you own it.
Whoever owns demand creation owns the gross margin.
one_liner: Peloton CEO Barry McCarthy discusses his experiences leading turnarounds, building high-performance cultures at Netflix and Spotify, and how owning 'demand creation' is the key to controlling gross margin.

title: Keith Rabois on Rejoining Khosla Ventures | E1102
key_insights: Khosla Ventures' culture of rigorous, collaborative partner debate sharpens investment decisions, contrasting with Founders Fund's more individualistic, 'PM-driven' model.
For seed and Series A rounds, walking away over price is often a sign of insufficient conviction, as the potential upside of an iconic company can outweigh a high entry valuation.
A successful VC must have a clear, differentiated 'comparative advantage' to avoid regressing to the mediocre returns of the average venture fund.
The decision-making process for reserves and pro-rata investments is more of an art than a science, with Founders Fund favoring ad-hoc decisions and KV taking a more disciplined, top-down approach.
The most effective founder-VC pairings occur when the investor is directionally aligned with the founder's ambition and philosophy, acting as a complementary partner rather than a director.
fundraising_mentions: Rippling Seed: Rabois offered a term sheet at a ~$25M post-money valuation, but lost to a ~$35M valuation.
Robinhood Seed: Rabois passed on leading the round because the firm wouldn't allow him to join the board at the seed stage.
Fair Seed: Rabois agreed to join the board as a condition of leading the seed round, having learned from the Robinhood experience.
Ramp Seed: Invested at an 'extraordinarily high' valuation for a seed round, possibly around $40M post-money.
Stripe Series C: Co-led the round while at KV, which was an order of magnitude more expensive than any investment in the firm's history at that time.
OpenDoor Seed: Raised a $10M seed round, which was considered the correct 'dose' to prove the model.
Khosla Ventures new funds: Totaling ~$3B, broken down into a $415M seed fund, a $1.5B venture fund, and an $800-900M growth fund.
quotable: When at a seed round or a series A round when you're walking away at price, it is a bit of a lack of conviction and you really should be looking in the mirror and say why don't I have conviction.

If you don't have a strong answer to why you have a comparative advantage, you're going to regress to the middle of the bell curve, and the middle of the bell curve returns are just not acceptable, period.
one_liner: Keith Rabois details his return to Khosla Ventures, offering a masterclass on VC strategy by comparing the cultures of KV and Founders Fund, and sharing his framework for seed investing, valuation, and building generational companies.

title: Ed Sim & Jamin Ball: Did Figma Kill M&A Markets & 3 Requirements to IPO in 2024 | E1101
guest_role: Founder, bold start Ventures & Partner, Altimeter Capital
key_insights: 2024 is a year of reckoning where startups that raised huge rounds in 2020-2022 must face tough conversations about their viability and valuations.
The bar for IPOs is high: companies need ~30%+ growth, be near cash-flow break-even, and move towards a 'Rule of 40 or 50'.
Large-scale M&A is unlikely due to intense regulatory scrutiny (citing the failed Adobe-Figma deal), shifting focus to smaller, strategic acquisitions and aqua-hires.
Late-stage investors are more willing to accept a 1x return to recycle capital into better opportunities rather than wait for overvalued companies to grow into their 2021 valuations.
Founders are advised against taking excessively high valuations as it severely limits exit optionality and creates immense pressure to grow 10-13x just to break even on the valuation.
fundraising_mentions: Discussion of companies raising 5 years worth of capital in an 18-month period during 2021-2022.
Loom's last round valuation was $1.5 billion, but they sold for $950 million.
Mentions of '100x ARR rounds' being particularly dangerous for companies.
Ed Sim's firm, bold start, provided bridge rounds for successful companies like Sneak, BigID, and Customer before their Series A/B rounds.
quotable: This is the year that the shit's hitting the fan because you know you can only extend Runway so much and it doesn't mean much if you're not growing.

If you're gonna go public I think you've got to be cash flow break even, I think you have to have you know 30% plus growth...you've got to be moving towards a rule of 40 or 50 with slanted more towards growth than you are cash flow Break Even.
one_liner: Venture capitalists Ed Sim and Jamin Ball analyze the 2024 market reckoning for startups, covering the challenging M&A and IPO landscape and the tough strategic decisions facing companies that raised at peak 2021 valuations.

title: This BILLIONAIRE'S PREDICTIONS Always Come True (Part 2)
key_insights: Markets naturally evolve to become more efficient over time, reducing friction between buyers and sellers.
An inefficient market is characterized by transactions that should occur but don't, often due to a lack of discoverability or trust.
Intermediaries (like eBay) create value by making inefficient markets more efficient and capture a percentage of that value as a commission.
The speaker posits that the market will continuously find more efficient ways to become efficient, potentially reducing the role or take-rate of intermediaries.
We may be at a historical turning point where technology enables a non-linear leap in how markets are made more efficient, surpassing the progress of Web1 and Web2.
quotable: The definition of an inefficient market is when a buyer and sellers should be coming together but don't as a result of non-discoverability as a result of non-rust any number of reasons a transaction that should have happened doesn't.
My thesis is that the market over the fullness of time will find increasingly efficient ways to make the market more efficient.
one_liner: Chamath Palihapitiya discusses his thesis on the long-term trend of markets becoming more efficient, the role of intermediaries, and how technology is approaching a pivotal moment to fundamentally reshape value exchange.

title: Dara Khosrowshahi: How I Became CEO of Uber; Uber Eats vs DoorDash; The Postmates Acquisition | E994
key_insights: A leader's job is to make mistakes and learn from them; avoiding mistakes means not taking necessary risks.
True high performance in leadership is about sustained excellence and results over a long period, not short-term glory.
The transition from focusing on personal happiness to focusing on making an impact can be a pivotal career motivator.
Effective leaders must be willing to be misunderstood for long periods and go against the grain to avoid average outcomes.
Uber's strategic focus shifted from speed and urban centers to selection and suburban markets after learning from competitors like DoorDash.
The best capital allocation involves focusing on core competencies, as seen in Uber's success with marketplace tech versus its struggles with hardware (e.g., bikes and scooters).
One-way door decisions are those with a significant blast radius, especially affecting third parties like earners, requiring more careful consideration.
quotable: If I didn't want to make mistakes I'd be a treasury bond manager right like my job is to make mistakes and learn from them.
Since when is life about happiness? It's about impact.
one_liner: Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi discusses his journey to leading the company, the strategic decisions behind acquisitions like Postmates and Kareem, the intense competition with DoorDash, and his core philosophies on leadership, decision-making, and building a lasting impact.

title: Databricks at $100BN, CoreWeave’s $11B Debt Bet & Nubank’s $2.5B Profit Shocker - Ep.19
key_insights: Private market valuations for high-growth AI companies like Databricks are soaring, potentially making them look undervalued compared to public counterparts like Snowflake due to faster growth.

one_liner: A deep dive into the massive valuations of AI and infrastructure companies like Databricks and CoreWeave, the surprising profitability of fintechs like Nubank, and the systemic risks and market dynamics shaping the current tech bubble.

title: How Y Combinator almost missed out on making billions on Dropbox investments 💰
key_insights: Persistence pays off, even if early attempts like showing up unannounced fail.
Getting attention from key people can be achieved through clever, indirect methods like hitting the top of Hacker News.

title: My Coming Out Story 🏳️‍🌈 | Facebook CMO Alex Schultz
key_insights: Alex Schultz shares his personal journey of coming out twice, first in university and then professionally at Facebook after a period of being closeted at eBay.
Being closeted in the workplace created significant personal distress and psychological challenges.
Visible support from senior leaders and a growing LGBTQ+ community within Facebook were crucial factors that enabled him to come out at work.
Despite progress, there remains a notable lack of openly gay individuals in senior leadership roles within the tech industry, with the trans community facing even greater difficulties.
Parents may initially struggle with a child's coming out, needing time to 'mourn their version of your future,' but can ultimately become immensely supportive.

Everyone around you has to mourn their version of your future.

title: AngelList CEO Avlok Kohli: The Funding Market Today; Last-Mile Delivery; Competing w/ Carta | E1005
key_insights: The venture market is experiencing one of its worst downturns, with a significant drop in investment activity and up-rounds, particularly from Series A onwards.

Being 'first to market' is overrated; it often means you're just building the 'idea maze' for future entrepreneurs who will learn from your journey.
AngelList leverages AI and LLMs to automate core operational tasks like email routing and document analysis, significantly increasing efficiency and maintaining high margins.

Defensibility at the early stage is minimal; the focus should be on building a product customers love, as competition is less of a threat than internal failure ('startups die of suicide, not homicide').

quotable: The only purpose for a company... it's just a group of individuals that are coming together to build product for your customers. Any process, anything that gets in the way of that, crush it.
Startups die of suicide not homicide.

John D. Rockefeller and Steve Jobs are cited as examples of highly successful entrepreneurs driven by vengeance.

The feeling of being wronged by the world or others can be a powerful, driving force for an entrepreneur.

when you find a Transcendent life's work entrepreneur with a company where there is a huge surface area they can capture where they're not going to stop because they have this extra motivator this extra ingredient of quite frankly being wronged in some way by the world or by someone else you ought to invest

title: Yamini Rangan, CEO @ HubSpot: How HubSpot Competes Against Salesforce
key_insights: Transitioning into a CEO role from a founder requires deliberate effort to manage relationships and align on vision, cadence, and decision-making processes.
HubSpot's strategy for AI is to deeply integrate it into the core platform to provide customer value, rather than creating separate, premium AI SKUs, believing monetization will follow usage.
B2B software markets, unlike consumer apps, are not 'winner-take-all,' allowing multiple major players like HubSpot and Salesforce to coexist by focusing on different segments.
When moving upmarket, an incremental approach to up-skilling teams and evolving the product is more effective than hiring a new enterprise team, which can break the existing culture.
AI is considered the 'greatest equalizer for smbs' because it helps them overcome constraints related to headcount, capital, and expertise.
A key leadership challenge in a scaled company is ensuring cross-functional alignment, which 'eats strategy for lunch' if not managed correctly.
Effective leaders must operate in different modes, optimizing for speed of execution in hard times and for consensus-building in peacetime.
quotable: When you are in a wartime or a hard time you are optimizing for Speed of execution when you are in peace time you are optimizing for getting a consensus around what you're trying to do.
AI is a you know equalizer for smbs it removes each one of those constraints.
one_liner: HubSpot CEO Yamini Rangan discusses leading a public company, the nuances of competing with Salesforce, and her conviction that deeply integrated AI will be the great equalizer for SMBs.

title: Ex-Coinbase employee reveals how hackers infiltrated his Coinbase account (and stole everything)
key_insights: A sophisticated phishing attack cost a then-Coinbase employee his entire Bitcoin holdings, valued at $50,000 at the time.

Human error, especially when tired or not paying close attention, is a major vulnerability that attackers exploit.
The guest used the devastating personal and financial loss as a motivator to 'level up' and deepen his commitment to the crypto industry rather than leaving it.
Hacks and theft are a widespread, 'unspoken secret' in the crypto world, affecting many more people than is commonly discussed.

I think I came close to to crying honestly... but at the end of the day it's like my belief in crypto more than anything else... led me to the the thinking like you need to use this to level up right so at the end of the day it was my, you know, mistake they caught me slipping right... you need to use it to to level up and motivate you to to go bigger.
one_liner: A former Coinbase employee shares the harrowing story of losing his life savings to a phishing attack and how he transformed the painful experience into a catalyst for growth within the crypto industry.

title: Peter Singlehurst: The Most Powerful Investor You've Never Heard of | 20VC #907
key_insights: The distinction between public and private company investing is an artificial construct of the financial industry; the fundamentals of a great business are consistent regardless of its public or private status.
Hiring from diverse academic backgrounds (like philosophy) over traditional finance fosters cognitive diversity, which is a key advantage that cannot be taught.
A company's shareholder base can be a significant competitive advantage or disadvantage; a successful IPO is about finding a small number of aligned, long-term partners, not appealing to everyone.
Traditional VC fund structures with limited life and carried interest can create misalignments, incentivizing premature exits rather than long-term value compounding.

Even with successful long-term investments, there will inevitably be periods where the investor looks and feels 'really stupid' due to market volatility, making conviction and a long-term mindset crucial.

Led a round in Grammarly in 2021.
quotable: I really think that the public private divide is an artifact of the financial universe rather than anything that you would come up with if you were thinking about investment or company formation from first principles.
If you are sufficiently long-term, even in your most successful investments there will always be a time when you look and feel really stupid.
one_liner: Peter Singlehurst of Baillie Gifford discusses a long-term, cross-platform investment strategy that blurs the lines between public and private markets, emphasizing fundamental analysis, cognitive diversity, and enduring partnerships with founders.

title: Ed Sim: Why Seed Has Never Been More Competitive & Why Pricing Has Never Been Higher | E1076
key_insights: The seed stage has fragmented into three types: 'Discovery' rounds (<$2M), 'Classic' rounds ($3-5M), and 'Jumbo' rounds (>$5M), each suiting different founder profiles and market situations.
Excess capital too early can be detrimental; constraints and pressure are crucial for innovation, and smart founders often prefer raising less money to maintain discipline.
Modern early-stage VC funds need the flexibility to write checks from $1M to $10M to compete with angels, multi-stage firms, and lead rounds at every level of the 'Inception' stage.
True value in AI will come from incumbent companies with data moats incorporating AI into their products, not from a flood of new 'AI startups' which are likely to vaporize capital.
The IPO market recovery is directly tied to the lowering of interest rates; high-growth company valuations have dropped from a peak of 35x forward revenue to ~6.8x, and may stabilize around 10-14x.

title: Was Frank Slootman Wrong?
key_insights: Culture isn't abstract; it's defined by the operational questions asked and decisions made daily within the company.
A culture of constant improvement is impossible without data and metrics to measure business operations and identify opportunities for growth.
In a high-performance environment, job security ('safety') is a direct result of performance, not just interpersonal trust.
Trust is giving team members the autonomy on 'how' they achieve goals, while safety is earned by delivering on the 'what'—the mutually agreed-upon performance metrics.
Clear alignment on performance expectations and the metrics that define success is the foundation for a culture where individuals feel secure to perform.

key_insights: Founders should be wary of generic advice and not believe everything they read or hear from sources like podcasts and social media.

Founders take a significant risk by betting on their unique insight, and they should not hedge or compromise that bet by listening to outsiders.
Instead of trying to replicate another's success story, founders should focus on 'making their own movie' and forging their unique path.
It's crucial for founders to have self-awareness to process advice, adapt it to their own style, and not just blindly implement it.
fundraising_mentions: Mentions seeing others 'raise some crazy round as some frothy price' but no specific details.
quotable: Don't believe everything you read in the newspaper.
Make your own movie. You know what you're not going to do? You're not going to replicate that movie.
one_liner: A discussion on why founders should be selective about the advice they take, trust their own vision, and focus on creating their own unique success story rather than mimicking others.

title: Maggie Hott: 3 Questions You Must Ask When Interviewing Sales Reps | 20VC #960
key_insights: In a Product-Led Growth (PLG) company, it's crucial to build product differentiation for enterprise tiers beyond just security (SSO), including features like advanced customer support, roles/permissions, and negotiable legal terms to avoid cannibalizing sales.
Build your outbound sales motion early and consistently, even alongside a PLG model. The primary goal of early cold outbound is brand awareness and educating the market, not immediate sales.
The first sales hire should not be a senior 'Head of Sales', but rather one or two proven AEs from a hyper-growth company who can handle ambiguity, embrace chaos, and build from the ground up.

Structure the sales interview process around a mock discovery call (not a product demo) to test for research skills, curiosity, and coachability. Key questions should focus on accountability, such as asking about a lost deal to see if they take ownership or assign blame.

When evaluating candidates and choosing a company, prioritize joining a 'rocket ship' company over chasing a specific title or a higher on-target earnings (OTE) without understanding the underlying quota, attainment rates, and true equity value.
fundraising_mentions: Advises founders to have around $1-2 million in ARR before starting to build an enterprise product and sales team.
Warns candidates to question the value of equity offers, noting that '$200,000 of equity at figma is very different than $200,000 at maybe a small company that doesn't have a good chance of success'.
quotable: It is so important to choose that rocket ship and you know what is it hit your wagon to it hit your saddle and join on with that rocket ship.
A hiring mistake can cost a company to the tune of $1 million.
one_liner: Webflow's Director of Sales, Maggie Hott, shares her playbook on building an early-stage sales team, covering how to layer sales onto a PLG motion, structure the hiring process to find the right reps, and avoid common pitfalls in compensation and team building.

title: Behind Duolingo Viral Success
key_insights: It is impossible to reliably predict if a post will go viral; a better litmus test is if the creator found it genuinely funny and entertaining themselves.
Quality of content is far more important than the quantity and consistency of posting on platforms like TikTok.
Getting feedback on content from people within the target demographic, outside of your brand, is incredibly helpful.
Establishing a core brand truth (e.g., 'Language learning is hard, so we make it fun' or 'Duo is freaking everywhere') provides a north star for all content decisions.
A multi-platform strategy is only necessary if it aligns with the brand's core truth and strategy; for Duolingo, being everywhere is the point.
quotable: I believe that the quality of content is far more important than the quantity.
If I didn't work at dualingo and if I didn't give a crap about Brands would I want to post this in my group chat and that's kind of my litness test.
one_liner: Duolingo's Global Social Media Manager discusses the strategy behind their viral success, emphasizing content quality over quantity and adhering to a core brand truth to guide their multi-platform presence.

title: What Questions to Ask in Customer Research
topics: Falling in Love with the Problem
key_insights: Effective customer development focuses on exploring the customer's problem, not pitching a solution.
Good customer research involves asking questions 'around' the customer's life and observing workarounds, rather than directly about the problem or solution.
Product managers should form sharp hypotheses but remain agnostic, approaching them as a judge rather than an advocate.
It's counter to human nature to maintain distance from an idea one has invested time and commitment in.
The key is to fall in love with the 'problem' (e.g., underserved market) rather than a specific 'solution', allowing for flexibility in finding the best path.
quotable: "it's about exploring the customer's problem rather than the solution"
"to have a sharp hypothesis but to be entirely agnostic not in love with any of those ideas to approach it more as a judge than a lawyer"
one_liner: This episode delves into the art of customer research, emphasizing the importance of exploring customer problems indirectly, maintaining an agnostic stance towards hypotheses, and falling in love with the problem rather than a specific solution.

title: Collective: Investing Lessons from Seeding Coupang, Pillpack & Suno|E1214
key_insights: Pro-rata rights are described as the 'original sin against entrepreneurs' because they create a free option for VCs and can complicate future fundraising, especially for struggling companies.
A fund's size relative to its check size is a critical indicator of an investor's alignment and the amount of attention a founder can expect to receive.
To succeed as a traditional seed fund in a market of mega-rounds, focus on non-consensus areas: non-traditional founders, overlooked markets (like cat food DTC), or old markets that are out of favor.
The most you can lose is all your money, but the most you can make is unlimited; this unfair feature of capitalism means if you're not experiencing some losses, you may not be taking enough risk.

When facing powerful incumbents ('leeches'), a startup's primary weapon is having customers who absolutely love the product; VCs can add significant value by providing a playbook for the legal, lobbying, and PR battles that will ensue.
fundraising_mentions: Seed rounds of $6-10 million are becoming more common.
AI deals priced at '5 on 20' (million) are within Founder Collective's range, but deals at '25 on 100' are not.
An AI company reached a $100 million pre-money valuation at the seed stage.
Kong's round at a $4 billion pre-money valuation, with Black Rock offering to invest $1 billion.
Josh Kushner's investment in OpenAI at a $100 billion valuation.
Mistral's first round was at a valuation of around $250 million.
During the ZIRP era, deals like '10 on 40' or '20 on 80' were common, often sourced from firms like Tiger Global.
quotable: I still think of like pro rata as like the original sin against entrepreneurs.
You own your own destiny by minding your monthly burn.
one_liner: David Frankel of Founder Collective shares lessons on disciplined, non-consensus seed investing, the challenges of fund strategy and reserves, and why pro-rata is a sin against entrepreneurs in a market grappling with AI hype and a liquidity crunch.

title: OpenAI’s $6BN Jony Ive Deal & YC Is Both Chanel and Walmart, and Has Officially Won!
key_insights: The venture model for large, late-stage funds differs from early-stage; it relies less on single 'fund returners' and more on a portfolio of solid returns, with a few concentrated, large bets.
Late-stage, high-priced investment rounds are losing their power to block IPOs, as public markets and companies are finding ways to work around complex cap tables (e.g., the Hinge Health IPO).
Y Combinator has 'won' the accelerator game by successfully combining mass-market scale (Walmart) with a prestigious, aspirational brand (Chanel), creating a powerful and enduring business.
In the current AI talent war, the power is shifting from capital providers to elite technical talent, as demonstrated by OpenAI's $6B+ acquihire of a hardware team.
The speed to $100M ARR has become a critical proxy for success because it creates a flywheel, attracting the best talent and follow-on capital, even if the underlying business quality varies.
fundraising_mentions: Builder AI raised $500M across rounds before shutting down.
Insight Partners' last fund size is mentioned as $12B.
Hinge Health raised at a $6B valuation in 2021, before its IPO at a $2-3B valuation.
Chime's $6B round has a mandatory conversion clause, which could force late-stage investors to realize losses upon IPO.
OpenAI's acquisition of Jony Ive's startup is valued at ~$6.5B, representing 2% of the company.
RevenueCap raised a round at a $500M valuation.
quotable: The wars that you choose to engage in dictate what it has to take to win.
What I think is so special about YC is it's Walmart and Chanel. They have scale and they've retained brand.
one_liner: VCs Rory O'Driscoll and Jason Lemkin break down OpenAI's hardware play, YC's market dominance, and the new rules for unicorn IPOs and venture returns in the age of AI.

title: Why My Bid to Buy Chelsea FC Failed
guest_role: Senior Advisor at Bain Capital and Managing Partner and Co-Owner of the Boston Celtics
key_insights: The Pax Group (Steve Pagliuca's organization) seeks to acquire iconic assets with strong fan bases and growth potential, viewing themselves as stewards.
The initial bidding requirements for Chelsea FC specified no debt, which later changed, allowing debt and demanding a higher price.
Steve Pagliuca's group withdrew their bid due to the altered terms, as the increased price would hinder necessary investments in the stadium, facilities, and players.
A core investment philosophy: 'the only thing worse than losing a deal is doing a bad deal.'
They prioritize preparing for the worst and hoping for the best in their investment approach.
fundraising_mentions: purchase prices of two to three billion pounds with no debt
asked for a much higher price than what we were talking about
quotable: the only thing worse than losing a deal is doing a bad deal
one_liner: Steve Pagliuca discusses why his group's bid to acquire Chelsea FC failed, highlighting changes in the bidding terms, his investment philosophy, and the importance of stewardship for iconic assets.

title: The Perfect Cold Email (according to David Sacks, Keith Rabois, & Jason Lemkin)
key_insights: A high-quality, detailed cold inbound email can be so compelling that an investor might want to invest even before the first meeting.
The quality of a founder's communication in a cold email can be a strong proxy for their overall capability.
Top investors have radically different preferences for cold outreach; Jason Lemkin prefers a detailed email with metrics, David Sacks wants two lines, and Keith Rabois wants a lengthy deck.
Even a great investor can miss a huge opportunity (like monday.com) if the initial cold email is poor, highlighting the limitations of relying on this as the sole filter.
The best founders are great communicators, and a well-crafted email is one way to demonstrate that skill.
fundraising_mentions: The core topic is how founders should approach investors via cold email for fundraising.
quotable: I like it a cold email that's so good that I already want to invest before the meeting.
You can you can judge a human being in a company just from that email if it's a plus.
one_liner: Jason Lemkin of SaaStr breaks down what makes a perfect cold email for fundraising, sharing his preference for hyper-detailed metrics and storytelling, while noting that other top VCs like David Sacks and Keith Rabois have entirely different approaches.

title: Why you SHOULDN’T go into product 🙅‍♂
key_insights: Product management is often misunderstood as being the 'CEO of the product', but it primarily involves navigating complex compromises.
The core job of a product manager is to make 'baby steps towards the vision while staying alive', constantly balancing conflicting demands.
A product manager is rarely universally liked; if sales is happy, engineering might be frustrated, and vice-versa, leading to a perception that 'everybody thinks you suck'.
The role requires finding 'possible compromises' between diverse stakeholders including customers, sales, engineering, and finance.
Product managers are often perceived as incompetent by others because of the necessary compromises and the frustration experienced by different departments.
quotable: if you're rocking it as a product manager everybody thinks you suck
It's finding a way to make baby steps towards the vision while staying alive
one_liner: This podcast snippet explores the often-frustrating reality of product management, highlighting the constant need to compromise between conflicting stakeholder demands, which can lead to widespread dissatisfaction despite making progress.

title: Antoine Le Nel, CGO @Revolut: How Revolut Launch and Grow Products & Why CAC is a BS Metric | E1216
key_insights: A focus on ROI (Return on Investment) is superior to focusing on CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost), as chasing low CAC can lead to acquiring low-quality user cohorts.
Good product managers should have strong enough conviction and product sense to not need A/B tests for every decision, especially for 10x features where the impact is obvious.
The idea of localization in marketing is often overrated; the same core strategies and creatives can work across very different markets, with rare exceptions like Japan.
Growth is a 'bidding war' won through the accumulation of many small optimizations (1-2% improvements) across the entire funnel, rather than relying on big 'moonshot' bets.
A true growth engine integrates the upper, mid, and lower funnels, where brand and awareness activities feed a highly-optimized conversion funnel.
Early-stage startups should invest everything in product rather than brand marketing; if the product is good enough, people will find out about it.
quotable: I have no belief in anything... there's no CAC discussion at re we only talk about Roi because if you talk about CAC you'll always acquire the worst cohorts.
If you're a good product manager you don't need an AB test you should be able to know what is the right product.
one_liner: Revolut's CGO, Antoine Le Nel, deconstructs their rapid growth, arguing for a focus on ROI over CAC, questioning the value of A/B testing and localization, and explaining how to build a multi-faceted growth engine.

title: Who is Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke?
key_insights: A deep curiosity and refusal to accept 'black boxes' is a fundamental driver for understanding and innovation.
The goal of life can be framed as minimizing the difference between the person you are and the person you could have become.
Maintaining an accurate, continuously updated mental model of the world is critical for high-quality decision-making.
Early exposure to technology and the agency it provides can be a powerful, life-defining experience.
Entrepreneurs are driven by a need for frontiers—spaces where they can build and create new value.
quotable: It's as if at the end of life you meet the person you could have become and the work of life is really try to minimize the diff between that person and the one that actually showed up.
I hate black boxes... we do not like black boxes in my house everyone everything is understandable and everything is way more interesting than it seems.
one_liner: Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke discusses how his early fascination with computers and a deep-seated hatred for 'black boxes' shaped his philosophy on continuous learning, self-improvement, and leadership.

title: Why Public Market Investors Are Better Than VCs -- Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince
key_insights: Public market investors foster more honest relationships due to the ease of disengagement (selling stock) compared to the 'unhealthy marriages' often found with VCs.
The 'no-fault divorce' analogy suggests that the ability for investors to easily exit an investment leads to healthier and more truthful interactions.
VC relationships can be problematic because both founders and VCs find it difficult to 'fire' each other, often leading to prolonged unhealthy partnerships.
Contrary to popular belief, some public market investors (e.g., Baillie Gifford) can have significantly longer holding periods than traditional VCs.
Founders should prioritize the specific individuals on the investment team, not just the firm, as they will be 'stuck' with those partners for a considerable time.
fundraising_mentions: Public Market investors sell your stock if they don't like what you're doing
Baillie Gifford, one of Cloudflare's top investors, has an average holding period of 16 years
quotable: Public Market investors are great because if they'll tell you the truth CU you know if they don't like what you're doing they sell your stock
it turns out that being able to get divorced is is really makes for a better relationship
one_liner: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince advocates for public market investors over VCs, emphasizing their honesty enabled by the ease of selling stock, which fosters more transparent and healthier company-investor relationships.

title: What was it like working with Bill Gates & Steve Ballmer? | Hadi Partovi
key_insights: Steve Ballmer's contribution to Microsoft's earnings growth is significantly underestimated, as he built the financial powerhouse that Satya Nadella later capitalized on.
Both Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer were intensely detail-oriented, often knowing a product better than the teams presenting it, which fostered a culture of extreme preparedness and excellence.

Effective leadership in major consumer tech companies often involves being deeply in the weeds, citing examples like Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, and Elon Musk, as opposed to pure delegation.
Bill Gates' leadership style was more focused on technology and products, whereas Steve Ballmer's was centered on numbers, sales, and motivational charisma.
Ballmer's energetic and motivational leadership style, though sometimes mocked, was incredibly effective at inspiring and energizing employees in the moment.
quotable: Steve bomber does not get anywhere near enough credit for having built Microsoft's into the PowerHouse that it is right now.

If you look at at you know who are the greatest technologists for Consumer companies... if you think of Steve Jobs Bill Gates Mark Zuckerberg Elon Musk none of these folks are just trust that the team will get it done they're getting very involved in little details.
one_liner: Hadi Partovi reflects on his experiences working with Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer at Microsoft, contrasting their intense, detail-oriented leadership styles and highlighting Ballmer's underestimated impact on the company's success.

title: Michael Eisenberg and Adi Levanon: Israeli Resilience in Crisis | E1072
key_insights: The Israeli tech community has shown extreme resilience, with members volunteering, creating rescue-coordination tech on the fly, and ensuring business continuity despite widespread reserve duty call-ups.
The conflict is framed not just as a political or territorial issue, but as a moral battle against terrorism, with a call for the global community to unequivocally condemn Hamas's actions.

Despite the immense personal and national trauma, with nearly every Israeli knowing someone affected, there's a determination to maintain normalcy and economic activity, including closing investment deals.
There is a strong belief that the crisis will ultimately lead to a more united and resilient Israel, attracting more investment due to the demonstrated creativity and fortitude of its people.
Personal stories, like a wedding held on the Gaza border, highlight the human aspiration for life and happiness even in the darkest of times, underscoring the deep-seated resilience of the society.
fundraising_mentions: Adi Levanon mentioned she was supposed to be on a two-and-a-half-week fundraising roadshow in San Francisco for her new fund but cancelled it.
Michael Eisenberg mentioned an investment he had been working on for a long time was closing the next day and they were issuing a capital call.
quotable: We're safe but we're not okay.
We're wounded but not down.
one_liner: Israeli VCs Michael Eisenberg and Adi Levanon share a raw, on-the-ground perspective of the Israel-Hamas war, detailing the tech community's incredible resilience, the profound personal impact on every citizen, and a powerful call for global moral clarity against terrorism.

title: Michael Mauboussin: The Single Biggest Mistake Investors Make In Decision-Making | 20VC #945
guest_role: Head of Consilient Research, Counterpoint Global
key_insights: Luck is distinguished from randomness in that luck happens to an individual (and can be good or bad), while randomness is at the system level; being positioned for good luck often requires a willingness to lose.

A robust investment process must be congruent with your perceived source of edge. The most common failures are deviating from the process and letting biases like overconfidence and confirmation creep in.
To combat confirmation bias in thesis-driven investing, pre-define and write down specific 'signposts' with probabilities that must be met for the thesis to be considered valid.
The persistence of high returns in top venture capital firms can be attributed to 'preferential attachment,' where success attracts more high-quality deal flow, creating a positive feedback loop.

While detailed DCF models are unrealistic for early-stage ventures, every investment is ultimately a DCF problem; the focus should be on the basic unit of analysis: how the company will fundamentally make money and generate cash flows over time.

Historically, market shocks and periods of high volatility, while dramatic at the moment, tend to appear less significant in retrospect on a long-term chart; this historical perspective is crucial for maintaining equilibrium.
fundraising_mentions: Firms like Benchmark are still raising funds with millions instead of billions, suggesting a craft-based, hands-on approach.
The influx of capital into venture should make investors worry about future returns.
quotable: Skill is what's in your control and luck is what's out of your control.
It's not how often you make money that matters. It's how much money you make when you're right.
one_liner: Investment strategist Michael Mauboussin breaks down the critical distinction between luck and skill, how to build a resilient investment process that mitigates cognitive biases, and why all investing ultimately boils down to a discounted cash flow problem.

title: The Impact of H1B Visas on Startups in the US & NVIDIA Invests $100BN Into OpenAI
key_insights: Nvidia's $100B investment in OpenAI represents a market-backed experiment to test the limits of AI scaling laws, where capital will continue to flow until a hard limit is reached.
The AI sector is characterized by extreme revenue concentration, with a few hardware giants like Nvidia serving a small number of massive customers who are locked in a high-stakes spending race.

Venture capital is mirroring the tech market's concentration, with the majority of funds flowing into a handful of late-stage AI companies, creating a distinct 'ultra late-stage' private investment category.
The current venture climate for hot AI deals is marked by a return to 2021-style frothiness, where due diligence is often compressed or bypassed entirely in favor of speed and securing access.

While outlier growth is prized, fundamentally strong SaaS companies with significant revenue and moderate growth can still pursue successful IPOs, though they will be valued on fundamentals, not hype.
fundraising_mentions: Nvidia invests $100 billion into OpenAI.
OpenAI commits $300 billion to Oracle.
75% of VC dollars in 2025 went to 19 companies.
NetScope had an $8.5 billion exit.
Atlassian bought DX for $1 billion.
Navan filed its S1 for IPO.
Notion reached $500 million in ARR.
Airtable and Notion raised at high valuations ($10B+) in 2021.
quotable: Any hot AI deal, there is no diligence provided, nor is any done. It's just done on Saturday. All you can lose is one extra money.

It's just this really weird dynamic. You've got this company what 4.5 trillion with only six customers. That's bad news. But the good news is all six of them are determined to spend themselves into oblivion to win the prize. It's a fascinating game.
one_liner: A panel of VCs analyzes the massive capital concentration in the AI arms race, the shifting dynamics of venture funding and IPOs, and the impact of US immigration policy on the tech ecosystem.

title: How to get journalists to write about you
key_insights: Condense your startup's story into a powerful one-liner with impressive 'signifiers' (metrics, prestigious names, funding) to immediately capture a journalist's attention.
Manufacture scarcity and importance by scheduling talks at prominent institutions (like top universities or tech conferences) and framing founder availability as limited.
Leverage partnerships with credible entities, like governments or major companies, for PR value, even if the direct business impact of the partnership is minimal.
Ensure you have tangible proof of partnerships (e.g., a logo on a government website) to use as validation when pitching to journalists.
Identify what signals matter to journalists (e.g., government backing, academic invitations) and strategically create those signals to make your story seem important and newsworthy.
fundraising_mentions: Mentioned having money from an angel investor as a potential 'signifier' for journalists, but no specific details were discussed.
quotable: You need to condense that story down into one line... when you're messaging someone for the first time they really don't care who you are.
You generate scarcity and you generate those levers and points of significance even when you don't have them by thinking what matters to people.
one_liner: Gina Gotthilf explains how to manufacture credibility and scarcity through powerful one-liners and strategic partnerships to secure media coverage for an unknown startup.

title: Scott Galloway on Billionaire Happiness, Money & Self-Worth | Why We Should Drink More & Not WFH
guest_role: Professor of Marketing at NYU Stern School of Business, Author, and Entrepreneur
topics: Work from home vs. office culture
key_insights: The concentration of market value in a few 'Mag Seven' tech companies stifles competition, making the economy less robust and hindering small and medium-sized businesses.
For the first time in US history, 30-year-olds are economically worse off than their parents were at the same age, due to policies and tax codes that favor the older, wealthier generation.
A small percentage of men on dating apps receive the vast majority of female attention, leading to widespread rejection, resentment, and radicalization among average men.

Men derive more emotional and mental stability from romantic relationships than women do; without these 'guardrails,' they are more prone to substance abuse, video games, porn, and conspiracy theories.
True fulfillment often comes after achieving economic security and then redefining one's purpose beyond accumulating wealth, focusing instead on generosity, relationships, and legacy.
fundraising_mentions: Scott Galloway mentions he was in the midst of raising a private equity fund to become a billionaire before having a change of heart.
He mentions the fear people have of asking for '$30 million for their VC fund' due to fear of rejection.
quotable: If you want to score above your weight class economically and romantically, get out a big spoon. Get ready to eat [__] Endure rejection.
I'm paid to be an extrovert. So, how I relax is I just like to listen to other people and and be, you know, an observer as opposed to participant.
one_liner: Scott Galloway discusses the dangers of wealth concentration in big tech, the economic and social challenges facing young men, and the personal journey to find happiness and purpose beyond money and career success.

title: The Broken Nature of LP Incentives
key_insights: LP (Limited Partner) compensation models are split, with some paid on DPI (Distributions to Paid-in Capital) and others on TVPI (Total Value to Paid-in Capital), leading to skewed incentives.
TVPI, once a reliable signal for future cash returns (DPI), has become less effective due to the recent phenomenon of rapid, successive funding rounds at escalating valuations.
A conflict exists between LPs who may want conservative portfolio markups and auditors who typically require marking to the price of the most recent financing round.
The rapid appreciation of company valuations (e.g., a company raising 3 times in one year) has broken traditional venture capital performance tracking systems.
Portfolio valuation affects not only an LP's direct compensation but also their external rankings in publications like US News and World Report.
fundraising_mentions: A company raising three times in a year, reaching a 10 billion valuation, from a 50 million seed fund.
quotable: LPS some get paid on DPI some get paid on tvpi meaning that how they're holding their portfolio is relevant to how they are viewed not just for their personal paycheck but how they might be measured by an external US News and World Report and other things.
it's hard to then argue to the Auditors you can't mark it to the last round if it was like two months ago because the Auditors will say typically they're like use the most recent last round
one_liner: A discussion on how conflicting LP incentives tied to DPI versus TVPI, combined with rapid startup valuation growth, creates inefficiencies and challenges in the venture capital market.

title: How Education Needs to Change
key_insights: Modern digital media like TikTok leverages compounding intelligence to retain user attention, a mechanism that traditional, static media like books cannot compete with.
The current education system is an outdated 'industrial age' model that treats students uniformly ('by manufacturing date') and is not designed to foster individual curiosity and learning.
The future of learning is being shaped by companies like Quizlet, Duolingo, and Sora Schools, which offer personalized and new educational models.
Despite disillusionment with current political leaders, there are promising signs of change with a new generation of entrepreneurs and activists entering politics.

Societal transformation is occurring through both incremental changes within existing systems and the creation of entirely new systems, such as the rise of homeschooling and concepts like the network state.
quotable: Education is not the filling of buckets, it's the lighting of flames.
We are in a bucket filling system by manufacturing date and that's not going to survive this transition.
one_liner: Albert Wenger argues that our industrial-age education system is obsolete and discusses the green shoots of a new societal paradigm emerging in learning, politics, and technology.

title: Daniel Khachab: "We Are in the Middle of a Cold War for AI Talent" | E1220
key_insights: The future of software is the 'agentification' of SaaS, where natural language prompts will replace traditional user interfaces, making current software models obsolete.

A global 'Cold War' for AI talent and infrastructure (chips, energy, foundation models) is underway, with governments actively competing to attract AI teams and resources, putting Europe at a disadvantage.

Pivoting to an AI-first model can lead to significant changes, including automating roles like customer service, which requires difficult but necessary leadership decisions to ensure business survival and progression.

True company value is created by focusing on fundamentals like product-market fit and a solid go-to-market strategy; fundraising success and high valuations are symptoms of a healthy business, not the goal itself.

Great founders must be willing to commit 15-20 years to their mission, persevere through extreme hardship (like losing 98% of revenue overnight), and stop making excuses about regulation or capital, especially in Europe.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a total of $330 million.
Most recent round was in early 2023 at a $1.1 billion valuation.
Company's annualized GMV is at $2.5 billion.
quotable: I think SAS is dead. I call it agentification of of SAS.
Who the [ __ ] wants to be a rainbow colored pony? Like I don't want to be a unicorn.
Lions don't lose sleep over sheep. We need to focus on what we are doing and not focus on winning against competition but at achieving our mission.
one_liner: Daniel Khachab, CEO of Choco, details his company's pivot from a traditional SaaS model to being 100% AI-driven, arguing that SaaS is dead and the future lies in software 'agentification', while also exploring the global 'cold war' for AI talent and the resilient mindset required to navigate crises like COVID-19.

title: We had to close that first round so that I could pay my rent.
key_insights: Founders often face significant personal financial challenges during a startup's early days.
Initial fundraising can be crucial for a founder's personal survival, beyond just company operations.
There can be stressful delays between VC commitment and the actual wiring of funds.
Founders might resort to personal measures like borrowing from family or delaying payments while awaiting funding.
The first funding round directly enabled the founder to set up payroll and pay his own rent.

close that first round

I was like trying to stall my landlord so I didn't get didn't get a victed
one_liner: Cloudflare founder Matthew Prince recounts the personal financial difficulties of starting a company, emphasizing how the first funding round was essential for him to pay his rent and cover basic living expenses.

title: This Billionaire has always been a Misfit | Mailchimp Founder Ben Chestnut
key_insights: Being a 'misfit' in early life can foster a unique perspective and independent thinking that is valuable for an entrepreneur.
Childhood experiences, such as being bullied, can create a powerful, lifelong drive to prove one's own value, fueling entrepreneurial ambition.

Effective leadership involves a duality: possessing high emotional intelligence (EQ) to understand people, while also being capable of making cold, logical, and sometimes harsh decisions for the good of the business.
A strong sense of stubbornness and a desire to 'do it my way' can be a defense mechanism from past experiences, leading to decisions like refusing early acquisition offers or investor funding.
Painful lessons, particularly those from formative years, often provide the most durable and impactful business philosophies.
fundraising_mentions: The business could have been sold early, as there were many suitors and investors knocking on the door, but the founder's stubbornness led him to decline these offers and build the company his own way.
quotable: I was leader of the Misfits always and I think MailChimp is like the Island of Misfit Toys sometimes.
