key_insights: The Total Addressable Market (TAM) for AI coding assistants is expanding dramatically as they shift from productivity tools to necessities for developers, with penetration approaching 100%.
Entry price is critical when the TAM is unclear, but when TAM expansion is massive, as with AI, winning is the only thing that matters for VCs.

The late-stage venture market is experiencing hyper-velocity, with companies like Cursor and Ramp doing multiple, significant valuation step-ups within a single year, blurring the lines with public market trading.
AI companies face a unique challenge where their core technology supplier (e.g., Anthropic, OpenAI) is also a direct competitor, raising questions about long-term margins and defensibility.

The traditional IPO market is being challenged by a robust private secondary market and the rise of retail capital in venture, creating an 'access premium' for elite private companies and delaying the need to go public.
fundraising_mentions: Cursor raised $2.3 billion at a $29.3 billion valuation.
Ramp's valuation increased from $13 billion to $32 billion in the same year over four financing rounds.
GCI raised from Scale at a $550 million post-money valuation.
Kleiner and Mamoon invested in Anthropic at a $180 billion valuation.
Bessemer co-led a Ramp round at a $32 billion valuation.
quotable: I think we're at a point where if there's some wobble, the magnitude of the correction will be fast and brutal.
As the models improve in performance dramatically, people switch. [...] But as the improvements in coding start to asmtote, I'm going to stay where I am.
one_liner: Tomas Tunguz discusses the explosive growth and sky-high valuations of AI coding companies like Cursor, the shifting dynamics of late-stage venture capital versus the IPO market, and the systemic risks of a market operating at its absolute limit.

title: How I Negotiated DiDi's $7BN Acquisition of Uber China
key_insights: In high-stakes negotiations, building genuine trust and rapport with your counterpart is more effective than superficial small talk.
Establishing a shared perspective on a non-central issue can be a powerful way to build initial trust with a competitor.
Daily check-ins to 'clear the air' and resolve any friction are crucial for maintaining momentum and trust during intense, multi-day negotiations.
Demonstrating reliability by consistently following through on your commitments is the foundation of trust that enables complex deals to close.

To convince a reluctant internal stakeholder (like a CEO) to agree to a major deal, presenting it as a finalized, well-structured opportunity with clear industrial logic is more effective than starting from scratch.
fundraising_mentions: Raised three and a half billion from the Saudis.
quotable: Every day I made sure at the end of the day said Gene how are we doing... did I say anything that you didn't like that you thought was wrong let's clear it out sort of like a marriage before you go to bed you clear your air we cleared our hour every day and then we closed the deal.
You told me what you're gonna do and you did it every single time no matter what it was... and I trusted that and that allowed me to get through the deal.
one_liner: Former Uber executive Emil Michael reveals the intense, trust-based negotiation tactics used to orchestrate the $7 billion sale of Uber China to its fiercest competitor, Didi.

title: POV: Your dad is a BILLIONAIRE internet entrepeneur
key_insights: Connecting abstract concepts like programming to tangible, real-world projects can be a powerful teaching method for children.
The internet enables rapid product development and global launch, allowing an idea to become a functional product in a weekend.
A successful product launch involves more than just coding; it requires understanding analytics, marketing through social media, and observing user behavior.
Involving family, like a son, in product management and bug testing can provide valuable feedback and create a shared learning experience.
A simple project, born from a desire to teach, can scale to millions of users, demonstrating the potential of simple, well-executed ideas.
fundraising_mentions: No fundraising mentioned.
quotable: I know it's possible to take an idea that can be solved through software and I can actually launch something. This is the beauty of the internet you don't have to ship floppy back you couldn't do this 20 years ago but now you can.
That helps connect the dots in his head right so now when he has ideas he's like okay well I don't have the skills yet to do the thing that Dad just did but I know it's possible.
one_liner: An internet entrepreneur recounts building a Wordle competitor in a single weekend to teach his son about software development, product launching, and the power of bringing ideas to life on the internet.

title: The Story Behind Ariana Grande's Performance at One Love Manchester
key_insights: Ariana Grande, despite being traumatized by the Manchester attack, chose to return and perform, demonstrating immense courage and character.
The decision to hold the concert was a direct response to terrorism, aimed at preventing fear from winning.
The city of Manchester showed incredible resilience by attending the concert in massive numbers, even after a terror alert was issued for London the previous night.
True leadership involves making difficult requests for a greater purpose, as seen when the guest asked Ariana to perform.
The unity of the artists and the community in the face of tragedy was a powerful statement against terrorism.
quotable: I'm not who I say I'm unless I do this.
The hero was the city of Manchester.
one_liner: Scooter Braun recounts the emotional and powerful story of how the One Love Manchester concert came together, highlighting Ariana Grande's heroism and the city's incredible resilience in the face of terrorism.

title: Hunter Somerville: Biggest Mistake LPs Make; Deep Dive into Secondary Markets | 20VC #985
key_insights: The secondary market is categorized into three main types: company secondaries (from founders, employees, early investors), traditional fund secondaries (LP interests), and GP-led restructurings (e.g., strip sales, tender offers, continuation funds).

The 'denominator effect'—where public market downturns leave LPs over-allocated to their private equity/venture portfolios—is a major forcing function for LPs to sell on the secondary market to rebalance.

Secondary discounts have deepened significantly, with LP interests trading at 30-45% discounts and company secondaries at 20-35% discounts, creating what is effectively a 'down round without the drama'.

In the current climate, DPI (Distributions to Paid-in Capital) is becoming far more important than TVPI (Total Value to Paid-in Capital) as LPs prioritize realized cash returns over paper gains, pressuring GPs to find liquidity.
GPs should be thoughtful about fund size, as many oversized growth funds raised in 2020-2021 may struggle to deploy capital effectively in a market with smaller rounds and fewer opportunities.
quotable: On the secondary side you can actually create it effectively a Down Round without the drama and disruption of doing that by buying at a 30 to 40 percent discount off of last round and creating an Arbitrage that you're comfortable with.

Venture at its core is all about outsourced Innovation and it's the job growth engine for our country... I'll always be long on Venture even if I'm disappointed by some of the behaviors that that we've seen in in recent years.
one_liner: A deep dive into the venture capital secondary market, explaining the mechanics of company, LP, and GP-led secondaries, and analyzing how market conditions are creating significant opportunities for buyers and liquidity pressure for sellers.

title: George Arison, Grindr CEO: How Grindr Built a Free Flow Cash Machine | E1234
key_insights: Grindr operates with extreme efficiency, generating over $2 million in revenue per full-time employee with a team of less than 150, driven by zero user acquisition spending and a lean organizational structure.

The platform is positioned as a social network for the gay community, not just a dating or hookup app, evidenced by users spending an average of one hour per day and plans to expand into travel and healthcare verticals.

Grindr embraces its identity as a 'hookup app' with features like 'Right Now', recognizing that in gay culture, sexual encounters often form the basis for friendships, social connections, and relationships.
CEO George Arison's management philosophy centers on lean teams, high accountability, and empowering employees by staying in the details without micromanaging.

Future growth is expected from increasing payer penetration (currently ~7%), international expansion, and leveraging AI to create better matches and user experiences, rather than focusing on growing the monthly active user base.
fundraising_mentions: The company was bootstrapped by its founder, Joel Simkhai.
It was acquired by Chinese company Kunlun, which was later forced to divest by the US government (CFIUS).
An ownership group called San Vicente acquired Grindr in 2020.
The company went public via a SPAC process in November 2022.
quotable: Second thing that I think Silicon Valley showed and has learned is that there's insane inefficiency in each individual that you have working for you because there's very bad management. Management does not mean micromanagement.

We shouldn't be just comped to dating apps when they talk about kind of what the multiple on the stock should be. that we should be comped as much as to social network products as much as we are comped to dating products.
one_liner: Grindr CEO George Arison breaks down the highly efficient, cash-flow positive business model of the world's largest social network for gay and bi men, detailing its unique user engagement, future expansion into new verticals, and his philosophy on lean management.

title: Imran Khan: Why the IPO Market is Not Closed & Lessons From Taking Snap & Alibaba Public | E1194
guest_role: Former Chief Strategy Officer, Snap Inc.
key_insights: The IPO market isn't closed; companies' valuation expectations are simply too high, preventing them from going public.
Companies should go public earlier rather than later to gain the discipline and feedback of public markets, which ultimately makes them better.
Revenue multiples are a 'BS multiple'; the focus should be on a business's potential for long-term cash flow and profitability.
A company's IPO price is just a snapshot in time and doesn't matter if the company is building a sustainable, long-term business.
Founders who hire 'missionaries' (employees who believe in the mission) rather than 'mercenaries' (employees motivated by stock price) can build a culture that withstands stock price volatility.
Technology landscapes shift every ~15 years, which makes holding companies private for too long risky for investors as the original investment thesis may become obsolete.
fundraising_mentions: Alibaba bought back 20% of its stake from Yahoo for approximately $8 billion.
Alibaba raised $1.75 billion from global investors for the Yahoo stake buyback.
Alibaba invested $200 million into Snap.
quotable: I don't think IPO market is closed I think the issue is companies don't want to go public because their expectations are too high.
Revenue multiple is a BS multiple... why would somebody give a about Revenue multiple?
When they're babies cats and tiger look same but a cat never become a tiger.
one_liner: Former Snap CSO and Alibaba IPO banker Imran Khan argues that the IPO market is open but company expectations are too high, advocating for earlier IPOs and focusing on long-term business fundamentals over short-term valuation.

title: How Netflix HACKED Hollywood 🎬
key_insights: Netflix disproved the industry's belief that consumers only want new releases, with 70% of its DVD rentals being catalog titles compared to Blockbuster's 10%.
Netflix effectively created the first mass-market for catalog home video content by making thousands of titles easily accessible.
By collecting user data and personalizing recommendations, Netflix learned individual user tastes (e.g., 'what Ben likes vs. what Harry likes').
This deep understanding of user preference allowed Netflix to 'demand shift' customers from high-cost content (e.g., Universal) to lower-cost content (e.g., Warner) without reducing satisfaction.
Netflix's ability to influence demand gave it significant leverage in content acquisition negotiations, rewarding partners with more favorable pricing models.
quotable: It actually for the first time ever creates a catalog in the home video Marketplace.
That strategy only works for someone like Netflix if they're able to demand shift you from a universal title to a Warner title without sacrificing your satisfaction.
one_liner: An analysis of how Netflix disrupted the home video market by leveraging its extensive catalog and data-driven personalization to shift consumer demand away from expensive new releases.

title: Matthieu Rouif: The Story of PhotoRoom, Is This YC’s Most Capital Efficient Company? | E1074
key_insights: Achieving extreme capital efficiency ($20M ARR with $2M cash) is possible on mobile by leveraging app store distribution and yearly subscriptions for a short payback period.
Intense focus is critical in the early stages; PhotoRoom narrowed from photo/video to just photo, then to sellers, and saw 10x growth with each step.
The 'McDonald's Test'—offering to buy people's food in exchange for user testing the app on the spot—provides rapid, invaluable, real-world feedback.
A feature becomes a product when it provides depth and opens up a wide range of new use cases (e.g., background removal enabling templates, thumbnails, etc.).
The future of UI/UX with AI is not text prompts; AI will enable more natural inputs like images and voice, making interfaces like on-screen keyboards obsolete.

Incumbents often build 'co-pilot' AI features on existing products, while startups have the advantage of building 'autopilot' systems that create entirely new product categories for users who previously lacked the skills or time.
fundraising_mentions: Scaled to $20 million in ARR with only $2 million of cash.
quotable: people don't like to write prompts... it's kind of a command line interface and for a lot of things it doesn't make sense to like to input text.
We're like pushing for that like on impact like we actually measure how much revenue per per teammate we have at fot room so that's that's one one thing we look at.
one_liner: Matthieu Rouif shares how PhotoRoom became one of YC's most capital-efficient companies by relentlessly focusing on user needs, leveraging mobile app store dynamics for growth, and building a product-led culture prepared for an AI-driven future.

title: Lessons from Keith Rabois
key_insights: Companies are constrained by the number of 'barrels' (key people who can run initiatives), not 'ammunition' (people who can do tasks).
The number of 'barrels' dictates how many major projects a company can execute simultaneously and how fast it can move.
When a 'barrel' is identified, a company should do everything in its power to retain them, including giving them more responsibility and equity.
Great growth leaders, especially early hires, often become the 'barrels' a company needs to succeed.
High-impact 'barrel' employees tend to attract and hire other 'barrels', multiplying their value to the organization.
quotable: No matter how much ammunition you have, if you only have five barrels you can only do five things simultaneously.
When you find that person, man you do whatever it takes to kind of keep them around because they'll probably hire other barrels too.
one_liner: A discussion on Keith Rabois' framework of 'barrels vs. ammunition' to explain why identifying and retaining key, high-leverage employees is critical for a company's ability to scale and execute effectively.

title: WILD STORY of how I became Duolingo’s Head of Growth
key_insights: When you identify a high-impact area or an inflection point, it's worth doubling down on it, even if it has been previously optimized.
A small, focused team can achieve significant results by targeting high-leverage areas, such as notifications which reach a broad user base.
Experiments that produce statistically significant negative results are valuable because they reveal what truly matters to users, providing a rich area for further learning and manipulation.
True experimental failure is not a negative outcome, but a lack of statistically significant results or meaningful learnings.
Challenging internal assumptions, even from founders, can lead to breakthroughs; the growth team tested notifications despite being told they were already fully optimized.
quotable: I went back to my desk and Googled what is growth... and I found Andrew Chen's blog and I started reading Andrew Chen's blog and like that's when I was like yeah I can do this.

If you run an experiment with statistical significance and it harmed your product, that means that you found a moment that really matters to users and if you found a moment that really matters to users you can manipulate it in multiple ways for positive and for negative.
one_liner: Duolingo's Head of Growth recounts how she got the job without prior experience and drove significant results by challenging assumptions and focusing on optimizing notifications, revealing that even small teams can find major inflection points for growth.

title: Harry debates Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince: "Should startups target niche markets?"
key_insights: For venture-backed startups, the worst outcome is not quick failure, but 'the slog'—a slow, draining journey with just enough growth to keep going but not enough to succeed, consuming years of a founder's life.
Founders should start with a huge, ambitious vision ('run the internet') rather than a narrow niche, as this is crucial for recruiting top-tier talent who are motivated by world-changing problems.
Quick failure is the second-best outcome for a VC-backed company because it frees up the entrepreneur's time and resources for the next venture.
Many stories of famous companies starting in a tiny niche (e.g., eBay with Beanie Babies) are often revisionist history; the founders likely had a massive vision from the very beginning.
Casting a wide net initially allows a company to discover its true initial market, which may be unexpected (e.g., Cloudflare finding traction with human rights organizations, not startups).
fundraising_mentions: Cloudflare intentionally did not raise money from angels or friends and family until the IPO to protect them from the high likelihood of failure.
Raised from VCs like Venrock.
Venture capital is a specific path with its own rules, distinct from bootstrapping.
quotable: The worst outcome by by far is the slog. Where you have these companies that are growing just enough that it feels like success is just over the next Hill and they and so they can't stop but they nobody cares about them anymore.
I think it's very rare to find someone who said I started out just trying to build the platform for people to sell snowboards and I ended up building Shopify.
one_liner: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince argues that venture-backed startups should pursue a massive, ambitious vision from day one, rather than focusing on a narrow niche, to attract the best talent and avoid the dreaded 'slog' of mediocrity.

title: Oren Zeev: How I Raised $1 BILLION in 12 Months
key_insights: A solo capitalist structure allows for faster, more contrarian, and conviction-based decision-making compared to traditional VC partnerships, which can tend towards mediocrity.
Investment pace should be opportunity-driven, not managed for vintage diversification; it's better to deploy capital into great deals when they appear rather than adhering to a rigid timeline.
When evaluating follow-on rounds in high-growth companies, it's better to err on the side of paying a higher price than to miss out, as strong growth can quickly justify the valuation.
Founders are the primary customers for a VC, not LPs. Building a reputation as the best partner for founders is the most critical driver of long-term success.

The traditional VC concept of 'protecting ownership' via pro-rata is flawed; investors should either increase their stake with conviction or thoughtfully pass, rather than blindly maintaining an arbitrary percentage.
fundraising_mentions: Raised three funds in 2021 totaling about $1 billion.
Was in the process of raising another $500 million fund at the time of the interview.
Invested in Riverside's seed round and later preempted and led a subsequent round.
Mentioned a missed opportunity to invest in Facebook at a $500 million valuation.
Discussed a potential take-private deal for Audible at $300 million which was blocked by his former partners.
quotable: It's all about being the best alternative for the founders. The founders are the customers, not the LPs, and the customer is always right.
I think pro-rata is bs. I think you should either be in and try and increase to 20 or 25 percent, or be out and have that hard conversation.
one_liner: Solo capitalist Oren Zeev shares his contrarian approach to venture capital, emphasizing rapid deployment, high-conviction bets, and why treating founders as the true customer is the key to building a top-performing fund.

title: Suchit Dash: Scaling Dubsmash to 43M Users, Battling TikTok & Joining Reddit | E1060
key_insights: Good products make it to your home screen, but great products make it into your mind; you think about them even when you're not using them.
Understanding creator motivation is key; it often boils down to the 'Three C's': Community, Clout, and Cash.
A product can be massively viral without having true product-market fit, as evidenced by high initial growth but poor long-term retention.
When facing an existential threat (like a competitor buying the market), you must be intellectually honest about your chances and consider strategic alternatives like M&A.
Pivoting the entire company towards a small but highly retentive user segment, even if it means abandoning larger, less engaged markets, can be the key to survival and finding true fit.
fundraising_mentions: Raised a Series B.
Had $7 million in cash in the bank at one point.
quotable: Good products make it to your home screen, great products make it into your mind.
The reality is consumer internet is what didn't you nail the user motivation. We didn't get users to spend to shift their time or spend their time daily using the product.
one_liner: Suchit Dash shares the tumultuous journey of building the viral app Dubsmash, navigating near-death experiences, finding a second life by pivoting to a niche community, and the eventual decision to sell to Reddit after battling TikTok.

title: Lessons from Quibi's Failure | Jeffrey Katzenberg & Sujay Jaswa
key_insights: Southern California (Hollywood) culture punishes failure with public humiliation, whereas Silicon Valley culture views it as a learning experience and part of the entrepreneurial journey.
Quibi's failure was attributed primarily to a lack of product-market fit, despite achieving high-quality content.
Launching a mobile, on-the-go product during a global pandemic was a significant, though not the only, factor in its failure.
When it's clear a venture is failing (a 'living dead' company), quickly shutting it down to return as much capital as possible to investors is a responsible, albeit rare, action.
There is a coming wave of 'Series B' stage companies with significant capital but no product-market fit, leading to a reckoning where investors may ask for their money back.
fundraising_mentions: Quibi returned $600 million out of an initial billion dollars raised to its investors.
quotable: If you want to do something that is original and unique it equals risk. If you are going to do something that is risky it means there needs to be the provision for failure. If you take out the equation the ability to ever fail you will not take risk if you don't take risk you'll never do anything unique and original.
For me actually the thing that was humiliating to me is I lost money.
one_liner: Jeffrey Katzenberg discusses the failure of Quibi, contrasting the cultural views on failure between Hollywood and Silicon Valley, and emphasizing the importance of product-market fit and the responsibility of returning capital to investors when a venture fails.

title: How Harry Would Fix Shopify
key_insights: Shopify's current homepage messaging is perceived as bland and fails to convey the empowering, dream-enabling potential of its platform.
A more effective brand message should focus on the outcomes Shopify enables for its merchants, such as funding their passions and achieving their dreams, rather than just listing features.
As companies scale to serve a diverse customer base (from small businesses to large enterprises), their messaging often becomes diluted and less potent in an attempt to appeal to everyone.

There is a fundamental tension in product marketing between crafting an authentic, aspirational message that resonates with the core user base and not alienating large, risk-averse enterprise customers.

The strategy for acquiring large enterprise clients (e.g., C-suite discussions, boardroom meetings) is fundamentally different from the broad, inspirational messaging needed to capture the long tail of smaller businesses.
quotable: I want empowerment. I want 'we deliver dollars to your pocket to pay for your children's favorite hobbies'... we make your life and your dreams possible.

You're getting to the true art of like product marketing which is how do you have a message which still speaks authentically to who you are and what you actually give a **** about without alienating an unacceptably large part of your customer base.
one_liner: A critique of Shopify's corporate messaging, arguing for a more inspirational, community-focused brand identity to better reflect its mission of empowering entrepreneurs.

title: David Tisch: The 3 Most Important Variables When Raising Your Seed Round | 20VC #983
key_insights: When fundraising, founders should prioritize the investors ('who') and the amount of capital over the valuation ('price').
Valuation is determined by the market; if a founder secures an investment at a certain price, that becomes the market price, and an investor's only choice is to accept it or pass.
Multi-stage firms have permanently changed the seed landscape by productizing a '$5-7M check at a $20-30M valuation' deal, creating a bifurcation in the market.
Generic startup advice is dangerous; founders should seek customized, nuanced guidance because every company's journey and circumstances are unique.
Signaling risk from seed investors not participating in a subsequent round is largely overstated, as later-stage investors form their own independent opinions.
fundraising_mentions: BoxGroup raised two funds totaling $255 million in 2021 ($127.5M each).
BoxGroup's typical check size is $500k, $750k, or $1 million.
Multi-stage funds offer a standard seed deal of $5-7 million at a $20-30 million valuation.
Traditional seed rounds (not led by multi-stage firms) are typically $2-4 million at a $10-15 million valuation.
quotable: Everybody can ask for whatever they want and everybody can say yes or no that's the way this business works if somebody says yes that's the price.
Make your own movie. You know what you're not gonna do? You're not gonna replicate that movie. You're not gonna replicate anyone else's movie. So figure out what movie is yours and make that.
one_liner: David Tisch of BoxGroup shares his founder-centric approach to seed investing, detailing his firm's flexible strategy, the three crucial variables of any fundraise (people, amount, price), and why long-term partnership is more important than short-term market fluctuations.

title: Joost de Valk: How I Founded Yoast; The Ultimate Guide to SEO; The Threat of AI | E1000
key_insights: Open-source freemium models are difficult but have incredible, often underestimated, potential. Their success hinges on balancing free features to attract users with premium features that convert, while building a strong brand to foster trust.

When building a product, especially in open source, focus on making the default settings excellent, as 90% of users will never change them ('Decisions not options'). Avoid over-optimizing for power users at the expense of simplicity for the majority.

Effective SEO starts with understanding the language customers use to describe their problems. You can't create demand with SEO; you can only capture existing demand. Therefore, branding and recognizability in search results are critical.

AI will dramatically increase content supply and development productivity, but it will also increase the importance of unique, high-quality, human-authored content. Search engines will likely focus more on author credibility (Expertise, Authority, Trust) to surface the best results.

When starting with SEO, a big mistake is focusing too much on minor technical fixes. Instead, fix the biggest technical issues and then focus on the overall Brand Story and creating content that addresses user needs.
fundraising_mentions: Never took external funding for Yoast as the company was cash-flow positive and grew organically alongside WordPress.

As an angel investor, he tends to write checks of 100k-200k, prefers companies that can become self-sustaining quickly, and is not interested in founders who have mapped out multiple funding rounds before building the product.
quotable: I was like if I'm going to make 100k with this in the first year then it's actually worth continuing doing this and then I made more than 100K in the first months.
The default is what 90% of your users will end up using, so it better be damn good.
one_liner: Yoast founder Joost de Valk shares insights on bootstrapping a massively successful open-source business, the core principles of effective SEO and branding, and why AI makes human creativity more valuable than ever.

title: AJ Tennant: How to Build a Sales Machine and Where Most Go Wrong | E2118
key_insights: Sales skills are learned, not innate; work ethic and a desire to learn are more important than a naturally gregarious personality.

To move upmarket, first prove repeatable success in the mid-market, then strategically target a few key large accounts (e.g., T-Mobile for Glean) to build a playbook before scaling the enterprise motion.
Founders must be deeply involved in the initial 0-$10M ARR phase to define the go-to-market strategy alongside the first sales hires.

'Collaborative tension' between GTM and R&D is crucial; sales leaders should get product and engineering teams on customer calls to build empathy and drive necessary product evolution for enterprise clients.

When hiring AEs, test for 'creative problem-solving' and the ability to handle 'collaborative tension'. A chronological interview to understand motivations and a practical panel presentation are key evaluation methods.
Many enterprises are still in an 'experimental budget phase' for AI, so sales must focus on turning AI excitement into clear, ROI-driven business value with defined success criteria to avoid churn.
quotable: If you do not have the ability to collaborate effectively in a way that's driving your point of view that does require some tension and you are steamrolling people people don't want to work with you you're gone it just doesn't work.

I want the world to see that this is a career path that enables you to become a CEO of another company... I want that next grad that regardless of whether you go to college or you're at an Ivy League or at a state school to realize that you can have a massive like career by investing in Tech sales.
one_liner: Glean's Head of Sales, AJ Tennant, details his playbook for building a world-class enterprise sales organization, covering everything from hiring and creating 'collaborative tension' with product teams to the strategy for moving upmarket and navigating the experimental nature of current AI budgets.

title: 2022 M&A PREDICTIONS 🔮
company: Mega-cap tech (Microsoft, Facebook, Google, Amazon, Apple, Salesforce)
key_insights: M&A activity in mega-cap tech was expected to be higher in 2022 than 2021.
Fear of regulatory intervention from the FTC, DOJ, and European authorities has had a chilling effect on M&A for companies like Facebook, Google, and Amazon.
Microsoft is now perceived as being in a better position to make acquisitions without facing the same level of antitrust scrutiny.
Salesforce was expected to be quiet on the M&A front as it digested its acquisition of Slack.
It was surprising that companies like Adobe and Workday were not more active in M&A.
quotable: It's kind of a funny world where Microsoft is now the one that's allowed to buy things and not considered the Anti-Trust you know sort of monopolist type of business.

Now Facebook's market cap is below 600 billion there's actually the chance that they could avoid Anti-Trust problems and so it's just a strategic decline from Zuckerberg to be allowed to acquire again.
one_liner: An analysis of the M&A landscape for mega-cap tech companies in 2022, highlighting the chilling effect of regulatory scrutiny and the unique position of Microsoft.

title: How I Convinced Steve Ballmer and Microsoft to Give Us $800M for Tellme Networks - Emil Michael
key_insights: Tellme Networks successfully pivoted from a consumer to an enterprise model after the dot-com crash, eventually reaching $100 million in revenue.
Having an 'owner's mindset' and feeling the weight of responsibility, regardless of your position, makes you stronger and more effective.
Direct, high-stakes negotiation with top leadership can dramatically alter outcomes, as seen in the jump from a $300M offer to an $800M acquisition from Microsoft.
Demonstrating sheer determination and an unwavering commitment to stay and execute the vision post-acquisition is a powerful tool in M&A negotiations.
A small, bold action, like securing a one-hour meeting with a key decision-maker (Steve Ballmer), can create hundreds of millions of dollars in enterprise value.
fundraising_mentions: Raised $150 million in four rounds over 12 months in the late 90s.
Received an initial acquisition offer for $300 million.
Ultimately sold to Microsoft for $760 million plus cash on the balance sheet, totaling approximately $800 million.
quotable: When you care that much, no matter what position you are, you feel the weight. But that weight makes you better, right? It makes you stronger.
I begged Hottie for one hour with Steve Ballmer at Microsoft... I said, every minute you talk to Steve, Gibbs is going to get me a hundred million more dollars for the company.
one_liner: Emil Michael shares the story of Tellme Networks' pivot from a consumer-facing app to a successful enterprise voice recognition platform, culminating in a bold negotiation with Steve Ballmer that increased their acquisition price from $300M to $800M.

title: Sarah Tavel: Will Foundation Models Be Commoditised? | E1149
key_insights: The application layer in AI is where a tremendous amount of value will be created and captured because it owns the end-user relationship.

A crucial differentiator for AI startups is to sell the 'work product' or outcome, rather than just a productivity tool, which changes the market size from being based on seats to the cost of headcount.
A strong, tangible 'why now'—like a new technology catalyst—is critical for a startup's success, creating a powerful current that propels the company forward despite mistakes.
The most defensible AI startups will own more of the workflow and create unique experiences not easily replicated by incumbents simply using an API.
Frontier AI models will likely remain closed-source due to the immense and escalating compute costs required for training, creating an oligopolistic market structure.

Benchmark's investment model focuses on deep, non-delegated partnerships with a small number of companies, acting as operators alongside founders, particularly in critical functions like executive recruiting.
Venture boards should be truth-seeking partners who ask critical questions to help founders scale, rather than just being cheerleaders.
