The founder believes smart investors want founders to have peace of mind regarding their personal finances so they can focus on the company.
He advises against taking secondaries too early (like at a Series A) and suggests a more systematic approach in later rounds (Series B and beyond).
The right amount for a secondary is a personal decision based on what makes the founder comfortable, rather than a fixed rule.
fundraising_mentions: Founder took ~$10M in secondaries.
Secondaries were taken at Series B and a subsequent round.
Investors' desire for a certain ownership percentage was a factor in the secondary transaction.
~15 early employees participated in secondaries, taking out up to 10% of their earned equity.
quotable: If you have a Savage and you give them 10 million they'll be even more of a Savage.
I think smart investors understand I don't want the guys that are running the company to be worrying about, you know, basketball [personal finances].
one_liner: A founder details his experience taking $10M in secondaries, advocating for the practice in later stages to provide founders and early employees with financial peace of mind, ultimately making them more focused and motivated.

title: Windsurf x Google x Cognition: Full Breakdown: Who Made Money, Who Did Not
guest_role: Founder of SaaStr & Founding Partner at Scale VP
key_insights: The complex structure of the Windsurf acquisition by Google and Cognition was primarily designed to navigate and avoid FTC antitrust scrutiny, setting a potential new playbook for large tech acquisitions.

Even founders of hyper-growth AI companies are opting for the security of an acquisition over independence, revealing deep concerns about competition, market defensibility, and the stress of M&A processes.

The rise of 'vibe coding' platforms like Lovable and Replit is creating a new, potentially massive market for non-professional developers, but the long-term durability of their consumer-like revenue models and churn rates remains a key question.

In a crowded AI market, brand recognition is becoming a powerful moat; users, overwhelmed with choice, are increasingly defaulting to the most well-known tools like ChatGBT, Replit, and Lovable, making it harder for new entrants to break through.

Elon Musk's Grok has evolved from a perceived 'spite app' to a serious competitor that has rapidly achieved technical parity with leading models, posing a significant future threat due to vast resources, a lack of corporate baggage, and Musk's singular vision.
fundraising_mentions: Windsurf was valued at $3 billion in a proposed OpenAI acquisition.
Google acquired Windsurf's IP and team for ~$2.6 billion.
Cognition acquired the remaining Windsurf assets (revenue, cash, employees) for ~$400 million.
Windsurf was about to raise at a $3 billion pre-money valuation before the acquisition talks.
An undifferentiated startup was mentioned raising at $300M pre-money with <$1M revenue.
Lovable is mentioned as raising at a 20x multiple and a $2 billion price.
Lovable's previous round was at a $200M price on $4M revenue, which grew to $19M by the deal's close.
Kleiner's round in Windsurf was at a $450-500M post-money valuation.
Grok is reportedly raising at a $200 billion valuation.
quotable: This entire podcast is basically the FTC [__] up normal business operations so now we've all got to do weird [__] podcast.

If you look at the crappy multiples we see for some startups, undifferentiated company raising at 300 pre with less than a million of revenue... And then you see what is Windurf selling for? 20x revenue. Lovables raising at 20. Ready to go.
one_liner: A deep dive into the complex Windsurf acquisition by Google and Cognition, analyzing the impact of FTC regulations on M&A, the rise of 'vibe coding' platforms, and Elon Musk's emerging threat with Grok.

title: PREDICTION: Crypto Will Bounce Back
key_insights: Crypto's performance as an inflation hedge is relative; while it may not have been effective for dollar-denominated users, it has been an 'amazing hedge' in countries with significant currency devaluation.

Centrally controlled government digital currencies (CBDCs) pose a significant threat to citizen freedom and can be used as a tool for financial power and control, as seen with the freezing of Canadian trucker accounts.

A healthy financial system requires a balance between total government control and complete anonymity, suggesting a future with regulated, multi-tiered stablecoins rather than a single, state-controlled digital currency.
The FTX collapse is a short-term 'blip' for the crypto ecosystem, analogous to major dot-com busts like Webvan, which ultimately serve to wash out bad actors and strengthen the industry long-term.
The best times to invest in crypto are during market downturns, with the current environment (early 2023) being the second-best opportunity since the launch of Bitcoin in 2009.
fundraising_mentions: The interviewer, Harry Stebbings, mentions making two crypto investments in Q4.
quotable: I don't want to live in a society where somebody with a button in Washington can control everybody's Bank balances.
The best time to have been in crypto was January 2009... and the second best time is January of 2023.
one_liner: VC Albert Wenger argues that despite recent turmoil, crypto's role as a decentralized alternative to state-controlled finance is more important than ever, and the current bear market represents a prime investment opportunity.

title: Akshay Kothari: How Notion Has More Money Than Ever & Why Startup Fundraising is Broken | E1203
key_insights: Applying first-principles and systems design from product development can effectively scale other business functions like support, avoiding linear headcount growth.
Being cash-flow positive provides ultimate control, allowing a company to fundraise strategically for talent or market signals, not out of necessity, leading to better terms.
Maintaining a lean, high-quality team, even if it means waiting months for the right hire, enables faster long-term execution and forces prioritization.

Don't reinvent the wheel on established functions like enterprise sales; traditional structures (like quotas) are effective because they align with the core motivations of top performers in that field.
Boards can be intentionally recruited to serve as expert coaches for the executive team, rather than being passively assembled based on who invested.
fundraising_mentions: Raised $50 million at a $2 billion valuation in early 2020.
Raised $270 million at a $10 billion valuation in H2 2021.
quotable: There's more cash in Notion's bank today than the history of its raise... we've produced cash we we haven't spent any of it.
Founder mode is really good if you have a Founder who's right a lot. If they're not, God bless that company.
one_liner: Notion COO Akshay Kothari discusses the strategic advantages of being cash-flow positive, raising capital on their own terms, and how a lean, first-principles approach has guided their hiring, sales, and board-building strategies.

title: Why is Character AI used by 20M people every day?
key_insights: Character AI reached 20 million daily active users and 450 million daily messages by empowering users to create their own use cases.
The platform's growth is driven by unexpected user behavior, such as using video game characters for therapy.
The core strategy is to provide a general AI platform and allow users' creativity to define its primary functions.
A significant emerging use case is the blend of entertainment, companionship, and emotional support.
The company embraces the motto 'a billion users inventing a billion use cases' to highlight the power of user agency in technology.
quotable: I like this sort of motto of a billion users inventing a billion use cases because that's sort of the superpower of this technology.
I'm talking to a video game character who's now my new therapist and this makes me feel better.
one_liner: Character AI's co-founder explains how the platform's massive growth is fueled by users discovering novel applications at the intersection of companionship, entertainment, and therapy.

title: ElevenLabs CEO/Co-Founder, Mati Staniszewski:The Untold Story of Europe’s Fastest Growing AI Startup
key_insights: ElevenLabs achieved rapid growth, reaching $200M in ARR by scaling from $100M in approximately 10 months.
The company prioritizes speed of execution and a focus on a specific niche (voice AI) as a key competitive advantage against larger players like OpenAI.
They deliberately time fundraising announcements with major product launches or milestones to maximize impact beyond just the financial news.
Despite raising significant capital, they maintain a 'small and mighty' team culture, believing it fosters higher ownership and faster iteration.
Building a global company from Europe is possible, and a key advantage is access to incredible, often underestimated, talent that is eager to work on ambitious projects.
fundraising_mentions: Pre-seed: $2 million at a $9 million post-money valuation.
Series A: $19 million led by Andreessen Horowitz, Nat Friedman, and Daniel Gross.
Last Round: Raised at a $3.3 billion valuation when the company was at $100M-$120M ARR, announced in January 2025.
quotable: What do you believe that most around you disbelieve? That you can build a company from Europe at the global scale.
For us even from investor from product perspective is like especially now the speed of execution speed of investing is is the only thing you have.
one_liner: ElevenLabs co-founder Mati Staniszewski shares the story of building Europe's fastest-growing AI startup, detailing their rapid journey to $200M ARR, fundraising strategies, and the belief that focus and speed can win against giants.

title: What I Learned Working at Facebook
key_insights: Facebook's approach to internal disagreements emphasizes quick resolution by agreeing, disagreeing, and understanding why, followed by rapid escalation.
The speed of escalation is directly linked to Facebook's historical agility and execution speed.
To counteract corporate slowness and maintain agility, organizations like Newbank focus on keeping teams very small.
When encountering obstacles, swift escalation and decision-making (even if potentially imperfect but reversible) is preferred over prolonged inaction.
Newbank cultivates a strong culture of autonomy, empowering its general managers and junior staff to make significant product and business decisions.
quotable: you think X I think why by the end of this week the latest we are going to either agree disagree and know why and escalate
A bad decision which can be iterated on is better than no decision at all because you start learning from the market and from customers and very few decisions are as as Bezos would say one-way doors
one_liner: An executive discusses lessons learned from Facebook regarding rapid execution, conflict resolution, and organizational agility, and how these principles are applied at Newbank through small teams, quick escalation, and high autonomy.

title: Phil Carter: Growth Loops, CAC + LTV Benchmarks, Pricing, Discounts, Paywalls... | E1204
key_insights: The biggest wins in growth often come immediately after a failed A/B test reveals an unexpected user insight.
Consumer subscription apps face high churn, losing over 50% of annual subscribers in the first year and over 50% of monthly subscribers in the first three months.
For most companies, Customer Acquisition Costs (CACs) inevitably increase over time as they expand beyond their highest-intent early adopters.
A good payback period for consumer subscription is under 6 months, while a great one is within the first month, due to high churn and low LTV.
Early-stage startups should focus on big swings rather than small optimizations, as they often lack the user volume for statistically significant A/B testing and still have low-hanging fruit.
fundraising_mentions: The guest mentions a common mistake is raising too much capital too fast before understanding the product and target customer, and mentions the 'raise a series A' playbook.
quotable: often times the biggest wins come right on the heels of a failed AB test
the average consumer subscription app is losing more than 50% of its annual subscribers in the first year and more than 50% of its monthly subscribers in the first 3 months
one_liner: Growth leader Phil Carter breaks down the nuanced strategies for scaling consumer subscription businesses, covering everything from managing CAC and LTV to optimizing pricing, paywalls, and retention loops.

title: How to Nurture Cross Functional Relationships | Sales Tips from Maggie Hott
guest_role: Sales Leader (formerly at Slack, currently at Webflow)
key_insights: Sales leaders must dedicate time to educate cross-functional partners about sales and foster strong collaborative relationships.
Sales representatives should proactively engage with other teams, demonstrate empathy, and approach requests with a partnership mindset.
It is vital for companies, especially those in PLG, to establish and invest in outbound sales motions early in their growth trajectory.
When building sales infrastructure and selecting tools, always plan and invest for future scale and hyper-growth, not just immediate needs, to prevent costly replacements.
Establishing the right tools and processes correctly from the outset is more efficient and effective than trying to fix or replace them later on.
quotable: your business is your brand
it is so much easier to get it right in the beginning than to try to buy and build for now and then have to rip and replace down the road
one_liner: Maggie Hott, a sales leader, shares actionable advice on fostering cross-functional relationships, building effective outbound sales strategies, and scaling sales operations by choosing future-proof tools, drawing from her experience at Slack and Webflow.

title: Marc Benioff: The Future of San Francisco and What He Would Do if in Charge | E1064
key_insights: AI is evolving through four simultaneous waves: predictive, generative, autonomous agents, and eventually AGI.
San Francisco remains the number one AI city in the world due to its concentration of talent, startups, and universities, despite narratives to the contrary.
Benioff uses a five-question framework called V2MOM (Vision, Values, Methods, Obstacles, Measures) to focus and guide his projects and decision-making.
True fulfillment and happiness come from integrating giving back with creating and building; philanthropy should be built into a company's model from the start.
A hybrid work model is most effective, with different requirements for different roles (e.g., engineers vs. sales), balancing productivity at home with in-person collaboration and customer time.
fundraising_mentions: When Salesforce started, they put 1% of their equity, 1% of their product, and 1% of their employees' time into a foundation.
quotable: You're only going to get to the happiness and fulfillment if not only are you creating but you're giving. You've got to give back.
My priorities are constantly out of whack... it's a dance.
one_liner: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff discusses the future of AI, his vision for improving San Francisco, his personal leadership framework (V2MOM), and the integral role of philanthropy in achieving happiness and success.

title: Geoff Charles: How To Hire Product Teams & Increase Product Velocity | E1091
key_insights: In the early stages, product managers should be deeply involved in the sales process, even selling to the first 100 customers, to directly understand pain points.
Structure development into two-week sprints with minimal, highly-focused meetings (a Monday leads meeting, a Tuesday team scrum) to maximize velocity.
When hiring, prioritize candidates who have experience at a similar company stage over those with category-specific experience, as scrappiness and adaptability are more critical.
To assess senior hires, don't give them headcount for at least six months; make them do the work themselves to truly evaluate their performance.
Instead of getting bogged down by rigid OKRs, focus on being product-strategy driven, defining a clear goal, hypothesis, and a path to win that is more actionable for the team.
When launching a second product, keep the go-to-market team focused on the first product until the new product achieves its own product-market fit to avoid distracting the main growth engine.
quotable: The founder or the first product manager should be selling the first 100 customers absolutely.
Don't treat your employees like babies because they will become babies or you will hire babies or you will retain babies instead like treat them like Founders themselves.
one_liner: Geoff Charles from Ramp shares his tactical playbook on how to build and scale high-velocity product teams, emphasizing direct customer interaction, efficient two-week sprints, and a strategy-driven approach over rigid OKRs.

title: Christian Kleinerman: Do OpenAI and Anthropic Have a Sustaining Moat? Who Wins the AI Wars? | E1063
key_insights: A robust data strategy is the essential foundation for any successful AI strategy; without it, AI initiatives will fail.
The value in the AI ecosystem accrues to those who own the data, not the models. Models are becoming commoditized, while proprietary data provides a sustainable competitive advantage.

Enterprises are concerned about the security and privacy implications of sending their data to external AI models. The winning solution will involve bringing AI models to the data, not the other way around.

Companies should build with model optionality, creating an abstraction layer to easily switch between different LLMs as the technology rapidly evolves, rather than getting locked into a single provider.
The immediate impact of AI on jobs will be incremental productivity boosts and co-pilot assistance, not mass firings or wholesale replacement of employees in the short to medium term.
quotable: There is no AI or gen AI strategy without a data strategy. It's not just a line, it's a truth that we strongly believe in.

The vast majority [of value] goes to data. I don't know if it's 90 plus percent... At the end of the day it's a data problem and models, these are strong words, but I think they're getting commoditized until the next big innovation comes.
one_liner: Snowflake's SVP of Product, Christian Kleinerman, argues that data is the ultimate moat in the AI wars, discusses why enterprises must prioritize a data-first strategy, and explores the future of model development, security, and enterprise adoption.

title: Ariel Cohen: The Death of Salesforce; How OpenAI is Changing the Travel Industry | 20VC #975
key_insights: Incumbent enterprise software giants like Salesforce and SAP have stopped innovating and will be replaced by user-centric, AI-powered platforms.
True innovation requires the courage to make your own products obsolete and embrace new technologies, even when it's difficult.
The best time to drive major change management (like switching software vendors) is during a crisis when normal operations are disrupted.
Integrating advanced AI like OpenAI can dramatically improve service efficiency, with Navan's bot expected to handle 90% of support interactions.
A people-centric product approach, where employees want to use the software, eliminates the friction and enforcement costs of traditional corporate tools.
Technology and AI can drive high gross margins (75-80%+) even in service-oriented industries, enabling new business models like freemium and investments in loyalty.
fundraising_mentions: Raised money during COVID-19 after being turned down by 28 of 30 investors.
Greenoaks led a round during the pandemic.
Did a round at a $5 billion valuation when the vaccine was announced.
Recently raised at a $9.2 billion valuation in the middle of a market correction.
quotable: I would say maybe AI is hitting the world and eating software and companies that will not join the party will not be around.

In five years from now nobody is using going to use Concur and Amex, nobody. But nobody is going to use Salesforce. Nobody is going to use software that makes you put something inside a ticket and then it goes through a workflow... People today are asking for something else.
one_liner: Navan Co-Founder Ariel Cohen discusses how relentless product innovation and the integration of AI are disrupting the corporate travel and expense industry, arguing that incumbent giants like Salesforce are destined for obsolescence because they've lost the ability to innovate.

title: Aaron Levie: How the Business Model of SaaS Changes Forever & Startups vs Incumbents:Who Wins?|E1155
key_insights: We are in a temporary, decade-defining architecture shift with AI, creating a rare window for new platform-scale companies to emerge, but this time incumbents with data and workflow have a strong advantage.
The pace of AI model improvement, such as the 500x increase in token window size in 18 months, is unprecedented in technology history and is showing no signs of slowing down.

The next big breakthrough is AI agents, which will shift software from a tool humans use to a system that autonomously performs tasks, acting as 'autopilots' rather than 'co-pilots' for business functions.

The traditional seat-based SaaS business model is being challenged by AI, with the industry experimenting with consumption-based, value-based, and bespoke pricing models to capture the value of AI-driven automation.

Incumbents must be willing to drop their inferior, proprietary technology and adopt superior AI models from leaders like OpenAI, even if it feels like supporting a competitor, to survive the disruption.
quotable: We are in at one of these moments with AI which is a period where we are going to see not only breakthrough technology but the Breakthrough application of those technologies that is as much going to be an Encompass game as a startups game this time around.

The big breakthrough is what if we could go from a world where software is something that you or I use to get our jobs done... to where software is something that you or I use to basically farm out work to AI to go do.
one_liner: Box CEO Aaron Levie analyzes the current AI-driven technological shift, exploring the battle between startups and incumbents, the rise of AI agents automating work, and the profound impact on business models, organizational structures, and the very nature of software.

title: What Silicon Valley Bank Did Wrong
key_insights: SVB's announcement of a capital raise to fill a $1.5B hole backfired, creating panic instead of confidence.
The psychology of a bank run is driven by the fear of being the last depositor in an illiquid bank.
The tech community's rapid communication amplified the panic, leading to a swift withdrawal of funds.
A better strategy would have been to secure the capital first, then announce the successful raise to project strength.
The sequence of events (announcing a need for money before securing it) was a critical and unusual error for a bank in a precarious situation.
fundraising_mentions: Announced a $500 million Capital raise with General Atlantic.
Planned a market offering to fill a billion and a half dollar hole.
quotable: No one wants to be the last man standing in that bank with your deposits as the FDIC shows up in an illiquid situation.
They should have raised the money made the announcement that they raised the money and that they were in great position.
one_liner: The episode analyzes how Silicon Valley Bank's poorly timed announcement of a capital raise triggered a panic-driven bank run within the tech community, leading to its collapse.

title: Jonathan Ross, Founder & CEO @ Groq: NVIDIA vs Groq - The Future of Training vs Inference | E1260
key_insights: Inference is a 10-20x larger and more critical market than training; Groq is built specifically for this, viewing it as a separate market from NVIDIA's training dominance.
Groq's LPU (Language Processing Unit) architecture avoids external memory (HBM), the primary bottleneck for GPUs, allowing for faster, more energy-efficient (3x), and scalable inference.

Groq's business model involves partners funding the capex for chip deployment in exchange for a revenue share, allowing Groq to scale without being capital-constrained. A $1.5B deal mentioned is revenue, not a funding round.
The next major bottleneck for AI in 3-4 years will be power availability, not chips, due to a mismatch in infrastructure investment cycles.
Groq believes in focusing on unsolved problems rather than direct competition. They are ceding the training market to NVIDIA to own the high-volume, lower-margin inference market.
fundraising_mentions: Clarified a $1.5 billion deal with a partner in Saudi Arabia is a revenue deal, not a funding round.
Mentioned a previous $300 million funding round.
Discussed 'Grock Bonds', an internal program where employees traded salary for equity to save the company from running out of money.
quotable: Your job is not to follow the wave your job is to get positioned for the wave.

If you are competing you have done something seriously wrong. If you're competing it means that you haven't found an unsolved customer problem because if you're competing someone else has already solved the problem.
one_liner: Groq CEO Jonathan Ross details his strategy to dominate the massive AI inference market by using a fundamentally different, faster, and more scalable chip architecture (LPU) than NVIDIA's GPUs, funded by an innovative partner-led capex model.

title: Marty Cagan: Product Lessons from Steve Jobs and Elon Musk; Why do we idolize engineers? | 20VC #957
guest_role: Founder at Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG)
key_insights: Founders should focus on the primary risk: creating a product people will buy, rather than secondary risks like business models or go-to-market strategies.
The difference between a feature and a product is about 'output vs. outcomes'. A product solves a real problem for customers, whereas features are just output.
Product discovery involves answering four key questions: is it valuable, usable, feasible, and viable?
When conducting customer interviews (qualitative feedback), the goal is to find all the things wrong with the product, not to seek affirmation.
It's better to hire product people with high potential and teach them the domain, as domain experts can be hindered by 'domain dogma'.
Empowering engineers is crucial for innovative companies; just using them to code is only realizing half their potential value.
quotable: The most important thing is to know what you can't know.
If you're just using your engineers to code, you're only getting about half their value.
one_liner: Product legend Marty Cagan shares lessons on building great products, focusing on primary risks, the art of product discovery, and the importance of empowering engineers.

title: Steeve Morin: Why Google Will Win the AI Arms Race & OpenAI Will Not | E1262
topics: Future of AI (Agents, Reasoning, World Models)
key_insights: The AI market will shift heavily towards inference, which will constitute 95% of compute needs in five years, compared to just 5% for training.
The ultimate winner in AI will be the entity that controls the entire stack: products, data, and compute. Steeve argues this is Google, not OpenAI, which relies on Microsoft's compute.

The future of AI applications, particularly agents and reasoning, requires a shift from throughput-bound hardware (like current GPUs) to latency-bound hardware, creating an opening for specialized chips (e.g., Cerebras, Etched) that can challenge Nvidia's dominance.

There is an unsustainable 'bubble' in the pricing of Nvidia's H100s for inference, as their cost is not justified by their performance gains, which will lead to a market correction and opportunity for more efficient hardware from AMD and others.

Software abstraction layers that make it seamless to switch between different hardware providers (Nvidia, AMD, TPUs) are critical to breaking vendor lock-in and will allow developers to choose the most efficient compute, fostering true competition on price and performance.
quotable: you have the products the data and the computer who has all three Google that's like you know Android Google Docs whatever they have everything they can sprinkle everywhere this is the sleeping giant in my mind
open AI is amazing but it's not their compute ultimately if you don't own your compute you're starting with you know something at your ankle
one_liner: Steeve Morin of zml argues that the future of AI will be dominated by inference, where Google's ownership of the full stack (products, data, compute) gives it a decisive advantage over competitors like OpenAI, and explains how the hardware landscape will shift away from Nvidia's expensive, training-focused GPUs towards more efficient, latency-optimized chips for reasoning and agents.

title: Alexis Ohanian: The Full P&L Breakdown of the World's Most Valuable Women's Sports Team | E1187
key_insights: Women's sports are a massively undervalued asset class, with low entry costs and significant upside potential driven by underdeveloped media rights, sponsorships, and fan engagement.

Modern sports franchises should operate as tech-driven media companies, focusing on storytelling and content creation around players to build brand equity and drive revenue far beyond ticket and merch sales.

The 'Drive to Survive' effect demonstrates that telling the human story behind the athletes (a 'female lens') can unlock huge, previously untapped audiences and commercial opportunities for any sport.

The traditional sports ownership model is inefficient and ripe for disruption; applying a startup mentality with a focus on software, data, and relentless execution can create a significant competitive advantage.

Apex creators like Mr. Beast are building vertically integrated empires (CPG, SaaS) that leverage their massive, direct distribution to bypass traditional industry gatekeepers, representing a new model for business.

There is a huge arbitrage opportunity in marketing for brands that align with women's sports, which are often more brand-safe and have a more engaged, loyal audience compared to their male counterparts.

The NWSL has the potential to become more valuable than the MLS in the next decade because it can authentically claim to be the pinnacle of excellence in its sport globally, a story the MLS cannot tell.
fundraising_mentions: Angel City FC's NWSL expansion fee was $1 million.
The initial funding round for Angel City FC was around $6 million.
Alexis Ohanian personally invested $250,000 in Angel City FC in a trust for his daughter.
Ohanian invested in Mr. Beast's 'Feastables', buying 10% for a $40 million pre-launch valuation.
The new NWSL media rights deal is worth $60 million a year for four years.
Ohanian's early investment of about $10,000 in Ethereum's token sale grew to $17.1 million.
The Washington Commanders were purchased for ~$500 million and sold for $6 billion.
quotable: If you can't show me a sport where the highlights go viral on social media, the freest Market of ideas that has ever existed in the world, you might have some stuff missing.
I look at this and I think my God, like the bar is actually really low.
In the same way that I think Venture Capital should be run like a tech company, I think sports teams should... be software companies.
one_liner: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian explains his investment thesis for building billion-dollar women's sports franchises by operating them as tech-forward media companies, using his team Angel City FC as a primary case study.

title: Emil Michael tells the wild story of how he negotiated the $4B merger of Uber-China and DiDi
key_insights: In high-stakes negotiations, building genuine trust with your counterpart is more effective than superficial small talk.
Establishing rapport can be achieved by discussing non-central topics to find common perspectives, such as analyzing past competitive incidents together.
Maintaining open communication and resolving disagreements daily, like in a marriage, is crucial during long negotiations to prevent misunderstandings from derailing the process.
Being a fair negotiator who consistently follows through on promises is essential for building the trust needed to close a complex deal.
Cross-border M&A deals often require extreme discretion, including meeting in secret locations, to prevent premature leaks.
fundraising_mentions: $4B merger of Uber-China and DiDi
quotable: sort of like a marriage before you go to bed you clear your air we cleared our air every day and then we closed the deal.
You told me what you're going to do and you did it every single time no matter what it was... and I trusted that and that allowed me to do the deal.
one_liner: Emil Michael shares the inside story of the intense, relationship-driven negotiation that led to the $4 billion merger between Uber-China and DiDi, emphasizing the critical role of trust and fairness in closing the deal.

title: Why smart companies should reset their valuations — Woody Marshall
key_insights: Smart companies reset valuations to make optimal long-term business decisions.
Holding onto inflated valuations can lead to suboptimal decision-making.
Level-setting valuations is crucial for motivating employees.
Efficient capital allocation is vital given the current economic environment.
Investors may experience longer return periods when market multiples decrease.
quotable: The problem with companies that hold on to some of those valuations is they're going to make decisions that are suboptimal when you think about how to build the business over the long term.
one_liner: Woody Marshall explains why companies should reset their valuations to foster optimal decision-making, boost employee motivation, and ensure efficient capital allocation in a shifting market.

title: Benchmark's GP, Everett Randle on Why Mega Funds Will Not Produce Good Returns
key_insights: A new taxonomy is needed for AI companies, prioritizing absolute gross profit dollars per customer over traditional SaaS gross margin percentages, as AI's value capture can be significantly larger.

A VC firm's strategy is dictated by its fund size and team structure ('you invest your fund size'), leading to a bifurcation between large-scale, capital-velocity-focused mega-funds and smaller, craft-oriented, high cash-on-cash return-focused firms like Benchmark.

Mega-funds may generate large absolute dollar returns but struggle to produce the high net multiples (e.g., 5x+) that LPs traditionally seek from the venture asset class due to the sheer size of capital they must deploy.

Technology and the ability to build a superior, differentiated AI product remains the primary moat, rather than just distribution, because creating truly great AI products is incredibly difficult and talent is scarce.
Early in an investor's career, it is crucial to 'see excellence up close' by working with top-tier founders and companies to develop an instinct for what A++ teams and execution look like.
Even with lower ownership percentages in highly competitive deals, a firm can succeed by being the founder's highest ROI and closest partner, delivering exceptional cash-on-cash returns to LPs.
fundraising_mentions: OpenAI round at $32 billion
SpaceX at $150 billion
Rippling Series A at $250 million post-money
Figma at 100x ARR ($4M ARR, $400M valuation)
quotable: I think we should not be placing that much emphasis on margins today. We need a new taxonomy for AI companies.

I think you ship your fund size or you invest your fund size and your team structure. So, if you have a $7 billion fund and you have 50 people, uh you definitively need to get in on these mega rounds.
one_liner: Benchmark's newest partner, Everett Randle, discusses why mega-funds will struggle to produce venture-like returns and argues for a new evaluation framework for AI companies based on absolute profit rather than SaaS margins.

title: Klaus Hommels: Why "Portfolios are Merely a Construct to Make LPs Happy"? | E1231
key_insights: Venture is not about building portfolios to please LPs, but about finding and taking over-proportional risks on truly great companies.
Europe is under-financing innovation by a factor of eight (0.5% of GDP vs. a historical 4%), which hampers its economic progress and wealth creation.
The geopolitical situation necessitates a huge increase in European defense spending, creating a massive new market for deep tech and venture investment focused on sovereignty.

When you find the right company, you should not be price sensitive; the cost of a great company being 30% more expensive is negligible compared to the final outcome, whereas a bad company isn't worth it even if 30% cheaper.
The quality of technical founders in Europe has significantly increased, shifting from 'copycat' models to genuine technological innovation.
The greatest currency for an investor is not the financial multiple, but the 'thank you' emails from the best founders for making a real impact on their journey.
The lack of deep capital pools and financial literacy in Europe, particularly the low allocation of pension funds to venture (0.02% vs. 10-13% in the US), is a major structural problem.
fundraising_mentions: The guest started his investing journey with 20,000 bucks from his grandmother.
Mentions the NATO Innovation Fund, a billion-euro fund he chairs.
quotable: Venture is not sitting in a nice office with borrowed power of LPs and playing like in Old Caesar's times thumbs up thumbs down.
I'm not so keen of building portfolios if I find cool companies that make a difference that is where the beef is and if you have one or two of them every portfolio looks great.
I had a rule for long that when I had an exceptional hit I would stop investing for three months because success makes you feel that you can walk over water.
one_liner: Lakestar's Klaus Hommels argues that VCs should focus on taking concentrated, disproportionate risks on game-changing companies rather than just building portfolios, makes the case for a massive ramp-up in European defense tech investment, and shares the stories behind his iconic investments in Spotify, Revolut, and Facebook.

title: Moving from Founders Fund to Khosla with @Khosla Managing Director Keith Rabois
key_insights: Keith Rabois returned to Khosla Ventures from Founders Fund, valuing its culture of vigorous, collaborative debate in partner meetings which he felt made him a sharper investor.
Khosla Ventures' weekly partner meetings are described as extensive, unstructured, and dense with preparation, fostering deep analytical rigor.
Founders Fund's operational model is depicted as more individualistic, where partners run their own investment strategies with less structured group debate.
Rabois missed the continuous learning about deep-tech sectors like AI, robotics, and biotech at Khosla, which he described as a 'free education.'
Strong co-investment relationships with Khosla partners continued even while at Founders Fund, indicating a persistent collaborative bond.
fundraising_mentions: Partner in Khosla Ventures funds KB4, KB5, and KB6.
Samir (from Khosla) led a financing round in OpenStore.
Samir led the Series A for a company named Truema.
Rabois led a growth round for Ultima Genomics.
Samir led an investment round in a Florida-based company.
quotable: I felt that they made me a sharper investor, a smarter investor... by listening to them and occasionally I made the mistake of over listening but it was always my mistake and I felt like I was doing my job better.
It was like getting a free education in the world of technology every week.
one_liner: Keith Rabois details his move back to Khosla Ventures, contrasting its rigorous, debate-driven partnership culture with the individualistic approach at Founders Fund, and explaining why he missed the intellectual sharpening and deep-tech education.

title: Mark-to-Market is Corrupting the VC Market
key_insights: The practice of 'mark-to-market' valuations has corrupted the venture capital industry by creating perverse incentives.
VCs are incentivized to over-fund companies to achieve high paper markups, which helps them raise subsequent funds.
Limited Partners (LPs) are often compensated based on paper markups, which fuels the demand for endless funding rounds and inflated valuations.
The venture industry would be healthier and more disciplined without markups, or by using a conservative Black-Scholes analysis for valuation.
Extremely high Internal Rates of Return (IRR) in the early years of a fund are a 'moronic' indicator of a frothy market, not necessarily skill, and are unsustainable.
fundraising_mentions: Speaker's fund valuation at $50-60 million, previously at $1.7M and $1.4M.
Achieved a 140% IRR in the first year of a fund.
quotable: Venture would be radically different if there were no markups... and I'm confident it would be a better industry with no markups.
My last Fund in the first year at 140 irr that's moronic but it wasn't it can't last I'm not that good.
one_liner: A critical analysis of how mark-to-market valuations incentivize VCs and LPs to over-fund companies, leading to distorted behavior and a corrupted venture capital ecosystem.

title: Carlos Delatorre, CRO @Harness: Why Every Sales Rep Should Do Pipeline Generation | E1251
key_insights: Hiring for sales should prioritize innate attributes (curiosity, empathy, drive) and a proven history of pipeline generation over charisma or past success at brand-name companies.
Pipeline generation is a non-negotiable skill for all AEs; they should source a significant portion of their own pipe, which increases win rates, accountability, and the value of inbound leads.
A structured weekly cadence for pipeline generation (e.g., 'Pipeline Generation Tuesdays') with dedicated time for research, prep, training, and execution is critical for consistent results.
Effective sales reps are not 'closers'; buyers buy. The rep's job is to create an environment conducive to a purchase decision through discovery, education, and demonstrating value.
When hiring the first sales reps at an early-stage company, the CEO should act as the primary rep to refine the messaging and playbook before hiring a leader.
The ability to generate pipeline helps reps get 'unstuck' in deals by enabling them to reach higher-level stakeholders or other business units directly.
In-person sales teams are significantly more productive; they learn faster, morale is higher, and managers can provide real-time coaching and course correction.
When evaluating sales candidates, it's crucial to test for non-negotiable skills like a history of self-sourcing pipeline, as it's a difficult skill to learn and requires a specific tenacity.
fundraising_mentions: Advises a series A company to have the founder act as the first rep and hire individual contributors before a sales leader.
quotable: I don't believe salespeople sell, buyers buy. All salespeople can do is create an environment that is conducive to that purchase decision.
Pipeline generation... hiring AEs that have not built their own pipeline, that one is non-negotiable because if they say they will, if they say they want to, they just don't know how hard it is.
one_liner: Harness CRO Carlos Delatorre shares his playbook for building elite enterprise sales teams, centered on the non-negotiable principle that every account executive must be an expert at generating their own pipeline through a highly structured, weekly process.

title: Roundtable #4 with Jason Lemkin, Woody Marshall, Deven Parekh, Harry Stebbings | E1071
guest: Deven Parekh, Woody Marshall, Jason Lemkin
guest_role: Deven Parekh (Managing Director, Insight Partners), Woody Marshall (General Partner, TCV), Jason Lemkin (Founder, SaaStr)
key_insights: The growth equity market has slowed dramatically from its 2021 peak, but is not dead; high-quality companies with strong fundamentals are still able to raise capital at a more measured pace.
Valuation resets are becoming common and are viewed as healthy for aligning employee incentives and making sound long-term business decisions, despite the near-term pain for investors and founders.

Highly structured financing rounds, while sometimes used to bridge valuation gaps, are often dangerous as they can create misalignment between investors and management, particularly in future M&A scenarios.
The IPO market is cautiously reopening, but the emphasis has shifted from pure growth to a 'Rule of 40' balance of growth and profitability, with public investors valuing sustainable business models.
While AI is a fundamental technology shift, the current late-stage investment market for AI is in a 'hype cycle' with valuations far ahead of company fundamentals, warranting caution.
fundraising_mentions: A minority software investment of $100M+ in a business growing 50%.
A hypothetical $50M ARR company that previously raised at a $1B valuation.
Klaviyo's last private round was at a $9.5B valuation.
Instacart's prior valuation was mentioned at $38B-$39B.
Cisco's acquisition of Splunk.
quotable: You can wake up in the morning and decide the glass is half empty or you can decide the glass is half full. We went over a year without any Tech IPO... you had three companies go public at real scale... that to me is a glass half full.
Structure never made a good company. At the end of the day, find a good company, make it great, and pay the right price.
one_liner: Top growth investors from Insight, TCV, and SaaStr dissect the current state of the SaaS market, debating valuation resets, the cautious reopening of the IPO window, and the strategic shift from hyper-growth to efficient, profitable scaling.

title: This is why you shouldn't outsource software engineers
key_insights: Leaders often coddle product people and engineers, limiting their broader business understanding.
Great product companies distinguish themselves by how they empower their engineers.
Empowered engineers are the foundational strength of leading tech companies like Tesla, SpaceX, Google, Amazon, Stripe, and Apple.
Using engineers merely for coding means leveraging only half their potential value.
Outsourcing engineering signifies a lack of seriousness about building a product-focused company.
quotable: if you're just using your engineers to code you're only getting about half their value
there is nothing more important than empowered engineers
one_liner: Marty Cagan passionately argues that empowering engineers is paramount for successful product companies, asserting that outsourcing engineering is a critical mistake that demonstrates a lack of commitment.

title: Turing CEO Jonathan Siddharth: Who Wins in Data Labelling & Why 99% of Knowledge Work Will Disappear
key_insights: The era of simple data labeling companies is over; it's now the era of 'research accelerators' that create complex data and reinforcement learning (RL) environments to train AI agents.
All knowledge work that involves a computer screen will eventually be automated, creating a $30 trillion opportunity and forcing incumbents to adapt or be replaced.
The future of AI training is shifting from simple imitation learning (SFT/RLHF) for chatbots to complex reinforcement learning in simulated business environments to build agentic AI.
The traditional SaaS model is 'completely over' because agentic foundation models will perform tasks directly and companies will easily build their own custom solutions.
Moats in the AI era are not based on technology, but on data-driven feedback loops from deploying models in the real world, which generates proprietary data for continuous improvement.
fundraising_mentions: Mentions the 'scale investment' event as a significant moment for the industry.
quotable: All knowledge work is going to be automated. It's only a matter of time.
SAS as we know it, I think is over. I think it's completely over.
I think the era of data labeling companies is over and it's now the era of research accelerators.
one_liner: Turing's CEO explains why the data labeling market is dead, how AI agents are trained using complex 'research accelerators', and why he believes all knowledge work and the traditional SaaS model will be completely automated.

title: Why Apple Needs a Management Overhaul & Why Google is Catching Up with Hyperscalers
guest_role: Founder, SaaStr & Partner, Scale Venture Partners
key_insights: A strong personal brand can now enable a VC to leave a top-tier firm like Benchmark and raise a successful solo fund, indicating a power shift in venture capital.
The revenue potential for AI developer tools is vastly underestimated, with projections of individual developer spend reaching $10,000/month, fueling massive valuations for companies like Anthropic.
Among the hyperscalers, Google is executing its AI strategy most effectively and gaining ground, while Microsoft's position is complex and AWS is seen as underperforming.
Apple's lack of a competitive proprietary AI product is a significant strategic vulnerability that may require a management overhaul, despite the strength of its hardware and App Store businesses.
The massive capital expenditure required for AI development is leading to a consolidation of power, but also creating oligopolies where new startups can still challenge incumbents in specific niches.
fundraising_mentions: Anthropic raising at a valuation between $150B and $180B, with revenue growing from $1B to a projected $4B.
OpenAI reportedly raising at a valuation between $360B and $380B.
Figma's IPO filing range was increased from $24-$28 to $32-$35 per share.
The Adobe acquisition of Figma for $20B in September 2022 was discussed.
quotable: Ironically, Google, whom we all piss on, has executed the best of the four. They have a model that works. Apple doesn't even have a product that works. Microsoft bought someone else's product, but doesn't quite own it... I don't think these guys are too powerful. If anything, I think they're a bunch of rich people on the back foot behind the new trend, desperately trying to catch up.

I think every developer at a top tech company growing is going to give them $10,000 a month of AI credits. Everyone's going to get 10,000, not 200, which is what we're thinking. We thought that was a lot a couple months ago. They're all going to get $10,000 a month.
one_liner: A deep dive into the shifting power dynamics in venture capital, the explosive growth of AI companies like Anthropic, the competitive landscape of hyperscalers, and the strategic challenges facing tech giants like Apple in the new AI-driven market.

title: The Ultimate AI Roundtable: What Happens Now in AI, Why Google are Vulnerable | E1085
guest: Emad Mostaque, Des Traynor, Jeff Siebert, Yann LeCun, Richard Socher, Cristóbal Valenzuela, Tom Tunguz, Miles Grimshaw, Christian Lang
guest_role: Founder, Founder, Founder, Head of AI, Founder, Founder, Investor, General Partner, Co-founder
company: Stability AI, Intercom, Digits, Meta, You.com, Runway, Theory Ventures, Benchmark, Beyond Work
topics: Future of Big Tech in AI
key_insights: A major debate exists on whether foundational models will be commoditized by open-source alternatives or dominated by a few large, closed-source companies.
Value in the AI stack is contested, with some arguing it will accrue to the application layer due to diverse needs, while others see infrastructure providers capturing immense value initially.
The dominant business model is expected to shift from seat-based pricing to consumption-based models that sell work and outcomes, not just software access (e.g., 'SLA on work, not on uptime').
Google is perceived as the most vulnerable incumbent due to the innovator's dilemma; AI-powered chat threatens its core search and ad-based business model.
The concept of 'co-pilots' is largely seen as an incumbent strategy to augment existing workflows, whereas true disruption will come from new, orthogonal applications that replace entire workflows.
fundraising_mentions: Anthropic 'did raise a lot of money too'
Universities collaborating to train models for '$20 or $50 million'
quotable: I mean who wants a co-pilot I I want to be a pilot... the better solution is to remove the application and just talk straight with AI.
AI is going to bring a new Renaissance for Humanity, a new form of Enlightenment... because AI is going to amplify everybody's intelligence.
one_liner: A panel of top AI founders and investors debate the commoditization of foundational models, the shift to outcome-based business models, and why incumbents like Google are vulnerable to disruption.

title: Max Levchin, Founder & CEO @ Affirm:The Biggest Surprise Scaling to $18.7BN Market Cap
key_insights: Brilliant people often have extreme personalities; the key is to manage their quirks to bring out their best, while drawing a hard line at issues of integrity.
A post-mortem culture, where failures are analyzed clinically without blame, is essential for learning and improvement. Create separate, documented spaces for each issue.
The real danger of 'B players' is not their work quality, but their fear-driven tendency to hire 'C players' to make themselves look better.
When giving direct and critical feedback, empathy is crucial. Frame it as a mutual problem to solve, separating the person's ability from the current work's quality.
In the short term, the market is a 'voting machine' driven by sentiment, but in the long term, it's a 'weighing machine' that values fundamentals like profitability and growth.
fundraising_mentions: The IPO and subsequent stock volatility are discussed.
Over-hiring was based on assumptions about the fundraising environment ('continuous cash tap') which did not materialize.
quotable: The hard red line for me is always once I can't trust you I can't ever trust you.
You have to completely separate any form of apologizing, responsibility taking... you have to be clinical about it. This happened, it wasn't good, here's why.
one_liner: Affirm's CEO Max Levchin shares insights on managing extreme talent, the importance of a clinical post-mortem culture, and navigating the pressures of being a public company CEO.

title: Prediction: Future of Work 🔮
guest_role: Managing Partner at Union Square Ventures
key_insights: Automation has historically been beneficial, evidenced by the shift from over 80% of the population in agriculture to under 5% in advanced economies.
Just as technology liberated the majority from agricultural work, it can now liberate them from the 'economic sphere' (work incentivized by prices).
The goal is to shrink the economic sphere to create more room for the 'non-economic sphere'—activities not driven by financial incentives, such as community, family, and creativity.
This shift could lead to a future where most of humanity is not primarily engaged in economically incentivized labor.
The current structure, where 80%+ of people are in the economic sphere, can be viewed as a temporary phase, similar to how we now view the agrarian age.
quotable: Just Like We Shrunk agriculture we can shrink the economic sphere and make room for the non-economic sphere.

I believe that if we play our carts right we can get to a place where we will look back at the current time and we'd be like oh my God 80 plus percent of humanity is engaged in what I think of as the economic sphere.
one_liner: Albert Wenger of USV explains his vision for a future where automation shrinks the traditional economy, allowing humanity to focus more on fulfilling, non-economically incentivized activities.

title: Millionaire CEO's Top 5 Interview Questions He Asks Every Applicant
key_insights: A consistent interview 'Playbook' allows for faster identification of red flags across numerous candidates.
The question 'how did you find the job' can reveal valuable recommendations or prior managerial relationships.
Effective responses to 'biggest achievement' should focus on individual, data-backed contributions, not just team collaboration.
Asking about 'lowest point' can expose a candidate's tendency to complain or their approach to adversity.
Examining 'why did you leave' across multiple roles helps uncover patterns, such as being pushed out versus genuine career advancement.
quotable: I run all the interviews with the same Playbook and that helps me because now I have seen thousands of candidates with the same Playbook the same questions right and so I can identify certain red flags faster
I improve the CVR of the website from 8% to 9.2 by doing a b and c that is a great thing if they're fluffy still struggling
one_liner: A Millionaire CEO details his five key interview questions and methodology to effectively screen applicants, identify red flags, and assess genuine contributions and resilience.

title: Thomas Plantenga & Alex Taussig: Vinted CEO's Ultimate Guide to Scaling Marketplaces | E1114
guest_role: CEO of Vinted & Partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners
key_insights: Vinted's successful turnaround involved a radical pivot from a standard seller-fee model to a low-cost, multi-stream revenue model that prioritized user value, a move that was highly counterintuitive at the time.
A key strategy for scaling was to first dominate a single, large, culturally relevant market (France) to perfect the business model and create a repeatable playbook before expanding internationally.

Reducing shipping costs was identified as a critical strategic weapon, not just for winning individual countries but for enabling the cross-border network effects necessary to build a pan-European marketplace.

In resale, where every item is unique, the user experience must be optimized for browsing and discovery (a 'window shopping' feel), leading to high engagement and session times comparable to social media.

The leadership team focused on improving fundamental input metrics (product, shipping, trust & safety) rather than chasing output metrics like the 'Rule of 40', which they view as a dangerous distraction for operators.
fundraising_mentions: Vinted's valuation during its last fundraise in the COVID era was $3.75 billion.
quotable: Bottom line it comes down to you completely switch your business model, you you practically kill all your current revenue streams, build new ones, and then the last money that you have available you blow it on television.

I think it's very important to build a growth framework that has all these things together... if you're going to steer your whole marketing investment on one metric like a cost per or a certain payback then like you're by definition you're wrong because all these variates are moving around.
one_liner: Vinted's CEO Thomas Plantenga and investor Alex Taussig detail the counterintuitive strategies behind scaling Europe's largest secondhand marketplace, from its radical business model pivot to its disciplined, data-driven approach to international expansion.

title: How Elon Can Still Save Twitter | Albert Wenger w/ Harry Stebbings
key_insights: Twitter's main problems were lack of programmability, a flawed blue check program, and ineffective content moderation.
Twitter was too dependent on advertising, leading to misaligned incentives.
It's not too late to save Twitter if it transitions to a steward ownership model and becomes fully programmable, allowing third-party clients.
The blue checkmark was a fiasco because it conflated identity verification with importance, when it should only be about identity.
All large social systems, including Twitter and TikTok, need to be programmable to prevent users from being programmed by them.
fundraising_mentions: Elon Musk is up to his eyes in debt due to the acquisition, but has the financial wherewithal to pay it off and implement changes.
quotable: I still believe that there's an opportunity today even after all the damage that has been done both by the prior uh regime and by the current one uh I still think it's not too late because Twitter is hard to kill it's a network of networks
These systems need to become programmable if they're not programmable we're being programmed by them
one_liner: Albert Wenger discusses the flaws of Twitter under both previous and current management, proposing a 'steward ownership' and 'fully programmable' model as the solution for its future, and extending the need for programmability to all major social media platforms like TikTok.

title: How Ed Sim Saved This $7B Startup 🤯
key_insights: An investor's deep involvement from the beginning allows them to see positive signals that outsiders might miss.
Early-stage startups may require multiple rounds of funding from their initial, high-conviction investor before they can attract outside capital.
A founder's ability to quickly prototype and sell a new feature (like the 'agent broker' for $50k) is a powerful signal of traction and execution.
Without continued support from an early backer with sufficient capital, a promising company might have failed to secure follow-on funding and gone out of business.
Concentrated portfolios enable investors to be more actively engaged and identify unique signals in their companies.
fundraising_mentions: Snyk raised three seed rounds from a single investor before their Series A.
In 2016/2017, the founder built an 'agent broker' feature in days to sign enterprise customers for $50k.
quotable: If you are actively involved and engaged on the board from the very beginning as well and you have a very concentrated portfolio you see signals and the signals that we see may not be the signals in Outsider sees.
If guy went out trying to raise capital from someone else and I didn't have enough Capital to give to him he would have gone out of business.
one_liner: Investor Ed Sim explains how his deep conviction and continued financial support through three seed rounds were crucial for Snyk's survival and eventual success, highlighting the importance of seeing signals that outside investors might miss.

title: Private Equity and Venture Capital are Not So Different #shorts
key_insights: All forms of capital gains, from private equity to venture capital, follow a similar evolutionary curve.
Early-stage asset classes are characterized by being subscale, volatile, and non-zero-sum, fostering collaboration as no clear formula for success exists.
As an asset class matures and a consensus path to profit emerges, the dynamic shifts towards zero-sum competition.
Once an industry reaches consensus, firms must specialize their strategy, choosing between being zero-sum vs. collaborative and generalist vs. specialist.
In a mature, consensus-driven market, firms prioritize hiring individuals who can execute an established playbook rather than disruptive 'rebels'.
fundraising_mentions: In the early days of venture, no single firm could raise enough money, which necessitated collaboration.
quotable: all capital gains end up looking the same
in those consensus games is you're looking for less rebels and you're looking for people who fit the organization right and can run the playbook that you've laid out
one_liner: Financial asset classes like venture capital evolve from a collaborative, subscale, and volatile stage to a competitive, zero-sum game once a consensus on strategy and sufficient scale are achieved.

title: William Hockey: How I Founded Plaid; The Ultimate Cold Email Tip; Hiring Lessons | 20VC #955
key_insights: Building inside the regulatory perimeter, while requiring significant upfront capital and time, allows for fixing core financial infrastructure problems rather than just creating abstractions on top of flawed systems.
True high performance for a founder is the ability to work diligently for years without needing external recognition or validation, as valuable companies take over a decade to build.
Maintaining an exceptionally high hiring bar, even if it causes short-term business pain, is critical. It's better to wait months for an 'A' player than to compromise.

The perceived weaknesses of the US financial system are often issues with the outdated implementations by legacy banks, not the underlying protocols themselves, which are powerful and can support modern financial products.

The future of financial services will likely involve vertical-specific software companies with deep customer relationships bundling financial products, while large banks recede into the background as infrastructure providers.
fundraising_mentions: Column is completely self-funded and employee-owned.
Plaid's acquisition by Visa was blocked by the DOJ, after which the company raised at a triple valuation nine months later.
Will had the chance to invest in Deel at the seed stage and ended up investing in the Series A.
quotable: Being able to be quiet, grinding and building in the shadows and be okay not being recognized, I think is the highest sort of high performance.
What's broken is the implementation of the US financial system that's flawed, not the underlying protocols and product.
one_liner: Plaid co-founder William Hockey discusses his new venture, Column, the philosophy of building a regulated bank from scratch, lessons on leadership, hiring, and his contrarian views on the strength of the US financial system's underlying protocols.

title: What is the role of a Head of Growth?
key_insights: A Head of Growth is responsible for accelerating a company's pace of learning, typically through experiments.
The growth team should operate at a faster drumbeat than the rest of the company.
Learnings from the growth team should be integrated back into the core product.
A Head of Growth engineers systems that help a company build more control over its North Star metrics.
The definition of a Head of Growth is inconsistent, but it can broadly apply to product, marketing, and sales functions.
quotable: Someone who's responsible for for two things one is accelerating the company's pace of learning this is typically done through experiments.
Engineering Systems that help a company build more control over its North Star metrics.
one_liner: A Head of Growth is defined as a role focused on accelerating a company's learning pace through experimentation and building systems to control its key North Star metrics.

title: I Built a $12BN Business on Accident 🤷‍♂️💰
key_insights: A side project built to solve a customer problem can unintentionally become a massive business.
The power of recurring revenue models was not initially recognized, but proved to be crucial for growth.
Transitioning from a service-based agency to a product-focused company is a significant but potentially rewarding pivot.
Organic growth, even if initially underestimated, can be a strong indicator of market fit.
Sometimes, the most successful ventures are those not taken 'seriously' at first.
quotable: we built it on the side and it kind of got annoying to log in and use it on behalf of our customers so we just made it self-serve
Mailchimp was growing and our agency was flat or and kind of declining that was all we needed to say let's stop the agency business and let's focus on management
one_liner: The speaker recounts how their web design agency accidentally created Mailchimp as a side project, which, due to organic growth and recurring revenue, eventually led them to pivot away from their original business.

title: When the CEO put the CTO in charge of culture at HubSpot
key_insights: Initial attempts to formally define company culture can be met with negativity and skepticism from employees.
Employees often react negatively to traditional corporate culture exercises like creating mission statements.
Framing culture definition as a data-collection and analysis problem can be a more effective approach, especially in a tech-oriented company.
Identifying the attributes of people who are successful within the company is a practical way to define its 'cultural coefficients'.
HubSpot's core cultural values identified through this process included transparency, humility, and empathy.
quotable: If I could write a function like literally code what would the kind of coefficients of that function be... let's identify the things that seem to be maybe not causal but at least correlated with success at HubSpot.
Dharmesh I just don't think hubspot's the kind of company now that I thought I joined.
one_liner: HubSpot's Co-founder & CTO, Dharmesh Shah, explains his data-driven approach to defining company culture after being unexpectedly tasked with it by his CEO, turning initial employee skepticism into a set of core values.

title: Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn & Paypal Founder: Trump Administration, Elon Musk and DOGE | E1239
key_insights: The next major advancements in AI will still come from larger models trained with more compute, contradicting the idea that we've reached the upper limits of LLMs.

Trade wars are broadly destructive to US prosperity; however, targeted tariffs are a necessary tool to counteract specific unfair practices, such as China's subsidized car industry or geopolitical aggression.
Elon Musk's immense conviction is both his greatest strength, enabling ventures like SpaceX and Tesla, and his greatest weakness, leading him to amplify conspiracy theories.
AI can be a net positive for climate change by optimizing energy consumption (e.g., in data centers) and by driving massive investment into new green energy sources to power its growth.

The biggest investment mistakes are not the ones that go to zero, but the opportunities missed, such as passing on early investments in companies like Stripe and Square due to over-analyzing the risks.
fundraising_mentions: Invested in Airbnb's Series A at a $60 million post-money valuation.
quotable: The worst thing is is saying no to the things that went to the moon.
The difficulty of making decisions is that in the short term it reduces your opportunity set because you've made a decision but it's the only way you have long-term opportunity.
one_liner: LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman discusses the political landscape of the Trump administration, the dual nature of Elon Musk's power, the future of AI and nuclear energy, and key lessons from his venture capital career.

title: Liquid Death CEO Mike Cessario: How I Turned Canned Water to a $700M Company
key_insights: A strong brand means more to people than the product itself, transcending functional benefits.
If people truly love something, there must be people who truly hate it. It's impossible to create something that everyone loves.
Healthy products can and should be marketed with the same fun and irreverence as unhealthy products.
Your unique brand, tone of voice, and marketing style are your true defensible moat, not functional differentiators like ingredients which can be easily copied.
Marketing should be viewed as creating entertainment. The goal is to make people feel something (like laughter) rather than just communicating functional benefits like hydration.
Don't be afraid of alienating some customers; trying to please everyone results in a brand that no one truly cares about.
Operational execution in the beverage industry, such as managing distribution and in-store placement, is just as critical as the brand itself.
fundraising_mentions: The beverage industry is very capital-intensive, requiring startups to be almost constantly fundraising.
Early on, the company got into bad distributor contracts that they had to pay to get out of.
Bringing the wrong investors on board can become a nightmare and almost tank a company.
Many celebrity investors in Liquid Death are fans who genuinely love the brand and get involved in creative marketing campaigns.
quotable: If there are people who truly love something, there has to be people who truly hate it. It is not possible to make something that everybody loves.

The brand is what you can truly own and that really is your moat more so than most brands think it is. They think their moat is an ingredient or they think it's something else... anybody can replicate your formula.
one_liner: Liquid Death CEO Mike Cessario breaks down his counter-intuitive approach to building a $700M water company by treating it as an entertainment brand, prioritizing humor and irreverence over traditional health-focused marketing.

title: Oana Olteanu: Why Founders Should Expect More From Their VCs | 20VC #950
key_insights: The concept of a 'Schrodinger's VC' describes an investor who appears helpful before a deal but adds no value afterward; founders can manage them by giving them specific 'homework' and holding them accountable.

To vet VCs, founders should assess if they act in service of the founder during diligence, understand how they behave during tough times by speaking to their portfolio founders, and select the partner over the firm.
VCs can and should assist with hiring by sourcing diverse candidates, helping to filter for culture, and aiding in closing top candidates, without taking over the founder's core responsibility.

To build a diverse pipeline, founders must address unconscious biases, use recruiters who can deliver diverse candidates, and engage with communities of underrepresented talent respectfully and intentionally.
Effective board meetings require pre-alignment with board members, focusing discussion on meaty topics rather than recaps, and proactive management by the founder to ensure all voices are heard.
